## Dīgha Nikāya
## Mahāvagga-aṭṭhakathā
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## 1. Mahāpadāna Sutta Vaṇṇanā
## Pubbenivāsapaṭisaṃyuttakathā
The Mahāpadāna Sutta, beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" (Thus have I heard), was [delivered] at the Kareri monastery. In this sutta, this is the explanation of the terms not yet explained: Regarding "karerikuṭikāyaṃ," *karerī* is the name of the *varuṇa* tree. Because the Kareri pavilion stood at the door of that dwelling, it is called "Karerikuṭikā." It is like how [a dwelling] is called "Kosambakuṭikā" because it stands at the door of a *kosamba* tree. Within the Jetavana Monastery, there are four great dwellings: Karerikuṭi, Kosambakuṭi, Gandhakuṭi, and Salalāgāra. Each one was completed at an expense of one hundred thousand [units of currency]. Among those dwellings, King Pasenadi of Kosala built and donated the Salalāgāra. The remaining dwellings were built and donated by the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika. Thus, the Blessed One dwelt in the Karerikuṭi, which was built upon pillars by the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika and resembled a celestial mansion.

"Pacchābhattaṃ" (after the meal) means that for those who observe the practice of eating at one sitting (ekāsanika), even if they have eaten in the morning, it is still called "pacchābhatta" within the period before noon. However, in this context, "pacchābhatta" refers to the time after the regular meal. "Piṇḍapātapaṭikkantānaṃ" means [the monks] who have returned from the alms round, having finished their meal and risen [from their seats].

"Karerimaṇḍalamāḷe" refers to the sitting hall built not far from that Kareri pavilion. That Kareri pavilion was [situated between] the Gandhakuṭi and the hall.

## Bodhiparicchedavaṇṇanā
In the section on Enlightenment, "pāṭaliyā mūle" means at the foot of the *pāṭali* tree. On that day, the trunk of that *pāṭali* tree rose to a height of fifty cubits, and its branches extended fifty cubits; thus, its total height was one hundred cubits. On that day, that *pāṭali* tree was completely covered from its base with flowers as if crowned, and it emitted a fragrance like that of the devas. At that time, not only did this single tree bloom, but all the *pāṭali* trees in the ten thousand world systems also bloomed. Not only did the *pāṭali* trees bloom, but in the ten thousand world systems, trunk-lotuses bloomed on the trunks of all trees, branch-lotuses on the branches, vine-lotuses on the vines, and sky-lotuses in the sky; moreover, great lotuses emerged, bursting through the surface of the earth. The great ocean was also covered with five-colored lotuses, as well as blue and red lotuses.

The entire ten thousand world systems were crowded with banners and streamers, spread with flower garlands and bouquets tied here and there, and shining with flowers of various colors, resembling the Nandana, Cittalatā, Missaka, and Phārusaka groves. Banners hoisted at the edge of the eastern world system struck the edge of the western world system. Banners hoisted at the edges of the western, southern, and northern world systems struck the edge of the southern world system. In this way, the world systems were filled with mutual glory. "Abhisambuddho" means that he realized the Four Noble Truths while penetrating the power and glory of all the Buddha's qualities.

In the phrases such as "The Blessed One Sikhī attained enlightenment at the foot of the *puṇḍarīka* (white mango) tree," the explanation should be understood in this same manner. Here, "puṇḍarīka" refers to the white mango tree. The dimensions of that tree were also the same. On that day, that tree was also well-covered with flowers having the fragrance of the devas. Not only was it covered with flowers, but it was also covered with fruits. On one side of that tree, young fruits hung; on another side, medium-sized fruits; on another side, semi-ripe fruits; and on another side, fully ripe fruits hung down, as delicious as if infused with celestial essence. Just like that tree, in the entire ten thousand world systems, flowering trees were adorned with flowers, and fruit-bearing trees were adorned with fruits.

"Sālo" refers to the *sāla* tree. The dimensions of that tree were also the same, and the glory and power of its flowers should be understood in the same way. The same method applies to the *sirīsa* tree. In the case of the *udumbara* tree...
24:
It is said that the Great Kings lifted the Queen together with her bed and took her to Lake Anotatta. Having bathed her, they clothed her in divine garments, anointed her with divine scents, and adorned her with divine flowers. Not far from there is the Silver Mountain, and inside it is a Golden Mansion. There, they laid her down with her head towards the east. Then the Bodhisatta, having become a noble white elephant, wandered on a Golden Mountain not far from there. Descending from it, he climbed the Silver Mountain, entered the Golden Mansion, circumambulated his mother, and appeared to enter her womb after piercing her right side.

Then the Queen awoke and informed the King of that dream. When the night had turned to dawn, the King summoned sixty-four eminent Brahmins. Having prepared costly seats on a ground smeared with fresh cow-dung and consecrated with parched grain and such, he filled gold and silver bowls with choice milk-rice prepared with ghee, honey, and sugar, and covering them with other gold and silver bowls, he offered them to the Brahmins. He also satisfied them with other gifts such as new clothes and red cows. Then, having satisfied them with all their desires, he told them the dream and asked, "What will happen?" The Brahmins said, "Do not worry, Great King; a conception has taken place in the Queen's womb. It is a male child, not a female. You will have a noble son. If he lives the household life, he will become a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti). If he goes forth from the household life into homelessness, he will become a Buddha in the world, one who has rolled back the veil [of ignorance]." This is the sequence of explanation for the phrase "He descended into the mother's womb."

"Ayamettha dhammatā" means: in this context of descending into the mother's womb, this is the natural way (dhammatā), this is the nature (sabhāva), this is the fixed law (niyāma). Fixed law (niyāma) is fivefold: the law of kamma (kammaniyāma), the law of seasons (utuniyāma), the law of seeds (bījaniyāma), the law of mind (cittaniyāma), and the law of phenomena (dhammaniyāma).

Among these, the giving of desirable results by wholesome actions and undesirable results by unwholesome actions is the law of kamma. To illustrate this, the stories of the verse beginning with "Na antalikkhe" should be told. Furthermore, it is said that a certain woman, having quarreled with her husband, hanged herself...
51:
The Bodhisatta, not through any other cause but through such wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) and through this attention to means (upāya-manasikāra), attained penetration through wisdom. His wisdom met with the cause of aging and death (jarāmaraṇa), [realizing] that when 'that' exists, aging and death come to be. What is that? It is birth (jāti). Therefore, it is said: "When birth exists, aging and death come to be." The meaning here is that the Bodhisatta's wisdom met with the wisdom that discerns the cause of aging and death. In this manner, all the terms should be understood.

In the phrase "When name-and-form exist, consciousness comes to be," it could have been said "When formations (saṅkhāra) exist, consciousness comes to be" and "When ignorance (avijjā) exists, formations come to be," but both were not taken. Why? Because ignorance and formations belong to the past life, and this insight (vipassanā) does not connect with them. For the Great Being (Mahāpurisa) was intent upon the present. Is it not true that one cannot become a Buddha without seeing ignorance and formations? True, one cannot. However, those [ignorance and formations] have already been seen through the power of becoming (bhava), clinging (upādāna), and craving (taṇhā). At this point, the discourse on Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) should be explained in detail. That discourse has already been explained in the Visuddhimagga.

"Turns back" (paccudāvattati) means it retreats. Which consciousness turns back here? Both the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa) and the insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa). There, the rebirth-linking consciousness turns back from the cause (paccaya), and the insight-knowledge turns back from the object (ārammaṇa). Both do not transcend name-and-form; they do not go beyond name-and-form. To this extent, in phrases such as "he would be born," etc., while consciousness is a condition for name-and-form, and name-and-form is a condition for consciousness—both being mutual conditions—to this extent he would be born... (pe) ... upapajjetha (would arise). Beyond this, what else would be born... (pe) ... would arise? Is it not this alone that is born... (pe) ... and arises? Thus, having shown the five terms together with the preceding and succeeding death and rebirth, and again assigning the meaning stated as "to this extent"—having said, "With name-and-form as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form"—thereafter, in order to show birth, aging, and death that will occur in the future based on name-and-form as the root with consciousness as condition through the power of the forward order of conditions, he said "With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases (saḷāyatana)," and so on. There, "the origin of this entire mass of suffering" means the arising of the entire mass of suffering consisting of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Thus, the Great Being saw the arising of the entire mass of suffering in the round of rebirth (vaṭṭadukkha).
53:
On the very day of [his son's] birth, he went forth into the forest, became a monk, and exerted himself in meditation. Having ascended the Bodhi-seat and defeated the army of Māra, he recollected his past lives (Pubbenivāsanussati-ñāṇa) in the first watch of the night. In the second watch, he purified the divine eye (Dibba-cakkhu). In the third watch, he contemplated dependent origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda), and emerging from the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (Ānāpāna), he entered into the five aggregates. Seeing the fifty characteristics by way of rise and fall (udayabbaya), he developed insight (Vipassanā) up to the knowledge of change-of-lineage (Gotrabhū-ñāṇa), and through the Ariyan Path, he penetrated all the qualities of a Buddha. This Great Man (Mahāpurisa) was one who had fulfilled the Perfections (Pāramī). That Great Man, having performed everything in the aforementioned order, emerged from the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing in the final watch and entered into the five aggregates to begin the various types of insight into rise and fall as described. To show this, these words were spoken.

In that context, "Thus is form" means: this is form, this much is form, there is no form beyond this. This refers to the comprehensive grasping of form without remainder by way of its nature of being deformed (ruppana), its divisions into the primary elements (mahābhūta) and derived form (upādā-rūpa), and its characteristics (lakkhaṇa), function (rasa), manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna), and proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna). By the words "Thus is the origin of form," it is meant to show the cause of form thus grasped. In that context, "Thus" means "in this way the cause arises." The detail of that is: "With the arising of ignorance (avijjā), there is the arising of form; with the arising of craving (taṇhā), there is the arising of form; with the arising of kamma, there is the arising of form; with the arising of nutriment (āhāra), there is the arising of form." One who sees the characteristic of production also sees the arising of the aggregate of form; thus it should be understood. Regarding its cessation: "With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of form... (pe) ... one who sees the characteristic of change also sees the cessation of the aggregate of form." This is the detail of that.

In the passages "Thus is feeling" and so on: this is feeling, this much is feeling, there is no feeling beyond this. This is perception, these are formations, this is consciousness, this much is consciousness, there is no consciousness beyond this. This refers to the comprehensive grasping of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness without remainder by way of their natures of experiencing, perceiving, constructing, and cognizing, and their divisions such as pleasant feeling, perception of forms, contact, and eye-consciousness, and by way of their characteristics, function, manifestation, and proximate cause. By the words "Thus is the origin of feeling" and so on, it is meant to show the cause of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness thus grasped. There too, "Thus" means "in this way the cause arises." The detail of those should be understood in the same manner as stated for form: "With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of feeling." However, there is this distinction: for the three [mental] aggregates, instead of saying "with the arising of nutriment," one should say "with the arising of contact (phassa)." In the aggregate of consciousness...
56:
This (Dhamma) is the designation for ignorance and so on, which have formations and such as their causes. All terms such as 'the stilling of all formations' (sabba-saṅkhāra-samatha) refer only to Nibbāna. Because, having reached that Nibbāna, all the stirrings of formations are stilled and quieted; therefore, it is called 'the stilling of all formations.' And because, having reached that Nibbāna, all acquisitions (upadhi) are relinquished, all cravings (taṇhā) are exhausted, all defilements and lust (kile-sarāga) fade away, and all suffering ceases; therefore, it is called 'the relinquishment of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, and cessation.'

That craving is called 'vāna' because it weaves and binds one existence to another, or kamma together with its result. Because of the departure from that 'vāna', it is called 'Nibbāna'. 'That teaching would be a weariness to me' means that teaching those who do not know or understand would be my weariness, my vexation. It means it would be a weariness of the body and a vexation of the body; as for the mind, neither of these exists for the Buddhas.

'Apissu' is a particle in the sense of addition. It shows: 'Not only did this thought occur, but these verses also became clear.' In the words 'Vipassī' and so on, it means of the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One, Vipassī. 'Anacchariyā' means things that are wonderful and appropriate. 'Paṭibhaṃsu' means they became the objects of the knowledge known as intuition (paṭibhāna); they reached the state of being contemplated.

'Kicchena' means with difficulty [it was attained], but not through a difficult practice (dukkha-paṭipadā). For the Buddhas, all four paths are indeed a pleasant practice (sukha-paṭipadā). However, this is said in reference to the preparatory practice (āgamanīya-paṭipadā) during the time of fulfilling the Perfections, when, while still possessing lust, hate, and delusion, he gave to all who came to beg: his head adorned and prepared, cutting it and drawing out the throat-blood; his well-anointed eyes, plucking them out; his son who was the lamp of the lineage, and his pleasing wife; and in other existences like that of the Preacher of Patience (Khantivādī), he underwent cutting and dismembering.

In the word 'Halaṃ', the letter 'ha' is merely a particle; it means 'alaṃ' (enough). 'Pakāsituṃ' means to teach. Thus, it is not necessary to teach the Dhamma attained with such difficulty; what benefit would there be in teaching it? This is the intended meaning. 'Rāga-dosa-paretehi' means by those overcome by lust and hate, or those followed by lust and hate.

'Paṭisotagāmiṃ' means the Dhamma of the Four Truths which goes against the stream of [views such as] permanence and so on, and is thus impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul. 'Rāgarattā' means those infatuated with the lust for sensual pleasures, the lust for existence, and the lust for views. 'Na dakkhanti' means they will not see by way of this nature of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness...
58:
Alternatively, because of the desire to teach when requested by the Brahmā, the Blessed One's mind inclined in this way. Indeed, the Blessed One knew: "If my mind inclines toward inaction and not teaching the Dhamma, the Great Brahmā will request me to teach. These beings hold the Brahmā in high regard; they will think, 'The Teacher was reportedly unwilling to teach the Dhamma, but then the Great Brahmā requested him to do so. How wonderful is the Dhamma! How noble is the Dhamma!' and they will be keen to listen." It should be understood that his mind inclined toward inaction for this reason, and not because of a lack of desire to teach the Dhamma.

In the phrase 'aññatarassa', although it says 'a certain [Brahmā]', it should be understood that he was the senior Great Brahmā in this universe. He reportedly uttered the cry, "Alas, the world is perishing!" so loudly that the Brahmās of the ten thousand world systems heard it and assembled. 'Yatra hi nāma' means 'in which world'. 'Appeared before him' means he appeared together with those ten thousand Brahmās. 'Apparajakkhajātika' refers to those who have little dust of greed, hatred, and delusion in their eye of wisdom; such is their nature. 'Assavanatā' means 'due to not hearing'. 'There will be [those who understand]' indicates that there will be many—not just one or two, but hundreds of thousands—who, having performed meritorious deeds through the ten bases of meritorious action under previous Buddhas and reached maturity like lotuses touched by sunlight, are longing for the Dhamma and are capable of entering the stage of the Noble Ones at the end of a four-line verse.

'Ajjhesana' means requesting in this manner three times. 'Buddha-cakkhu' (the Buddha-eye) refers to the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties of beings (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of their inclinations and latent tendencies (āsayānusaya-ñāṇa). These two knowledges are called the 'Buddha-eye'; omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) is called the 'All-seeing eye' (samanta-cakkhu); and the three lower path knowledges are called the 'Dhamma-eye' (dhamma-cakkhu).

In the terms 'apparajakkha' and so on, those who have little dust of greed and so forth in their eye of wisdom, as previously explained, are called 'apparajakkha' (those with little dust). Those who have much dust are 'mahārajakkha'. Those whose faculties such as faith are sharp are 'tikkhindriya'. Those whose faculties are weak are 'mudindriya'. Those whose dispositions such as faith are good are 'svākāra'. Those who can notice the reasons explained and are easy to make understand are 'suviññāpaya'. Those who are accustomed to seeing danger in the next world and in faults are called 'paralokavajjabhayadassāvino'.

## 
"Even now, the burden is mine alone; I myself will serve those Buddhas with the four requisites and will not give the opportunity to others." Thinking thus, he had a fence of catechu wood constructed on both sides from the entrance of the monastery to the gate of Rājagaha. He had it covered with mats, draped with cloths, and roofed over. He had various flower-garland canopies made, adorned with golden stars and hanging down like palm trunks. He had the ground below spread with ornate carpets. Inside, on both sides, he had small flower plants and full jars placed. To make the entire path fragrant, he had flowers placed between perfumes and perfumes between flowers. Then, he had the Blessed One informed that it was time.

The Blessed One, surrounded by the community of monks, went to Rājagaha within the curtained enclosure, performed his meal duties, and returned to the monastery. No one else had the opportunity even to see him, let alone offer alms, pay homage, or listen to the Dhamma. The citizens thought: "Today, it has been over seven years and seven months since the Teacher appeared in the world, yet we do not even get the chance to see him, let alone offer alms, pay homage, or listen to the Dhamma. The King, being attached, thinking 'The Buddha is for me alone, the Dhamma is for me alone, the Sangha is for me alone,' serves them himself. When a Buddha appears, does he not appear for the benefit and happiness of the world including the devas? It is not as if hell is hot only for the King and cool like a forest of blue lotuses for others. Therefore, let us speak to the King. If he gives us [access to] the Teacher, it is well. If he does not, we will even fight with the King, take the Sangha, and perform meritorious deeds such as giving." (They consulted:) "However, the citizens alone cannot do this; let us also take a leader."

They approached the General and, having informed him of the matter, asked, "Lord, will you be on our side or on the King's side?" The General said, "I will be on your side; however, the first day must be given to me." They accepted. The General approached the King and said, "Great King, the citizens are angry with you." When asked, "For what reason, friend?" he replied, "They say that only you are serving the Teacher and they get no opportunity. If they get it now, they will not be angry; if they do not, they wish to fight with you, O King." The King said, "Friend, I will fight; I cannot give up the community of monks." When asked, "Great King, your own loyal servants say they will fight with you; whom will you take to fight? Are you not the General?" [The King replied,] "Without the citizens..."
75:
Sitting too close manifests a lack of respect. If one sits directly in front and wishes to look, one must look eye-to-eye. If one sits too far back and wishes to look, one must turn the neck. Therefore, this Venerable Ānanda also circumambulated the Blessed One three times, paid homage respectfully, and avoiding these six faults of sitting, sat down in a position facing the right knee-cap. He sat as if entering within the six-colored Buddha-rays, like descending into a pool of clear lac-dye, like being wrapped in a golden cloth, or like entering the middle of a canopy of red lotus garlands—thus sat Venerable Ānanda, the Treasurer of the Dhamma. Therefore, it is said, "he sat to one side."

At what time and for what reason did this venerable one approach the Blessed One? It was in the evening for the purpose of asking a question about Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda). On that day, it is said, this venerable one, like placing a thousand-coin bundle at every house door for the benefit of families, wandered for alms in the village of Kammāsadhamma. After returning from the alms round and performing duties for the Teacher, when the Teacher entered the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), he paid homage to the Teacher and went to his own place for the day's rest. After performing duties for his pupils and when they had departed, he swept the resting place, spread out the leather mat, took water from the water-pot, cooled his hands and feet with water, and sat down cross-legged, entering the attainment of the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala-samāpatti). Then, emerging from the attainment at the designated time, he applied his knowledge to Dependent Origination. He contemplated the twelve factors of Dependent Origination three times: from the beginning starting with "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise" to the end, from the end to the beginning, from both ends to the middle, and from the middle to both ends. As he contemplated thus, Dependent Origination became very clear to him, appearing like something placed on or turned over in the palm of the hand.

Then he thought: "This Dependent Origination has been described by every Buddha as 'profound and having a profound appearance.' Yet to me, though I am a disciple established in partial knowledge (padesañāṇa), it appears very shallow and clear. Does it appear shallow only to me, or to others as well?" Then this thought occurred to him: "Let me take this question and ask the Blessed One. Surely the Blessed One, taking this matter as the starting point, will preach a discourse (suttanta-kathā) to me, like raising a grain of rice or lifting Mount Sineru. When Buddhas reach these four topics—the Vinaya regulations, the different planes of existence (bhummantara), Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), and different philosophical views (samayantara)—their roar is great, their knowledge penetrates, and the Buddha-knowledge..."
77:
## Explanation of the Praise (Ussādanāvaṇṇanā)

In that context, while praising him: "Ānanda, you are one of great wisdom, one of clear knowledge. Therefore, even the profound Dependent Origination appears shallow to you. However, it should not be considered that this Dependent Origination is shallow for others; it is indeed profound and has a profound appearance." In this regard, they tell four similes. It is said that a great wrestler (Mahāmalla), who had been nourished with the essence of good food for six months, had practiced well, and was accustomed to wrestling stones at festivals, was going to the battlefield. On the way, people showed him a wrestling stone. The wrestler asked, "What is this?" They replied, "It is a wrestling stone." He said, "Bring it here." When they said, "We cannot lift it," he went himself and asked, "Where is the heavy part of this stone?" and lifting two stones with both hands, he threw them up like toy balls and went on his way. In that case, although the wrestling stone is light for the wrestler, it should not be said to be light for others. Just like the wrestler nourished with good food for six months, Ven. Ānanda has fulfilled the perfections (pāramī) for a hundred thousand aeons. Just as the wrestling stone is light due to the wrestler's great strength, Dependent Origination is shallow (easy) due to the Elder's great wisdom. It should not be said to be shallow for others.

In the great ocean, the fish named Timi is two hundred leagues (yojana) long; the Timingala fish is three hundred leagues; the Timipiṅgala fish is four hundred leagues; the Timirapiṅgala fish is five hundred leagues. The Ānanda fish, Timinanda fish, Ajjhāroha fish, and Mahātimi fish—these four are each one thousand leagues long. Among these, let us illustrate with the Timirapiṅgala fish. When that fish moves its right ear, the water moves in an area of five hundred leagues. The same happens when it moves its left ear, tail, or head. When it begins to play by moving both ears, striking the water with its tail, and turning its head from side to side, the water boils like water placed in a pot on a stove in an area of seven hundred or eight hundred leagues. In an area of about three hundred leagues, the water is unable to cover the fish's back. That fish might say: "They say this great ocean is profound, profound. Where is its profundity? We do not even get enough water to cover our backs." In that case, although the great ocean is shallow for the Timirapiṅgala fish with its massive body, it should not be said to be shallow for other small fish. In the same way, although Dependent Origination is shallow for the Elder who is endowed with wisdom, it should not be said to be shallow for others.
78:
The King of Galons is also one hundred and fifty yojanas in size. His right wing is fifty yojanas, and his left wing is the same. The wing-fringe is sixty yojanas, the neck is thirty yojanas, the face is nine yojanas, and the feet are twelve yojanas. When that King of Galons begins to display the wind from his wings, even an area of seven or eight hundred yojanas is insufficient. That King of Galons might say: "They say this sky is infinite, infinite; where is its infinity? We do not even get enough space to spread our wing-wind." In that case, although the sky is narrow for the great-bodied King of Galons, it should not be said to be narrow for other small birds. In the same way, although Dependent Origination is shallow for the Elder who is endowed with wisdom, it should not be said to be shallow for others.

Rāhu, the Lord of Asuras, is four thousand eight hundred yojanas from the tips of his toes to the tips of his hair. The span between his two arms is one thousand two hundred yojanas. In thickness, it is six hundred yojanas. The palms of his hands and the soles of his feet are three hundred yojanas each; the face is the same. Each finger-joint is fifty yojanas, and the space between the eyebrows is the same. The forehead is three hundred yojanas. The head is nine hundred yojanas. When that Rāhu, the Lord of Asuras, descends into the great ocean, the deep water reaches only to his knees. That Asura might say: "They say this great ocean is deep, deep; where is its depth? We do not even get enough water to cover our knees." In that case, although the great ocean is shallow for the great-bodied Rāhu, the Lord of Asuras, it should not be said to be shallow for others. In the same way, although Dependent Origination is shallow for the Elder who is endowed with wisdom, it should not be said to be shallow for others. Aiming at this meaning, the Blessed One said: "Do not say so, Ānanda; do not say so, Ānanda."

Indeed, for four reasons, even the deep Dependent Origination appears as if it were shallow to the Elder. What are the four? They are: the perfection of past supporting conditions (pāramī), living in the presence of the Buddha, being a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), and being very learned (bahussuta).

## Pubbūpanissayasampattikathā

One hundred thousand aeons ago from this present one, the Teacher named Padumuttara arose in the world. For that Blessed One, there was a city named Haṃsavatī, and a king named Ānanda...
114:
Aparihāniya means that which does not cause decline, meaning it is a cause for growth. "I will teach the Dhamma" means he will teach it by making it clear, as if making thousands of moons and thousands of suns shine, or as if lighting thousands of oil lamps inside a four-cornered house.

Among those factors, the phrase "assembling frequently" is just the same as what was said regarding the seven conditions for non-decline of the Vajjī princes. In this Dispensation (Sāsana) as well, if they do not assemble frequently, they do not hear the news of the Sāsana coming from various directions. Because of not hearing it, they do not know such things as: "The Sīmā of such-and-such a monastery is in disorder; the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies have stopped; in such-and-such a place, monks are practicing medicine, acting as messengers, and so on; they live by making many requests and by offering flowers, etc." Evil monks, knowing that "the Community of Monks is negligent," gather together and cause the Dispensation to decline. However, monks who assemble frequently hear various news. Therefore, they send the Community of Monks to rectify the Sīmā, they cause the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies to proceed, they send monks who uphold the Ariyavaṃsa (Noble Lineage) to places where wrong livelihood is prevalent and have them preach the Ariyavaṃsa Dhamma, and they have the evil monks subdued by the Vinaya-experts (Vinayadhara). The evil monks, thinking, "The Community of Monks is diligent; we are not able to wander about in groups," become demoralized and flee. Thus, decline and growth in this matter should be understood.

Regarding the words "in harmony" (samagga) and so on: when the drum or the bell is struck with the intention of establishing a rule (katikavatta) for the purpose of repairing a shrine (cetiya), or for roofing a Bodhi-tree house or an Uposatha hall, or with the desire to give an exhortation, saying "Let the Saṅgha assemble," those monks who cause distraction by saying "I have robe-work to do," "I have a bowl to fire," "I have new construction work to do," are not said to assemble in harmony. But those who, setting aside all such business, assemble all at once, saying "I will arrive first, I will arrive first," are said to assemble in harmony. After assembling, if they do not rise together after having deliberated, consulted, and performed what was to be done, they are not said to rise in harmony. For when they rise in this way, those who go first might think: "We have only heard the external talk; now the talk of the decision will take place." But those who rise all at once are said to rise in harmony. Furthermore, having heard that "the monastery Sīmā in such-and-such a place is in disorder, the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā have stopped, evil monks who practice medicine etc. are numerous in such-and-such a place," [they ask] "Who...
117:
... hears the sound; because of that sound, he obtains forest-born rapture. Reflecting on that very rapture, the monk stands firm in the highest fruit, Arahatship. Thus, the Blessed One praises even a monk sleeping in the forest more than a monk sitting in a village monastery without attaining jhāna. Therefore, based on that reason, He said: "They will have regard for forest dwellings."

"They will establish mindfulness in themselves" means they will establish mindfulness within their own internal continuity. "Pesalā" means those of dear virtue. In this Dispensation, resident monks who do not desire the arrival of fellow practitioners are without faith and without devotion. They do not perform the duties of welcoming arriving monks, receiving their bowls and robes, preparing seats, or holding fans. Then, a bad reputation of those monks spreads: "The monks residing in such-and-such a monastery are without faith and without devotion; they do not perform major and minor duties for those entering the monastery." Hearing this, monks do not enter the monastery even when passing by its gate. Thus, those who have not yet arrived simply do not come. As for those who have arrived, if there is no comfortable living, those who arrived without knowing think: "We came intending to stay, but who can live with such behavior from these resident monks?" and they depart. Thus, that monastery becomes uninhabited by other monks. Consequently, the resident monks, not getting to see virtuous monks, do not get to dispel their doubts, find a teacher of conduct and training, or hear the sweet Dhamma. For them, there is no learning of the Dhamma not yet learned, nor the recitation of the Dhamma already learned. Thus, for them, there is only decline, not growth.

Regarding the phrase "But those who desire the arrival of fellow practitioners," those who desire the arrival of fellow practitioners are indeed endowed with faith and devotion. They perform the duties of welcoming arriving fellow practitioners and prepare seats for them. They take those monks and enter for alms, dispel their doubts, and get to hear the sweet Dhamma. Then, the fame of those monks spreads: "The monks residing in such-and-such a monastery are thus endowed with faith and devotion, perfect in their duties, and are hospitable." Hearing this, monks come even from afar. The resident monks perform the duties for them; approaching them, they pay homage to and sit near a visiting monk who is senior to them, and they take a seat and sit near a monk who is junior to them. Having sat down, they ask, "Will you reside in this monastery or will you depart?" If it is said, "I will depart," they say, "The lodging is suitable, alms are easy to obtain," etc., and do not allow them to leave. If the visitor is a master of the Vinaya, they recite the Vinaya in his presence. If he is a bearer of the Suttas, etc., they recite that respective Dhamma in his presence. Abiding by the advice of the visiting elders, they attain Arahatship together with the analytical insights. The visitors also...
123:
Regarding the phrase "one who shares possessions in common with virtuous fellow practitioners" (sādhāraṇabhogī), the characteristic of one who shares possessions in common is as follows: Whatever exquisite items are obtained, he does not give them to laypeople with the aim of seeking gain with gain, nor does he consume them alone. Even while receiving them, he thinks, "Let this be a possession shared with the Sangha," and views it like Sangha property to be used after striking the bell.

Who fulfills this quality of communal harmony (sāraṇīyadhamma), and who does not? An immoral person (dussīla) cannot fulfill it. This is because virtuous people do not accept his possessions. Only a person of pure virtue can fulfill it without failing in the duties. The duty of fulfillment is this: If one gives by dedicating it to mother, father, teacher, preceptor, etc., it is merely giving what should be given; it is not yet sāraṇīyadhamma, but rather attending to an impediment (palibodha). Sāraṇīyadhamma is suitable only for one free from impediments. One who gives by such dedication should also give to the sick, the attendants of the sick, visitors, traveling monks, and to a newly ordained monk who does not yet know how to handle the outer robe and bowl. After giving to them, whatever remains should be given to whoever takes it, starting from the seat of the elders, without giving just a little. If nothing remains, one should go for alms again, and after giving whatever exquisite alms are obtained starting from the seat of the elders, one should consume the remainder. Because it is said "with the virtuous," it is also proper not to give to an immoral person.

This sāraṇīyadhamma is easy to fulfill in a well-trained assembly, but difficult in an untrained assembly. In a well-trained assembly, one who receives from elsewhere does not take from here. Even one who does not receive from elsewhere takes only in moderation, not in excess. This sāraṇīyadhamma is fulfilled only after twelve years for one who gives whatever is obtained by repeatedly going for alms; not earlier than that. If, in the twelfth year, the one fulfilling the sāraṇīyadhamma leaves a bowl full of alms in the refectory and goes to bathe, and the Elder of the Sangha asks, "Whose bowl is this?" and is told, "It belongs to the one fulfilling the sāraṇīyadhamma," and the Elder says, "Bring it here," and after distributing and consuming all the alms, leaves the empty bowl; then, if that monk sees the empty bowl and feels displeasure (domanassa), thinking, "They have consumed it without leaving any remainder for me," the sāraṇīyadhamma is broken. It must be fulfilled again for another twelve years. This is similar to the probation (parivāsa) of the sectarians; if it is broken once, it must always be fulfilled again.
124:
"It is good for me, it is a great gain for me, that my fellow practitioners enjoy the food in my bowl without even asking me"—if such joy (somanassa) arises, his fulfillment of the sāraṇīyadhamma is said to be complete (puṇṇa).

For one who has thus fulfilled the sāraṇīyadhamma, there is no envy (issā) or stinginess (macchariya). He is beloved by people and easily obtains the four requisites. Even when giving away the food in his bowl, it does not run out. He receives the most excellent of the items to be distributed. When danger or famine arrives, the deities take care of him.

In this regard, there are these stories: The Elder Tissa, residing on Senagiri Mountain, lived depending on the village of Mahāgiri. Fifty great elders, while traveling to Nāgadīpa to worship the shrine, entered the village of Giri for alms but left without receiving anything. The Elder, entering the village, saw them and asked, "Venerables, did you receive alms?" They replied, "Friends, we have made our rounds (but received nothing)." Knowing they had received nothing, the Elder said, "Venerables, please wait here for a moment until I return." They said, "Friend, we fifty people did not even get enough to moisten our bowls." "Venerables, resident monks are capable; even if they don't receive alms, they know the nature of the alms-round path," he replied. While the elders waited, the Elder entered the village. At the very first house, a great female lay follower had prepared milk-rice and was looking out for the Elder. As soon as the Elder reached the door, she filled his bowl to the brim. Taking that food, the Elder went to the great elders and said to the Sangha Elder, "Venerables, please accept this." The Sangha Elder looked at the faces of the other monks, thinking, "We, so many of us, received nothing, yet this monk has returned so quickly with food. How can this be?" The Elder, knowing this just by their look, said, "Venerables, this alms-food was obtained rightfully and justly. Please accept it without hesitation." Starting from the first, he gave to all until they were satisfied, and he himself ate until satisfied.

Then, after the meal, the elders asked, "Friend, when did you realize the supramundane Dhamma?" He replied, "Venerables, I have no supramundane Dhamma." "Friend, are you an attainer of jhāna?" they asked. "Venerables, I do not have that either," he replied. "Friend, is this not a miracle (pāṭihāriya)?" they asked. "Venerables, I have fulfilled the sāraṇīyadhamma. From the time that Dhamma was fulfilled, even if there were a hundred thousand monks, the food in my bowl does not run out." Hearing this, they said, "Sādhu, Sādhu, virtuous one! This is appropriate for you." This is the story regarding "the food in the bowl does not run out."

This same Elder went to the place of donation during the Giribhaṇḍa Great Offering at Cetiyapabbata Mountain and asked, "What is the most excellent item in this place?" "Venerable, it is two cloths (robes)," they replied. That...

"One who lacks confidence" means: First, a layperson approaches a gathering with fear, thinking, "Surely, in this place where many people assemble, someone will know of my deed, and then they will suppress me," or "They will hand me over to the royal family." He sits dejected, with drooping shoulders, looking down, scratching the ground with his finger. He is unable to speak with confidence. A monk also approaches with fear, thinking, "Many monks are assembled; surely someone will know of my deed, and then they will bar me from the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā, cause me to fall from the monkhood, and expel me." He is unable to speak with confidence. Even if some immoral person wanders about as if proud, he is still inwardly dejected.

"Dies confused" means: To that person lying on his deathbed, the immoral deeds he had undertaken and performed appear in his mind. Opening his eyes, he sees this world; closing his eyes, he sees the next world. The four woeful states appear to him. It is as if he is being struck on the head with a hundred spears. He dies crying out, "Stop it! Stop it!" Therefore, it is said, "He dies confused." The fifth point is quite clear.

The benefits should be understood as the opposite of what has been stated.

"With a Dhamma talk for much of the night" means: With other Dhamma talks outside of the Pali Canon and with the appreciation (anumodanā) at the dwelling, he showed the Dhamma, gladdened them, and sent them away throughout the night, as if bringing down the celestial Ganges or as if squeezing a great honeycomb a league in size and giving the honey-drink. "Passed" (abhikkantā) means: transcended, exhausted, reached destruction and decay. "Empty house" (suññāgāra) means: there is no separate place called an empty house, but right there, on one side, they enclosed an area with a curtain-wall and prepared a couch, thinking, "The Teacher will rest here." The Blessed One, thinking, "This place used by me with the four postures will be of great fruit for these people," took up the lion's posture (sīhaseyya) there. Referring to that, it is said, "He entered the empty house."
131: There is either a place of buying and selling by virtue of the collection of goods brought there, or a place where merchants reside. 'This will be the chief city' means among the trade routes where these noble ones (Ariyas) reside, this city will be the most excellent, the greatest, and the foremost. 'A place for breaking open the bundles' means a place for opening bundles of goods, a place for unloading merchandise. Even goods not obtainable in the whole of Jambudīpa will be found here; and goods that do not sell elsewhere will come here. Therefore, it means they will break open the bundles right here. It is shown that five hundred thousand in taxes will arise daily—four at the four gates and one at the assembly hall. In the phrase 'from fire or...' and so on, the word 'or' (vā) has the meaning of 'and' (ca). It means it will be destroyed by fire, by water, and by mutual dissension. One part will be destroyed by fire, which they will be unable to extinguish. One part the river Gaṅgā will carry away. One part will be destroyed by the mutual dissension of people who are divided by slanderous speech, saying, 'This person did not tell that to him, that person did not tell this to him.' Having said this, the Blessed One went to the bank of the Gaṅgā at dawn, washed his face, and sat down waiting for the time to go for alms. Sunidha and Vassakāra also thought: 'Our king is an attendant of the recluse Gotama. He will ask us, "I heard the Teacher went to Pāṭaligāma; did you approach him or not?" If we say we approached him, he will ask, "Did you invite him or not?" If we say we did not invite him, he will blame and rebuke us. Furthermore, we are building a city in the place where we have arrived. In every place the recluse Gotama goes, inauspicious beings depart; we will have that spoken of as the city's auspicious blessing.' Thinking thus, they approached the Teacher and invited him. Therefore, it is said, 'Then Sunidha and Vassakāra...' and so on. 'In the morning' means at the time of the forenoon. 'Having dressed' means having dressed in the inner robe in the manner of entering a village and having tied the waistband. 'Taking bowl and robe' means having taken the bowl and robe and having made them connected to the body. 'To the virtuous here' means to the virtuous ones in this place. 'To the restrained' means to those restrained in body, speech, and mind.
132:
"One should share the portion with those deities" means that one should share the merit of the four requisites offered to the Saṅgha with those house-guarding deities; one should give them the portion of merit. "Being honored, they honor in return" means they think, "These people are not even our relatives, yet they share merit with us in this way," and thus they provide excellent protection. "Being revered, they revere in return" means when they are revered by the offering of bali from time to time, they think, "These people are not our relatives, yet every four or six months they give us bali offerings," and so they revere them. Deities who revere humans remove the dangers that arise.

"That person" refers to that wise person. "Like a son born of her own breast" means a child raised at the breast; just as a mother has compassion for her own son, and exerts effort only to remove the dangers that arise for him, so do they have compassion. This is the meaning. "Sees auspicious things" means sees good things.

"Raft (uḷumpa)" means a raft made by driving in pegs to cross to the other shore. "Raft (kulla)" means a raft made by binding with creepers and such.

In the verse "Those who cross the ocean," "ocean (aṇṇava)" is a name for a body of water that is, at the very least, one league (yojana) deep and wide. Here, "lake (sara)" refers to a river. The meaning is: those who cross the deep and wide river of craving (taṇhā), they cross by making a bridge known as the Noble Path (ariya-magga). "Leaving the marshes" means leaving behind the low-lying areas filled with water without touching them. While these people, even if they wish to cross only a small amount of water, must bind a raft, the Buddha and the disciples of the Buddha are wise people who cross even without a raft.

## Explanation of the Discourse on the Noble Truths (Ariyasaccakathāvaṇṇanā)

Koṭigāma means the village built at the pinnacle (koṭi) of King Mahāpanāda's palace. "Of the Noble Truths" means of the truths that make one a Noble One (ariya). "Through not understanding" means through not knowing or not comprehending. "Through not penetrating" means through not penetrating. "Has wandered" means has wandered by way of going from one existence to another. "Has circled" means has circled in saṃsāra by way of repeatedly coming and going.

"Mamañceva tumhākañca" means "of myself and of you as well." Alternatively, the meaning of "sandhāvitaṃ saṃsaritaṃ" in this context should be understood as "the running and wandering has been mine and yours." "Bhavanetti samūhatā" means the rope of craving, which is capable of leading from one existence to another, has been well destroyed, cut, and made not to arise again.

## Description of the Non-returning Nature and Enlightenment (Anāvattidhammasambodhiparāyaṇavaṇṇanā)

"Nātikā" refers to two villages belonging to two sons of brothers (cousins) located near a pond. "Nātike" means in a small village of relatives. "Giñjakāvasathe" means in a residence made of bricks.

"Orambhāgiyānaṃ" means [the fetters] that occur in the lower realm, which cause rebirth only in the sensual realm (kāmabhava). Alternatively, they are called "orambhāgiyāni" because they are to be abandoned by the three paths known as "ora" (lower). Among those fetters, sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and ill-will (byāpāda), if not yet suppressed by meditative attainment (samāpatti) or not yet eradicated by the path (magga), prevent one from going to the higher realms of the fine-material (rūpabhava) and immaterial (arūpabhava) spheres by the power of their arising. The three fetters starting with self-identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), even if they arise in those higher realms, bring one back and cause rebirth in this sensual realm; thus, all of them are called "orambhāgiyā" (lower fetters). "Anāvattidhammā" refers to those whose nature is not to return by way of rebirth.

In the phrase "rāgadosamohānaṃ tanuttā" (the thinning of lust, hatred, and delusion), the state of being thin should be understood in two ways: by occurring only occasionally and by the weakness of the outbursts of defilements (pariyuṭṭhāna). Indeed, for a Once-returner (Sakadāgāmi), lust and so on do not arise frequently as they do for worldlings (puthujjana); they arise only occasionally. And when they do arise, they do not arise thickly like those of worldlings, but very thinly, like a fly's wing. However, the Dīghabhāṇaka Tipiṭaka Mahāsīva Thera said: "Because a Once-returner has sons, daughters, and a harem, the defilements are thick. This statement about 'thinning' is spoken with reference to the thinning of existences (fewer births)." This view is rejected in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) which states: "For a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), excluding the seven existences, there is no thinning of existence in the eighth. For a Once-returner, excluding two existences, there is no thinning of existence in the five. For a Non-returner (Anāgāmi), excluding the fine-material and immaterial realms, there is no thinning of existence in the sensual realm. For an Arahant (Khīṇāsava), there is no thinning of existence in any realm."

"Imaṃ lokaṃ" (this world) is spoken with reference to this sensual realm. The meaning here is: if one who has attained the fruit of Once-returning among humans [is reborn] in the celestial realm...

## Description of the Story of Ambapālī the Courtesan (Ambapālīgaṇikāvatthuvaṇṇanā)

Regarding "Vesāliyaṃ viharati," the prosperity of Vesālī should be understood according to the method described in the Khandhaka, starting with "At that time, Vesālī was prosperous and flourishing." "Ambapālivane" means in the mango grove which was the park of the courtesan Ambapālī. "Sato bhikkhave" (Mindful, O monks) means the Blessed One specifically began this discourse on the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) here to establish mindfulness upon seeing Ambapālī. In that phrase, one is called "sato" because of recollecting. One is called "sampajāno" because of clearly comprehending. The meaning is that one should dwell endowed with both mindfulness and clear comprehension. Whatever needs to be said regarding the terms "kāye kāyānupassī" (contemplating the body in the body), etc., will be explained in the description of the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta.

"Nīlā" (blue/dark) is an inclusive description. "Nīlavaṇṇā" (blue-colored), etc., is the detailed classification of that same description. Although their natural complexion was not blue, it is said so because they were anointed with blue-colored ointments. "Nīlavatthā" means their lower garments, blankets, silk cloths, etc., were also blue. "Nīlālaṅkārā" means they were adorned with blue gems and blue flowers. Their chariots were also inlaid with blue gems, draped with blue cloths, had blue banners, and were yoked to blue horses with blue armor and blue ornaments; even the goad-sticks were blue. In this way, the meaning should be understood for all the terms. "Parivaṭṭesi" means struck or collided. In the phrase "kiṃ je Ambapālī," "je" is a form of address, meaning "Lady Ambapālī, for what reason?" There is also a variant reading "kiñcā," but the meaning is the same. "Sāhāraṃ" means together with one's own territory. "Aṅguliṃ phoṭesuṃ" means they snapped their fingers. "Ambakāyā" means because of a woman.

"Yesaṃ" is the genitive case used in the sense of the instrumental (karaṇattha), meaning "by whom [they] have not been seen." "Oloketha" means look. "Avaloketha" means look repeatedly. "Upasaṃharatha" means bring near. Bring this assembly of Licchavīs near to your mind as being like the Tāvatiṃsa gods; compare them. Just as the Tāvatiṃsa gods are beautiful, inspiring, and have various colors like blue, etc., so too are these Licchavī kings. Thus, the meaning is: look at them by making them equal to the Tāvatiṃsa gods.

Why did the Blessed One, after forbidding the taking of signs (nimittaggāha) in the eyes, etc., regarding forms, etc., in hundreds of discourses, now encourage the taking of signs with great effort here? It is because he desired their welfare. For there, some monks were slack in their energy...

Standing in the air at a height of seven palm trees, he displayed psychic powers and preached the Dhamma. The entire city gathered. The Elder descended, paid homage to the Blessed One, and said, "Venerable Sir, it is time for me to go." The Blessed One, thinking "I will see off the General of the Dhamma," rose from the Dhamma-seat, went towards the Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), and stood on a jeweled slab. The Elder circumambulated him three times, paid homage at the four directions, and said: "Venerable Sir, at the feet of the Buddha Anomadassī, more than a hundred thousand aeons and an incalculable period ago, I prostrated and aspired to see you. That aspiration of mine has been fulfilled; I have seen you. That was the first sight, and this is the last. There will be no more seeing you again." Having said this, he raised his hands in salutation, shining like the union of ten fingernails, and backed away facing the Buddha as long as he was within sight. He paid homage, saying, "From this day forth, there is no more coming and going to any place by way of death and rebirth," and departed. The earth shook violently as far as the water's edge. The Blessed One said to the monks standing around, "Monks, follow your elder brother." The monks followed as far as the gateway. The Elder turned them back, saying, "Stay, friends, be diligent," and departed only with his own retinue. People followed him weeping, saying, "Previously the Venerable One went on a journey from which he would return; now he goes on a journey from which he will not return." He turned them back too, saying, "Friends, be diligent; such is the nature of conditioned things."

Then, the Venerable Sāriputta, showing compassion to the people along the way for seven days, reached Nālaka village in the evening and stood at the foot of a banyan tree at the village gate. At that time, a nephew of the Elder named Uparevata, while going out of the village, saw the Elder, approached, paid homage, and stood there. The Elder asked him, "Is your grandmother at home?" He replied, "Yes, Venerable Sir." "Go and tell her of our arrival here. If she asks why we have come, say: 'He will stay inside the village for just one day today. Prepare the birth chamber. Arrange lodging for five hundred monks.'" He went and said, "Grandmother, my uncle has arrived." "Where is he now?" "At the village gate." "Is he alone, or is there anyone else?" "There are five hundred monks." "For what reason has he come?" He told her the whole matter. The Brahmin lady thought, "For so many people, a place to stay..."

The Elder ascended the mansion with the monks. Having ascended, he entered the birth chamber and sat down. As soon as he sat, he dismissed the monks, saying, "Go to your own lodgings." Just as they had gone, a severe illness arose in the Elder; painful feelings of dysentery leading to death occurred. Blood entered one vessel and left another. The Brahmin lady, thinking "I do not like my son's condition," stood leaning against the door of her own room. The Four Great Kings, looking to see where the General of the Dhamma was staying, thought, "He is lying on his deathbed in the birth chamber in Nālaka village; let us go for a final sight." They arrived, paid homage, and stood there. The Elder asked, "Who are you?" "We are the Four Great Kings, Venerable Sir." "Why have you come?" "We have come to attend to the sick." "Let it be, there is an attendant. You may go," he dismissed them. After they had gone, in the same manner, Sakka, the King of Devas, and after he had gone, Suyama and others, and Mahābrahmā also came. The Elder dismissed them in the same way.

The Brahmin lady, seeing the coming and going of the deities, thought, "Who are these people who pay homage to my son and then leave?" She went to the door of the Elder's room and asked, "Dear Cunda, what is the situation?" Cunda explained the situation and said, "Great Lay-Devotee, they have come to the Venerable One." The Elder asked, "Why have you come at an unusual time?" She said, "Dear son, I have come to see you," and asked, "Dear son, who came first?" "Great Lay-Devotee, it was the Four Great Kings." "Dear son, are you greater than the Four Great Kings?" "Great Lay-Devotee, these are like temple attendants; from the time our Teacher took conception, they have provided protection with swords in their hands." "Dear son, who came after they left?" "Great Lay-Devotee, he is like a novice who carries a bundle; when our Teacher descended from Tāvatiṃsa, he descended carrying the bowl and robes." (The earth) shakes because it is struck. When the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta was preached, it shook while established in the nature of giving applause. When the life-principle was relinquished, it shook while established in the nature of compassion, unable to endure the agitation of the mind. "Ānanda, these eight are the causes"—in these words, "these" refers to the things pointed out. By this much, the Venerable Ānanda noted, "Indeed, today the Blessed One has relinquished the life-principle." Although the Blessed One knew that [Ānanda] had noted this, without giving an opportunity [for further questioning], he combined other groups of eight and said, "There are these eight," and so forth.

## Explanation of the Eight Assemblies

In that context, "many hundreds of the assembly of nobles" is similar to the meetings with King Bimbisāra, meetings with relatives, meetings with the Licchavīs, and so on; such an assembly is also found in other world-systems. "Sallapitapubba" means having engaged in conversation before. "Sākacchā" means having previously engaged in Dhamma discussion. "What was their appearance like?" means they might be fair, dark, or of a golden hue, but the Teacher is always of a golden color. This statement, however, is made with reference to the physical form. The physical form appears only to their perception; the Blessed One does not become like a barbarian, nor does he wear jeweled earrings; he sits only in the form of a Buddha. They, however, see only a form similar to their own. "What was their voice like?" means they might have broken voices, hoarse voices, or voices like a crow's, but the Teacher's voice is like that of Brahmā. This statement is made with reference to the specific language. For if the Teacher, seated on a royal throne, speaks, they think, "Today the King speaks with a sweet voice." When the Blessed One has departed after speaking, and they see the King arrive again, the inquiry arises, "Who was that?" In this context, "Who was that?" means they do not know even when they investigate, "Who was this person who just now spoke so sweetly in the Māgadha or Sīhaḷa language and then disappeared? Was it a god or a human?" Why does he preach the Dhamma to those who do not know him in this way?
151:
It is for the purpose of establishing a latent tendency (vāsanā). For even Dhamma heard in this way becomes a condition in the future; thus he preaches with reference to the future. The occurrence of many hundreds of the assembly of Brahmins and so on should be understood through the meetings with Soṇadaṇḍa the Brahmin, Kūṭadaṇḍa, and so forth, as well as through other world-systems.

For what purpose did the Blessed One bring up these eight assemblies? It was only to show his state of fearlessness. Having brought up these assemblies, he said: "Ānanda, for the Tathāgata who approaches these eight assemblies and preaches the Dhamma, there is no fear or nervousness. Who could conceive the idea that the Tathāgata would be afraid upon seeing Māra alone?" (He said:) "Ānanda, the Tathāgata, fearless, unshakeable, mindful, and clearly comprehending, has relinquished the life-principle."

## Explanation of the Eight Bases of Transcendence (Abhibhāyatana)

"Bases of transcendence" (abhibhāyatana) means the causes for transcending. What do they transcend? They transcend both opposing states and objects. They transcend opposing states by being their opposites, and they transcend objects through the excellence of the person's knowledge.

In the phrases such as "perceiving form internally," one is called "perceiving form internally" by virtue of performing preliminary work (parikamma) on the forms within one's own continuity. One who performs the preliminary work on blue internally does so on the hair, the bile, or the pupils of the eyes. One who performs the preliminary work on yellow does so on the fat, the skin, the backs of the hands and feet, or the yellow parts of the eyes. One who performs the preliminary work on red does so on the flesh, the blood, the tongue, or the red parts of the eyes. One who performs the preliminary work on white does so on the bones, the teeth, the nails, or the white parts of the eyes. That (internal preliminary work), however, is not intensely blue, intensely yellow, intensely red, or intensely white; it is indeed impure.

"One sees forms externally" means that for such a person, this preliminary work has arisen internally, but the sign (nimitta) is external. Such a person is said to be "perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally" by virtue of the internal preliminary work and the external attainment (appanā). "Limited" (paritta) means objects that are not enlarged. "Beautiful or ugly" (suvaṇṇa-dubbaṇṇa) means they are either fair or foul. It should be understood that this base of transcendence is spoken of only by way of the limited (small object). "Having transcended those forms" means, for example, a person with good digestion, having received a mere spoonful of rice—
152:
Just as one might pull [food] towards oneself, thinking, "What is there to be eaten here?" and make only a single mouthful, so too, a person of superior wisdom and clear knowledge, thinking, "What is there to be attained in this limited object? This is not my burden," masters those forms and enters into attainment. The meaning is that as soon as the sign (nimitta) arises, he reaches absorption (appanā) in that object. By the words "he knows, he sees," his reflection (ābhoga) is mentioned. And that reflection occurs only to one who has emerged from the attainment, not within the attainment itself. "He is one who has such a perception" means he has such a perception either through the perception of reflection or through the perception of jhāna. For him, the perception of mastering (abhibhavana-saññā) exists even within the attainment, but the perception of reflection (ābhoga-saññā) occurs only to one who has emerged from the attainment.

"Immeasurable" means having a developed measure, meaning "great." Regarding "having mastered" (abhibhuyya): just as a man who eats a lot, having received a single serving of rice, does not see it as great, thinking, "Let there be another; what will this much do for me?" so too, a person of superior wisdom and clear knowledge, thinking, "How should I enter into attainment here? This is not immeasurable; there is no burden for me in achieving one-pointedness of mind," masters those forms and enters into attainment. The meaning is that as soon as the sign arises, he reaches absorption in that object.

"Perceiving no form internally" means being devoid of the perception of preliminary work (parikamma-saññā) regarding internal forms, either because of not obtaining them or because of their absence.

"Alone, he sees forms externally" means for whom both the preliminary work and the sign have arisen only externally. Such a person is said to be "perceiving no form internally, he alone sees forms externally" by virtue of both the preliminary work and the absorption externally. The rest here is the same as the method stated in the fourth base of mastery (abhibhāyatana). Among these four, the limited (paritta) object comes by way of the temperament of initial thought (vitakka-carita); the immeasurable (appamāṇa) object by way of the temperament of delusion (moha-carita); the beautiful (suvaṇṇa) object by way of the temperament of hatred (dosa-carita); and the ugly (dubbaṇṇa) object by way of the temperament of lust (rāga-carita). For these types of people, these objects are suitable. Their suitability is stated in detail in the Description of Temperaments (Carita-niddesa) in the Visuddhimagga.

In the fifth base of mastery and so on, "blue" is said by way of including everything. "Blue-colored" is said by way of color. "Showing blue" is said by way of appearance; it means that because of not knowing, the openings of conceit (mānavivara) have unmixed colors and appear as a single blue. "Having a blue luster" is said by way of radiance; it means having a blue radiance, endowed with blue light. By this, the purity of those objects is shown. Pure color...
155:
The neck bones of the Buddhas, however, stand connected like the links of a chain; therefore, at the time of looking back, it is not possible to turn the neck. Just as a noble elephant, wishing to look at the rear, turns with its whole body, so too the Buddha must turn. For the Blessed One, while standing at the city gate, as soon as the thought "I shall look at Vesālī" arose in his mind, [thinking] "O Blessed One, you who have fulfilled the perfections for more than a hundred thousand crores of aeons have never performed the act of looking by turning the neck," this great earth turned like a potter's wheel and made the Blessed One face the city of Vesālī. It is with reference to this that it was said.

Is it not only at Vesālī? At Sāvatthī, Rājagaha, Nālandā, Pāṭaligāma, Koṭigāma, and Nātika village, at the time of departing from each place, all those were also the last sightings; why then did he not look with the elephant look (nāgāpalokita) in those places? Because it was not extraordinary. For one who turns and looks in those places, such looking is not extraordinary; therefore, he did not look in that way. Furthermore, the princes of Vesālī were close to destruction; they would perish within three years. Those princes would establish a shrine (cetiya) named "Nāgāpalokita" at the city gate and worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so on; that worship would be for their welfare and happiness for a long time. Thus, he looked out of compassion for them.

"The ender of suffering" means the one who makes an end to the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha). "The one with vision" means the one who has vision through the five eyes. "The one who is extinguished" means the one who is extinguished through the extinction of defilements (kilesa-parinibbāna).

## Explanation of the Four Great Authorities (Caturamahāpadesa-vaṇṇanā)
"Great Authorities" (Mahāpadesa) means in a great opportunity, or a great reason; the meaning is great causes stated by citing great personages such as the Buddha.

"Should not be rejoiced at" means one should not accept it beforehand by saying "Sādhu" with joy and delight. For if this is done, later when it is said, "This does not agree [with the Dhamma]," one might not give up his view, saying, "Was this Dhamma before, and now it is not Dhamma?" "Should not be rejected" means one should not say beforehand, "What is this fool saying?" For if this is said, the person will not say even what is fit to be said. Therefore, He said, "Without rejoicing, without rejecting." "Words and syllables" (Pada-byañjanā) means the syllables known as words. "Having learned well" means...
166:
The lion stretches its body, shakes its mane, roars the lion's roar three times, and goes out in search of food.

"Sleeping with the fourth jhana is called the Tathāgata's sleep" (Aṅguttara Nikāya). Among those ways of sleeping, the lion's posture (sīhaseyya) is mentioned here. This posture is called the noble sleep because it is a posture where the fire element (tejo-dhātu) is predominant.

"Foot on foot" means the left foot on the right foot. "Overlapping" means placing it slightly beyond. If ankle touches ankle or knee touches knee, pain often arises repeatedly, the mind is not concentrated, and the sleep is uncomfortable. If placed overlapping so they do not touch, pain does not arise, the mind is concentrated, and the sleep is comfortable. Therefore, he lay down in this manner. Because he reached the sleep from which he would not rise, it is not said here, "keeping the thought of rising in mind." Here, "not rising" should be understood by way of the physical body; however, by way of sleep, there was no opportunity for the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) to occur for the Blessed One that night. For in the first watch, he preached the Dhamma to the Malla princes; in the middle watch, to Subhadda; in the last watch, he exhorted the Saṅgha of monks; and at the break of dawn, he attained Parinibbāna.

"Bloomed on all branches" means they bloomed everywhere from the roots to the tips; not only the Twin Sal trees, but all trees were in full bloom. Not only in that park, but in the entire ten-thousandfold world system, flowering plants bloomed and fruiting plants bore fruit. On the trunks of all trees, trunk-lotuses bloomed; on the branches, branch-lotuses; on the vines, vine-lotuses; in the sky, sky-lotuses; and stalk-lotuses bloomed, breaking through the surface of the earth. The entire Great Ocean was covered with five-colored lotuses. Mount Himavanta, three thousand yojanas wide, was extremely delightful, like a thick bundle of peacock feathers, like being decorated with continuous garlands and flower-tassels, like a flower-circlet tightly bound, and like a well-filled flower basket.

"Those deities scatter over the Tathāgata’s body" means the deities dwelling in those Twin Sal trees shook the trunks and branches to scatter flowers over the Tathāgata’s body; it means they scattered flowers over his body. "They cover" means they scatter as if covering him. "They scatter all around" means they scatter repeatedly and continuously.
169:
Why did the Blessed One, while praising the immeasurable fruit of an offering made by even holding a single ummā flower and reflecting on the Buddha's virtues in other places, reject such a grand offering here? It was for the sake of favoring the assembly and for the long-lastingness of the Dispensation (Sāsana). If the Blessed One had not rejected it thus, in the future, people would not fulfill virtue (sīla) where it should be practiced, they would not fulfill concentration (samādhi) where it should be practiced, and they would not undertake the work of insight (vipassanā) where it should be practiced. They would live merely encouraging attendants to make offerings. What is called material offering (āmisa-pūjā) cannot support the Dispensation even for a single day, or even for the duration of drinking a cup of gruel. Even a thousand monasteries like the Mahāvihāra and a thousand stupas like the Mahācetiya cannot maintain the Dispensation. Whoever performs the deed, it belongs to that person alone. Only right practice (sammā-paṭipatti) is the offering appropriate for the Tathāgata. That practice alone is what the Blessed One desired, and it can also support the Dispensation. Therefore, wishing to show that practice, he said, "Ānanda, whoever..." and so on.

In that passage, "dhammānudhammapaṭipanno" means one who practices the preliminary path (pubbabhāgapatipadā), which is the practice appropriate for the ninefold supramundane Dhamma. Because that practice itself is appropriate, it is called "sāmicī" (proper). Because of practicing that proper practice, one is called "sāmicīpaṭipanno". One practices and fulfills that "anudhamma" known as the preliminary path; therefore, one is called "anudhammacārī".

The preliminary path should be understood as the right practice (sammā-paṭipatti) starting from virtue (sīla), the regulations of conduct (ācāra-paññatti), and the undertaking of ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), up to the stage of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū). Therefore, a monk who does not stand in the six types of respect, violates the regulations, and makes a living through improper search is not a dhammānudhammapaṭipanno. A monk who does not transgress even slightly all the training rules prescribed for him, the Buddha's instructions, the Buddha's boundaries, and the Buddha's laws is called a dhammānudhammapaṭipanno. The same method applies to nuns. A layman who lives undertaking the five enmities (breaking the five precepts) and the ten courses of unwholesome action is not a dhammānudhammapaṭipanno. But one who fulfills the three refuges, the five precepts, and the ten precepts, observes the eight-day Uposatha every month, gives alms, makes offerings of incense and flowers, attends to parents, and attends to righteous recluses and brahmins is called a dhammānudhammapaṭipanno. The same method applies to laywomen.
171:
Why is it that only the Venerable Mahākassapa Thera possesses such abundant majesty (tejas), while other Arahants do not? It is because he had once been a guardian deity at the stupa of Kassapa Buddha.

It is said that when Vipassī Buddha attained Parinibbāna, a single stupa was built for his relics, which were like a solid mass of gold. Indeed, it is the nature of long-lived Buddhas to have only a single stupa. People constructed that stupa to a height of one league (yojana), using golden bricks that were one span in width and two inches thick, using orpiment and realgar as clay, and sesame oil instead of water. From that point, the earth-dwelling (bhumma) deities raised it by one league, the sky-dwelling (ākāsaṭṭha) deities by one league, the cloud-dwelling deities of heat (uṇhavalāhaka) by one league, the cloud-dwelling deities of mist (abbhavalāhaka) by one league, the deities of the Four Great Kings (cātumahārājika) by one league, and the deities of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven by one league. Thus, the stupa became seven leagues high. When people arrived carrying flowers, scents, garments, and so on, the guardian deity would take those items and offer them to the stupa even while the people were watching.

At that time, this Venerable Mahākassapa Thera was a wealthy Brahmin (Mahāsāla) and went there carrying a bright yellow cloth. The deity took the cloth from the Brahmin's hand and offered it to the stupa. Seeing this, the Brahmin was filled with inspiration and made a wish: "May I also become a guardian deity at the stupa of such a Buddha in the future." After passing away from that life, he was reborn in the celestial realm. While he was wandering between the celestial and human realms, Kassapa Buddha appeared in the world and attained Parinibbāna. For that Buddha too, there was only a single mass of relics, and a stupa one league high was built. He became the guardian deity there, and when the Dispensation (Sāsana) disappeared, he was reborn in heaven. Passing away from there during the time of our Buddha, he took rebirth in a great family, went forth into homelessness, and attained Arahantship. Thus, because he had been a guardian deity at a stupa, the Elder should be known as one abundant in majesty (Tejussada).

"Ananda, the deities are complaining" means, "Ananda, the deities are complaining; there is no other fault in my son (Mahākassapa)."

Why did he ask, "Of what nature are they, Bhante?" The Buddha said, "The deities are complaining," and this was a question to ask what Ananda understood to be the nature of those deities.
173:
If anyone misinterprets the Pali or the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), they are questioned, "From whom did you learn this?", and are corrected and retaught properly. The monks living on the other side of the Ganges do the same at the Tissa Mahāvihāra. Thus, when monks assemble during these two annual occasions, those who had previously departed after taking meditation subjects for the rains retreat return to report their attainment of distinction. Referring to such monks, it was said, "Bhante, those who previously resided for the rains," and so on.

"Manobhāvanīya" means those who are developed or esteemed by the mind. Alternatively, it means those who develop the mind, cause it to grow, and wash away the dust of lust (rāga) and so forth. It is said that the Elder Mahākassapa, being perfect in duties (vatta), would not remain still upon seeing an elder monk; he would go out to meet him, take the umbrella, bowl, and robes from his hands, dust the seat, and offer it. He would perform duties for the monk sitting there and look after his dwelling. Even upon seeing a novice monk, he would not remain silent but would stand nearby and perform the major and minor duties. The Elder spoke thus because he did not want these duties and practices to decline.

Then the Buddha thought, "Ananda is thinking that he will no longer have the opportunity to see mind-developing (manobhāvanīya) monks. I will tell him the places where he can see them. By staying in such places, he will be able to see mind-developing monks without having to wander here and there." Thinking thus, he said, "These four places," and so on.

In that passage, "saddhassa" (of the faithful) refers to one who has a clear mind of faith in the Triple Gem and is perfect in duties, such as being known for performing all duties like sweeping the stupa terrace from early morning. "Dassanīyāni" means places worthy of seeing, places that should be visited for the purpose of seeing. "Saṃvejanīyāni" means places that arouse spiritual urgency (saṃvega). "Ṭhānāni" means causes or geographical locations.
