The phrase "Whoever they may be" was spoken to show the benefit of going on a pilgrimage to stupas. Among those wandering on pilgrimage to stupas, there is no need to speak of those who sweep the stupa terrace, wash the seats, or water the Bodhi tree. It shows that even those who set out with the intention, "We will worship the stupa," and die on the way with a clear mind of faith, will certainly be established in heaven without any hindrance.
174:
## Commentary on the Discourse on Ānanda's Questions

'Adassanaṃ Ānandā' (Not seeing, Ānanda) means that there is the non-seeing of women; the Buddha shows that this non-seeing is the noble practice in this Dispensation. For as long as a monk, sitting in his dwelling with the door closed, does not see a woman who has come and is standing at the door, greed certainly does not arise in him, nor does his mind waver. However, if there is seeing, both [greed and wavering] can occur. Therefore, He said: "Not seeing, Ānanda."

'Dassane Bhagavā sati kathaṃ' (If there is seeing, Blessed One, how...) means asking how one should practice if there is seeing in places such as where one goes for alms.

Then the Blessed One said: "It is better to speak with a man standing with a sword in hand, saying, 'If you speak with me, I will cut off your head right here,' or with an ogress standing and saying, 'If you speak with me, I will crunch and eat your flesh right here.'" This is because, due to that [speaking with the man or ogress], destruction occurs only in a single existence; there is no experiencing of boundless suffering in the lower realms. But if there is conversation with a woman, intimacy arises; when there is intimacy, there is an inclination [of the mind]; one whose mind is inclined reaches the destruction of virtue and becomes one who fills the lower realms. Therefore, He said: "No conversation (anālāpo)."

It was also said:
"One may speak with a person with a sword in hand,
One may even speak with a pisāca demon,
One may approach even a venomous snake whose bite is fatal,
But one should not speak alone, one-on-one, with a woman."

'Ālapantena pana' (But if speaking...) means if a woman asks about the day, requests the precepts, wishes to hear the Dhamma, asks a question, or if there is a duty to be performed by monks, and if [the monk] remains without speaking, people will say, "This one is mute, this one is deaf, he sits with his mouth closed after eating." Therefore, one must inevitably speak. This is asking how one should practice when one has to speak in this way.

Then the Blessed One, referring to this advice: "Bhikkhus, establish the thought of a mother toward those who are like mothers, the thought of a sister toward those who are like sisters, and the thought of a daughter toward those who are like daughters," said: "Mindfulness, Ānanda, should be established (sati Ānanda upaṭṭhapetabbā)."

'Abyāvaṭā' means be those who are unconcerned and without effort [in worldly affairs].

'Sāratthe ghaṭatha' means strive for the noble benefit, which is Arahantship.

'Anuyuñjatha' means devote yourselves to the attainment of that Arahantship.
178:
'The deity makes the rain fall well; the crops are abundant'—thus he engages in pleasant conversation. To the monks, he speaks pleasantly: 'Venerable sirs, are the requisites of a monk easily obtained? Do not be negligent in the practice of a recluse.'

## Commentary on the Mahāsudassana Sutta Discourse

'Khuddakanagarake' means in a small town that is like a minor town, a cramped small town. 'Ujjaṅgalanagarake' means in an uneven small town. 'Sākhānagarake' means just as the branches of trees are small, so too it is a small town like a branch of other great cities. 'Khattiyamahāsālā' refers to great nobles who have attained the status of 'Mahāsāla'. This method applies everywhere.

Among them, 'Khattiyamahāsāla' refers to those who have buried and stored wealth amounting to a hundred or a thousand crores; the daily expenditure is one cartload of kahāpaṇas going out, and two cartloads coming in during the evening. 'Brāhmaṇamahāsāla' refers to those who have buried wealth of eighty crores; the daily expenditure is one pot of kahāpaṇas going out, and one cartload coming in during the evening. 'Gahapatimahāsāla' refers to those who have buried wealth of forty crores; the daily expenditure is five baskets (ambaṇa) of kahāpaṇas going out, and one pot coming in during the evening.

'Mā hevaṃ Ānanda avaca' means: Ānanda, do not say so; this city should not be called a 'small town'. To describe the prosperity of this city, the Buddha said, "I have come here with great effort and great exertion, standing and sitting many times," and then spoke the words beginning with 'Bhūtapubbaṃ'. 'Subhikkhā' means being endowed with food and provisions. 'Hatthisaddena' means when one elephant makes a sound, eighty-four thousand elephants make a sound; thus, it is not quiet from the sound of elephants; the same applies to the sound of horses. Meritorious beings travel in the streets, chasing one another in chariots drawn by four Sindh horses; thus, it is not quiet from the sound of chariots. Musical instruments such as drums are always played in this city; thus, it is not quiet from the sound of drums and so forth. There, 'sammasaddo' means the sound of bronze gongs. 'Pāṇitāḷasaddo' means the sound of striking a square vessel (ambaṇa) with the hand. They also say 'kuṭabherisaddo'.
189:
In the phrase "sandhisamalasaṅkaṭīrā," 'sandhi' refers to an alley (the space between houses). 'Samala' refers to a heap of excrement and a drain for wastewater. 'Saṅkaṭīra' refers to a place where rubbish is piled. Celestial dances occurred above, while human dances occurred below. This was also the case with singing and so on. Furthermore, humans moved among deities, and deities moved among humans, making offerings as they went. While the Buddha's body was being carried through the center of the city, Mallikā, the wife of General Bandhula, heard, "The Buddha's body is being brought." She had the Mahālatā ornament—similar to Visākhā's—brought out, which she had kept without wearing since her husband's death. Thinking, "I will honor the Teacher with this ornament," she had it washed with scented water and stood at the doorway.

That ornament had existed in only three places: with those two women and in the house of the thief Devadāniya. When the Buddha's body reached the doorway, she said, "Friends, please lower the Buddha's body for a moment," and she adorned the Buddha's body with that ornament. It covered him from head to the soles of his feet. The golden-hued body of the Buddha, adorned with the Mahālatā ornament made of the seven jewels, was exceedingly beautiful. Seeing this, Mallikā, with a heart full of faith, made a wish: "Lord, as long as I wander in Saṃsāra, may I have no need for separate ornaments; may my body always be as if it were already adorned."

Then, carrying the Buddha with that Mahālatā ornament made of the seven jewels, they exited through the eastern gate and placed the Buddha's body at the Mallas' shrine called Makuṭabandhana, to the east of the city.

## Mahākassapattheravatthuvaṇṇanā

"Pāvāya Kusināraṃ" means that after wandering for alms in the city of Pāvā, he entered the road, thinking, "I will go to Kusinārā." In the phrase "rukkhamūle nisīdi" (sat at the foot of a tree), why is it not called "divāvihāra" (day-rest)? Because he did not sit for the purpose of the day-rest. The monks accompanying the Elder Mahā Kassapa were all those who had grown up in comfort and possessed great merit. At midday, they became exhausted from walking barefoot on the ground, which was like a hot stone slab. Seeing those monks, the Elder thought, "The monks are tired, and the destination is not far. After resting for a while to relieve the fatigue, I will go to Kusinārā in the evening and pay respects to the Buddha."
190:
Leaving the road, he spread his double-robe (saṅghāṭi) at the foot of a tree, cooled his hands and feet with water from a water-pot, and sat down. The accompanying monks also sat at the foot of the tree, practicing wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra) and reciting the virtues of the Triple Gem. Because they sat for the purpose of dispelling fatigue, it is not called "divāvihāra."

"Mandārava-pupphaṃ gahetvā" means holding a flower the size of a large storage jar, placed on a fresh stalk, like an umbrella. "Addasa kho" means he saw [someone] coming from afar. Having seen him, he thought:

"In the hand of this Ājīvaka, a Mandārava celestial flower is seen. This flower does not usually appear on the paths of humans. It appears only when someone of psychic power performs a feat, or when the Omniscient Bodhisatta descends into his mother's womb, and so on. Today, however, no performance of psychic power by anyone is seen. My Teacher has not descended into a mother's womb, nor has he been born, nor has he attained Buddhahood today, nor has he preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, nor has he performed the Twin Miracle, nor has he descended from the celestial realm, nor has he relinquished the life-force. My Teacher, the Buddha, being advanced in age, must surely have attained Parinibbāna."

Then, the thought arose, "I will ask him." Thinking, "If I ask while remaining seated, it would be disrespectful to the Teacher," he rose from his seat. He put on the rag-robe (paṃsukūla) given to him by the Buddha, which was like the hide of the Chaddanta elephant king or the color of a rain cloud. Placing his joined palms, shining with the meeting of ten fingernails, upon his head, he faced the Ājīvaka out of respect for the Teacher and said, "Friend, do you know our Teacher?"

Did he ask knowing that the Buddha had attained Parinibbāna, or without knowing? The knowledge of Arahants is connected to reflection (āvajjana). Some say he asked without knowing because he had not yet reflected. The Elder frequently entered meditative attainments (samāpatti). He spent his time through the power of attainment in the night, the day, in caves, and in pavilions. Even when entering a village of his relatives, he would enter attainment at the gate and only receive alms after emerging from it. The Elder thought, "In this final existence, I will favor the people. May the merit of those who offer me alms or honor me with scents and garlands be of great fruit."
192:
“When the Blessed One arrives, we shall make an offering of congee (yāgu); collect the materials,” he said. (Mahāvagga, 303). They did as instructed.

Seeing those boys, who were lovely and bold in speech, people—whether they wished to or not—made the offerings. After making them, they asked, “Dear boys, what will you take?” The boys replied, “We have no need for anything else; our father wishes to offer congee when the Blessed One arrives.” Hearing this, the people gave everything they could carry without limit. What they could not carry themselves, they had others deliver. Then, when the Blessed One arrived at Atumā and entered the chaff-house (bhusāgāra), Subhadda went to the village gate in the evening, called the people, and said: “Lay devotees, I do not expect anything else from you. The rice and other items brought by my sons are sufficient for the Saṅgha. Just give me your manual labor (service).”

“Take this and that,” they said, and having taken all the equipment, he had ovens built in the monastery. Wearing a dark dyed robe and wrapping himself in a similar one, he went about all night directing, “Do this, do that,” spending a hundred thousand, and had edible congee and honey balls prepared. “Bhojjayāgu” refers to congee that is drunk after eating. Into that congee, he put everything called edible, such as ghee, honey, molasses, fish, meat, flowers, and fruit juices. It was so fragrant that it was like something suitable for anointing the heads of those who wish to play.

Then, the Blessed One, having performed his morning ablutions, set out towards the city of Atumā for alms, surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks. People told Subhadda, “The Blessed One has entered the village for alms; for whom have you prepared the congee?” Subhadda, still wearing those dark dyed robes, holding a large ladle in one hand and a small ladle in the other, knelt with his right knee on the ground like a Brahmā, paid homage, and said, “Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept my congee.”

Then, following the method in the Khandhaka where “Tathāgatas ask even though they know,” the Blessed One asked and, upon hearing the answer, rebuked that one ordained late in life (vuḍḍhapabbajita). He then laid down two training rules regarding this matter: the rule on accepting what is unallowable (akappiyasamādāna) and the rule on carrying barber's tools (khurabhaṇḍapariharaṇa). He said, “Monks, those who for many millions of aeons [spent their lives] seeking food...
193:
...have passed away. But this food of yours is unallowable, arisen through unrighteous means. Those who consume this food will be reborn only in states of deprivation (apāya) for many thousands of existences. Cast it away; do not take it.” Having said this, he proceeded for alms. Not a single monk took anything.

Subhadda, being displeased, thought: “This man wanders about saying, ‘I know everything.’ If he did not want to take it, he should have sent word. This cooked food (pakkāhāra), even if it lasts a long time, would only last about seven days. This was something I had strived for all my life. He has destroyed it all; this man wishes me harm.” Thus, he harbored a grudge against the Blessed One but could say nothing while the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala) was alive. It is said he thought: “This man is a Great Being (Mahāpurisa) ordained from a high noble family; if I say anything, he will only rebuke me.” Hearing today that “The Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna,” he spoke thus, feeling relieved and joyful.

When the Elder Mahākassapa heard those words, he felt as if his heart had been struck or as if a thunderbolt had fallen on his head. Spiritual urgency (saṃvega) arose in him: “The Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna only seven days ago; even today his golden-hued body still remains. In the Dispensation (Sāsana) that the Blessed One attained with great difficulty, such a great and vile impurity, a thorn, has appeared so quickly. If this wicked person prospers and gains similar companions, they will surely cause the Dispensation to decline.” Then the Elder thought:

“If I were to make this old man wear rags here and now, sprinkle him with ashes, and expel him, people would see our fault, saying, ‘While the body of the Ascetic Gotama still remains, his disciples are already quarreling.’ Therefore, I shall endure it for now.

The Dhamma taught by the Blessed One is like a heap of unstrung flowers. Just as flowers in such a heap are scattered here and there when the wind blows, so too, as time passes under the influence of such wicked persons, one or two training rules in the Vinaya will disappear, one or two sets of questions in the Sutta will disappear, and one or two levels in the Abhidhamma will disappear. In this way, when the root is gradually destroyed, we shall become like ghosts and demons. Therefore, let us perform a rehearsal (Saṅgāyana) of the Dhamma and Vinaya. If this is done...”
196:
The Blessed One's funeral pyre (citaka) ignited spontaneously; this statement was made because no one was seen making an effort to ignite it. However, by the power of the devas, the pyre ignited from all sides simultaneously.

"Only the bodily remains (relics) were left" means that previously, because it existed as a single solid mass, it was called "sarīraṃ" (the body). Now, because they have dispersed, they are called "sarīrāni" (the bodily remains/relics). It means that the relics remained, which were like jasmine buds, like washed pearls, and like gold. Indeed, the bodies of long-lived Buddhas are a single solid mass like a block of gold. But the Blessed One, [thinking,] "I shall not remain for long before attaining Parinibbāna, and my Dispensation (Sāsana) has not yet spread everywhere; therefore, even after I have attained Parinibbāna, let the great multitude of people, taking even a mustard-seed-sized relic of mine and building a stupa in their respective places of residence to worship, be destined for heaven," made a resolution for the dispersal of the relics. How many of the Blessed One's relics were dispersed, and how many were not dispersed? These seven relics—the four canine teeth, the two collarbones, and the frontal bone (uṇhīsa)—were not dispersed; the rest were dispersed. Among those relics, the smallest relic was about the size of a mustard seed; the medium-sized relic was about the size of a broken grain of rice; and the largest relic was about the size of a broken mung bean.

"Streams of water" means that streams of water, some as thick as an upper arm, some as thick as a lower leg, and some as thick as a palm tree trunk, fell from the sky and extinguished the fire. "Udakasālato" is said in reference to the Sāla trees that stood surrounding [the pyre]; indeed, streams of water also came out from the gaps between the trunks and branches of those trees to extinguish it. The Blessed One's funeral pyre was very large. Even by piercing the earth, circles of water about the size of a plowshare rose up like crystal beads and enveloped the pyre. "Gandhodakena" means with various kinds of scented water brought in golden and silver jars. "Nibbāpesuṃ" means they extinguished the sandalwood pyre by sprinkling it with eight-handled ladles made of gold and silver.

And while this pyre was burning, although flames rose from between the branches, forks, and leaves of the Sāla trees standing around it, there was no such thing as a leaf, a branch, or a flower being burnt. Even ants and spiders [lived] right between the flames...
198:
## Exposition on the Distribution of the Relics

"The King heard"—how did he hear? It is said that at first, the ministers, having heard [of the Buddha's Parinibbāna], thought: "The Teacher has attained Parinibbāna; it is no longer possible to bring him back. In terms of the faith of worldlings (puthujjana), there is no one like our King. If he hears this news in this manner (suddenly), his heart will break. We must protect the King." Thinking thus, they brought three golden troughs, filled them with the four sweet foods (catumadhura), and went to the King, saying: "Great King, we have seen a bad dream. To avert the danger of that dream, you should wear fine dukūla cloth and lie in the trough of catumadhura in such a way that only your nostrils are visible."

Hearing the words of the ministers who sought his welfare, the King agreed, saying, "Let it be so, dear ones," and did as they said. Then, one minister removed his ornaments, disheveled his hair, and facing the direction where the Teacher attained Parinibbāna, raised his hands in salutation and said to the King: "Great King, there is no being who is free from death. That Blessed One, our Teacher, who increased our life, who is the site for stupas, who is like a field of merit, and who is like the pouring of anointing water, has attained Parinibbāna in Kusinārā."

As soon as the King heard this, he lost consciousness and released heat into the catumadhura trough. Then they lifted him and placed him in the second trough. When he regained consciousness, he asked, "Dear ones, what did you say?" "Great King, the Teacher has attained Parinibbāna," they replied again. The King lost consciousness again and released heat into the catumadhura trough. Then they lifted him from there and placed him in the third trough. When he regained consciousness, he asked again, "Dear ones, what did you say?" "Great King, the Teacher has attained Parinibbāna," they replied again. The King lost consciousness once more; then they lifted him, bathed him, and poured water over his head from jars.

When the King regained consciousness, he rose from his seat, disheveled his ruby-colored hair that had been soaked in scented water, and spread it over his back which was the color of a golden plate. Beating his breast with his palms, and clutching his chest—which was the color of a golden image—with his well-rounded fingers that were the color of coral sprouts as if he were stitching it, he descended into the middle of the street wailing like a madman. That King, surrounded by adorned dancers, left the city and went to Jīvaka's Mango Grove, looking at the place where the Blessed One used to sit and preach the Dhamma...
209:
The term 'susira' refers to instruments such as flutes. The term 'ghana' refers to instruments such as cymbals. 'Suvinītassa' means well-played (producing sound) by means of tightening or loosening the strings and so forth. 'Suppaṭitāḷitassa' means well-struck or beaten in order to know the state of remaining within the proper measure. 'Sukusalehi samannāhatassa' means played by those who are skilled and proficient in playing. 'Dhuttā' refers to gamblers who play with dice. 'Soṇḍā' refers to those addicted to liquor. These very people, by the power of wanting to drink repeatedly, are as if thirsty. 'Paricāresunti' means they danced and made merry by moving their hands or feet.

## Description of the Wheel Treasure (Cakkara-tana-vaṇṇanā)

'Sīsaṃ nhātassa' means having bathed the head along with the body with scented water. 'Uposathikassa' means of one who has undertaken the factors of the Uposatha. 'Uparipāsādavaragatassa' means of one who has ascended to the upper part of the noble palace; having consumed excellent food, entered the auspicious chamber on the upper floor of the noble palace, and is reflecting on the precepts (sīla). At that time, it is said that the King, having given a great gift (mahādāna) by relinquishing hundreds of thousands of wealth early in the morning, performed the auspicious head-washing with sixteen pots of scented water, and after eating breakfast, placed a clean upper robe over one shoulder, sat cross-legged on the auspicious couch in the upper palace, and remained reflecting on his collection of merit such as giving (dāna). This is the natural custom (dhammatā) of all Universal Monarchs.

While those kings are reflecting on such merit, due to the aforementioned meritorious actions and seasonal conditions (utu-samuṭṭhāna), the divine Wheel Treasure appears, resembling a mass of blue sapphires, as if breaking through the surface of the eastern ocean, and decorating the sky. That Wheel Treasure appeared to King Mahāsudassana in the same way. This is called 'divine' (dibba) because it is endowed with divine power. Because its spokes are one thousand, it is called 'thousand-spoked' (sahassāra). Because it has a rim and a hub, it is called 'with a rim' (sanemika) and 'with a hub' (sanābhika). Because it is complete in every aspect, it is called 'complete in every aspect' (sabbākārapari-pūra).

In that context, it is called 'Wheel Treasure' (cakkara-tana) because it is a wheel (cakka) and also a treasure (ratana) in the sense of producing delight. As for the hub because of which it is called 'with a hub' (sanābhika), that hub is made of Indanīla (blue sapphire). In the center of that hub, however, there is a tube made of pure silver. That tube shines beautifully as if smiling, like a row of pure, smooth teeth. It is also like the moon's orb with a hole in the middle. On both the inner and outer edges, it is surrounded by silver plates. In suitable places on those silver plates...
210:
...surrounding the hub-tube, the dividing lines and markings are well-distributed and distinct without being blurred. This is the completeness of the hub of that Wheel Treasure in every aspect.

As for the spokes because of which it is called 'thousand-spoked (sahassāra)', those spokes are made of the seven treasures and are endowed with a radiance like sunbeams. On those spokes as well, the dividing lines and markings such as the shapes of water-pots and pearls are well-distributed and distinct. This is the completeness of the spokes of that Wheel Treasure in every aspect.

As for the rim because of which it is called 'with a rim (sanemika)', that rim is made of very red, pure, and smooth coral (pavāḷa), as if mocking the beauty of the rays of the rising sun. At the joints of that rim, circular dividing lines made of red Jambu-gold plates, having a splendor like the glow of twilight, are well-distributed and distinct. This is the completeness of the rim of that Wheel Treasure in every aspect.

On the outer surface of the rim-circle, between every ten spokes, there is a coral rod that is hollow inside like a vein, decorated with small circular holes, and capable of catching the wind. When the wind blows, the sound produced from that coral rod is melodious, enchanting, lovely, and intoxicating, like the sound of a five-fold musical ensemble played by a very skillful person. Above that coral rod is a white umbrella (setacchatta). On both sides of that umbrella, there are two rows of hanging flower garlands. In this way, on the rim-circle beautified by a hundred coral rods carrying a hundred white umbrellas surrounded by two hundred rows of flower garlands, there are two lion-faces (mouths) inside both sides of the hub-tube. From those lion-mouths, two clusters of pearls hang down, about the length of a palmyra trunk, as beautiful as the mass of rays of the full moon, ending in red woolen balls resembling the rising sun, as if mocking the beauty of the flow of the celestial Ganges. Because of those pearl strings rotating in the sky along with the Wheel Treasure, it appears as if three circles are rotating together. This is its absolute completeness in every aspect.

This Wheel Treasure, complete in every aspect, usually appears when people are sitting on seats prepared at their doors and conversing after having their evening meal, and when children are playing at crossroads and such. It beautifies the sky near the tops of forests, neither too high nor too low, and its sound is heard from twelve leagues (yojanas) away...
211:
(That Wheel Treasure) approached the royal capital, delighting the ears of beings with a melodious sound audible from twelve yojanas away, and attracting their eyes with a complexion brilliant with the emergence of various radiances from one yojana away, as if proclaiming the power of the Universal Monarch's merit.

Then, upon merely hearing the sound of that Wheel Treasure, among those people who were looking toward the east with hearts wondering, "From where does this sound come? What object makes this sound?", one man said, "Friends, look at this wonder! Previously, only one full moon rose, but today a second has risen with it. Like a pair of royal swans, this pair of full moons ascends the sky in succession." Another said to him, "Friend, what are you saying? Where have you ever seen two full moons rising together? Is this not the sun risen, possessing golden rays and shimmering beams?" Another laughed and said, "Are you mad? Has the sun not just set? How could that sun rise while following this full moon? Surely, this must be the celestial mansion of a meritorious person, brilliant with the radiance of many jewels." Rebuking them all, others said, "Friends, why do you lament so much? This is neither the full moon, nor the sun, nor a divine mansion. Those moons, suns, and mansions do not possess such splendor and glory. This must surely be the Wheel Treasure."

Even as they were conversing thus, the Wheel Treasure left the lunar orb and headed straight toward them. Then, when asked, "For whom has this appeared?", the answer was given, "For no one else; has our Great King not fulfilled the duties of a Universal Monarch? It is for him that this has appeared." Then that great multitude, and everyone else who saw it, followed the Wheel Treasure. That Wheel Treasure, as if wishing to make known its arrival for the sake of the King, circled the city seven times above the walls, then circled the King's inner palace clockwise, and came to a standstill at a place like the northern lion-window of the inner palace, as if fixed to an axle, so that it could be easily honored with perfumes and flowers.

As it stood thus, the King, seeing the mass of radiance entering through the windows and other openings, illuminating the interior of the palace with the brilliance of various multicolored gems, felt a desire to see it...
212:
The King felt a desire to behold the Wheel Treasure. Then his attendants, bringing the gift of pleasant words, reported the matter to him. Thereupon the King, his body suffused with powerful joy and rapture, released his cross-legged posture, rose from his seat, went near the lion-window, and seeing the Wheel Treasure, thought: "I have heard of this..." and so on. For King Mahāsudassana, everything happened in that very way. Thus it is said: "Having seen it, King Mahāsudassana... (pe)... Am I then a Universal Monarch?"

In that phrase, "Am I then a Universal Monarch?", if one asks to what extent one becomes a Universal Monarch: when the Wheel Treasure rises into the sky and revolves even by the measure of one or two finger-breadths, one is a Universal Monarch. Now, wishing to show the action to be performed to make that Wheel Treasure revolve, he said: "Then, Ānanda," and so forth.

In that passage, "rising from his seat" means getting up from where he was sitting and coming near the Wheel Treasure. "Taking a golden ceremonial vessel" means lifting a golden water-pot with a spout like an elephant's trunk. I shall further explain the words: "King Mahāsudassana followed with the fourfold army." All Universal Monarchs, after sprinkling water and saying, "May the noble Wheel Treasure conquer," the Wheel Treasure immediately ascends into the air and revolves. At the very moment it revolves, that king is called a Universal Monarch. When the Wheel Treasure revolves, the King, following it, mounts the excellent vehicle of a Universal Monarch and ascends into the air. Then his attendants carrying the parasol, yak-tail whisk, and so on, as well as the women of the harem, and then the sub-king, the general, and others, together with their own troops—adorned with various types of well-fitted tunics and armor, brilliant with the radiance of diverse ornaments, and decorated with raised banners and flags—ascend into the air and surround the King.

Those employed in the King's service had drums beaten through the city streets to gather the people, saying: "Friends, the Wheel Treasure has appeared to our King. Assemble, adorned according to your wealth!" The great multitude, having already abandoned all their tasks upon hearing the sound of the Wheel Treasure and having gathered with perfumes and flowers, all ascended into the air and surrounded the King. Indeed, whoever felt the desire to go with the King found themselves already in the sky. Thus, an assembly twelve yojanas in length and breadth was formed. In that assembly, there was not a single person with a deformed body or soiled clothes. A Universal Monarch has a pure retinue. The assembly of a Universal Monarch is like wizards (viddhyādharas) traveling in the sky, or like jewels scattered upon a surface of blue sapphire. Therefore, it is said: "Then King Mahāsudassana..."
213:
In the retinue of that Wheel-turning Monarch, there is no one with physical defects or dirty clothes. This is because the Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti) is surrounded by a pure retinue. The retinue of a Cakkavatti is like wizards (Vijjādharas) traveling in the sky, or like gems scattered upon a surface of sapphire (indanilamaṇi). It was the same for King Mahāsudassana. Therefore, it was said: "King Mahāsudassana followed [the Wheel Treasure] together with his fourfold army."

That Wheel Treasure (Cakkaratana) revolves in the sky at a height that is neither too high nor too low above the treetops. Those who desire the flowers, fruits, and sprouts of the trees are able to take them easily. Those on the ground are also able to identify: "This is the King, this is the Crown Prince, this is the General." Among the postures such as standing, whichever posture a person wishes to travel in, they travel in that very posture. Even those engaged in arts such as painting travel while performing their respective tasks in this aerial journey. Just as all tasks are accomplished on the ground, so too are all their tasks accomplished in the very sky. Thus, carrying the Cakkavatti's retinue, that Wheel Treasure travels to the Eastern Continent (Pubbavideha), which is seven thousand yojanas in extent, passing over the Great Ocean while keeping Mount Sineru on its left.

In that Eastern Continent, there is a pleasant area of land, twelve yojanas in width and thirty-six yojanas in circumference, suitable for the assembly and residence of the retinue, where food and provisions are easily obtainable, which is endowed with shade and water, and which is pure and level. Above that area of land, the Wheel Treasure stands still like a wheel fixed to an axle. Then, by that sign, the multitude of people descend and take up residence, performing all their tasks such as bathing and eating according to their wishes. It was entirely the same for King Mahāsudassana. Therefore, it was said: "Ānanda, in whatever region the Wheel Treasure settles, there King Mahāsudassana takes up residence together with his fourfold army."

When the Cakkavatti thus takes up residence, even if the kings of that region hear that "an enemy army has arrived," they do not assemble their forces or prepare for war. This is because, immediately upon the appearance of the Wheel Treasure, there is no being who would dare to raise a weapon against that King with the thought of him being an enemy. This is the power (ānubhāva) of the Wheel Treasure.
214:
By the power of the Wheel Treasure,
All the enemies of that King come under his discipline;
Because he subdues his enemies, that King of men
Is said to possess that very Wheel.

Therefore, all those kings, taking gifts appropriate to their own royal glory and wealth, approach that Wheel-turning Monarch and, bowing their heads, worship the King's feet with the consecration of the radiance of the crest-jewels on their heads. They address him with words such as "Come, Great King," and ask, "What task shall we perform?" They did the same for King Mahāsudassana. Therefore, it was said: "Ānanda, those in the eastern direction... [said] 'Govern us, Great King.'"

In that context, 'Svāgataṃ' means a good arrival. For when some people arrive, others grieve, and when they leave, others rejoice. When some others arrive, people rejoice, and when they leave, people grieve. A Cakkavatti of such nature causes joy upon arrival and grief upon departure. Therefore, your arrival is called a 'good arrival' (svāgataṃ). When thus addressed, the Wheel-turning Monarch does not say, "Pay me this much annual tax," nor does he seize the wealth of one to give to another. Instead, with wisdom befitting his status as a Righteous King (Dhammarāja), he investigates matters such as killing (pāṇātipāta) and, with a lovely and melodious voice, teaches the Dhamma in this manner: "Look, dear ones, the taking of life, when practiced, developed, and frequently cultivated, leads to hell," and gives advice such as "Life should not be taken." King Mahāsudassana did the same. Therefore, it is said: "King Mahāsudassana said, 'Life should not be taken... enjoy only the wealth you have obtained.'" If it is asked whether all kings accept this advice of the Cakkavatti—even the advice of the Buddha is not accepted by all beings, so how could all accept the advice of a King? Therefore, only the wise who can discern the meaning accept it. However, all become followers. Therefore, it was said: "Ānanda, those who..."

Then, after giving such advice to the inhabitants of the Eastern Continent and having finished the morning meal, that Wheel Treasure, by the power of the Cakkavatti, rises into the air and enters the Eastern Ocean. As it enters, it stills the waves like a Naga king that has smelled the scent of Agada medicine and retracted its hood. It descends about one yojana into the waters of the Great Ocean and stands within the ocean like a wall of beryl (veḷuriya). At that very moment, as if wishing to see the merit and glory of that King, various treasures scattered at the bottom of the Great Ocean emerge from that place and fill the area. Then, the King's retinue, seeing the surface of the Great Ocean filled with various treasures, take as much as they desire in their waist-cloths and so on, and thus the King's retinue obtain great treasures.
215:
Various scattered jewels arriving from various places filled that area. Then, the King's retinue, seeing the floor of the great ocean filled with various jewels, gathered them as they pleased in the folds of their garments and so forth. When the retinue had taken as many jewels as they desired, the Wheel Treasure turned back. As the Wheel Treasure turned back, the retinue was in the front, the King in the middle, and the Wheel Treasure at the very rear. The water of the great ocean followed continuously, striking against the rim of the wheel, as if enticed by the splendor of the Wheel Treasure or as if unable to bear separation from it. In this way, the Wheel-turning Monarch, having conquered Pubbavideha bounded by the eastern ocean, proceeded toward the southern ocean along the path shown by the Wheel Treasure, desiring to conquer Jambudīpa bounded by the southern ocean. King Mahāsudassana also proceeded in the same manner. Therefore, it is said: "Then, Ānanda, the Wheel Treasure, having plunged into the eastern ocean and emerged, rolled on towards the southern direction."

The manner of the rolling of the Wheel Treasure as it proceeded, the encamping of the troops, the coming of rival kings to pay homage, the giving of instructions to them, the plunging into the southern ocean, the receding of the ocean water, and the taking of jewels—all should be understood in the same manner as previously described.

Having conquered Jambudīpa, which is ten thousand yojanas in extent, and emerging from the southern ocean, he went according to the previous method to conquer Aparagoyāna, which is seven thousand yojanas in extent, and conquered that island bounded by the ocean in the same way. Then, emerging from the western ocean, he went in the same manner to conquer Uttarakuru, which is eight thousand yojanas in extent, and having conquered that island bounded by the ocean, he emerged from the northern ocean.

By this extent, the Wheel-turning Monarch attained sovereignty over the entire earth bounded by the four oceans. Having thus achieved successive victories, the Wheel-turning Monarch, in order to display the splendor of his royal majesty, flew up into the sky with his retinue. Looking down upon the four great continents, each surrounded by five hundred small islands, which appeared like four natural lakes (Jātassara) adorned with beautifully blooming red, blue, and white lotuses, [he returned] by the path shown by the Wheel Treasure...
216: He returns to his royal capital in due order by the path indicated by the Wheel-treasure. Then, that Wheel-treasure remains as if beautifying the palace gate. When that Wheel-treasure is thus established, there is no need for torches or lamps within the royal palace; the radiance of the Wheel-treasure alone dispels the darkness of the night. For those who desire darkness, however, there is only darkness. For King Mahāsudassana, all this happened in the same way. Therefore, it is said: "Having descended into the southern ocean... etc... such a Wheel-treasure appeared." ## Commentary on the Elephant-treasure To the Wheel-turning Monarch for whom the Wheel-treasure has thus appeared, the ministers have the usual auspicious elephant stable prepared so that the ground is level and clean. Having had it smeared with fragrant perfumes such as red sandalwood, they scatter beautiful and fragrant flowers below. Above, they prepare a canopy like a divine mansion, adorned with delightful garlands of flowers interspersed with golden stars. They then say, "O King, please contemplate the arrival of such an Elephant-treasure." That Wheel-turning Monarch, having given great gifts and undertaken the precepts as previously mentioned, sits reflecting on the perfection of that merit. Then, urged by the power of his merit, a noble elephant—wishing to enjoy that exceptional honor—comes from either the Chaddanta lineage or the Uposatha lineage and stands in that place. It has a pure white body adorned with feet, neck, and mouth as red as the rising sun. It stands on seven points touching the ground, with well-proportioned limbs. It has a beautiful trunk like a blooming red lotus. Possessing psychic power, it is capable of traveling through the air like a yogi. It is like a silver mountain with edges tinged with red arsenic powder. If it comes from the Chaddanta lineage, the youngest elephant comes. If it comes from the Uposatha lineage, the eldest elephant comes. In the Pāḷi text, however, it only appears as "Uposatha, the king of elephants." The commentaries state that since the Chaddanta king of elephants is not to be used by anyone, the youngest from the Chaddanta lineage comes. That noble elephant comes while the Wheel-turning Monarchs, who fulfill the duties of a Wheel-turning Monarch, are contemplating in the manner described. For King Mahāsudassana, it came to the usual auspicious elephant stable of its own accord, displaced the existing elephant, and stood there. Therefore, it is said: "Again, Ānanda... etc... the king of elephants."
217:
Upon seeing the Elephant Treasure that had appeared in this way, the elephant keepers and others were overjoyed and went quickly to inform the King. The King also arrived in haste, and upon seeing the Elephant Treasure, his heart was filled with clarity. Thinking, "Friends, this elephant vehicle is truly excellent; if only it could be tamed," he extended his hand. Then, the elephant, like a domestic calf, lowered its ears and approached the King, showing a gentle and docile manner. The King desired to mount the elephant. Knowing the King's wish, his attendants adorned the Elephant Treasure with golden banners, golden ornaments, and covered it with a golden net, then brought it near. Without making the elephant kneel, the King ascended by a ladder made of the seven kinds of jewels, his mind intent on traveling through the sky. As soon as the King's thought arose, that king of elephants, like a king of swans, leaped into the dark blue sky which shone with the brilliance of sapphires. Just as described regarding the movement of the Wheel Treasure, the entire royal retinue followed. Thus, the King, together with his retinue, traveled around the entire earth and returned to the capital within the time of the morning meal. In this way, the Elephant Treasure of a Universal Monarch possesses great psychic power. For King Mahāsudassana as well, there was such an Elephant Treasure. Therefore, it is said: "Having seen... the King... appeared."

## Explanation of the Horse Treasure

After the Elephant Treasure had appeared in this way, the ministers of the Universal Monarch prepared and adorned the natural auspicious horse stable to be clean and level. Following the previous method, they exerted effort to make the King think of the Horse Treasure. The King, having performed acts of giving, honoring, and worshiping as before, and having undertaken the moral precepts, reflected repeatedly on the fulfillment of his merit while sitting comfortably atop the palace. Then, prompted by the power of the King's merit, the king of horses named Valāhaka, capable of traveling through the sky, arrived and stood in that auspicious horse stable. He was of the Sindhu breed, as glorious as a mass of white clouds in the autumn season entwined with streaks of lightning, with red feet and a red muzzle. His body was pure, smooth, and solid like a mass of moonlight. Because his head was black like a crow's neck or a sapphire, he was called "Kāḷasīsa" (Black-headed). Because his mane was fine, round, and straight like Muñja grass, as if well-groomed, he was called "Muñjakesa" (Muñja-haired). For King Mahāsudassana, this horse arrived just like the Elephant Treasure. All the rest...
218:
...should be understood in the same manner as described for the Elephant Treasure. Regarding such a Horse Treasure, the Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Ānanda..." and so on.

## Explanation of the Jewel Treasure

After the Horse Treasure had appeared in this way, the Jewel Treasure arrived from Mount Vepulla for the Universal Monarch. It was four cubits in length and had a circumference like the hub of a chariot wheel. It was adorned at both ends with two golden lotuses and very pure strings of pearls emerging from the edges of the pericarp. It was surrounded by eighty-four thousand attendant gems and spread its glory like the full moon surrounded by a host of stars. When that Jewel Treasure arrived, it was placed in a pearl net and raised into the sky to a height of about sixty cubits by a succession of bamboo poles. During the night, its radiance spread over an area of one league all around. By that radiance, the entire area became illuminated as if it were the time of dawn. Then, farmers performed their plowing, merchants opened their shops, and various artisans carried out their respective works, thinking, "It is daytime." For King Mahāsudassana as well, all of that happened in the same way. Therefore, it was said: "Furthermore, Ānanda... the Jewel Treasure appeared."

## Explanation of the Queen Treasure

After the Jewel Treasure had appeared in this way, the Queen Treasure, who is the cause of the excellence of the Universal Monarch's special sensual pleasures, appeared. They brought a chief queen for him from the Madda royal family, or she arrived of her own accord from the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru) due to the power of merit. Her remaining accomplishments are mentioned in the Pāḷi text itself in this manner: "Furthermore, Ānanda, for King Mahāsudassana, the Queen Treasure appeared, beautiful, lovely..." and so on.

In that Pāḷi, "Abhirūpā" means having extraordinary beauty due to the perfection of her physical form. "Dassanīyā" means lovely, because she pleases the eyes just by being seen, such that one should behold her even by setting aside other distractions. "Pāsādikā" means graceful, because she clarifies the mind through the power of joy just by being seen. "Paramāyā" means supreme, because she brings about such inspiration. "Vaṇṇapokkharatāya" means endowed with beauty of complexion. "Samannāgatā" means possessed of. Alternatively, she is "Abhirūpā" because she is neither too tall nor too short. She is "Dassanīyā" because she is neither too thin nor too fat.
219:
She is inspiring (pāsādika) because she is neither too dark nor too fair. She is endowed with the supreme beauty of complexion because she has surpassed the human appearance but has not yet reached the divine appearance. For the radiance of humans does not emanate outward, but the radiance of deities emanates even to a very great distance.

The radiance of that queen's body illuminates an area of about twelve cubits. Among the descriptions such as 'not too tall,' the first pair describes her perfection in height, the second pair her perfection in girth, and the third pair her perfection in complexion. Alternatively, these six terms indicate the absence of physical defects, while the phrase 'surpassing the human appearance' indicates physical perfection. 'Silk-cotton or cotton' refers to the softness like silk-cotton or cotton that has been beaten a hundred times and soaked in clarified butter. 'When it is cold' means when it is the cold season for the King. 'When it is hot' means when it is the hot season for the King. 'Scent of sandalwood' means the fragrance of yellow sandalwood, well-ground, fresh, and mixed with the four types of perfumes, wafts from her body at all times. 'Scent of lotus wafts' means that at the time of laughing or speaking, the extremely fragrant scent of a blue lotus, as if just blossomed at that moment, wafts from her mouth.

To show the conduct appropriate to the physical perfection of the queen, who is thus endowed with the perfection of form, touch, and scent, the passage beginning with 'Taṃ kho pana' is stated. In that regard, she is one who rises first (pubbuṭṭhāyinī) because, upon seeing the King, she rises from her seat first like one burnt by fire. She is one who retires later (pacchānipātinī) because she performs duties such as fanning with a palmyra fan while the King is seated and only then sleeps or sits. She is one who is obedient (kiṃkārapaṭissāvinī) because she asks with her voice, 'O Lord, what shall I do?' She is one who acts pleasingly (manāpacārinī) because she practices and performs only what is pleasing to the King. She is one who speaks endearingly (piyavādinī) because she speaks only what is dear to the King.

Now, to show that this conduct of the queen is due only to the purity of her disposition and not through deceit, the passage beginning with 'Taṃ kho pana' is spoken. Therein, 'no aticarī' means she did not commit adultery; it means she did not desire another man even in her mind, setting aside the King.

The qualities mentioned at the beginning of the queen's description, such as 'beautiful' (abhirūpā), and those at the end, such as 'rising first' (pubbuṭṭhāyinī), are her natural qualities. However, the qualities such as 'surpassing the human appearance' should be understood as having arisen through the power of past meritorious deeds, starting from the appearance of the Wheel-treasure, depending on the merit of the Universal Monarch.
220:
Alternatively, qualities such as exceeding beauty also become fully perfected in every aspect from the time the Wheel-treasure appears. Therefore, it is said: 'Such a Queen-treasure appeared.'

## Explanation of the Householder-treasure
For the Universal Monarch to whom the Queen-treasure has thus appeared, the Householder-treasure appears so that the infinite tasks involving wealth may be carried out comfortably. This householder is naturally very wealthy and born into a very wealthy family. He is a treasurer-householder who increases the King's accumulation of wealth. To that Householder-treasure, a divine-like eye arises due to the result of kamma, accompanied by the power of the Wheel-treasure, by which he sees treasure-pots within the earth up to a distance of one yojana. Seeing that abundance of wealth, he, with a joyful mind, goes and invites the King with wealth, fulfilling all tasks to be done with wealth. He fulfilled them in the same way for King Mahāsudassana. Therefore, it is said: 'Furthermore, Ānanda... such a Householder-treasure appeared.'

## Explanation of the Counselor-treasure
For the Universal Monarch to whom the Householder-treasure has thus appeared, the Counselor-treasure appears, who is capable of managing all affairs. That Counselor-treasure is indeed the King's eldest son. He is naturally wise, learned, sagacious, and capable of clearly explaining to others the meanings he understands. Depending on the power of the King's merit, the knowledge of others' minds (paracittañāṇa) arises in him due to the power of his own past kamma. By that knowledge, he is able to know the mental behavior of the King's retinue within twelve yojanas and to determine what is beneficial or harmful to the King. That eldest son, too, seeing that power of his own, with a joyful heart, invites the King by offering counsel in all state affairs. He invited King Mahāsudassana in the same way. Therefore, it is said: 'Furthermore... the Counselor-treasure appeared.'

In that Pali, 'thapetabbaṃ thapetuṃ' means to appoint those who should be appointed to various respective positions.

## Explanation of the Endowment with the Four Psychic Powers
'Samavepākiniyā' means having the quality of digesting food evenly. 'Gahaṇiyā' refers to the fire element (tejo-dhātu) born of kamma. Regarding that digestion, for whom the food is digested as soon as it is eaten, for whom...
221:
Otherwise, the food eaten remains in the stomach like a bundle of rice. Neither of these two is endowed with the digestive fire element born of kamma (kammaja-tejo-dhātu) that digests food evenly. For whoever has the desire to eat arise again at the next mealtime, only he is endowed with the digestive fire element born of kamma that digests food evenly.

## Explanation of the Dhamma Palace and the Lotus Ponds

"Māpesi kho" means that it was not a creation made by having a drum beaten in the city and gathering a crowd of people. Rather, as soon as the King's thought arose, eighty-four thousand lotus ponds appeared, splitting the earth. It is in reference to these ponds that appeared according to the King's wish that this was said. "Dvīhi vedikāhi" means being surrounded by one railing (vedikā) at the edge of the bricks, and by another railing at the outer boundary of the precinct. Why did "Etadahosi" (this thought occurred) happen? It is said that one day, the Great Man (King Mahāsudassana), seeing the great multitude of people coming and going after bathing and drinking, thought: "These people are going about like madmen. If they had flowers to wear, it would be good." Then, this thought occurred to the King. In that thought, "Sabbotukaṃ" means that flowers usually bloom only in one season. I, however, will make them bloom in all seasons. "Ropāpesi" (he caused to be planted) does not mean he had various lotus seeds and so on brought from various places and planted; rather, everything was accomplished as soon as the King's thought arose. Because the people thought the King had planted them, it is said "ropāpesi." From then on, the great multitude of people went about wearing various kinds of water-born and land-born flowers, as if playing at a constellation festival.

Then the King, wishing to make the people even more happy, planned for the welfare of the people, saying, "What if I, at the banks of these lotus ponds..." and so on, and did everything. There, "nhāpesuṃ" means that one person rubbed the body, another prepared scented powders, another fetched water for the person bathing on the bank, and another received and gave clothes.

How did he "Paṭṭhapesi kho" (establish)? He had suitable ornaments made for women and men, and placed women there for a short time to provide service, while placing all the remaining food and drinks for the purpose of charity, and had a drum beaten, saying, "King Mahāsudassana gives these gifts; enjoy these offerings." The great multitude of people, having come to the banks of the ponds, bathed, changed clothes, anointed themselves with various scents, and wore various beautiful flowers.
222:
Going to the place of almsgiving, among the many kinds of congee, rice, and hard food, and the eight kinds of drinks, whatever food or drink a person desired, they ate and drank that. Then, wearing delicate linen clothes of various colors from the Khome region, they enjoyed prosperity. Those who already possessed such items left them behind and went away. Those who did not possess them took them and went away. Even with elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, and so on, after riding and wandering for a while, those who did not want them left them behind and went away, while those who wanted them took them and went away. After sleeping on noble beds and enjoying prosperity, those who did not want them left them behind and went away, while those who wanted them took them and went away. Even after enjoying prosperity with women, those who did not want them left them behind and went away, while those who wanted them took them and went away. Even after adorning themselves with the seven kinds of jewels and enjoying prosperity, those who did not want them left them behind and went away, while those who wanted them took them and went away. That almsgiving was also given repeatedly and continuously. The inhabitants of Jambudīpa had no other work; they just wandered about enjoying the King's alms.

Then the Brahmins and householders thought: "Even though this King is giving such alms, he does not have us bring anything like rice or milk. Even if the King does not have us bring anything, it is not proper for us to remain silent." They collected much wealth and offered it to the King. Therefore, it was said: "Then, Ānanda, the Brahmins and householders," and so on. Why did they plan together equally? From some people's houses, a little was brought; from others, much was brought. If that collected wealth were to be redistributed, disputes might arise, such as: "Is only what came from your house good, and not what came from mine? Is only what came from your house much, and not what came from mine?" To prevent such sounds of quarreling from arising, they planned together equally in this way.

"Come, friend" means "Come, friend/companion." He gave the command by assigning the name "Dhamma" to the palace. Vissakamma, the celestial architect, asked, "O King, how large should the palace be?" When told, "Let it be one league in length and half a league in width, and let it be made entirely of all kinds of jewels," he replied, "So be it, your word is excellent," and after accepting the command from the King of Dhamma, King Mahāsudassana, he created it. In that context, "Ānanda, this is good for you" means the intended meaning is "Ānanda, this is good for you." "Having accepted" means accepting and speaking. By remaining silent...
223:
Thinking, "There will be an opportunity for me to practice the Dhamma of a recluse," he accepted by remaining silent. 'Sāramaya' means made of the heartwood of sandalwood. In the phrase "with two railings (vedikā)," one railing was at the top of the pinnacle of that palace, and one railing was above the lower boundary.

"It was difficult to look at" means 'du-uddikkha'; it means difficult to look at because of the perfection of its radiance. 'Musati' means it attracts (the eyes), it causes them to flutter, and it does not allow them to remain still. 'Viddhe' means pierced and high, or distant due to the absence of clouds. 'Deve' means in the sky.

"He created" does not mean he caused them to be created by saying, "I will create a pond in this place; destroy your houses." Rather, by the mere arising of a thought, the ground of that king split open and such a pond appeared. "Satisfied them with all sensual pleasures" means he satisfied them with all desired objects; the recluses with the requisites of a recluse, and the Brahmins with the requisites of a Brahmin.

## The Commentary on the First Recitation Section is finished.

## Commentary on the Attainment of Jhana

"Mahiddhika" means possessing great psychic power, being endowed with the great power known as the production of eighty-four thousand ponds by the mere arising of a thought. "Mahānubhāva" means being endowed with great majesty because of the greatness of those very fruits to be experienced. 'Seyyathidaṃ' is an indeclinable; its meaning is "which three?" 'Dāna' means the relinquishing of perfect gifts. 'Dama' means that although wisdom is called 'dama' in the Āḷavaka Sutta, in this context, it refers to the Uposatha practice performed by one who restrains himself. 'Saṃyama' means virtue (sīla).

## Commentary on the Bodhisatta's Past Connection

Standing here, the past effort (pubbayoga) of that king should be understood. In detail: Formerly, the king was born into a householder's family. At that time, during the dispensation of the living Kassapa Buddha, an Elder lived in the forest. The Bodhisatta...
224:
Entering the forest on his own business, the Bodhisatta saw the Elder, approached him, paid homage, and after looking at the Elder's dwelling place and walking path, asked: "Venerable sir, does the noble one live here?" Hearing the reply, "Yes, lay follower," he thought, "It is proper to build a leaf-hut for the noble one here." Abandoning his own business, he cut timber and other building materials, built a leaf-hut, roofed it, plastered the walls with fine clay, fitted a door, and made a wooden floor. Then, thinking, "Will the noble one use it or not?" he sat to one side.

The Elder returned from the village, entered the hut, and sat on the wooden floor. The lay follower also came, paid homage, and sitting nearby, asked: "Venerable sir, is the leaf-hut comfortable to live in?" "Lay follower, it is pleasant to live in and suitable for a recluse," the Elder replied. When asked, "Venerable sir, will you reside in this hut?" the Elder said, "Yes, lay follower." Knowing by the Elder's manner of acceptance that he would reside there, the Bodhisatta made him promise, "Please come to my house door regularly," and then said, "Venerable sir, please grant me a boon." "Lay follower, recluses have transcended boons," the Elder replied. "Venerable sir, please grant a boon that is allowable and blameless." The Elder said, "Speak, lay follower."

"Venerable sir, in a place where one resides regularly, people desire the noble one's presence on both auspicious and inauspicious occasions; they get angry when he does not come. Therefore, even if you go to another place where you are invited, please enter my house first to complete your meal," the Bodhisatta requested, and the Elder accepted.

The Bodhisatta spread a mat in the leaf-hut, arranged a couch and a stool, placed a headrest, and a footstool. He dug a pond, made a walking path, and scattered sand. Seeing deer coming to rub against the walls and causing clods of earth to fall, he surrounded it with a thorn fence. Seeing deer entering the pond and making the water muddy, he lined the inside with stones, surrounded the outside with a thorn fence, and planted rows of palm trees along the edge of the fence. Seeing deer disturbing the smooth ground of the great walking path, he also surrounded the path with a fence and planted rows of palm trees along the edge. Having thus completed the monastery, he offered the Elder the three robes, alms-food, medicine, water pots for drinking and washing, an awl for piercing needle-eyes, a small razor, a nail cutter, a needle, a walking stick, sandals, a water gourd, an umbrella, a lamp stand, an ear-pick, a water strainer, a dhammakaraka (water filter), an alms-bowl, a cup, and all other items used by recluses. There was no requisite that the Bodhisatta had not offered to the Elder. That Bodhisatta, observing the precepts and performing the Uposatha...
225:
He served the Elder for the rest of his life. The Elder, residing in that very monastery, attained the fruit of Arahatship and passed into Parinibbāna.

The Bodhisatta, having performed meritorious deeds until the end of his life, was reborn in the celestial realm. Passing away from there and coming to the human world, he was reborn in the royal city of Kusāvatī and became King Mahāsudassana.

“Even if the merit performed in this Dispensation is not very great,
It yields great results; therefore, a wise person should perform such merit.”

“Mahāviyūha” refers to a great peaked mansion (pāsāda) made of silver. Desiring to dwell there, he went to it. Regarding “this much of sensual thought,” it means he stopped the three types of thoughts at the door of the peaked mansion, saying, “Sensual thought, you must retreat and stop at this point; beyond this is not your place. This is called the House of Jhana; this is not a place for dwelling with you.”

In the passages starting with the first Jhana, there is no separate task of preliminary work (parikamma) for the kasinas. When there is a need for the blue kasina, he sees a blue gem; for the yellow kasina, gold; for the red kasina, a red gem; and for the white kasina, silver. In every place he looks, the kasina itself becomes manifest.

Everything that should be said regarding the passages starting with “accompanied by loving-kindness” has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga. Thus, in the Pali text, only the four Jhanas and the four Boundless States (appamaññā) are taught. However, the Great Being, having attained all eight meditative attainments and the five superknowledges, enters the attainments in fourteen ways, such as in forward and reverse order. He dwells sustained by the bliss of attainment, just as a king bee entering a honeycomb is sustained by the taste of honey.

## Explanation of the Eighty-four Thousand Cities and Others

“Kusāvatīrāja-dhānippamukhāni” means that the royal city of Kusāvatī is the chief and most excellent among those cities. “Bhattābhihāro” refers to the food (alms-food) that is to be brought.
226:
Why did he think “Vassasatassa vassasatassa” (every hundred years)? He thought so because he was weary of the sound of those elephants. For it is said, “Sound is a thorn to one who has entered a meditative attainment.” Therefore, the Great Man, being weary of the sound, had this thought. If he was weary of the sound, why did he not say, “Do not come”? He did not say it because he thought, “These eighty-four thousand elephants will think, ‘Now we can no longer see the King,’ and thus lose their regular duty. Let that loss of duty not happen to those elephants.”

## Explanation of Queen Subhaddā’s Approach

Regarding “This thought occurred,” when did it occur? It occurred on the day the King passed away. At that time, it is said the deities thought, “Let the King not die a helpless death; let him die surrounded by his harem, many daughters, and sons.” Then, influencing the Queen, they caused such a thought to arise in her. “Golden-colored clothes” refers to those clothes which naturally please the King’s mind. Therefore, she said, “Put on those clothes.” “Queen, stand right there” means, “Queen, this so-called House of Jhana (jhānāgāra) is not a place for dwelling with you; it is only a place for me to experience the bliss of Jhana. Do not enter here.”

Regarding “This thought occurred,” it is the nature of beings in the world to shine very brightly when death is near. Therefore, seeing the King’s exceptionally clear faculties, this thought occurred to her. Then, not wishing for the King to die, she thought, “I will speak of the King’s virtues and act in a way to make him remain,” and she said, “Great King, these are your possessions,” and so on. In that speech, “Arouse desire” means to arouse love and find delight. “Regard for life” means to have regard, attachment, and craving for life.

In the phrase “Queen, you... to me thus,” the meaning is: When the Queen, thinking “This is a monk,” said to the King, “Great King, we women do not know the proper way to address and speak to monks; how should we speak?”, the King replied, “Queen, speak to me in this way,” and so on. “Censured” means censured by Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, disciples, and other wise and learned persons. For what reason? Because dying with attachment to life is a cause for being reborn in one's own house as a yakkha, a dog, a goat, an ox, a buffalo, a mouse, a chicken, a louse, or a bedbug.
227:
Then, Ānanda, Queen Subhaddā wiped away her tears means that the queen went to a suitable place, wept and lamented, and then, having wiped her tears, spoke these words.

## Description of Reaching the Brahma Realm

Why is it said "or of a householder"? It is because they possess great wealth and heritage, like Soṇa, the merchant's son, and others. It is said that a single bowl of rice for Soṇa, the merchant's son, was worth two hundred thousand. Thus, for those who eat such food, there is a momentary intoxication with food, stupor from food, and exhaustion from food.

"At that time, in whichever city he lived" means that the city where he resided was only one. In the remaining cities, sons, daughters, and servants lived. The same applies to palaces and gabled houses. Among thrones and such, he used only one throne; the rest were for the use of his sons and others. Among women, only one attended to him; the rest were merely attendants. "I wear" means I wear only one pair of garments; the rest are for the sixteen hundred thousand men, plus eighty thousand more, who follow in his train. "I eat" means I eat at most only a measure of rice (a nāḷi) as the supreme limit; the rest is for the eight hundred thousand men, plus forty thousand more, who follow in his train. Indeed, a pot of cooked rice is sufficient for ten people.

Those eighty-four thousand cities, eighty-four thousand palaces, and eighty-four thousand gabled houses arose as the result of the gift of a single leaf-roofed hut. The eighty-four thousand thrones arose as the result of the gift of a couch for reclining. The eighty-four thousand elephants, horses, and chariots arose as the result of the gift of a stool for sitting. The eighty-four thousand gems arose as the result of the gift of a single lamp. The eighty-four thousand lotus ponds arose as the result of the gift of a single pond. The eighty-four thousand women, eighty-four thousand sons, and eighty-four thousand householders arose as the result of the gift of utility pots, alms-bowls, cups, water-strainers (dhammakaraṇa), filters, needles, needle-cases, hooks, nail-cutters, ear-picks, footstools, sandals, umbrellas, and walking sticks. The eighty-four thousand cows arose as the result of the gift of milk and dairy products. The eighty-four thousand crores of garments arose as the result of the gift of clothing for wearing and wrapping...
228:
(Continued from the previous page) ...arose. The eighty-four thousand pots of cooked rice should be understood to have arisen as the result of the gift of the five kinds of food.

Thus, the Blessed One, having preached in detail the prosperity of King Mahāsudassana from the beginning, and wishing to show all that prosperity as being like children playing at building houses with dust, spoke while lying on his deathbed: "Look, Ānanda," and so forth. In that context, "vipariṇatā" (transformed) means they have reached a state where they can no longer be designated, like a lamp that has gone out by abandoning its natural state. "Ānanda, thus indeed are formations impermanent" means they are called impermanent because of their nature of non-existence after having come into being.

By this sequence of teaching, the Blessed One—just as a man might bind a ladder to a Champaka tree a hundred cubits high, climb it, pluck a Champaka flower, and then descend by letting go of the ladder—similarly, as if binding a ladder (of craving for prosperity), he ascended to the prosperity of King Mahāsudassana, which was many hundreds of thousands of crores of years high, and then, taking the characteristic of impermanence that stands at the peak of prosperity, he descended as if letting go of the ladder. For that very reason (showing prosperity at the beginning and impermanence at the end), in ancient times, King Vasabha, while listening to the words of the Elders who were reciters of the Dīgha Nikāya (Dīgha-bhāṇaka) reciting this Mahāsudassana Sutta at the young mango grove on the eastern side of the Brazen Palace (Lohapāsāda), thought: "Friends, what has my grandfather (the Buddha) preached in this Sutta? He speaks only of prosperity in the place where he himself ate and drank." But when the Buddha preached, "Ānanda, thus indeed are formations impermanent," the King, with a joyful heart, gave a cry of "Sādhu! Sādhu!", saying, "Friends, having seen this matter, the Buddha, who possesses the five kinds of eyes, has preached thus," while bending his left arm and striking it with his right hand.

"Addhuvā" means they are devoid of stability, like water bubbles and such. "Anassāsikā" means they provide no solace, like water drunk in a dream or like sandalwood paste applied to the body. "Sarīraṃ nikkhipeyya" means one should discard the body. Now, he says, "Ānanda, for the Tathāgata, since defilements have been eradicated, there is no more laying down or nurturing of another body." Having said this, he addressed the Elder again: "The power of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) disappears on the seventh day after the king has gone forth (renounced). But in the case of King Mahāsudassana, on the seventh day after his death, the seven-gemmed walls, the seven-gemmed palm trees, the eighty-four thousand lotus ponds, the Dhamma Palace, the Dhamma Pond, and the Wheel Treasure—all these structures disappeared." Regarding elephants and such, this is the natural law: those whose lifespan is exhausted die together (with the king).
229: If life still remains, the Elephant-treasure goes to the Uposatha elephant lineage, the Horse-treasure goes to the Valāhaka horse lineage, and the Gem-treasure goes only to Mount Vepulla. The power of the Woman-treasure disappears. The eyes of the Householder-treasure become just ordinary. The ability of the Counselor-treasure vanishes. "The Blessed One said this" means that the Blessed One spoke everything, both what is included in the Pāḷi text and what is not. The remaining words have clear meanings. ## The Commentary on the Mahāsudassana Sutta is finished.
230: ## 5. Commentary on the Janavasabha Sutta ## Commentary on the Explanation of Nātika, etc. 273-275. "Thus have I heard" and so forth is the Janavasabha Sutta. In that sutta, the explanation of obscure terms is as follows: "Parito parito janapadesu" means in the surrounding districts. "Paricārake" refers to those who attend upon the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. "Upapattīsu" means in the occurrences of knowledge, destiny, and merit. "Kāsikosalesu" means in the Kāsī and Kosala regions, in the kingdoms of Kāsī and Kosala. This method is the same in all places. However, in the six kingdoms of Aṅga, Magadha, Yonaka, Kamboja, Assaka, and Avanti, the Blessed One did not make a declaration. Among these sixteen great nations, he made declarations only in the first ten. "Nātikiya" refers to the inhabitants of Nātika village. "Tena" means by way of being a Non-returner and so forth. Having heard the Blessed One's answer to the questions, which he declared after discerning with his omniscient knowledge, they reached a final conclusion regarding their status as Non-returners and so forth, and were delighted by that status. In the Commentary, however, "tena" is said to mean "te Nātikiya" (those people of Nātika). In this sense, the syllable "na" is merely a particle. ## Commentary on Ānanda’s Discussion "Bhagavantaṃ kittayamānarūpo" means praising thus: "Oh, the Buddha! Oh, the Dhamma! Oh, the Saṅgha! Oh, the Dhamma is well-expounded!" and he passed away while thus praising. "Bahujano pasīdeyya" means: "Our father, mother, brother, sister, son, daughter, and friends used to eat and sleep together with us; we did pleasant things for them; they are said to be Non-returners, Once-returners, and Stream-enterers. Oh, how good! Oh, how excellent!" In this way, many people would gain confidence. "Gatiṃ" refers to the occurrence of knowledge. "Abhisamparāyaṃ" refers to the future life to be attained through knowledge. He saw two million four hundred thousand people.
231:
"Upasantapadisso" means having a peaceful vision. "Bhātiriva" means he shines exceedingly, he appears exceedingly beautiful. "Indriyānaṃ" refers to the faculties, with the mind (mano) as the sixth. By the words "Ānanda, I have seen," he meant that he saw not just ten, twenty, a hundred, or a thousand, but exactly two million four hundred thousand (2,400,000) people.

## Commentary on the Janavasabha Yakkha

Seeing that "so many people have been liberated from suffering depending on me," great joy (somanassa) arose; his mind became clear. Because the mind was clear, the blood produced by the mind became clear. Because the blood was clear, the faculties, with the mind as the sixth, became clear. After saying all this, he spoke the words beginning with "Atha kho Ānandā."

In that context, because that deity (deva) became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) after hearing the Blessed One's Dhamma discourse and became the leader of one hundred and ten thousand (110,000) people, the name "Janavasabha" (Lord of Men) arose for him.

"Ito sattā" means passing away from this deva world seven times. "Tato sattā" means passing away from that human world seven times. "Saṃsārāni catuddasa" means throughout the entire sequence of fourteen aggregates (rounds of rebirth). "Nivāsamabhijānāmi" means knowing the previous dwellings by way of rebirth. "Yattha me vusitaṃ pure" means: "In those deva worlds where I lived as a companion of King Vessavaṇa, and in the human worlds where I lived as a king, I have lived before this present existence."

Because of having lived thus before, and now being a Stream-enterer having performed much merit in the Triple Gem, although he is capable of being reborn in higher deva worlds by the power of that merit, he was reborn right here (in the Cātumahārājika realm) due to strong attachment (nikanti) to the place where he lived for a long time.

By the words "Āsā ca pana me santiṭṭhati," he shows that he did not spend his time heedlessly or sleeping just because he was a Stream-enterer. Rather, he had begun insight (vipassanā) to attain the path of Once-returning (Sakadāgāmi-magga). He shows that he lives with effort, thinking, "Today, even today, I shall penetrate [the higher path]."

"Yadagge" refers to the day he first saw the Blessed One at the Laṭṭhivana (Palm Grove) garden and became a Stream-enterer. "Venerable Sir, from that day on, I know that for a long time I have been free from falling into states of woe (avinipāta)" means that starting from that day, he knows he is free from falling into states of woe in the fourteen previous existences; he knows the nature of non-falling (avinipāta-dhamma) attained by the power of the Path of Stream-entry at the Laṭṭhivana garden.
232:
"Anacchariya" means repeated wonder (anu-acchariya). Seeing the Blessed One on the road while traveling for some business is a wonder even when contemplated repeatedly. It is also a wonder to hear in person from the Great King Vessavaṇa words that are identical to what the Blessed One had seen. "Two reasons" refers to the fact of seeing [the Buddha] on the road and the desire to report what was heard in the presence of Vessavaṇa.

## Description of the Assembly of Devas

Regarding "they assemble," why do they assemble? It is said they assemble for four reasons: to support monks entering the rains retreat, to support monks performing the pavāraṇā ceremony, to listen to the Dhamma, and to enjoy playing near the Pāricchattaka tree. Among these four, on the full moon day of Āsāḷhī, which is said to be "tomorrow the rains retreat begins," the devas assemble in the Sudhammā assembly hall and deliberate: "In such-and-such a monastery, one monk has entered the rains retreat; in such-and-such a monastery, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, or a thousand monks have entered the rains retreat. In these various places, provide well-arranged protection for the venerable ones." In this way, support for the monks entering the rains retreat is provided.

At that time also, they assembled for this very reason. "This is their seat" means this is the seat of the Four Great Kings. Only after these Great Kings have sat down does our seat come to be.

"For which purpose" means for the purpose of supporting those entering the rains retreat. "Thinking of that purpose and deliberating on that purpose" means thinking of the protection of the Saṅgha of monks who usually dwell in the forest, and deliberating with the Four Great Kings, saying, "In these various places, arrange protection for the Saṅgha of monks who have completed the rains retreat."
