"There are spoken words" means the thirty-three deities speak, and the Great Kings are those to whom the words are spoken. Likewise, the thirty-three deities advise, and the others are those who have been advised. In both phrases, the word "taṃ" is merely a particle. "Avipakkantā" means they have not departed (they remain present).

"Uḷāra" means extensive or great. "Divine splendor" (devānubhāva) refers to the radiance of the clothes, ornaments, mansions, and bodies of all deities, which extends for twelve yojanas. However, the bodily radiance of those with great merit extends for a hundred yojanas. Surpassing that divine splendor...

"That preliminary sign of Brahmā" means that just as the rising of the dawn is the precursor and preliminary sign of the sunrise, so too the natural appearance of Brahmā is the preliminary sign of his arrival. "Anabhisambhavanīyo" means unattainable (unbearable). The Tāvatiṃsa devas [cannot endure] that natural appearance of Brahmā...
233:
Just as the rising of the dawn is the precursor and preliminary sign of the sunrise, so too it is shown that when Brahmā is about to arrive, this radiance is the preliminary sign of Brahmā.

## Description of the Talk of Sanaṅkumāra

"Anabhisambhavanīyo" means unattainable; the meaning is that the Tāvatiṃsa devas cannot see that natural appearance of Brahmā. "Cakkhupathasmiṃ" means either in the sensitivity of the eye (cakkhu-pasāda) or in the field of vision. It means that the natural appearance of Brahmā does not come into the range of the devas' eye sensitivity; it does not become an object of their experience. Indeed, devas of lower realms can only see the forms created by devas of higher realms by making them gross (oḷārika). "Vedapaṭilābhaṃ" means obtaining delight. "Adhunābhisitto rajjena" means one who has recently been anointed in kingship. This meaning of a recently anointed king's delight is illustrated by the story of King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī Abhaya.

It is said that after conquering thirty-two Damiḷa kings and receiving his anointment in the city of Anurādhapura, King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī was so filled with joy and happiness that he could not sleep for a whole month. Then he informed the Saṅgha of monks, saying, "Venerable sirs, I cannot sleep." The Saṅgha said, "Great King, if that is so, undertake the Uposatha today." So the king undertook the Uposatha. The Saṅgha went and sent eight monks who were masters of the Abhidhamma, saying, "Recite the Cittayamaka." They went and said, "Great King, please lie down," and began the recitation. While listening to the recitation, the king fell into a sleep. The elders said, "Do not wake the king," and departed. On the second day, the king woke up at sunrise and, not seeing the elders, asked, "Where are the venerable ones?" They replied, "They left after knowing you had fallen asleep." The king said, "Friends, there is no such thing as a medicine unknown to the sons of my grandfather, the Buddha; they even know the medicine for sleep."

"Pañcasikho" means becoming like the Gandhabba Pañcasikha. It is said that all the deities cherish the form of the Gandhabba deity Pañcasikha. Therefore, Brahmā also manifested by creating such a form. "Pallaṅkena nisīdi" means he sat down after folding his legs cross-legged.

"Vissaṭṭho" means a voice that is well-released from defects, not oppressed by bile or phlegm. "Viññeyyo" means a voice that makes the meaning understood. "Mañjū" means a voice that is sweet and soft. "Savanīyo" means a voice that is worthy of being heard and pleasant to the ear.
234:
"Bindu" means being compact. "Avissārī" means being very clear and not scattered. "Gambhīro" means arising from a deep place, starting from the base of the navel, and not arising merely from the impact of the tongue, teeth, lips, and palate. Indeed, a sound arising in such a [superficial] way is not sweet and does not carry far. "Ninnādī" means being resonant, like the sound of a great rain cloud or a drum. Furthermore, in this context, it should be understood that each subsequent word is simply the meaning of the preceding word. "Yathāparisaṃ" means making the sound known only to as many people as there are in the assembly. His voice resonates only within the assembly and does not spread outside. The words beginning with "Ye hi keci" are spoken to show that he practiced for the benefit of many people. The words "Saraṇaṃ gatā" do not refer to those who have taken refuge in any ordinary way, but specifically to those who have taken refuge with a mind free from doubt. "Gandhabbakāyaṃ paripūrenti" means filling the host of Gandhabba deities. Thus, it means that from the time our Teacher, the Blessed One, appeared in the world, the six deva worlds and so on have been filled without gaps, like a tube filled with pounded flour or like a forest of reeds or rushes.

## Commentary on the Development of the Bases of Power

"Yāva supaññattā ca ime tena bhagavatā" means "these have been very well-formulated and well-expounded by that Blessed One, my Teacher." In this term "Iddhipāda," it should be understood that it is called "Iddhi" in the sense of completion or success, and "Pāda" in the sense of being a foundation. "Iddhipahutāya" is because of the ability to perform miracles. "Iddhivisavitāya" is because of being suitable and appropriate for performing miracles. It means having mastery (vasībhāva) through repeated practice. "Iddhivikubbanatāya" is because of the state of performing various transformations of power, for the purpose of demonstrating them in various ways. In the phrases such as "Chanda-samādhi-padhāna-saṅkhāra-samannāgataṃ," concentration that has desire as its cause or concentration where desire is predominant is called "Chanda-samādhi." This is a designation for the concentration obtained by making the desire to act (kattukamyatā-chanda) the predominant factor. Volitional formations that are primary are "Padhāna-saṅkhāra." This is a designation for the right effort (sammappadhāna-vīriya) that accomplishes the four tasks. "Samannāgataṃ" means being endowed with both concentration due to desire and volitional formations of effort. "Iddhipādaṃ" refers to the collection of the remaining mental states and consciousness which serve as the foundation (pāda) for desire, concentration, and volitional formations of effort associated with the direct-knowledge mind, which are reckoned as "Iddhi" either in the sense of completion through the method of accomplishment, or by the method that "by this, beings are successful, prosperous, and reach excellence." For this was said in the Vibhaṅga: "The base of power (iddhipāda) is the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of volitional formations, and the aggregate of consciousness of one who is such."
235:
In this manner, the meaning should be understood in the remaining cases as well. Just as the concentration obtained by making desire the predominant factor is called "Chanda-samādhi," so too the concentration obtained by making energy, consciousness, or investigation the predominant factor is called "Vīmaṃsā-samādhi" (and so on). In another way, access concentration (upacāra-jhāna) is the base (pāda), and the first absorption (jhāna) is the success (iddhi). The first absorption together with its access is the base, and the second absorption is the success. Thus, the meaning of "Iddhipāda" should be understood as the preceding part being the base and the subsequent part being the success. The discussion on the bases of power (iddhipāda-kathā) has been stated in detail in the Visuddhimagga and the Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā.

However, some teachers say, "Iddhi is (paramattha-wise) accomplished, while Iddhipāda is not yet accomplished." To refute their view, the section called "Uttara-cūḷika-vāra" is brought forward in the Abhidhamma: "There are four bases of power: the base of power consisting of desire, the base of power consisting of energy, the base of power consisting of consciousness, and the base of power consisting of investigation. Therein, what is the base of power consisting of desire? Here, a monk, at the time he develops supramundane jhāna which is leading out, leading to the undoing [of rebirth], for the abandoning of views, for the attainment of the first stage, secluded from sensual pleasures, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is painful practice with slow intuition. Whatever desire, state of desiring, desire to act, or wholesome desire for the Dhamma there is at that time—this is called the base of power consisting of desire. The remaining states are the states associated with the base of power consisting of desire" (from the Vibhaṅga). These states are presented only in terms of the supramundane. Among those four, the Elder Raṭṭhapāla produced the supramundane state by making desire the leader. The Elder Soṇa by making energy the leader, the Elder Sambhūta by making consciousness the leader, and the Venerable Mogharāja by making investigation the leader.

The parable for these four individuals is as follows: Among four sons of ministers who lived depending on the king, desiring a high position, one son, having a strong desire for service and knowing the king's intention and preference, served day and night, pleased the king, and attained a high position. Just as he attained the high position by making desire the leader, so should one who produces the supramundane state by making desire the leader be understood.

Another son of a minister thought, "Who can serve every single day? When a matter of importance arises, I will please the king through my effort." When a rebellion occurred in a frontier region, he was sent by the king, and by exerting effort, he crushed the enemy and attained a high position. Just as he attained the high position by making energy the leader, so should one who produces the supramundane state by making energy the leader be understood.
236:
One son of a minister thought, "Attending [the king] day after day is a burden, as is shielding oneself from spears and arrows with one's chest; I shall please the king through the power of counsel." Because he was well-practiced in the art of knowing the battlefield (khattavijjā), he pleased the king through the arrangement of counsel and attained a distinguished rank. Just like that minister's son, Ven. Sambhūta should be understood as one who brings about the supramundane Dhamma by making the mind the chief factor.

Another son of a minister thought, "What is the use of such attendance and so on? Kings usually grant distinguished ranks to those of noble birth; if they give to such persons, they will give to me as well." Relying solely on the excellence of his birth, he attained a distinguished rank. Just like that minister's son, Ven. Mogharāja should be understood as one who brings about the supramundane Dhamma by making wisdom the chief factor, relying on extremely purified wisdom.

'Anekavihita' means having many kinds. 'Iddhividha' means the portions of psychic power.

## Explanation of the Threefold Attainment of Opportunity

'Sukhasādhigamāya' means for the sake of attaining the bliss of Jhana, the bliss of the Path, and the bliss of Fruition. 'Saṃsaṭṭha' means [living] with an associated mind. 'Ariyadhamma' means the Dhamma taught by the Noble Buddha. 'Suṇāti' means hearing what is taught either in the presence of the Blessed One or by monks, nuns, and so forth. 'Yoniso manasikaroti' means reflecting by way of means, by way of the path, and by way of cause, as "impermanent" and so on. It is said: "What is called wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) is attention by way of means, attention by way of the path; it is the turning of the mind, the repeated turning, the application, the focused attention, and the reflection upon the impermanent as impermanent, the painful as painful, the non-self as non-self, the foul as foul, or in accordance with the Four Noble Truths." This means that one exerts effort in such wise attention as described. 'Asaṃsaṭṭha' means living unmixed with either objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) or defilement-based sensuality (kilesa-kāma). 'Uppajjati sukhaṃ' means the arising of the bliss of the first Jhana. 'Sukhā bhiyyo somanassaṃ' means the successive joy that arises for one who has emerged from the attainment, based on the bliss of Jhana. 'Pamudā' means weak rapture which is merely the aspect of being pleased. 'Pāmojja' means stronger rapture and joy. 'Paṭhamo okāsādhigamo' (the first attainment of opportunity) is so called because the first Jhana stands having displaced the five hindrances and taken its own opportunity.
237:
Regarding the word "Oḷārika" (gross), let bodily formations (kāya-saṅkhāra) and verbal formations (vacī-saṅkhāra) be gross first; but why are mental formations (citta-saṅkhāra) gross? Because they have not yet been abandoned. In detail, bodily formations are abandoned by the fourth Jhana, verbal formations by the second Jhana, and mental formations by the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). Thus, even when bodily and verbal formations are abandoned, those mental formations still remain; therefore, in comparison to what has been abandoned, they are called gross because they are not yet abandoned. "Sukha" refers to the bliss of the fruition attainment associated with the fourth Jhana that arises for one emerging from the attainment of cessation. "Sukhā bhiyyo somanassaṃ" refers to the successive joy and gladness for one who has emerged from the fruition attainment. "Dutiyo okāsādhigamo" (the second attainment of opportunity) is so called because the fourth Jhana stands having displaced pleasure and pain and taken its own opportunity. In this context, when the fourth Jhana is taken, the second and third Jhanas are already included, which is why they are not mentioned separately.

In the words "Idaṃ kusalaṃ" and so forth, "wholesome" (kusala) refers to the ten wholesome courses of action. "Unwholesome" (akusala) refers to the ten unwholesome courses of action. The dyad of blameworthy (sāvajjaduka) and so forth should also be understood by way of these wholesome and unwholesome states. All these states are called "kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāga" because they are dark (kaṇha), bright (sukka), and have counterparts (sappaṭibhāga). Nibbāna alone is "appaṭibhāga," having no counterpart. "Avijjā pahīyati" means the abandoning of ignorance that conceals the round of rebirth. "Vijjā uppajjati" means the arising of the knowledge associated with the path of Arahantship. "Sukha" refers to both the bliss of the path of Arahantship and the bliss of fruition. "Sukhā bhiyyo somanassaṃ" refers to the successive joy and gladness for one who has emerged from the fruition attainment. "Tatiyo okāsādhigamo" (the third attainment of opportunity) is so called because the path of Arahantship stands having displaced all defilements and taken its own opportunity. The remaining paths are included within that path of Arahantship, which is why they are not mentioned separately.

These three attainments of opportunity should be explained in detail by way of the thirty-eight meditation objects. How? By defining all objects by way of access (upacāra) and absorption (appanā) as stated in the Visuddhimagga, the first Jhana in twenty-four places is called the "first attainment of opportunity." The second and third Jhanas in thirteen places, and the fourth Jhana in fifteen places, having reached the attainment of cessation, are called the "second attainment of opportunity." The ten access concentrations, which are the proximate cause for the path, belong to the third attainment of opportunity. Furthermore, among the three trainings, the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) belongs to the first attainment of opportunity, the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā) to the second, and the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā) to the third; thus it should also be explained by way of the trainings. In the Sāmaññaphala Sutta as well, from the minor section on virtue (cūḷasīla) up to the first Jhana is the first...
238:
The attainment of opportunity (okāsādhigama) is also spoken of by way of the Sāmaññaphala Sutta as follows: the second attainment of opportunity is from the second jhāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; the third attainment of opportunity is from insight (vipassanā) up to the fruit of arahantship. Furthermore, it is also spoken of by way of the Piṭakas: the Vinaya Piṭaka belongs to the first attainment of opportunity, the Suttanta Piṭaka to the second, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka to the third.

It is said that in ancient times, the Great Elders would begin reciting this very sutta on the day of entering the rains retreat (vassa) with the intention: "We shall have the opportunity to preach by analyzing the three Piṭakas." It cannot be said that one who preaches by combining and comparing the three Piṭakas has preached poorly. This sutta, when preached by leading others to resort to the three Piṭakas, is indeed well-preached.

## Commentary on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness

'For the attainment of the wholesome' (kusalassādhigamāya) means for the sake of attaining the wholesome of the Path and the wholesome of the Fruit. Both of these are called 'wholesome' (kusala) because they are blameless (anavajja) and because they are secure (khema). In that teaching on the foundations of mindfulness, 'he is well-concentrated' (sammāsamādhiyati) means he has a well-placed mind, a one-pointed mind, within his own internal body. 'He produces the knowledge and vision of external bodies' (bahiddhā parakāye ñāṇadassanaṃ abhinibbatteti) means he directs insight-knowledge from his own body towards the bodies of others. This method applies to all terms. In all instances, the word 'mindful' (satimā) refers to the mindfulness that grasps the body and so forth. By the word 'world' (loko), the body and so forth that are grasped are themselves the world. It should be understood that these four foundations of mindfulness are preached as a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.

## Commentary on the Seven Requisites of Concentration

In the term 'requisites of concentration' (samādhiparikkhāra), there are three types of requisites (parikkhāra). In the passage, "The chariot has virtue as its ornament (parikkhāra), jhāna as its axle, and energy as its wheels" (SN 5.4), 'parikkhāra' means ornament. In the passage, "It is well-protected by the seven city-requisites (parikkhāra)" (AN 7.67), 'parikkhāra' means surroundings or fortifications. In the passage, "Medicinal requisites (parikkhāra) for the support of the sick," 'parikkhāra' means equipment or necessities. In this context, however, 'seven requisites of concentration' is spoken of by way of 'surrounding requisites.' 'Equipped' (parikkhata) means surrounded. 'This is called the Noble Right Concentration' means that just as a Wheel-turning Monarch is surrounded by seven treasures, so too, by the seven factors...
239:
Concentration surrounded (by the seven factors) is called "Noble Right Concentration." "Saupanisa" is also called "saupanissaya" (with its prerequisites); it means being together with its retinue. "Sammādiṭṭhissa" means for one established in Right View. "Sammāsaṅkappo pahoti" means Right Intention arises. This method should be understood for all terms. 

This meaning should be understood by way of the Path and by way of the Fruit. How? For one established in the Path of Right View, the Path of Right Intention arises... [pe]... for one established in the Path of Knowledge, the Path of Liberation arises. Likewise, for one established in the Fruit of Right View, the Fruit of Right Intention arises... [pe]... for one established in the Fruit of Knowledge, the Fruit of Liberation arises.

Terms such as "Svākkhāto" have already been explained in the Visuddhimagga. "Apārutā" means opened. "Amatassa" means of Nibbāna. "Dvārā" means the Paths which are the ways of entry. "Aveccappasādena" means with unshakeable confidence. "Dhammavinītā" means those who have emerged by the Path that leads well out of the cycle of suffering.

The phrase "Atthāyaṃ itarā pajā" is said with reference to Non-returners (Anāgāmīs); it means that there are also Non-returners. "Puṇyabhāgā" means those who are born from a portion of merit. "Ottappaṃ" means being possessed of moral dread. By that statement, he shows: "I am unable to count because I fear telling a lie; it is not that I lack the power to count."

By the words "Taṃ kiṃ maññati bhavaṃ," he is merely questioning King Vessavaṇa; that deity does not hold the view that such a Teacher never existed or will not exist. This is because there is no difference in the realization (abhisamaya) of all Buddhas.

"Sayaṃparisāyaṃ" means in one's own assembly. "Tayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ" means that entire holy life consisting of the Three Trainings. The remaining words are clear. These words were placed by the Elders who were the Reciters of the Dhamma (Dhammasaṅgāhaka).

## The Commentary on the Janavasabha Sutta is finished.
240:
## 6. Commentary on the Mahāgovinda Sutta

This sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Mahāgovinda Sutta. In this sutta, the explanation of the obscure terms is as follows: "Pañcasikho" refers to one who has five crests, or five locks of hair hanging down behind. It is said that when this celestial youth Pañcasikha was performing meritorious deeds in the human world, he was the chief cowherd while still a young boy with five locks of hair. He led other boys in performing various meritorious deeds such as building rest houses at the junctions of four roads outside the village, digging lotus ponds, constructing bridges, leveling uneven roads, and removing trees that obstructed the axles of carts. He passed away while still a youth. That individual existence (attabhāva) of the boy was desirable, lovely, and pleasing. After passing away, he was reborn in the realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājikā) with a lifespan of nine million years. The physical form of that celestial youth Pañcasikha was three gāvutas in height and resembled a block of gold. He adorned himself with ornaments equivalent to a thousand cartloads, anointed himself with perfumes amounting to nine jars (kumbhas), wore divine red garments, donned a diadem made of red gold, and wandered about with the five locks of hair on his back, just like the appearance of a young boy with five crests. Therefore, he is known only as "Pañcasikha."

"Abhikkantāya rattiyā" means when the first watch of the night has ended, or when a portion of the night has passed. "Abhikkantavaṇṇo" means one who has a complexion that is exceedingly desirable, lovely, and pleasing. Indeed, although that celestial youth was naturally of a pleasing complexion, he became one of surpassing beauty because he arrived fully adorned. "Kevalakappaṃ" means entirely, from all around without remainder. Here, the word "kevala" has the sense of being without remainder, as in the term "kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ." The word "kappa" has the sense of "all around," as in "kevalakappaṃ jetavanaṃ" and so on. "Obhāsetvā" means having suffused with his own radiance, making a single spread of light and brilliance like the moon or the sun.

## Description of the Assembly of Devas

"Sudhammāyaṃ sabhāyaṃ" means in the assembly hall named Sudhammā, which arose from the merit of donating a jeweled pinnacle made of wood by a woman named Sudhammā. It is said that the floor of that Sudhammā celestial assembly hall was made of crystal, and the other parts were made of rubies.
241:
The pillars are made of gold. The pillar-bases and joints are made of silver. The figures of wild animals are made of coral. The rafters, the roof-ridges, and the circular rims are made of the seven kinds of gems. The roof is covered with sapphire bricks, the roof-throne is made of gold, and the pinnacle is made of silver. It is three hundred yojanas in length and width, nine hundred yojanas in circumference, and five hundred yojanas in height. In such a Sudhammā assembly hall.

Regarding the words "Dhataraṭṭho" and so on: Dhataraṭṭha, the king of the gandhabbas, surrounded by a hundred thousand million gandhabba deities, having them hold a hundred thousand million golden shields and golden swords, sits in the eastern direction facing west, placing the deities from the two deva realms in front of him.

Virūḷhaka, the king of the kumbhaṇḍas, surrounded by a hundred thousand million kumbhaṇḍa deities, having them hold a hundred thousand million silver shields and golden swords, sits in the southern direction facing north, placing the deities from the two deva realms in front of him.

Virūpakkha, the king of the nāgas, surrounded by a hundred thousand million nāgas, having them hold a hundred thousand million large ruby shields and golden swords, sits in the western direction facing east, placing the deities from the two deva realms in front of him.

Vessavaṇa, the king of the yakkhas, surrounded by a hundred thousand million yakkhas, having them hold a hundred thousand million large coral shields and golden swords, sits in the northern direction facing south, placing the deities from the two deva realms in front of him. This is how it should be understood.

"Then there is a seat for us" means that the opportunity for us to sit arises behind those four great kings. Beyond that, they do not get the chance to enter or to see. The reason for the assembly here is the same fourfold reason mentioned previously. Among those four, the gathering related to the commencement of the rainy season (vassūpanāyika) has been explained in detail. Just as they assemble and consult on the day of entering the rains, so too on the full moon day of the Great Pavāraṇā, they assemble and consult, saying, "Where shall we go today, and in whose presence shall we perform the Pavāraṇā?" Among those deities, Sakka, the lord of the devas, usually performs the Pavāraṇā at the Piyangu-dīpa Mahāvihāra. The remaining deities...
242:
The devas take divine flowers such as the Pāricchattaka (coral tree) flowers and divine sandalwood powder, go to their respective favorite places, and perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony. Thus, they assemble for the sake of mutual hospitality through Pavāraṇā.

In the deva world, there is a creeper named Āsāvatī. Expecting that this creeper will bloom, the devas go to attend to it for a thousand years. However, when the Pāricchattaka tree blooms, they go to attend to it for a whole year. These devas are delighted from the time the leaves of that coral tree turn pale. As the Blessed One said: "Monks, at the time when the Pāricchattaka Kovīḷāra tree of the Tāvatimsa devas has pale leaves, at that time, monks, the Tāvatimsa devas are delighted, thinking: 'The Pāricchattaka Kovīḷāra tree now has pale leaves; before long, the leaves will fall.' Monks, at the time when the Pāricchattaka Kovīḷāra tree of the Tāvatimsa devas has fallen leaves, it produces shoots, it produces lattice-like buds, it produces flower-buds, it produces blossoms. At that time, monks, the Tāvatimsa devas are delighted, thinking: 'The Pāricchattaka Kovīḷāra tree now has blossoms; before long, it will be in full bloom.' Monks, the radiance of the Pāricchattaka Kovīḷāra tree in full bloom spreads for fifty yojanas all around, and its scent travels one hundred yojanas downwind. Such is the power of the Pāricchattaka Kovīḷāra tree."

When the Pāricchattaka tree blooms, there is no need to climb to pick the flowers, nor to use a hook to bend the branches, nor to use a basket to collect them. The 'cutting wind' (kantanaka-vāta) blows and severs the flowers from their stems. The 'receiving wind' (sampaṭicchanaka-vāta) catches them. The 'bringing wind' (pavesanaka-vāta) brings them into the Sudhammā assembly hall. The 'sweeping wind' (sammajjanaka-vāta) removes the old flowers. The 'spreading wind' (santharaṇaka-vāta) spreads the petals, pericarps, and stamens as if they were dancing. In the center is the Dhamma seat. There is a jeweled throne one yojana in size, over which a white umbrella three yojanas in size is held. Near that jeweled throne is the seat of Sakka,
243:
the King of Devas, which is prepared. Then, the seats for the thirty-three devas are arranged, and then for other powerful deities. For other obscure deities, the flower pericarps themselves serve as seats.

The devas enter the assembly hall and sit down. Then, pollen rises from the flowers, hits the flower-pericarp above, and falls, making the devas' bodies, which are three gāvutas in height, appear as if they were elegantly adorned with lac-dye. This play of theirs comes to an end after four months. Thus, they assemble to enjoy the play with the Pāricchattaka flowers.

For eight days every month, the great preaching of Dhamma is proclaimed in the deva world. In the Sudhammā assembly hall of that deva world, either Sanankumāra Mahābrahmā, or Sakka the King of Devas, or a monk who is a Dhamma-preacher, or another deva who is a Dhamma-preacher, delivers a Dhamma discourse. On the eighth day of the fortnight, the ministers of the Four Great Kings; on the fourteenth day, the sons of the Great Kings; and on the fifteenth day, the Four Great Kings themselves go forth, taking golden plates and cinnabar, and wander through the villages, market towns, and royal capitals. They record on the golden plates with cinnabar: "Such a woman or man has gone to the Buddha for refuge, has gone to the Dhamma for refuge, has gone to the Saṅgha for refuge. They observe the five precepts. They keep the Uposatha eight days a month. They fulfill the duty of attending to their mother. They fulfill the duty of attending to their father. In such a place, an offering was made with a hundred handfuls of lotuses and flower-pots. A thousand lamps were lit as an offering. They listened to the Dhamma at an unusual time. They donated turned pillars for the umbrella of a stupa, for the surrounding stupas, and for the stupa enclosure, as well as a lion throne and a lion-staircase. They fulfill the three types of good conduct. They undertake and practice the ten wholesome courses of action." Having recorded this, they bring it and place it in the hands of the deva Pañcasikha. Pañcasikha places it in the hands of Mātali. Mātali, the charioteer, places it in the hands of Sakka, the King of Devas.

When those who perform meritorious deeds are not many, the record is small. Seeing that it is small, the devas are displeased, saying: "Alas, the people live heedlessly; the four woeful states will be filled, and the six deva worlds will be empty." But if the record is large, seeing that large golden plate, the devas [rejoice], saying: "Alas, the people truly live heedfully; the four woeful states will be empty..."
244: If the gold plate is large, just by seeing that gold plate, the deities rejoice, saying: "Friends, the multitude of humans are indeed living mindfully. The four woeful planes will be emptied. The six deva realms will be filled. We shall have the opportunity to celebrate the festival of the stars, placing at the forefront the highly meritorious deities who have arrived after performing meritorious deeds in the Buddha's Dispensation." Sakka, the king of devas, takes that manuscript and reads it. The voice of that Sakka, speaking in his natural tone, spreads for twelve yojanas. When speaking with a loud voice, it remains covering the entire city of devas, ten thousand yojanas in extent. Thus they assemble to hear the Dhamma. Here, however, it should be understood that they have assembled for the sake of the Pavāraṇā gathering. "Tathāgataṃ namassantā" means venerating the Tathāgata through nine reasons. "Dhammassa ca sudhammataṃ" means the excellent nature of the Dhamma, which is endowed with special qualities such as being well-expounded (svākkhāta). "Saṅghassa ca suppaṭipattiṃ" means the good practice of the Saṅgha, consisting of various aspects such as practicing uprightly (ujuppaṭipanna) (while venerating them). ## Aṭṭhayathābhuccavaṇṇanā "Yathābhucce" means according to what is true, according to nature. "Vaṇṇe" means virtues or qualities. "Payirudāhāsī" means he spoke or uttered. Regarding "Bahujanahitāya paṭipanno" (He practiced for the benefit of the many), how did he practice? Even while making the aspiration for Buddhahood at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha, having combined the eight factors, he is said to have practiced for the benefit of the many. While fulfilling these ten perfections—the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramī), the perfection of virtue (sīla-pāramī), the perfection of renunciation (nekkhamma-pāramī), the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramī), the perfection of energy (viriya-pāramī), the perfection of patience (khanti-pāramī), the perfection of truthfulness (sacca-pāramī), the perfection of resolution (adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī), the perfection of loving-kindness (mettā-pāramī), and the perfection of equanimity (upekkhā-pāramī)—for four incalculable periods and a hundred thousand aeons, he was indeed practicing for the benefit of the many. When he was the ascetic Khantivādī, the prince Cūḷadhammapāla, the elephant king Chaddanta, the naga kings Bhūridatta, Campeyya, and Saṅkhapāla, and the monkey king Mahākapi, while performing such difficult deeds, he was indeed practicing for the benefit of the many. While existing in the life of King Vessantara, giving the great gift of seven hundred and shaking the earth in seven places, reaching the pinnacle of perfections, he was indeed practicing for the benefit of the many. Thereafter, while staying for the full lifespan in the immediate next existence in the Tusita heaven, he was indeed practicing for the benefit of the many. In that deva realm, having seen the five omens and being requested by the deities and Brahmas from ten thousand world-systems, having conducted the five great investigations and giving his word to support the deities and Brahmas...
245:
While passing away from the Tusita heaven and taking conception in his mother's womb, he was indeed practicing for the benefit of the many.

While dwelling in his mother's womb for ten months and being born from the womb in the Lumbinī grove; while living in the household life for twenty-nine years and then departing in the Great Renunciation to become a monk on the banks of the Anomā River; while exhausting himself through striving for six years and then ascending the Bodhi seat to penetrate Omniscient Wisdom; while spending the seven weeks at the site of enlightenment; while going to the Isipatana Deer Park to turn the peerless Wheel of Dhamma; while performing the Twin Miracle; while descending from the deva world; while remaining for forty-five rains retreats after becoming a Buddha; while relinquishing the life-force; and while attaining Parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu) between the twin Sāla trees—he was indeed practicing for the benefit of the many. It should be understood that as long as his relics, even the size of a mustard seed, remain, he is practicing for the benefit of the many. The remaining terms are merely synonyms of this "Bahujanahitāya". Among those terms, each subsequent term is the meaning of the preceding one.

"Not seen in the past, nor seen now" means that in the past, no person other than the Buddha was seen; in the future, none will be seen; and as for the present, because there is no other Teacher (Buddha), no one other than that Blessed One is seen. In the Commentary, it is also stated: "Past and future Buddhas are just like our Teacher; what is Sakka saying?" After investigating, it says: "At present, there is no other Teacher practicing for the benefit of the many except for our Teacher; therefore, he says he does not see [another]." Just as it is understood here, the same meaning should be understood in the subsequent terms. Terms like "Svākkhāta" and "Kusala" have the meanings already mentioned.

"The water of the Ganges and the water of the Yamuna" means that at the confluence of the Ganges and Yamuna, the waters merge and become one in color, scent, and taste; they become identical like a sheet of gold in the middle, not distinct as when merging with the water of the great ocean. The practice for the pure Nibbāna is also pure. It is not possible to see Nibbāna in old age after practicing medicine and the like in one's youth and wandering in improper places. The practice leading to Nibbāna is like the sky and must be pure. Just as the moon and sun traveling in the sky are unattached and pure in whatever place they desire, the practice of a monk going to Nibbāna must be like the sky, without attachment or bondage to families or groups. The Blessed One prescribed and taught that practice. Therefore, it is said that Nibbāna and the practice are in harmony. "Paṭipannānaṃ" refers to those established in the practice. "Sitānaṃ" refers to those who have utilized the practice of the Path. "Etesaṃ laddhasahāyā" means those Sekhas and Arahants are called companions (sahāya) because they tend to be together with the Blessed One in various tasks. However, the phrase "Dutiyo asahāyo appaṭisamo" (A secondless, companionless, peerless one) is said in terms of being without an equal. It means there is no second person, no equal companion, and no comparable individual. "Apakkantā" means that although he dwells among those Sekhas and Arahants through the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), he dwells mentally withdrawn, striving for and delighting in solitude. "Abhinipphanno kho panassa bhagavatā attho" means...
246:
A practice that is unattached, unbonded, and like the sky is appropriate. The Blessed One has prescribed, spoken, and taught only such a practice. Therefore, it is said: "Nibbāna and the practice are compatible." "Paṭipannānaṃ" refers to those established in the practice. "Vusitavatāṃ" refers to those who have completed the practice of the noble path. "Laddhasahāyo" means that these Sekhas and Arahants are called "companions" (sahāya) because they act together with the Blessed One in various matters. The phrase "adutiyo asahāyo appaṭisamo" is spoken in the sense of being peerless. It means there is no second person, no equal companion, and no rival. "Apanujja" means that even in their midst, He dwells in the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), withdrawing with His mind and repeatedly devoting Himself to solitary delight. Great gains arose for that Blessed One. From when did they arise? They arose from the time He attained omniscience, passed the seven weeks, turned the Wheel of Dhamma at Isipatana, gradually disciplined devas and humans, ordained the three Jaṭila brothers, went to Rājagaha, and disciplined King Bimbisāra. Referring to the great gains and honor that arose from the time He disciplined King Bimbisāra, it is said: "At that time, the Blessed One was honored, revered, respected, worshipped, and esteemed, and He was a recipient of the four requisites: robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick." The gains and honor, arising from the overflowing merit accumulated over four incalculable periods and a hundred thousand aeons, came flooding in like a great torrent.

Once, in the cities of Rājagaha, Sāvatthī, Sāketa, Kosambī, and Vārāṇasī, almsfood in succession (paṭipāṭibhatta) arose for the Blessed One. At that time, one person wrote a notice and hung it at the monastery gate, saying, "I will give alms by spending a hundred." Another wrote two hundred, another five hundred, another a thousand, another two thousand, another five, ten, twenty, fifty thousand, another a hundred thousand, and another two hundred thousand. Even when He was wandering through the countryside, the multitude followed Him with carts filled with goods, waiting for an opportunity to give alms. As it is said: "At that time, the people of the countryside followed behind the Blessed One with carts loaded with much salt, oil, rice, and hard food, thinking, 'Wherever we get a turn, there we will provide almsfood.'" Thus, many stories found in the Vinaya Mahāvagga and elsewhere should be understood. In the Incomparable Alms-giving (Asadisa-dāna), these gains reached their peak. Once, when the Blessed One arrived at Jetavana after wandering through the countryside, King Pasenadi of Kosala invited Him and gave alms. The next day, the citizens gave alms. Then the King gave more than them, and the citizens gave more than the King. After many days had passed in this way, the King thought, "These citizens perform more excellent alms-giving day by day. If I, the lord of the earth, am defeated by the citizens in giving alms, it will be a cause for reproach." He also thought, "Thus will the citizens' criticism be." Then Queen Mallikā gave him a suggestion on how to give alms in a way the citizens could not match. The King [built] a pavilion with Sal-wood planks in the palace courtyard...
247:
...thinking, "We shall get our turn, and there we will provide almsfood," they followed behind the Blessed One with carts loaded with provisions. Thus, many stories found in the Khandhakas and the Vinaya should be understood.

In the Incomparable Alms-giving (Asadisa-dāna), however, these gains reached their peak. Once, when the Blessed One arrived at Jetavana after wandering through the countryside, King Pasenadi of Kosala invited Him and gave alms. On the second day, the citizens gave alms. Then the King gave more than them, and the citizens gave more than the King. After many days had passed in this way, the King thought, "These citizens perform more excellent alms-giving day by day. If I, the lord of the earth, am defeated by the citizens in giving alms, it will be a cause for reproach." Then Queen Mallikā gave him a suggestion.

The King had a pavilion built with Sal-wood planks in the palace courtyard, covered it with blue lotuses, and had five hundred seats prepared. He placed five hundred elephants behind the seats and had each elephant hold a white umbrella over each monk. Between every two seats, a princess adorned with all ornaments ground the four types of perfume. As each perfume was finished, she placed it in a perfume casket in the center, and another princess stirred it with a bunch of blue lotuses. Thus, each monk was attended by three princesses. Another adorned woman held a palm-leaf fan and fanned them; another took a water filter (dhamakaraṇa) and filtered the water; another brought water from the bowl.

For the Blessed One, there were four invaluable items: a foot-scrubber (pādakathalikā), a bowl-stand (ādhāraka), a leaning board (apassenaphalaka), and a jewel at the base of the umbrella (chattapādamaṇī). Even the gift given to the most junior monk (saṅghanavaka) was worth a hundred thousand. In that alms-giving ceremony, Elder Aṅgulimāla was the most junior monk. The elephant brought near the Elder's seat did not dare to approach him. When they reported this to the King, he asked, "Is there no other elephant?" They replied, "There is only a fierce elephant, and it is not easy to bring him." The Blessed One asked, "Great King, who is the most junior monk?" "It is Elder Aṅgulimāla, Bhante," he replied. "In that case, Great King, adorn that fierce elephant and bring him," He said. They adorned the elephant and brought him. Due to the Elder's power, that elephant did not even dare to blow air from its trunk. In this way, alms were given continuously for seven days. On the seventh day, the King paid homage to the Blessed One and said, "Bhante, please preach the Dhamma to me."
248:
In that assembly, there were two ministers named Kāḷa and Juṇha. The minister Kāḷa thought: "The wealth of the royal family is being destroyed. What will all these people do? After eating, they will just go to the monastery and sleep. If a royal servant received this wealth, what could he not achieve? Alas, the King's wealth is being wasted." However, the minister Juṇha thought: "This kingship is truly great. Who else would be able to give such an offering? How can one be called a king if, while established in kingship, he is unable to give such an alms?"

When the Blessed One looked into the inclinations of the assembly, He knew the thoughts of those two ministers and reflected: "If I were to preach the Dhamma today according to Juṇha's inclination, Kāḷa's head would split into seven pieces. I have fulfilled the perfections out of compassion for all beings. Juṇha will penetrate the paths and fruits on another day when I preach the Dhamma. For now, I will look upon Kāḷa with compassion." Thus, He spoke only this four-line verse to the King:

"The stingy indeed do not go to the celestial realm,
Fools truly do not praise giving;
But the wise man rejoices in giving,
And because of that joy, he becomes happy in the hereafter."

The King became displeased and thought: "Although I have given a great alms, the Buddha preached only a little Dhamma to me. I suppose I was unable to capture the heart of the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala)."

After having his morning meal, the King went to the monastery, paid homage to the Blessed One, and asked: "Venerable Sir, I have given a great alms, but the blessing (anumodanā) given to me was not grand. Venerable Sir, what fault is there in me?" The Blessed One replied: "Great King, there is no fault in you. It was because the assembly was impure that the Dhamma was not preached." When asked why the assembly was impure, the Teacher revealed the thoughts of the two ministers.

The King called Kāḷa and asked: "Friend Kāḷa, is it true that you thought thus?" "It is true, Great King," he replied. "When I am giving my own property, where does it hurt you? I no longer wish to see you. Banish him from my kingdom!" the King commanded. Then he summoned Juṇha and asked: "Friend Juṇha, is it true that you thought thus?" "It is true, Great King," he replied. "May it be according to your heart's desire," the King said. In that very pavilion, on the prepared seats, he invited five hundred monks to sit, surrounded by those same royal princesses, and taking wealth from the royal house...
249:
"Give an alms equal to the one I gave for seven days," the King commanded. Juṇha gave accordingly. On the seventh day, after giving, he requested: "Blessed One, please preach the Dhamma." The Teacher, combining the blessing for both almsgivings, delivered a great Dhamma discourse, like two great rivers overflowing into a single current. At the conclusion of the discourse, Juṇha became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). The King, being filled with faith, donated the Veluvana Monastery (Bāhiravatthu) to the Blessed One. Thus, it should be understood how gain and honor arose for the Blessed One.

"Abhinipphanno siloko" refers to the praise of His virtues. That fame arose from the time the Blessed One turned the Wheel of Dhamma. From then on, even kings spoke of the Blessed One's virtues. Brahmins, householders, Nāgas, Garuḍas, Gandhabbas, devas, and Brahmās also spoke of His fame, starting with "Itipi so bhagavā..." (Such indeed is the Blessed One...). Other heretics (titthiyas) gave a thousand pieces of wealth to a man of royal descent (Vararāja) and sent him, saying, "Go and speak of the faults of the ascetic Gotama." He took the thousand pieces and looked at the One of Ten Powers from the soles of His feet to the tips of His hair. Seeing not even a fault the size of a louse's egg (likkhā), he thought: "If one speaks ill of this faultless physical form—adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor characteristics, surrounded by a fathom-wide radiance, resembling the Nandana Grove beautiful with celestial flowers, like the sky shining with fully bloomed Pāricchattaka flowers and hosts of stars—the mouth of the speaker would be twisted and his head would split into seven pieces. There is no way to speak of faults; I shall only speak of virtues." Thus, from the soles of the feet to the tips of the hair, he praised the Buddha's virtues with more than a thousand verses. At the time of the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya), this fame reached its pinnacle. Thus, fame (siloko) arose.

"Yāva maññe khattiyā" means that kings, brahmins, merchants, laborers, Nāgas, Garuḍas, Yakkhas, Asuras, devas, and Brahmās—all of them, being of a loving nature, live in joy and satisfaction. "Vigatamado kho pana" means that the Blessed One does not consume food with the intoxication of pride or for the sake of play, thinking, "So many people love me." On the contrary, the Blessed One consumes food while being entirely free from intoxication.
250: "Yathāvādī" means that whatever word he speaks with his voice, the bodily action of that Blessed One follows that speech. Whatever deed he performs with his body, the verbal action of that Blessed One follows that body. The body does not exceed the speech, and the speech does not exceed the body; the speech conforms to the body, and the body conforms to the speech. For example: "By the left side he is a pig, by the right side a deer; By the voice he is a calf, by the horns an old ox." This pig-ogre, upon seeing pigs, shows his left side which resembles a pig and catches and eats them. Upon seeing deer, he shows his right side of such nature and catches and eats them. Upon seeing calves, he makes the sound of a calf and catches and eats them. Upon seeing oxen, he creates horns resembling theirs and from afar, thinking "It looks like an ox," those oxen that approach are caught and eaten. Another example is the crow in the Dhammika-vāyasa Jātaka who, when asked by birds, said: "I eat only the wind; because I eat only the wind, I keep my mouth open, and for fear of killing insects, I stand on only one leg. Therefore, you all also— 'Practice the Dhamma, may it be well with you; practice the Dhamma, O kinsmen; He who practices the Dhamma sleeps happily, in this world and the next.'" Thus he created intimacy with the birds. Then, thinking "This bird is indeed good, a supreme practitioner of Dhamma; standing on one leg, he speaks 'Dhamma, Dhamma,'" the birds that became intimate were eaten. Therefore, the speech of those individuals does not conform to their body, and their body does not conform to their speech. The Blessed One is not like that. It is shown that the Blessed One's speech conforms to his body, and his body indeed conforms to his speech. He is called "Tiṇṇavicikiccho" because he has crossed over doubt. He is called "Vigatakathaṅkatho" because he is free from such perplexity as "How is this? How is this?". Just as the common people [wonder]: "This is a tree; what kind of tree is it? This is a village; this is a district; this is a country; what kind of country is it? Why is this tree's trunk straight? Why is this trunk crooked? Why are some thorns straight and some crooked? Why are some flowers fragrant and some foul-smelling? The fruit..."
251:
Some fruits are sweet, some are not sweet—thus people have doubts. The Teacher is not like that. Indeed, the Teacher is free from wavering indecision, knowing, 'Because of the predominance of such and such elements, this is so.' Just as those who have attained the first jhana etc. might have doubt regarding the second jhana etc.; and just as Paccekabuddhas might have doubt in terms of conventional expression regarding Omniscience because they lack the definitive realization of it—it is not so for the Buddha. It is shown that the Blessed One is free from wavering indecision in all things.

'Pariyositasankappo' means: just as some people have their intentions perfected and their wishes fulfilled through mere virtue, some through mere insight, some through the first jhana... some through the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, some through the mere state of a stream-enterer... some through the fruit of Arahantship, some through the knowledge of a disciple's perfection, and some through the knowledge of Paccekabodhi—my Teacher is not like that. It is shown that my Teacher has his intentions perfected through Omniscience (Sabbaññutañāṇa).

'Ajjhāsayaṃ Ādibrahmacariyaṃ': this term is in the nominative case used in the sense of the instrumental. It means one who has crossed over doubt, is free from wavering indecision, and has perfected his intentions through the Noble Path (Ariyamagga), which is characterized by superior inclination, being the supreme support, the primordial holy life, and the ancient holy life. For it is said: 'In things unheard of before, he realized the truths by himself, and therein attained Omniscience and mastery over the Powers (Balas).' Thus, it should be understood that the Blessed One's perfection of intentions is accomplished only through the Noble Path.

'Yathariva Bhagavā' means: just like our Buddha, they spoke with longing, 'Oh, how good it would be if four Conquerors (Jinas) were to wander in the four directions across the surface of this single Jambudīpa and preach the Dhamma!' Then others, desiring the state of wandering together in the three circles, said, 'Three Rightly Self-Awakened Buddhas (would be good).' Others thought, 'Having fulfilled the ten perfections, the arising of four or three Buddhas is difficult. However, if one Buddha were to reside permanently and preach the Dhamma, while another were to wander, in this way too, Jambudīpa would be graced and many would attain welfare and happiness.' Thinking thus, they said, 'O sirs, it would be good!'

'Aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso yaṃ': in this passage, both 'ṭhāna' and 'avakāsa' are terms for 'cause'. A cause is called 'ṭhāna' because the effect stays there, depending on it. It is called 'avakāsa' because it is like the room/space for that effect, as the effect cannot exist elsewhere without that cause. The word 'yaṃ' is in the nominative case used in the sense of the instrumental. This is what is meant: there is no cause for two Buddhas to arise simultaneously in a single world system. The moon and the sun revolve around Mount Meru in such a region, and they shine brilliantly in those directions. Because they shine thus, those regions are illuminated. That many thousands...
252:
It means there is no reason why two Buddhas should arise simultaneously in a single world system (lokadhātu). In this context, both terms "ṭhāna" and "avakāsa" refer to the cause (hetu). Because an effect can only exist in connection with its cause, it is called "ṭhāna" (basis). That cause is like the location of the effect, because without that cause, the effect cannot exist elsewhere; therefore, it is called "avakāsa" (space/location). The word "yaṃ" is a nominative case used in the sense of an instrument. It means there is no such cause by which two Buddhas could arise simultaneously in a single world system. In this regard also—

"As far as the sun and moon revolve, beautifying the quarters with their radiance,
So far the world extends a thousandfold; therein your power is exercised."

In this verse, a single world system (cakkavāḷa) is called one world system (lokadhātu). In the passage "A thousandfold world system (sahassī lokadhātu) shook," a thousand cakkavāḷas are called one lokadhātu. In the passage "Ānanda, if the Tathāgata so desires, he could make his voice heard throughout the three-thousandfold great-thousandfold world system (tisahassimahāsahassilokadhātu) and suffuse it with his radiance," a hundred billion cakkavāḷas are called one lokadhātu. In the passage "And this ten-thousandfold world system...," ten thousand cakkavāḷas are called one lokadhātu. It is with reference to those ten thousand cakkavāḷas that it is said "in a single world system." This extent of territory is called the field of birth (jātikhetta). Even within those ten thousand cakkavāḷas, Buddhas do not arise in any place other than the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa) of Jambudīpa in this particular cakkavāḷa. Beyond the field of birth, no place for the arising of Buddhas is known in the scriptures. "Yenatthena" means in the sense of including the invitation (pavāraṇā).

## Description of the Account of Sanaṅkumāra

"By complexion and by fame" means with ornaments and retinue, and with the glory and majesty of merit. In the phrase "It is well (sādhu), Mahābrahmā," the word "sādhu" is used in the sense of appreciation. "We rejoice after reflecting" means we rejoice after knowing.

## Description of the Story of the Brahmin Govinda

Regarding the statement "That Blessed One has been of great wisdom for a long time," it is not possible to define it as such-and-such a period; rather, he has indeed been of great wisdom for an exceedingly long time. "What do you think?" Then, wishing to answer the question himself, he said: "Friends, it is not yet a matter of wonder that now..."
253: 'Friends, what is surprising if the Blessed One, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), having crushed the heads of the three Māras upon the Throne of Enlightenment (Bodhi-pallaṅka), and having penetrated the unique knowledge (asādhāraṇañāṇa), should be of great wisdom? Friends, I shall indeed tell you how he was of great wisdom even during the time when his omniscience was not yet mature, while standing in partial knowledge (padesañāṇa) and even during the time of having lust, etc.' Thus, wishing to show the cause hidden by past lives, he spoke the words beginning with 'Bhūtapubbaṃ bhoti.' A chaplain (purohita) is one who advises on all matters. 'Govinda' is one who has been consecrated with the consecration of the office of Govinda. Although he originally had another name, from the time of his consecration, he became known as 'Govinda.' 'Jotipāla' is so called because of his brilliance (jotana) and because of his protection (pālana). It is heard that on the day Jotipāla was born, all weapons shone. The King, seeing his own auspicious weapon shining in the early morning, stood in fear. Govinda went to attend the King in the morning and asked if he had slept well. The King replied, 'Teacher, how could I have slept well?' and told him the reason. 'Do not fear, Great King, a son has been born to me; it is by his power that the weapons throughout the city are shining,' he said. The King thought, 'Could this boy be my enemy?' and became even more afraid. When asked, 'Great King, what are you thinking?' the King told him the matter. Then Govinda reassured him, 'Do not fear, Great King, this boy will not harm you; indeed, in the whole of Jambudīpa, there will be no one equal to him in wisdom. By my son's words, the doubts of the people will be cut off, and he will advise you on all your affairs.' The King was delighted and gave a thousand (pieces of money), saying, 'Let this be for the boy's milk-money,' and added, 'Show the boy to me when he is grown.' The boy grew up in due course. Because of his brilliance and his ability to protect, they named him 'Jotipāla.' Therefore, it is said: 'He is Jotipāla because of brilliance and protection.' 'Sammā vossajjitvā' means having properly relinquished. Or this is simply the reading. 'Alamatthadasataro' means one who is more capable and more endowed with seeing what is beneficial than others. By the passage 'by the instruction of the youth Jotipāla,' it is shown that even the father, the Brahmin Govinda, would consult Jotipāla before giving advice.
254:
"Bhavamattha bhavantaṃ Jotipālaṃ" means: "May there be prosperity, the attainment of special distinction, and all goodness and blessings for the venerable Jotipāla." "Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ" (courteous talk) means: after concluding the polite conversation intended to dispel grief and associated with death, in such a manner as: "Great King, do not worry; this death is a constant law for all beings," and so forth. "May the venerable Jotipāla not reject us from [his] instruction" means: do not let him abandon us from instruction by saying, "I will no longer instruct." "Abhisambhosi" means having arranged and completed [the tasks]. People said this—seeing that the son, the Brahmin Govinda, was even wiser than his father, instructing in all affairs and being able to accomplish all tasks, they were delighted in heart and said, "Sirs, the Brahmin is indeed a Govinda; sirs, the Brahmin is indeed a Great Govinda (Mahāgovinda)." The meaning is: "Sirs, this one's father was once the Brahmin Govinda, but this son is indeed the Great Brahmin Govinda."

## Description of the Division of the Kingdom
"Yena te cha khattiyā" refers to those six princes who were called "friends." It is said that those princes were younger brothers of King Reṇu, born of the same father. Therefore, Mahāgovinda, thinking, "I do not know whether this king, after being consecrated, will divide the kingdom among those princes or not; it would be good if I send those princes to King Reṇu in advance to obtain a promise," approached where those six princes were. "Rājakattāro" (king-makers) refers to the ministers who appoint the king.

"Madanīyā kāmā" refers to sensual pleasures that cause intoxication and negligence. As time passes, this King Reṇu might not be able to remember his promise; therefore, it means, "Sirs, please come, please come."

"Sarāmahaṃ bho" (I remember, sirs) refers to the fact that at that time, it was a period when people spoke only the truth; thus, without saying what was untrue, such as "When did I say it? Who saw it? Who heard it?", he said, "Sirs, I remember." "Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ" refers to polite conversation such as, "Great King, do not worry though the royal father has gone to the world of devas; this is a constant law for all beings; conditioned things are of such a nature." "Sabbāni sakaṭamukhāni paṭṭhapesi" means arranging all six kingdoms to be like the front of a chariot. Each king's kingdom was three hundred yojanas in size. At the place where they met King Reṇu's kingdom, it was about ten gāvutas, and in the middle, King Reṇu's kingdom was like a canopy. Why was it arranged in this way? So that when the kings come from time to time to see the Great King, they will come and go only through their own territories without harassing the kingdoms of others, and as they go...
255:
The Brahmin Mahāgovinda established the six kingdoms in a shape resembling the front of a chariot. Each king's kingdom was three hundred yojanas wide. The area reaching King Reṇu's kingdom was ten gāvutas, and in the middle, King Reṇu's kingdom was like a canopy. Why was it established in this way? So that when the kings come from time to time to see the [Great] King, they will come and go only through their own kingdom's boundaries without harassing the kingdoms of others. When entering another's kingdom, people reproach a king who says, "Give rice, give oxen," saying, "These kings do not travel through their own domains but are harassing us." However, for a king traveling through his own domain, people do not think they are being harassed, reflecting, "This king ought to receive such and such things from us." Thinking of this benefit, the Brahmin Mahāgovinda established it in this way, [wishing], "May the kings, in harmony and joy, rule the kingdoms for a long time."

"Dantapura of the Kaliṅgas, and Potana of the Assakas,
Māhissati of the Avantis, and Roduka of the Sovīras.
Mithilā of the Videhas, Campā was built among the Aṅgas,
And Bārāṇasī of the Kāsīs—these were built by Govinda."

These seven cities were built by Mahāgovinda himself for the benefit of those kings.

"Sattabhū and Brahmadatta, Vessabhū together with Bharata,
Reṇu and the two Dhataraṭṭhas—there were then seven Bhāradhas."

These are the names of all those seven kings. Among them, one was named Sattabhū, one was named Brahmadatta, one was named Vessabhū, one together with him was named Bharata, one was named Reṇu, and two were named Dhataraṭṭha. Thus, there were seven Great Kings, the Bhāradhas, who carried the responsibility of the kingdoms on the surface of Jambudīpa.

## End of the Explanation of the First Recitation Section.
256:
## Explanation of the Spreading of Fame

"Upasaṅkamiṃsu" means: "Our prosperity and sovereignty did not arise through the power of others, but only through the power of Mahāgovinda. Mahāgovinda has united us seven kings and established us upon the surface of Jambudīpa. It is not easy to repay the one who has first rendered us service. Let this Mahāgovinda alone advise us seven; let us appoint him to the positions of General and Chaplain. In this way, we shall prosper." Thinking thus, they approached him. Mahāgovinda also thought: "I have united these kings. If they were to have other generals and chaplains, they would listen to the words of their own generals and chaplains and become divided among themselves. Therefore, I shall accept the positions of General and Chaplain for them." Thinking thus, he consented, saying, "Very well, sirs."

"Satta ca brāhmaṇamahāsāle" means: "I may or may not be present in all places. In places where I am not present, they shall perform the necessary duties." Thinking thus, he appointed seven sub-chaplains. Referring to them, it is said, "Satta ca brāhmaṇamahāsāle." They are called "Nahātakā" (those who have bathed) because they bathe twice a day, in the evening and in the morning. Alternatively, they bathe upon the completion of their vows and practices; from the time they have thus bathed, they do not eat or drink with other Brahmins, and are therefore called "Nahātakā."

"Abbhuggacchi" means spreading or becoming widely renowned. At that time, people in every place they sat were saying: "It is not possible to advise the whole of Jambudīpa in this way without consulting with Brahma." "Na kho panāhaṃ" means that Great Man thought: "This false reputation has arisen for me. The arising of a reputation is not a heavy burden; only the maintenance of an arisen reputation is a heavy burden. This reputation has arisen while I was acting without reflection or consultation. If I were to act with reflection and consultation, it would spread even more widely." Thus, while seeking a means to see Brahma, he saw that reason and reflected on the meaning of "Sutaṃ kho pana metaṃ," and so on.
257:
The reason he approached King Reṇu was: "If I live thus in solitude, during the four months of the rainy season, there will be no one who wishes to see me or speak with me. Then, being free from impediments (palibodha), I shall live happily." Thus, he approached for the purpose of cutting off impediments. This method applies to all instances.

"Sādisiyo" means (wives) of similar appearance and similar caste.

"Navaṃ sandhāgāraṃ kāretvā" means having built a splendid lodging surrounded by reeds on the outside, suitable for living during the four months of the rainy season, and endowed with places for the night, places for the day, and a walkway (caṅkama). "Karuṇā jhānaṃ jhāyī" means he entered into the third and fourth jhānas based on compassion. Here, by mentioning compassion as the starting point, the other three Divine Abodes (brahmavihāra) are also included. "Ukkaṇṭhanā paritassanā" means that for one established in jhāna, there is no dissatisfaction-induced anxiety or fear-induced trembling; however, it means there was a craving or longing for the arrival of Brahma.

## Explanation of the Discussion with Brahma

"Bhaya" means the fear of mental terror itself. "Ajānantā" means being without knowledge. "How shall we know you?" means "How can we know you? Where does this person live? What is his name? What is his clan?" Among such characteristics, it means "By what characteristic shall we recognize you?"

"They know me as Kumāra" means they know me as "Kumāra" or as "Dahara" (the Young). "In the Brahma-world" means in the sublime world. "Sanantana" means ancient or traditional. He shows that "I am that ancient Kumāra, the Brahma named Sanaṅkumāra." "Know thus, Govinda" means "O wise Govinda, you should know thus; recognize me in this way."

"A seat, water, foot-water, and
Sweet vegetables (I offer) to Brahma.
We ask the Venerable One about hospitality;
May the Venerable One accept our hospitality."

Here, "Aggha" refers to that which should be offered to a guest. Therefore, he means: "This seat is prepared; sit here. This water is pure; drink this drinking water. Wash your feet. This foot-oil is oil prepared for the benefit of the feet; anoint your feet with this oil. This is a sweet vegetable broth." The holy life (brahmacariya) of a Bodhisatta is not like the holy life of others. That Bodhisatta does not (store things), thinking, "This will be for tomorrow, this will be for the third day."
258:
That Mahāgovinda did not practice storing [provisions], saying, "This item shall be for tomorrow, this item shall be for the third day." *Madhusāka* refers to cooked vegetables boiled only with water, without salt, without oil (spices), and without being sour (without buttermilk). Referring to those boiled vegetables, while saying, "Please partake of this," he said the words beginning with, "I ask the Blessed One for a worthy gift." All these valuable structures do not belong to Brahmā. They ask the Lord Brahmā about those structures. This means: "May the Blessed One accept our offering; may the Blessed One receive this offering of ours."

Why does this Govinda not know that "Brahmā does not partake of anything other than this offering"? It is not that he does not know; even though he knows, he asks on the basis of the duty (*vattasīsa*) that a guest who has arrived in one's presence should be questioned.

Then Brahmā, reflecting, "Does this wise man ask knowing that I do not partake [of food], or does he ask out of hypocrisy?" realized that "He asks on the basis of duty." Thinking, "Now it is proper for me to accept," he said, "Govinda, we accept your offering as you have spoken." This means: "Govinda, whatever words you speak, such as 'This seat is prepared, please sit here,' in those words, we are considered as having sat on your seat, as having drunk the drinking water; let my feet also be considered washed and anointed with oil; let the boiled vegetables also be considered consumed. From the time I consented to the gift you offered, whatever you say, it is as if I have already accepted it." Therefore, it is said, "Govinda, we accept your offering as you have spoken." Having thus accepted the offering, wishing to give the opportunity to ask questions, he spoke the words beginning with, "For the sake of welfare and happiness in the present life."

"I, who have doubts, ask the Lord Brahmā, who is free from doubt regarding the well-known questions made known by others," is the meaning of "*Kankhī akankhiṃ paravediyesu*."

"*Hittvā mamattaṃ*" means abandoning the craving for requisites, thinking, "This is mine, this is my property." "*Manujesu*" means among beings; the meaning is: whoever among men abandons the sense of "mine." "*Ekodibhūto*" means becoming solitary, standing alone, and sitting alone. In terms of word-definition, because one arises or proceeds alone, one is called "*Ekodi*"; being of such a nature, one is called "*Ekodibhūto*." "*Karuṇedhimutto*" means being intent on the jhāna of compassion, having produced that jhāna. "*Nirāmagandho*" means being free from the stench (of defilements). "*Ettha ṭhito*" means established in these qualities. "*Ettha ca sikkhamāno*" means practicing in those qualities. This is the summary of these passages; the detailed explanation was already spoken above by Mahāgovinda and Brahmā. In those words, Govinda...
259:
"*Sikkhamāno*" means one who is training and practicing in these qualities. This is just a summary here; the detailed explanation was already spoken above by the Brahmin Mahāgovinda and Brahmā.

In that detailed explanation, "*Ete avidvā*" means "I do not know these stenches (defilements)." "*Idha brūhi dhīra*" means "O wise one, tell me, speak to me about those stenches here." "*Kena āvaṭā vāti pajā kurutu*" means "By what kind of obstruction of defilements is the generation (beings) obstructed so that they become putrid and stink?" "*Āpāyikā*" means going to the lower realms (*apāya*). "*Nivuta-brahmalokā*" means that for such a being, the Brahma-world is obstructed and closed. It is a question asking: by which defilement is the path leading to the Brahma-world obstructed, closed, and concealed for beings?

"*Kodho mosavajjaṃ nikati ca dubbho*" refers to: anger (*kodha*) characterized by irritation; falsehood (*musāvāda*) characterized by deceiving others; deceit (*nikati*) characterized by trickery by showing something similar; and treachery (*dubbha*) characterized by betraying friends. "*Kadariyatā atimāno usūyā*" refers to: extreme stinginess (*kadariyatā*) characterized by harsh miserliness; arrogance (*atimāna*) characterized by thinking oneself superior; and envy (*usūyā*) characterized by disparaging the prosperity of others. "*Icchā vivicchā paraheṭhanā ca*" refers to: desire (*icchā*) characterized by longing; various forms of selfishness (*vivicchā*) characterized by stinginess; and harassing others (*paraheṭhanā*) characterized by violence. "*Lobho ca doso ca mado ca moho*" refers to: greed (*lobha*) characterized by attachment to anything; hatred (*dosa*) characterized by malice; pride (*mada*) characterized by intoxication; and delusion (*moha*) characterized by bewilderment.

"*Etesu yuttā anirāmagandhā*" means that a being associated with these fourteen defilements is not one free from stench; such a person is one who has a stench, a putrid smell like a rotting corpse. "*Āpāyikā nivuta-brahmalokā*" explains that such a being is one who goes to the lower realms and is one for whom the path to the Brahma-world is concealed. When preaching this Sutta, it should be explained by comparing it with the *Āmagandha Sutta*; the *Āmagandha Sutta* should also be explained by comparing it with this Sutta.

"*Te na sunimmadayā*" means those stenches (defilements) are not easily subdued; they are difficult to abandon and difficult to conquer. "*Yassa dāni bhavaṃ govindo kālaṃ maññati*" means: "Whatever time the venerable Govinda considers right for going forth (renunciation), let that going forth take place. If you renounce thus, my coming to your presence will be a good coming, and the Dhamma discourse spoken will be well-spoken. My dear..."
260:
"Being the foremost man in the whole of Jambudīpa, staying in the first stage of life, your renunciation—abandoning such great wealth, glory, and beauty—is exceedingly noble, like a scent-elephant breaking its iron bonds and departing. This is the tradition of the Buddhas (Buddhatanti)." Having thus strengthened the Great Being's resolve for renunciation, Sanankumāra Brahma returned to the Brahma realm.

## Commentary on the Consultation with King Reṇu

The Great Being also thought, "It is not proper for me to go directly from this place (of meditative absorption) to ordain. Since I am the advisor for the welfare of the royal family, I shall first inform the King. If the King also ordains, it would be very good. If he does not ordain, I shall ordain after handing over the office of the chaplain (purohita)." Thinking thus, he approached the King. Regarding this, it was said: "Then, the venerable Mahāgovinda... 'I no longer delight in the office of the chaplain,'" and so forth.

In that passage, "tvaṃ pajānassu rajjena" means: "You yourself should know (manage) your kingship (state affairs)." "Nāhaṃ porohicce rame" means: "I no longer delight in being a chaplain; I am weary of it. Seek another teacher who can advise you. I no longer delight in the office of the chaplain."

Then the King thought, "The wealth in the house of the Brahmin, who has been in seclusion for four months, must have become depleted." Wishing to invite him with wealth, he said, "If you are in need of sensual pleasures, I shall fulfill them for you." Then, thinking again, "Could this man have been harassed by someone while living alone?", he said:

"Whoever harasses you, I shall prevent them; I am the commander of the earth's army.
You are my father, and I am your son; O Govinda, do not forsake us."

The meaning of that verse is: If anyone harasses you, I shall prevent them; you only need to point out, "It is this person," and I shall know what must be done in this matter. "Bhūmisenāpati ahaṃ" means, alternatively, "I am the lord of the earth; as such, I shall hand over this kingdom to you alone." "Tuvaṃ pitā ahaṃ putto" means: "You shall stand in the position of a father, and I shall stand in the position of a son." O Govinda, you, having set aside my wish, act only according to your own wish; let it be as you desire. As for me, following only your wish and consuming the alms-food given by you, I shall serve you, holding a sword and shield in hand, or I shall drive your chariot. There is also a reading "mā no govinda pājahī." The meaning of that reading is: "You shall stand in the position of a father, and I shall stand in the position of a son. Venerable Govinda, do not forsake us; do not abandon us." Then, the Great Being, wishing to show that the points the King thought of did not apply to him, said: "I have no need for sensual pleasures, nor is there anyone harassing me..." and so forth.
261:
This is the text. The meaning of that text is: "May the venerable one stand in the place of a father, and I shall stand in the place of a son. O venerable Govinda, do not abandon us, do not forsake us entirely." Then, the Mahāpurisa, wishing to show that the King's thoughts did not apply to him, said:

"I have no lack of sensual pleasures, nor is there anyone to harass me. Having heard the words of a non-human (amanussa), I no longer delight in the home."

In that verse, "na matthi" means "I do not have." "Gahe" means "in the home." Then the King asked the Brahmin Govinda:

"What is the appearance of that non-human? What benefit did he speak to you? Having heard what words do you entirely abandon us, the home, and all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa?"

In that verse, "jahāsi no gahe amhe ca kevalī" means that the King, considering the Brahmin's wealth-filled houses as his own through the power of support, says: "Having heard what words do you abandon our home, us, and all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa without exception?"

Then the Mahāpurisa, wishing to tell the King, spoke the words beginning with "upavutthassa me pubbe." In that text, "upavutthassa" means having lived in solitude and seclusion for four months. "Yiṭṭhakāmassa me sato" means while I was desiring to perform a sacrifice (pūjā). "Aggi pajjalito āsi, kusapattaparitthato" means that having strewn kusa grass all around and adding ghee, curd, honey, etc., an effort was made to make the fire blaze. The meaning here is: "To me, who stood thinking, 'I shall give gifts to the multitude,' having thus lit the fire..." 

"Sanan tano" refers to Brahma Sanaṅkumāra. Thereafter, the King, wishing to renounce himself, spoke the words beginning with "saddahāmi." In that text, "kathaṃ vattetha aññathā" means "How would you conduct yourselves in any other way?" "Te taṃ anuvattissāma" means "We too shall follow and practice just as you do; we shall follow you into renunciation." There is also a reading "anuvajissāma," which means "we shall follow along." "Akāco" means flawless and not coarse. "Govindassānusāsane" means "in the instruction of you, Govinda." It means they will practice having the venerable Govinda alone as their teacher (satthāra).
262:
## Commentary on the Addressing of the Six Khattiyas

'Where are those six kings? He approached that place' means he approached King Reṇu. 'Great King, kingship is such that beings kill even mothers, fathers, brothers, and sisters to seize it. Your act of wishing to renounce such great royal splendor to become a monk is truly noble'—praising and supporting him in this way, he approached the king, making his effort even firmer.
