'They thought in unison' means they thought together just as the king had thought, thinking, 'At some time, the Brahmin's wealth and possessions might decrease.' It means, 'Let us entice and win him over with wealth.' 'Let that much wealth be brought, let it be taken; take as much as you desire'—this is the intended meaning. 'Only because of you, young princes' means that because of you as the cause, and because of what you have given, much wealth and property have arisen.

'If we renounce sensual pleasures' means renouncing both the objects of sensuality (vatthu-kāma) and the defilements of sensuality (kilesa-kāma). 'In which sensual pleasures the worldling is stuck' means that worldlings are attached and clinging to those sensual pleasures. 'Strive, be firm' means 'In this case, put forth effort; being one with unremitting exertion, be firm in your resolve.' 'Be endowed with the power of patience' means 'Be possessed of the power of patience,' thus generating effort in the kings.

'This path is a straight path' means this path of the compassion-jhana (karuṇā-jhāna) is called a straight path. 'This path is the unsurpassed noble path' means this alone is the unsurpassed, noble path for rebirth in the Brahma world. 'The Dhamma protected by the virtuous' means this is the Dhamma protected by the virtuous ones, namely the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples. Thus, by speaking of the virtues of the compassion-jhana, he makes their resolve firm so that those kings do not turn back.

'Sirs, who can know life?' means 'Sirs, what is called life (jīvita) is like a water bubble, like a dewdrop on the tip of a blade of grass; it is of a nature to perish in an instant. Who can know the destination of that life? At what moment will it break?' 'Going to the next world is certain' means that the next world (paraloka) must surely be gone to; therefore, a wise man of good family should investigate and understand it with wisdom. 'Mantā' is called wisdom; it means one should investigate, understand, reflect upon, and know with that wisdom. Alternatively, the locative case is to be understood in the sense of the instrumental (by wisdom). 'It should be known by wisdom' means it should be known with knowledge (ñāṇa). What should be known? The fact that life is difficult to know...
263:
...and the certainty of going to the next world. Having understood this, and having cut off all impediments (palibodha), one should perform meritorious deeds and lead the holy life (brahmacariya). Why? Because for a being who is born, there is no such thing as not dying.

## Commentary on the Addressing of the Great Wealthy Brahmins

'Sirs... monkhood has few followers and few gains.' Indeed, from the time of renunciation, people speak of one who has abandoned kingship to become a monk only by harassing and oppressing him, making him out to be a lowly and helpless person. Gains and honors are also very few; even after wandering through an entire village, it is difficult to obtain even enough food for sustenance. This Brahminhood (brahmañña), however, is of great influence because of having many followers, and it is abundant in gains because of being endowed with gains and honors. You are now the chief chaplain (purohita) in the whole of Jambudīpa; in all places, you receive the best seat, the best water, the best food, the best scent, and the best garland.

'Like a king among kings' means: 'Sirs, I am now like a Cakkavatti king among ordinary kings.' 'Like Brahma among Brahmas' means: 'Like a Mahābrahmā among ordinary Brahmas.' 'Like a god among householders' means: 'I am like Sakka, the king of gods, among the remaining householders.'

## Commentary on the Addressing of the Wives

'Forty similar wives' means there are forty wives who are similar in appearance and fortune. Besides them, that Brahmin Mahāgovinda had many dancing women in all three stages of life.

## Commentary on the Renunciation of Mahāgovinda

'Wandering on tour' means he wandered on tour through a succession of villages and market towns. In every place he went, there was a great stir, just as when a Buddha appears. When people heard, 'The wise Mahāgovinda is coming, it is said,' they had pavilions built beforehand, decorated the roads, went out to welcome him, and brought him along. Great gains and honors arose, overwhelming like a great flood. 'Of the seven chaplains' means the chaplain of the seven brother-kings. In this way, just as nowadays, in such times or when some suffering arises, people say, 'Namo Buddhassa' (Homage to the Buddha), so at that time, people said, 'Homage to the Brahmin Mahāgovinda, homage to the chaplain of the seven kings.'
264: In the Pali text, only the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) appear through the method beginning with 'accompanied by loving-kindness' and so forth. However, the Great Being (the Bodhisatta) actually attained all eight meditative attainments (samāpatti) and five superknowledges (abhiññā). He also taught his disciples the path (jhāna-magga) which is the cause for being reborn in the Brahma world together with the Brahmas. 'Sabbena sabbaṃ' refers to those who attained the eight meditative attainments and five superknowledges. 'Ye na sabbena sabbaṃ sāsanaṃ ājāniṃsu' refers to those who did not know even one of the eight meditative attainments and were unable to attain them. 'Amoghā' means they are with results (fruitful). 'Avañjhā' means they are not barren. 'Sabbanihīnaṃ pasavanti' means they produce the assembly of Gandhabba deities. 'Saphalā' means they are beneficial through rebirth in the remaining celestial realms. 'Sa-udrayā' means they have growth (benefit) through rebirth in the Brahma world. 'Sarāmahaṃ' means 'O Pañcasikha, I remember.' It is said that because of this word, this Sutta became known as the word of the Buddha (Buddhabhāsita). 'Na nibbidāya' means not for the sake of disenchantment with the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa). 'Na virāgāya' means not for the sake of dispassion toward the round. 'Na nirodhāya' means not for the sake of the cessation of the round. 'Na upasamāya' means not for the sake of the calming of the round. 'Na abhiññāya' means not for the sake of knowing the round with higher knowledge. 'Na sambodhāya' means not for the sake of awakening from the round by being free from the sleep of defilements. 'Na nibbānāya' means not for the sake of the benefit of the deathless Nibbāna. 'Ekantanibbidāya' means it is indeed for the sake of disenchantment with the round. In this context, 'nibbidāya' refers to insight (vipassanā). 'Virāgāya' refers to the Path (magga). 'Nirodhāya upasamāya' refers to Nibbāna. 'Abhiññāya sambodhāya' refers to the Path. 'Nibbānāya' refers to Nibbāna itself. Thus, the definitive explanation should be understood as: insight in one place, the Path in three places, and Nibbāna in three places. In a figurative sense (pariyāya), however, all these terms are synonyms for both the Path and Nibbāna. What should be said regarding Right View and so forth has already been stated in the 'Explanation of the Truths' in the Visuddhimagga. 'Ye na sabbena sabbaṃ' refers to those who do not know how to fulfill all four Noble Paths, but attain only three, two, or one (of the instructions). 'Sabbesaṃyeva imesaṃ kulaputtānaṃ' refers to the sons of good family who have practiced the holy life. He concluded the teaching by placing the fruition of Arahantship at the summit with the words 'amoghā... saphalā sa-udrayā'.
265:
"Having paid homage to the Blessed One and performed the circumambulation" (D. ii. 188): this phrase means that he (the deity) accepted the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One with his mind, rejoiced, praised it with his words, and expressed appreciation. Then, placing his hands in a great reverential salutation (añjali) upon his head, as if submerging himself in clear liquid lac, he entered into the net of six-colored rays of the Ten-Powered One. He paid homage at the four positions, circumambulated three times, and while repeatedly praising the Blessed One, he disappeared from right before the Teacher and went to his own celestial realm.

## The Commentary on the Mahāgovinda Sutta is finished.
266:
## 7. Commentary on the Mahāsamaya Sutta

## Commentary on the Introduction

This Sutta beginning with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' is the Mahāsamaya Sutta. Herein, the commentary on the words in sequence is as follows: By the method of origin stated in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta, 'Indeed, O friends, the princes are capable (sakya vata bho kumārā)', based on this solemn utterance of the father, King Okkāka, the princes obtained the name 'Sakka'. The single district which was the dwelling place of these princes is called 'Sakka' by conventional designation; 'among the Sakyans' means in that Sakyan district. 'Mahāvane' refers to a large forest that grew naturally, was not planted by anyone, and was connected in a single stretch with the Himālaya. 'Sabbeneva arahantehi' means together with all the Arahants who had reached the fruition of Arahantship on the very day this Mahāsamaya Sutta was preached.

Regarding the phrase 'sabbeneva arahantehi', the sequential narrative is as follows: It is said that the Sakyans and Koliyans, between the cities of Kapilavatthu and Koliya, had the river named Rohiṇī dammed by a single embankment to cultivate their crops. Then, in the month of Jeṭṭhamūla (May-June), when the crops began to wither, the laborers from both cities assembled. At that time, the laborers of Koliya city said, 'If this water is divided between both sides, it will not be enough for you nor for us. However, our crops can be brought to completion with just this one supply of water; therefore, give this water to us.' The laborers of Kapilavatthu city replied, 'When you have filled your granaries and remain settled, we will not be able to wander at your doorsteps carrying baskets and sacks, taking red gold, green emeralds, and black kahāpaṇas. Our crops can also be brought to completion with just this one supply of water; therefore, give this water to us.' 'We will not give it,' they said. 'We too will not give it,' the others replied. Thus, escalating the quarrel, one rose up and struck another, and that one struck another; thus, having struck one another and insulting the lineage of the royal families, they magnified the dispute.

The Koliya laborers said, 'You Kapilavatthu residents, relying on your Sakyan princes, shout loudly; those who, like domestic dogs and jackals, lived together with their own sisters. What can their elephants, horses, and shields and weapons do to us?' The Sakyan laborers also said, 'You now, relying on those leprous children, shout loudly; those who, being helpless and destitute like animals, lived in Kola trees (jujube trees). Their elephants, horses, and shields and weapons...'
267:
“What can their elephants, horses, and weapons do to us?” they said. Those farmers went and told the ministers appointed to that task, and the ministers informed the royal families. Then the Sakyan kings said, “We shall show the strength and power of those who cohabit with their own sisters,” and they set out, prepared for battle. The Koliyan kings also said, “We shall show the strength and power of those who dwell in the Kola trees,” and they set out, prepared for battle.

The Blessed One, having arisen from the attainment of Great Compassion at dawn, surveyed the world and saw these kings setting out prepared for battle. Seeing them, he reflected, “If I go, will this quarrel be settled or not?” He then concluded, “I will go there and preach three Jatakas to settle the quarrel; then the quarrel will subside. After that, to illustrate unity, I will preach two Jatakas and then deliver the Attadanda Sutta. Upon hearing the discourse, the kings of both cities will each offer two hundred and fifty princes. I will ordain them, and there will be a great assembly.” Therefore, while those kings were setting out for battle, without informing anyone, he took his bowl and robes and went alone. He sat cross-legged in the air between the two armies, emitting the six-colored rays.

When the inhabitants of Kapilavatthu saw the Blessed One, they thought, “Our noble kinsman, the Teacher, has arrived. Has he seen the cause of our quarrel?” They then considered, “It is not proper for us to let weapons fall on the bodies of others while the Blessed One has arrived. Let the people of Koliya city kill us or oppress us if they wish.” Thinking thus, they discarded their weapons and sat down, paying homage to the Blessed One. The inhabitants of Koliya city thought likewise, discarded their weapons, and sat down, paying homage to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One, though he already knew, asked, “Great kings, why have you come?” They replied, “Venerable Sir, we have not come to play at the water-side, nor to play on the mountain top, nor to play in the river, nor to see the hills. Indeed, we have come to this place having prepared for battle.” “Great kings, on account of what is your quarrel?” he asked. “Venerable Sir, it is on account of water,” they replied. “Great kings, how much is water worth?” “Venerable Sir, it is of little value.” “Great kings, how much is the earth worth?” “Venerable Sir, it is invaluable.” “Great kings, how much are kings worth?” “Venerable Sir, kings are invaluable.” “Great kings, why do you destroy invaluable kings on account of water which is of little value?” Having said this, he added, “There is no satisfaction in quarreling. Great kings, by the power of quarreling, a grudge was formed in an improper place between a tree deity and a black lion, which has followed them throughout the aeon.” He then preached the Phandana Jataka. Then, great kings...
268:
“This grudge has followed throughout this entire aeon,” he said, and preached the Phandana Jataka. Then he said, “Great kings, one should not be easily led by the words of others. For, by being led by others' words, because of the word of a single young rabbit, the four-footed animals in the Himalayan forest, which is three thousand leagues wide, once leaped into the great ocean. Therefore, one should not be easily led by others' words,” and he preached the Pathavī-undriya Jataka. Then he said, “Great kings, sometimes even the weak see a flaw or an opportunity in the strong, and sometimes the strong see an opportunity in the weak. Even a small female quail once killed a noble elephant,” and he preached the Latukika Jataka. Having thus preached three Jatakas to settle the quarrel, he preached two more Jatakas to illustrate unity. How? “Great kings, no one can find an advantage over those who are united,” he said, and preached the Rukkha-dhamma Jataka. Then he said, “Great kings, no one was able to find a flaw in those who were united. But when they quarreled with one another, the hunter's son took their lives and carried them away. There is no pleasure in quarreling,” and he preached the Vattaka Jataka. Having thus preached these five Jatakas, he preached the Attadanda Sutta at the conclusion.

The kings, being devout, said, “If the Teacher had not come, we would have killed one another with our own hands and caused a river of blood to flow. We would not have seen our sons and brothers at the doors of our houses. There would not even have been anyone to carry messages back and forth. We have gained our lives because of the Teacher. If the Teacher had lived the household life, the sovereignty of the four great islands surrounded by two thousand small islands would have come into his hands, and he would have had over a thousand sons. Then he would have traveled only with a retinue of warrior-kings. But he abandoned that prosperity, went forth, and attained Omniscience. Now also, let him travel only with a retinue of warrior-kings.” Thus, the inhabitants of both cities offered two hundred and fifty princes each. The Blessed One ordained those princes and went to the Mahāvana forest. Those monks, having been ordained only out of deep respect and not by their own desire, became dissatisfied. Their former wives also sent messages, saying, “Noble lords, be discontented; the household life is not stable,” and so on. Consequently, those monks became exceedingly dissatisfied.

The Blessed One, reflecting and knowing their dissatisfaction, thought, “These monks are dissatisfied even while living together with a Buddha like me. Now, I shall tell them the beauty of Lake Kunāla, take them there, and [remove] their dissatisfaction...”
269:
Thinking, "I shall dispel their dissatisfaction," the Blessed One spoke in praise of Lake Kunāla. Those monks felt a desire to see that Lake Kunāla. When asked, "Monks, do you wish to see Lake Kunāla?" they replied, "We wish to see it, Venerable Sir." "If so, come, let us go," he said. When they asked, "How can we go to the place where those with psychic powers go?" he said, "You only need the desire to go; I shall take you there by my own psychic power." They replied, "Very well, Venerable Sir." Then the Blessed One, taking the five hundred monks, flew into the sky and, standing at Lake Kunāla, said to those monks, "Monks, whatever fish in this Lake Kunāla whose names you do not know, ask their names."

The monks asked, and the Blessed One answered all their questions. He did not only have them ask and answer the names of the fish; he also had them ask and answered the names of the trees in that forest, and the names of the two-footed birds and four-footed creatures at the foot of the mountain. Then, they saw the cuckoo bird king named Kunāla, who was sitting on a stick held in the beaks of two birds, coming surrounded by a flock of birds in front, behind, and on both sides. Seeing him, they said, "Venerable Sir, this bird must be the king of these birds; we think these birds are his attendants." "Monks, it is just as you think; this bird king is also of my lineage, my ancestry," he said. "Venerable Sir, now we have seen these birds; we wish to hear the words the Blessed One spoke: 'This bird king is also of my lineage, my ancestry,'" they requested. When asked, "Monks, do you wish to hear?" they replied, "We wish to hear, Venerable Sir." Saying, "If so, listen," he dispelled their dissatisfaction by preaching the Kunāla Jātaka, adorned with three hundred verses. At the end of the teaching, all the monks were established in the fruit of Stream-entry, and through the path of Stream-entry itself, they also attained psychic powers. The Blessed One, saying, "Let this much benefit suffice for these monks for now," flew into the sky and went to the Mahāvana forest. Although those monks had gone by the psychic power of the Buddha, upon returning, they descended into the Mahāvana forest surrounding the Blessed One by their own psychic power.

The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat and addressed those monks, "Come, monks, sit down; I shall teach you the meditation subject for the abandoning of the defilements to be abandoned by the three higher paths." The monks thought, "The Blessed One, knowing our dissatisfaction, took us to Lake Kunāla and dispelled it. To us who attained the fruit of Stream-entry there, he has now given the meditation subject for the three higher paths here. It is not proper for us to spend time saying, 'We are Stream-enterers'; we should act like Great Men." Those five hundred monks paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One, stood up, shook their sitting cloths, and sat down individually in caves and at the feet of trees.
270:
The Blessed One reflected: "These monks, by nature, do not abandon their meditation subjects; for a monk who has obtained the proper method, there is no such thing as exhaustion. As they go on, they will develop insight, reach Arahantship, and come to me, saying, 'We shall report the special qualities we have individually attained.' When these monks arrive, deities from the ten thousand world systems will gather in this single world system; there will be a Great Assembly (Mahāsamaya). It is proper for me to sit in a secluded place." Then, he sat on the Buddha-seat prepared in a secluded spot.

The Elder who had taken the meditation subject and departed before all others reached Arahantship together with the analytical insights. Then, one after another, all five hundred monks blossomed like lotuses in a lotus pond. The monk who first reached Arahantship thought, "I shall report to the Blessed One," and releasing his cross-legged position, he shook his sitting cloth, stood up, and faced the Ten-Powered One. In this way, one after another, all five hundred arrived in order, as if entering a refectory.

The one who arrived first paid homage, spread his sitting cloth, and sat down in a suitable place. Wishing to report the special quality he had attained, he turned and looked back at the path he had come, thinking, "Is there anyone else besides me, or not?" and he saw the other monks. Thus, although all of them had arrived and were sitting in suitable places, it was a case of "This monk is shy before that monk and does not speak; that monk is shy before this monk and does not speak." It is said that for those whose taints are destroyed, two dispositions occur: the thought arises, "Oh, may the world with its devas quickly realize the special quality I have attained!" However, like a man who has found a hidden treasure, they do not wish to tell others of their attainment.

While that assembly of Noble Ones was thus approaching the Blessed One, the full moon—free from the five defilements of clouds, mist, smoke, dust, and Rāhu from behind the Yugandhara mountains—rose and entered the path of the wind, appearing like a great silver mirror held up in the east to show the loveliness of the world adorned by the appearance of a Buddha, or like a glorious silver wheel being turned by its rim. At such a moment, a second, a minute, the Blessed One was staying among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Mahāvana forest, together with a great community of monks, about five hundred monks, all of whom were Arahants.

There, the Blessed One was born in the lineage of King Mahāsammata, and those five hundred monks were also born in the clan of King Mahāsammata. The Blessed One was born in the womb of a Khattiya queen, and those monks...
271:
These monks were born in the royal lineage. Just as the Blessed One went forth from the royal lineage, so did these monks. Just as the Blessed One renounced the sovereignty of a Cakkavatti and the white parasol that were within his reach to go forth, so did these monks renounce their royal sovereignty and white parasols that were within their reach to go forth. Thus, the Blessed One, in an exceedingly pure place, during a pure time of night, being pure himself and surrounded by a pure retinue—free from lust and surrounded by those free from lust, free from hatred and surrounded by those free from hatred, free from delusion and surrounded by those free from delusion, free from craving and surrounded by those free from craving, free from defilements and surrounded by those free from defilements, peaceful and surrounded by those who are peaceful, tamed and surrounded by those who are tamed, liberated from defilements and surrounded by those who are liberated—shone most brilliantly. This passage is called 'Vaṇṇabhūmi' (the ground of praise); praise should be spoken as much as one is able. Thus, the words 'together with about five hundred monks, all of whom were Arahants' were spoken in reference to these monks.

The word 'Yebhuyyena' (mostly) means that although many devas and Brahmas assembled, the Asañña-satta Brahmas, the Arupa Brahmas, and those devas and Brahmas absorbed in meditative attainments did not assemble. The order of the assembly of those devas and Brahmas was as follows: The deities near the Mahāvana forest, thinking, 'Come, sirs! Beholding the Buddha is of great benefit, hearing the Dhamma is of great benefit, beholding the Saṅgha of monks is of great benefit; come, let us go!' made a great sound and arrived. They paid homage to the Blessed One and to the Arahants who had attained Arahantship at that very moment, and stood at a respectful distance. In this manner, hearing the sounds of various deities, at distances of half a gāvuta, one gāvuta, half a yojana, one yojana, and so on, deities from the Himavantā forest, which is three thousand yojanas wide; from the sixty-three thousand cities visited three times; from the nine million nine hundred thousand market towns; from the nine million six hundred thousand seaports; and from the fifty-six jewel mines (such as those in Sīhaḷadīpa and elsewhere)—thus from the entire Jambudīpa, Pubbavideha, Aparagoyāna, Uttarakuru, and the two thousand small islands, throughout the entire world-system, and then from the second and third world-systems, up to ten thousand world-systems, it should be understood that the deities assembled. Here, 'ten world elements' (dasa-lokadhātu) refers to the ten thousand world-systems. Therefore, it is said, 'Deities from the ten world elements mostly assembled.'

The interior of the entire world-system, up to the Brahma world, was so crowded with the assembled devas and Brahmas that it was like a needle case packed with needles without any gap. The height of that Brahma world should be understood thus: if a great stone the size of about seven pinnacles of the Lohapāsāda were dropped from the Brahma world, it would take four months to reach the earth. In such a vast space, flowers or smoke thrown from below could not find a gap to rise upward, nor could mustard seeds dropped from above find a gap to fall downward. In the same way, the deities were packed without any gap. However, just as the Cakkavatti's...
272:
If a stone were dropped, it would take four months to reach the ground; in such a vast space, flowers or smoke thrown from below could not find a gap to rise upward, nor could mustard seeds dropped from above find a gap to fall downward. In the same way, the deities were packed without any gap. Just as the place where a Cakkavatti sits is not crowded, and great powerful kings who arrive find a place, while it is very crowded further out and behind, so too the place where the Blessed One sat was not crowded. The great powerful deities and Great Brahmas who arrived certainly found a place. Indeed, in the immediate vicinity of the Blessed One, as described in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, even in a space the size of the tip of a horse-hair, ten, twenty, or even thirty deities created exceedingly subtle forms and stood there. At the outermost edge, the deities stood in groups of sixty each.

'Suddhāvāsakāyikānaṃ' refers to those living in the Suddhāvāsa (Pure Abodes). The Suddhāvāsa refers to the five Brahma worlds which are the dwellings of pure individuals—Non-returners (Anāgāmīs) and Arahants. Why is it said 'Etadahosi' (this thought occurred)? It is said that those Brahmas, having entered meditative attainments and emerged at the predetermined time, looked at the Brahma realm and saw it empty, like a kitchen after lunch has been eaten. Then, reflecting, 'Where have the Brahmas gone?' they realized there was a Great Assembly (Mahāsamāgama). They thought, 'This assembly is great; we have been left behind. It is difficult for those left behind to find an opportunity. Therefore, when we go, let us not go empty-handed, but let us each compose a verse and go. By that verse, we shall make our arrival known in the Great Assembly and also speak in praise of the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala).' Thus, because they reflected after emerging from their meditative attainments, this thought occurred to them.

'Bhagavato purato pāturahesuṃ' (they appeared before the Blessed One): although the Pali text says they descended right into the presence and before the Blessed One, this meaning should not be taken literally here. Those Brahmas, while still in the Brahma world, composed the verses, and then one descended to the edge of the eastern world-system, one to the edge of the southern world-system, one to the edge of the western world-system, and one to the edge of the northern world-system. Then, the Brahma who descended to the edge of the eastern world-system entered the Nīla-kasiṇa (blue kasina) and emitted blue rays, making his arrival known to the deities and Brahmas of the ten thousand world-systems as if he were clothing them in a jeweled robe, and then...
273:
No one is able to obstruct the path leading to the Buddha (Buddha-vīthi). Therefore, [the Brahma descending from the eastern world-system] arrived via the path habitually used by the devas and Brahmas when approaching the Blessed One, paid homage to the Blessed One, and stood at a suitable place. Standing at a suitable place, he recited a verse he had composed himself.

The Brahma who descended at the southern rim of the world-system also entered the yellow kasina attainment (pīta-kasiṇa), emitted golden rays, and stood there, making his arrival known as if covering the devas and Brahmas of the ten thousand world-systems with a golden cloth. The Brahma who descended at the western rim of the world-system also entered the red kasina attainment (lohita-kasiṇa), emitted red rays, and stood there, making his arrival known as if wrapping the devas and Brahmas of the ten thousand world-systems with a noble red blanket. The Brahma who descended at the northern rim of the world-system also entered the white kasina attainment (odāta-kasiṇa), emitted white rays, and stood there, making his arrival known as if covering the devas and Brahmas of the ten thousand world-systems with a cloth the color of jasmine flowers.

In the Pali text, however, it is stated: "They appeared before the Blessed One. Then those devas paid homage to the Blessed One and stood at a suitable place." Although it describes their appearance before Him and their standing after paying homage as if occurring simultaneously, it actually happened in this sequence and was presented collectively. The recitation of the verses, however, is mentioned separately in the Pali.

In those verses, "Mahāsamaya" means a great gathering. A forest grove is called "pavana." By both terms, the Blessed One said that today in this forest grove, there is a great gathering, a great assembly of devas and Brahmas. Then, to show who had arrived at that assembly, He said, "devakāyā samāgatā" (the groups of devas have assembled). In that phrase, "devakāyā" means groups of devas and Brahmas. "Āgatamha imaṃ dhammasamayaṃ" means, "Seeing the devas and Brahmas thus assembled, we too have come to this assembly for the Dhamma." For what reason did they come? As said in "dakkhitāye aparājitasanghaṃ," they came to see the Noble Sangha which no Māra can conquer. It means they came to see this unconquered Sangha, which cannot be defeated by anyone and which has today crushed the three Māras and won the battle. After reciting this verse, that Brahma paid homage to the Blessed One and stood at the eastern rim of the world-system.

Then the second Brahma arrived and recited in the same manner as mentioned. In the verse recited by that second Brahma, "tatra bhikkhavo" means the monks in that place of assembly. "Samādahaṃsu" means they composed themselves with concentration. "Cittamattano ujuṃ akaṃsu" means they removed all crookedness, curvature, and deviousness from their minds and made them straight. Like a charioteer [holding] the reins...
274:
"Gahētvā" means just as a charioteer, having laid down his weapon, stands holding all the reins of Sindhu horses running evenly, neither driving nor restraining them; likewise, these five hundred monks, who are wise, endowed with six-factored equanimity (saḷaṅgupekkhā), and have guarded sense-doors, protect their faculties. [He addressed:] "Blessed One, we have come to this place to see those monks." That [second Brahma] also went and stood in his place.

Then the third Brahma arrived and addressed in the same manner as mentioned. In that verse, "chetvā khīlaṃ" means having cut the spikes of lust, hatred, and delusion. "Palighaṃ" refers to the cross-bar of lust, hatred, and delusion. "Indakhīlaṃ" is also the threshold pillar of lust, hatred, and delusion. "Ūhacca maneja" means these monks are called "aneja" because they are free from the agitation of craving; it means having thoroughly uprooted the pillars of lust and so on. "Te caranti" means those monks wander without obstruction in the four directions. "Suddhā" means being free from defilements. "Vimalā" means being stainless. This word "vimalā" is a synonym for "suddhā." "Cakkhumatā" means [tamed] by the Blessed One who is endowed with the five eyes. "Sudantā" means those who are well-tamed in the eye-faculty, ear-faculty, nose-faculty, tongue-faculty, body-faculty, and mind-faculty. "Susunāgā" means those who are like noble elephants, having become Arahants even in their youth. [He addressed:] "Blessed One, we have come to see those noble young elephants tamed by such an unsurpassed teacher of meditation (the Blessed One)." That [third Brahma] also went and stood in his place.

Then the fourth Brahma arrived and addressed in the same manner as mentioned. In that verse, "gatāse" means they have gone for refuge with a mind free from doubt. That [fourth Brahma] also went and stood in his place.

## Description of the Assembly of Devas

Then, as the Blessed One looked out, He saw the assembly of devas and Brahmas extending from the surface of the earth to the rim of the world-system and up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma realm. He thought, "This assembly of devas is vast. The monks, however, do not know that there is such a great assembly of devas. Let me tell them." Having thought thus, the text beginning with "Then the Blessed One addressed the monks..." should be expanded in detail. In that passage, "etaparamā" means this is the highest extent or measure for those devas. Since there are no other Buddhas at this time, the third repetition, "Monks, at this time also...", was not spoken. Why did He say, "Monks, I will tell you"? It was to create clarity and joy in the minds of the devas. For the devas reportedly thought, "In such a vast assembly, the Blessed One will mention the names and clans of only the high-authority devas; how could He mention those of the low-authority devas?"
275: Then the Blessed One, reflecting, "What are these deities thinking?" knew their thoughts as if putting a hand into the mouth to knead the heart-flesh, or as if catching a thief with the stolen goods. He thought, "I shall announce the names and lineages of all the deities of lesser and greater power who have come from the ten thousand world systems (cakkavāḷa)." Buddhas are indeed great and exceptional beings. Whatever is seen, heard, sensed (through the senses of smell, taste, and touch), known, attained, sought after, or reflected upon by the mind of the world including the devas—there is no object whatsoever that does not appear before the threshold of their knowledge. Among the visual objects of various colors such as blue as analyzed in the Abhidhamma, or among the various auditory objects such as the sound of a great drum, there is not a single object that does not appear in the Buddha's knowledge. Referring to this meaning, he taught: "Monks, whatever in the world with its devas... whatever is seen, heard, sensed, known, attained, sought after, or reflected upon by the mind of devas and humans, that I know, that I have seen, that I have realized through higher knowledge." Thus, the Blessed One, whose knowledge is unobstructed in all objects, divided the assembly of deities into two groups: those capable of liberation (bhabba) and those incapable (abhabba). Those beings described by such terms as "possessed of the obstruction of kamma" are called incapable. Even if they live in the same monastery, the Buddhas do not look upon them. Others are called capable. Even if they live far away, the Buddhas go to them and favor them. Therefore, in that assembly of deities as well, he set aside the incapable ones and accepted the capable ones. Having accepted them, he divided them into six groups according to their temperaments: "This many deities are of lustful temperament, this many are of hateful temperament, and this many are of deluded temperament." Then, while considering the appropriate Dhamma teaching for them, he determined the discourse: "I shall preach the Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta to the deities of lustful temperament, the Kalahavivāda Sutta to those of hateful temperament, the Mahāvyūha Sutta to those of deluded temperament, the Cūḷavyūha Sutta to those of speculative temperament, the Tuvaṭṭaka practice to those of faithful temperament, and the Purābheda Sutta to those of intellectual temperament." Having thus determined the teaching, he again reflected on the assembly: "Will they understand through my own initiative, or through the initiative of another, or through a specific occurrence, or by way of a question?" Then, knowing that "They will understand by way of a question," he looked to see, "Is there anyone capable of taking the inclination of the deities and asking a question according to their temperament?" He saw that among those five hundred monks, not even one was capable. Then he considered the eighty great disciples and the two chief disciples...
276: Seeing that "They too are unable," he thought, "If there were a Paccekabuddha, would he be able?" Knowing that "Even he would not be able," he considered whether anyone among Sakka, Suyāma, and others would be able. If any of them were able, he would have them ask and he himself would answer; however, not one among them was able. Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One: "Only a Buddha like me would be able. Is there another Buddha anywhere?" Spreading his infinite knowledge throughout the infinite world systems and looking, he did not see another Buddha. This is not surprising, that he did not see anyone equal to himself now; for even on the day of his birth, as described in the commentary to the Brahmajāla Sutta, not seeing anyone equal to himself, he uttered the bold words like an irreversible lion's roar: "I am the foremost in the world." Thus, not seeing another equal to himself, he thought: "If I ask and I myself answer, these deities and Brahmas will not be able to penetrate the meaning. But if another Buddha asks and I answer, it will be marvelous, and the deities and Brahmas will be able to penetrate the meaning. Therefore, I shall create a duplicate Buddha (nimmitabuddha)." Having entered the jhāna which is the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññāpādakajjhāna) and emerged from it, he performed the preliminary work with the sense-sphere consciousness, resolving: "Let the holding of the bowl and robes, the looking ahead and looking aside, and the bending and stretching of this created Buddha be just like mine." Then, with the fine-material sphere consciousness, he resolved it to appear like the moon-disk emerging rapidly after breaking through the circumference of the eastern Mount Yugandhara. The assembly of deities and Brahmas, seeing that created Buddha, said, "Friends, has another moon arisen?" Then, as it came closer and appeared like the moon, they said, "It is not the moon, it is the sun that has arisen." As it came even closer, they said, "It is not the sun, it is a celestial mansion." As it came closer still, they said, "It is not a celestial mansion, it is a son of the devas." As it came closer still, they said, "It is not a son of the devas, it is a Great Brahma." As it came closer still, they said, "It is not a Great Brahma; friends, another Buddha has arrived!" At that time, the worldling deities thought, "When there was only one Buddha, this many deities and Brahmas assembled; if there are two Buddhas, how many more will there be?" The noble (ariya) deities, however, thought, "There is no such thing as two Buddhas in a single world system; surely the Blessed One has created another Buddha equal to himself." Then, while that assembly of deities and Brahmas was watching, the created Buddha arrived and, without bowing to the Blessed One, sat down in front of him on a seat created to be equal to his. The Blessed One possessed the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, and the created Buddha also possessed the same thirty-two marks.
277:
Six-colored rays emitted from the body of the Blessed One, and rays also emitted from the body of the created Buddha (Nimmitabuddha). The rays from the Blessed One’s body struck the body of the created Buddha, and the rays from the created Buddha’s body struck the body of the Blessed One. The rays emerging from the bodies of both Buddhas reached as far as the Akaniṭṭha realm, and from there, they returned, descending upon the heads of the deities and settled on the rim of the universe (Cakkavāḷa). The interior of the entire universe shone brilliantly, like a shrine-house (cetiya-ghara) adorned with golden rafters. Deities and Brahmās from ten thousand universes gathered in this single universe and stood within the aura of the rays of the two Buddhas. While remaining seated, the created Buddha, praising the abandonment of defilements at the Blessed One’s Throne of Enlightenment, spoke this verse:

“I ask the Sage of profound wisdom,
Who has crossed over, reached the far shore, attained Nibbāna, and is firm in self;
Having gone forth from the home and abandoned sensual pleasures,
How should that bhikkhu wander rightly in the world?” (Sn 361)

The Blessed One, intending to first gladden the minds of the deities by announcing the names and clans of those who had arrived, said: “Bhikkhus, I shall proclaim...” and so on. In that passage, “Silokamanukassāmi” means: I shall bring forth (proclaim) a collection of words composed in verse. “Yattha bhummā tadassitā” means: In whatever places the earth-bound deities (bhummā devatā) reside, they are dependent on those places. With the words beginning with “Ye sitā girigabbharaṃ,” he spoke of the virtues of those bhikkhus. It means those bhikkhus reside depending on mountain clefts. “Pahitattā” means those whose minds are directed toward Nibbāna (those who strive without regard for body or life). “Samāhitā” means those whose minds are not distracted.

“Puthū” means many bhikkhus. “Sīhāva sallīnā” means those who, like lion kings, dwell alone and have attained a state of oneness. “Lomahaṃsābhisambhuno” means those who stand having overcome the bristling of hair due to fear; it means they are fearless. “Odātamanasā suddhā” means those who are pure, having bright minds. “Vippasannāmanāvilā” means those who are exceptionally clear and undisturbed. “Bhiyyopañcasate ñatvā” means knowing more than five hundred bhikkhus together with the Blessed One. “Vane Kāpilavatthave” means in the forest grove located near Kapilavatthu. “Tato āmantayī satthā” means at that time the Teacher addressed them. “Sāvake sāsane rate” means the disciples who follow the Buddha’s word because it arose at the conclusion of hearing his Dhamma teaching, and who delight in the Dispensation (Sāsana) consisting of the threefold training. All these words beginning with ‘Bhiyyopañcasate’...
278:
“Disciples delighted in the Teaching” (Sāvake sāsane rate) means those who are called disciples (sāvaka) because they arose at the conclusion of hearing his Dhamma teaching, and who delight in the Teaching because they delight in the Dispensation (Sāsana) of the threefold training. Because he said, “I shall proclaim the verse,” he spoke all these words beginning with “Bhiyyopañcasate” as if they were spoken by another.

“The hosts of deities have arrived; bhikkhus, recognize them” means: Recognize those deities with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). He taught this to the bhikkhus to direct their minds toward the knowledge of the divine eye. Upon hearing that instruction of the Buddha, those bhikkhus immediately exerted effort to attain that divine eye.

By merely making such an effort, knowledge became manifest to those bhikkhus. What kind of knowledge? The divine eye knowledge that can see non-human beings (deities) arose. That divine eye was not produced by those bhikkhus through preliminary preparation (parikamma) at that moment; rather, it was accomplished through the Noble Path (Ariyamagga) itself. However, they merely directed their minds toward that knowledge in order to see the non-human beings. The Teacher, intending this very divine eye accomplished through the Noble Path, said: “You possess knowledge; bring forth that knowledge and recognize them with it,” thus he said, “Bhikkhus, recognize them.”

“Some saw a hundred” means among those bhikkhus, some saw a hundred non-human beings. “A thousand, then seventy thousand” means some saw a thousand, and some saw seventy thousand deities. “Some saw a hundred thousand” means some bhikkhus saw a hundred thousand deities. “Some saw an infinite number” means they saw a vast number; it means they saw deities and Brahmās without limit by hundreds or thousands. Why? Because all directions were pervaded and filled with deities and Brahmās.

“Knowing all that” means knowing all the deities and Brahmās seen by each of those bhikkhus. “The One with Eyes (Cakkhumā) having distinguished” means the Teacher, endowed with the five eyes, having distinguished them clearly as if seeing the lines on the palm of his hand. “Then he addressed” means he spoke the previously mentioned verse to proclaim their names and clans. “I shall proclaim to you which deities there are; you should recognize them, see them, and look at them”—this is the connection here. “Girāhi” means with words. “Anupubbaso” means in due order.

“Those seven thousand yakkhas are earth-bound deities of Kapilavatthu” means among these deities, first, the seven thousand deities are earth-bound deities (bhummā devatā) who arose depending on Kapilavatthu, and they are indeed called yakkhas.
279:
(The Buddha) said: *Iddhimanto* means those endowed with the psychic power of devas. *Jutimanto* means those endowed with the radiance and majesty of devas. *Vaṇṇavanto* means those endowed with physical beauty. *Yasassino* means those endowed with a retinue. *Modamānā abhikkāmun* means they have come with joyful hearts. *Bhikkhūnaṃ samitiṃ vanan* means they have come to this Mahāvana forest to the presence of the monks for the purpose of seeing the monks. Alternatively, *samitiṃ* means a group; thus, it also means they have come to see the assembly of monks.

*Chasahassā hemavatā, yakkhā nānattavaṇṇino* means six thousand Yakkhas born on Mount Hemavata, all of whom have various colors such as blue and so forth.

*Sātāgirā tisahassā* means three thousand Yakkhas born on Mount Sātāgira.

*Iccete soḷasasahassā* means all these devas total sixteen thousand.

*Vessāmittā pañcasatā* means five hundred devas born on Mount Vessāmitta.

*Kumbhīro rājagahiko* means the Yakkha named Kumbhīra born in the city of Rājagaha. *Vepullassa nivesanan* means his dwelling place is Mount Vepulla. *Bhiyyo naṃ satasahassaṃ, yakkhānaṃ payirupāsati* means more than one hundred thousand Yakkhas attend upon that King Kumbhīra. *Kumbhīro rājagahiko, sopāgā samitiṃ vanan* means that Kumbhīra, along with his retinue, has also come to this forest to see the assembly of monks.

*Purimañca disaṃ rājā, dhataraṭṭho pasāsati* means he rules and governs the eastern direction. *Gandhabbānaṃ adhipati* means he is the chief of the Gandhabbas in the four directions. All those Gandhabbas follow the will of King Dhataraṭṭha. *Mahārājā yasassiso* means this Great King has a large retinue.

*Puttāpi tassa bahavo, indanāmā mahabbalā* means King Dhataraṭṭha has many sons of great strength; all those sons bear the name of Inda, the king of devas.

*Virūḷho taṃ pasāsati* means King Virūḷha rules and governs that [southern] direction.
280:
The sons of King Dhataraṭṭha are just like the king himself. In the Pali text, it is written as '*mahabbalā*' (possessing great strength). However, in the Commentary, the reading is '*mahābalā*' in all instances.

'King Dhataraṭṭha in the eastern direction, Virūḷhaka in the south,
King Virūpakkha in the western direction, and Kuvera in the northern direction.
These four Great Kings, shining brilliantly in all four directions,
stood in the forest of Kapilavatthu.'

These verses are taught in a way that encompasses all the Four Great Kings. The meaning here is: there are Great Kings named Dhataraṭṭha in the ten thousand universes. All these kings, accompanied by retinues of hundreds of billions of Gandhabbas, have come and stood filling the entire interior of the universe, starting from the Mahāvana forest of Kapilavatthu in the eastern direction. Similarly, Virūḷhaka and others stand in the southern and other directions. Therefore, it is said: 'Shining brilliantly in all four directions, they stood.' This means: having come from their respective universes, they stood in the four directions like great masses of fire on mountain peaks, shining intensely. Because these kings came specifically aiming for the Mahāvana forest of Kapilavatthu, even though they fill the entire universe, it is said they are 'in the Mahāvana forest of Kapilavatthu'.

'The deceptive servants of those kings also came' means: those four Great Kings have servants who possess the characteristic of concealing their own wrongdoings (*māyā*) and who have crooked conduct. Because they deceive the world both in one's presence and behind one's back, they are called '*vañcanika*' (deceivers), and because they are full of fraud and craftiness, they are called '*saṭha*' (crafty). It means those servants also arrived. '*Māyā kuteṇဍu viṭeṇဍu, viṭucca viṭuṭo sahā*' means all those servants are indeed deceivers. By name, one is called Kuteṇḍu, and one is called Viteṇḍu. In the Pali text, it is written as '*veṭeṇဍū*'. One is named Viṭucca, and one is named Viṭuṭo. '*Saha*' means that Viṭuṭo also came together with them.
281: Candana, Kāma-seṭṭha, Kinnighaṇḍu, and Nighaṇḍu—among these names, another servant is named Kinnighaṇḍu. In the Pali text, however, it is written as 'Kinnughaṇḍū'. Nighaṇḍu refers to another person named Nighaṇḍu. These individuals are the servants [of the Four Great Kings]. Apart from these servants, others who arrived are: 'Panāda, Opamañña, Devasuta, Mātali, Cittasena the Gandhabba, Naḷarājā Janesabha, Pañcasikha, Timbarū, and Suriyavacchasā.' These are celestial kings. Among these kings, Devasuta is a divine charioteer. Cittasena refers to Citta, Sena, and Cittasena. 'Gandhabba' means this Cittasena is a deity belonging to the Gandhabba host. Not only him, but all these deities starting with Panāda are also Gandhabbas. Naḷarājā is a deity named Naḷakāra (the reed-maker). Janesabha is the deity Janavasabha. 'Āguṃ Pañcasikho ceva' means the deity Pañcasikha also arrived. Timbarū is the Gandhabba king named Timbarū. Suriyavacchasā is the daughter of that king. 'Ete caññe ca rājāno, gandhabbā saha rājūbhi' means that along with those Gandhabba kings mentioned by name, many other Gandhabbas also came together with those kings. 'Modamānā abhikkāmuṃ, bhikkhūnaṃ samitiṃ vanaṃ' means they came to this forest, the meeting place of the community of monks, with joyful and delighted minds. 'Athāguṃ nāgasā nāgā, vesālā sahatacchakā' means the Nagas living in Lake Nāgasa and the Nagas living in Vesālī arrived together with the Tacchaka Naga retinue. 'Kambalassatarā' refers to the Nagas Kambala and Assatara. It is said that these Nagas live at the foot of Mount Sineru; they are highly powerful Nagas whom even Garudas cannot carry away. 'Pāyāgā saha ñātibhi' means the Nagas living at the Pāyāga landing arrived together with their assembly of kinsmen. 'Yāmunā dhataraṭṭhā ca' refers to the Nagas living in the Yamunā River and the Nagas born of the Dhataraṭṭha clan. 'Erāvaṇo mahānāgo' refers to the deity named Erāvaṇa; by birth, he is not a noble elephant (Naga), but he is called so by the designation 'Naga'. 'Sopāgā' means that the deity Erāvaṇa also arrived.
282: Those Garudas (Supaṇṇas) who, overcome by greed, seize and carry away the Nagas of the aforementioned types by force. These Garudas are called 'Dibba' because they possess power similar to that of the devas. They are called 'Dija' (twice-born) because they are born twice: once from the mother's womb and once from the eggshell. They are called 'Pakkhi' because they are endowed with wings. They are called 'Visuddhacakkhu' (pure-eyed) because they have eyes capable of seeing Nagas at a distance of a hundred or a thousand yojanas. These Garuda kings arrived at this Mahāvana forest through the sky. Because they have variegated wings, these Garudas are named 'Citrasupaṇṇa'. At that time, the Blessed One granted the Naga kings freedom from fear, making them safe from the Garudas. Therefore, all those Nagas and Garudas, calling out to one another with gentle words, greeted each other joyfully like friends and relatives, embracing, holding hands, and placing their hands on each other's shoulders with delighted minds. Both Nagas and Garudas went to the Buddha alone for refuge. The Asuras were defeated by Sakka, the king of devas, who wields the Vajira weapon. All those Asuras, who usually dwell in the great ocean and are brothers of Vāsava (Sakka) because of the Asura princess Sujātā, are powerful and have great retinues. Among those Asuras, those named Kālakañja arrived, having manifested large and terrifying forms. Other archer Asuras named Dānavēghasa also arrived. The Asuras Vepacitti and Sucitti, as well as the Mara named Namuci, arrived together with those Asuras. These Asuras are dwellers of the great ocean, while Mara is a dweller of the Paranimmita-vasavatti heaven; why did he come with them? It is because of the lack of wholesome desire to attain the Path of Arhatship. Just as those Asuras lack wholesome desire and are incapable of becoming Noble Ones (Ariyas), Mara is the same. Therefore, they came together due to their similar natures (dhātu). The hundred sons of the great Asura king Bali also arrived. All of them took the name of their maternal uncle, Rāhu the Asura lord. All those Asuras, having assembled and prepared their own Bali army, approached Rāhu the Asura lord.
283:
"Samayo dāni bhaddante" means: "May there be blessings to the Great King of the Asuras; now is the opportune time for you to approach the Mahāvana forest, the meeting place of the monks, to see the Saṅgha of monks."

"Āpo ca devā pathavī, tejo vāyo tadāgamuṃ" means: The devas named Water (Āpo), and so forth, who were born by performing preliminary practice (parikamma) on the water-kasina and so forth, have arrived. "Varuṇā vāraṇā devā, somo ca yasasā sahā" means: The devas named Varuṇa, Vāraṇa, and Soma have arrived together with the deva named Yasasa. "Mettākaruṇākāyikā" refers to the devas born by performing preliminary practice on the meditations of loving-kindness (mettā) and compassion (karuṇā). "Āguṃ devā yasassino" means: Those illustrious devas with large retinues have also arrived.

"Dasete dasadhā kāyā, sabbe nānatta-vaṇṇino" means: These ten groups of devas, staying in ten ways, have arrived, possessing various colors such as blue and so forth.

"Veṇḍū ca devā" means: The Veṇḍu devas; "sahali ca" means: the Sahali devas; "asamā ca duve yamā" means: the Asama devas and the two Yama devas have arrived. "Candassūpanisā devā, candamāguṃ purakkhatvā" means: The devas dependent on the Moon-god have arrived, placing the Moon-god at the front. Similarly, the devas dependent on the Sun-god, placing the Sun-god at the front; "nakkhattāni purakkhatvā" means: the devas dependent on the stars have also arrived, placing the stars at the front. "Āguṃ mandavalāhakā" means: The Wind-cloud devas (Vātavalāhaka), the Mist-cloud devas (Abbhavalāhaka), and the Heat-cloud devas (Uṇhavalāhaka)—all these groups of cloud-devas are called "Mandavalāhaka." They have also arrived. "Vasūnaṃ vāsavo seṭṭho, sakkopāgā purindado" means: Vāsava, the chief of the Vasu devas, who is also called Sakka and Purindada, has also arrived.

"Dasete dasadhā kāyā" means: These ten groups of devas have also arrived in ten ways. "Sabbe nānatta-vaṇṇino" means: They possess various colors such as blue and so forth.

Then, the devas named "Sahabhū" arrived. "Jalamaggisikhāriva" means: They arrived shining like the crest of a flame. It is also said that "Jalamaggi" and "Sikhāri" are the names of those devas. "Ariṭṭhakā ca rojā ca" means: The Ariṭṭhaka devas and the Roja devas. "Umāpupphanibhāsino" means: These devas are called "Flax-flower devas" because they have a color like the flax flower (umā flower).
284:
The aura of the Ariṭṭhaka and Roja devas is like the flax flower (umā flower); therefore, they are called "Umāpupphanibhāsino."

The two devas, Varuṇa and Sahadhamma, as well as the Accuta and Anejaka devas, and the Suleyya and Rucira devas, have arrived. The devas named Vāsavanesī have also arrived. These ten groups of devas have arrived in ten ways.

The Samāna and Mahāsamāna devas, the Mānusa and Mānusuttama devas, the Khiḍḍāpadosika devas who pass away due to excessive indulgence in play and pleasure, and the Manopadosika devas who pass away due to excessive anger, have also arrived.

Then, the golden-colored devas named Hari have arrived, as well as the devas named Lohitavāsī. The two types of devas, Pāraga and Mahāpāraga, have also arrived. These ten groups of devas have arrived in ten ways.

The three types of devas—Sukka, Karambha, and Aruṇa—have arrived, along with the devas named Veghanasa. The leading devas named Odātagayha and the devas named Vicakkhaṇa have also arrived.

The Sadāmattā and Hāragaja devas, as well as the illustrious Missaka devas with their retinues, have arrived. The rain-god Pajjunna has also arrived, thundering. Wherever that rain-god Pajjunna goes, he causes rain to fall in those places. These ten groups of devas have arrived in ten ways.

The Khemiya devas, the devas residing in the Tusita heaven, and the devas residing in the Yāma heaven have arrived. The illustrious Kathaka devas have also arrived. (In the Pali text, however, it is written as "Kaṭṭhakā ca.") The Lambitaka and Lāmaseṭṭha devas have also arrived. There are devas named Joti, who are as bright as a bonfire of reeds lit on a mountain top; those Joti devas and the Āsā devas have arrived. (According to the verse order, the Āsa devas are called "Āsā.") These ten groups of devas have arrived in ten ways.
285:
In the Pali text, however, they write "Jotināmā". Deities named Āsā are called "Āsā" by the power of their desire (chanda). The Nimmānaratī deities have come; then the Paranimmitavasavattī deities have also come. "Dasethe dasadhā kāyā" means those ten groups of deities (starting from Khemiyā and ending with Āsā) have also come in ten different ways.

"Saṭṭhete devanikāyā" means the sixty groups of deities, such as the Āpo deities, have various colors by the power of their complexions, such as blue and so on. "Nāmanvayena āgacchuṃ" means they came according to their name-groups, such as the Āpo deities. "Ye caññe sadisā sahā" means those deities in other world systems who are similar to the Āpo deities and others in terms of appearance and name have also come. Thus, by using a single term, the Buddha refers to all deities as if making a collection or a bundle.

Having thus pointed out the groups of deities in the ten thousand world systems, He now spoke the verse beginning with "Pavuṭṭhajātiṃ" to show the purpose for which those deities had come. The meaning of that verse is: The Ariya Saṅgha is called "Pavuṭṭhajāti" because they have discarded birth (jāti). We shall see the Ariya Saṅgha who is called "Akhīla" because of the absence of the thorns of lust, hatred, and delusion; who is called "Oghatiṇṇa" because they stand having crossed the four floods (ogha); and who is called "Anāsava" because of the absence of the four taints (āsava). We shall also see the Dasabala Buddha, who is called "Oghatara" because He has crossed those same four floods; who is called "Nāga" because He does no evil; and who shines with glory like the moon, having transcended dark stains (asitātiga). For this purpose, all those deities came according to their names, and similar deities from other world systems also came together.

Now, wishing to show the Brahmas, He spoke the verse beginning with "Subrahmā paramatto ca". Therein, "Subrahmā" is one Brahma. "Paramatto" is also a Brahma. "Puttā iddhimato sahā" means the Ariya Brahmas, who are the sons of the Buddha, the Possessor of Great Power, have come together. "Sanaṅkumāro tisso ca" refers to Sanaṅkumāra Brahma and Tissa Mahābrahmā. "Sopāgā" means that Great Sanaṅkumāra Brahma also came.

"In the thousand Brahma worlds, the Mahābrahmā stands surpassing others; he is a Brahma who is reborn in the Brahma realm, possessing majesty, having a great body, and having a retinue."
286:
In this (Mahāsamaya Sutta), "Sahassaṃ brahmalokānaṃ" means a thousand Great Brahmas have arrived, who are capable of spreading light to a thousand world systems with one finger, and to ten thousand world systems with ten fingers. "Mahābrahmābhitiṭṭhati" means each Great Brahma stands surpassing other Brahmas (in appearance, retinue, and lifespan). "Upapanno" means one who is reborn in the Brahma realm. "Jutimanto" means one who is endowed with power. "Bhismākāyo" means one who has a large body, having a physical form equal in size to about two or three village-tracts in the Magadha country. "Yasassī" means one who is endowed with a retinue, which is described as the splendor of the physical form.

"Dasettha issarā āgūṃ, paccekavasavattino" means that among those thousand Brahmas, ten sovereign Great Brahmas of such nature, who can make others follow their own will individually, have arrived. "Tesañca majjhato āga, hārito parivārito" means that in the midst of those Brahmas, the Great Brahma named Hārita has arrived, surrounded by a retinue of one hundred thousand Brahmas.

"Te ca sabbe abhikkante, sainde deve sabrahmake" refers to all the groups of deities who came with Sakka, the king of gods, as their leader, and all the groups of Brahmas who came with Hārita Mahābrahmā as their leader. "Mārasenā abhikkāmī" means the army of Māra came overwhelmingly. "Passa kaṇhassa mandiyaṃ" means "Behold the foolishness of the dark Māra."

"Come, catch, bind!"—in this way, he (Māra) commanded his own assembly. "May this entire assembly of deities and Brahmas be bound by lust (rāga) for you all," he said. "Surround them from all sides; let not even one of you release even a single one of them," he said. There is also a reading "Mā vo muñcetha", which has the same meaning.

"Iti tattha mahāseno, kaṇho senaṃ apesayī" means thus, in that Great Assembly (Mahāsamaya), Māra, who has a large army, dispatched the army of Māra. "Pāṇinā talamāhacca" means by striking the surface of the earth with his hand. "Saraṃ katvāna bheravaṃ" means by making a terrifying sound to show the intimidation of Māra.

"Yathā pāvussako megho, thanayanto savijjuko" means shouting a great roar like a heavy monsoon cloud accompanied by lightning. "Tadā so paccudāvattī" means at that time, that Māra, having shown that intimidation, retreated and fled...
287:
That Māra retreated. "Saṅkuddho asayaṃvase" means that being extremely enraged and unable to bring anyone under his control, he retreated against his own will. The Blessed One knew, "This Māra, seeing this great assembly (Mahāsamaya), intends to create an obstacle to the realization of the Truths (abhisamaya)," and that he was showing terrifying threats by sending Māra's armies at intervals. This is the natural disposition of the Blessed One: in a place where the realization of the Truths will not occur, He does not prevent Māra from showing terrifying threats. However, in a place where the realization of the Truths will occur, He resolves (adhiṭṭhāna) so that the assembly neither sees Māra's form nor hears his voice. In this assembly, since many devas and Brahmās would attain the realization of the Truths, He resolved so that the devas would neither see Māra's form nor hear his voice. Therefore, it is said: "At that time, that Māra, being extremely enraged and unable to have his way, retreated."

"Tañca sabbaṃ abhiññāya vavatthitvāna cakkhumā" means that the Blessed One, having known and discerned all those actions of Māra, said: "O monks, the armies of Māra have fled; you should know them accordingly and enter into the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti)." "Ātappamakaruṃ" means they exerted effort to enter the attainment of fruition. "Vītarāgehi pakkāmuṃ" means that Māra and his army moved far away from the Noble Ones (Ariyas) who are free from passion. "Nesaṃ lomāpi iñjayuṃ" means they could not even make a single hair of those passion-free Noble Ones stir. Then, Māra spoke this verse concerning the community of monks:

"All your disciples, who have conquered the battlefield, transcended fear, possess great fame, and are well-known among the people, rejoice together with the Noble Ones."

In that verse, "modanti saha bhūtehi" means they rejoice together with the Noble Ones who have arisen within the Dispensation (Sāsana) of the Buddha. "Janesutā" means being famous and well-known among the people.

This Mahāsamaya Sutta is very dear and pleasing to the devas. Therefore, those who wish to speak auspicious words should recite this very sutta at new places of business or dwellings. It is said that devas wander about with their ears inclined, thinking, "We shall listen to this sutta." At the conclusion of the teaching...
288:
At the conclusion of that Mahāsamaya Sutta, one hundred thousand crores of devas attained Arahantship; the number of those who became Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna) and so forth is beyond counting.

Regarding the fact that this sutta is dear and pleasing to the devas, there is this story: It is said that a female deity (devadhītā) lived in a Naga tree at the entrance of the Nāga Cave in the Koṭipabbata Monastery. A young monk was reciting this sutta inside the cave. Having heard it, the deity uttered a loud "Sādhu" at the end of the sutta. When asked, "Who is this?", she replied, "Venerable sir, I am a female deity." When asked, "Why did you utter Sādhu?", she replied, "Venerable sir, I heard this sutta on the day the Blessed One, the Possessor of Ten Powers, sat and preached it in the Great Forest (Mahāvana), and I have heard it again today. You have preserved this Dhamma well, without omitting even a single syllable from the Pali text preached by the Blessed One." When asked, "Did you hear it yourself when the Possessor of Ten Powers was preaching?", she replied, "Yes, venerable sir." When asked, "I have heard that there was a great assembly of devas and Brahmās at that time; where did you stand to listen?", she replied:

"Venerable sir, I am a deity residing in the Great Forest. However, when powerful devas arrived, I found no space in Jambudīpa. Thus, I came to this island of Tambapaṇṇi and endeavored to listen while standing at the port of Jambukola. There too, as powerful devas arrived, I retreated step by step and eventually listened while standing in the sea, in water up to my neck, behind the village of Mahāgāma in the Rohaṇa region." When asked, "Could you see the Teacher from such a distance where you stood?", she replied, "Venerable sir, what are you saying? While the Teacher was preaching the Dhamma in the Great Forest, I felt as if He was constantly looking only at me. Thus, out of shame and respect, I remained hidden among the waves."

"It is said that on that day, one hundred thousand crores of devas attained Arahantship. Did you also attain Arahantship then?" she was asked. "No, venerable sir," she replied. "I suppose you attained the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-phala)?" "No, venerable sir." "I suppose you attained the fruit of Once-returning (Sakadāgāmi-phala)?" "No, venerable sir." (It is said that the devas who attained the three paths are beyond counting.) "Then, I suppose you became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna)?" Since the deity had attained the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) on that day, she felt shy and said, "Venerable sir, you are asking what should not be asked." Then that monk asked, "Deity, can you show your form to us?" She replied, "Venerable sir, I cannot..."
289:
"Venerable sir, I am unable to show my entire body. I shall show only a finger-joint to you." Saying this, she pointed her finger through the keyhole into the cave. At that moment, it was as if a thousand moons and a thousand suns had risen. The deity said, "Venerable sir, be diligent (appamatta)," and after paying homage to the young monk, she departed. In this way, this sutta is dear and pleasing to the devas; the devas cherish this sutta.

## The Commentary on the Mahāsamaya Sutta is finished.
290:
## 8. Sakkapañhasutta Vaṇṇanā
## Commentary on the Introduction

This discourse beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Sakkapañha Sutta. In this sutta, the explanation of the obscure terms is as follows: Regarding the Brahmin village named Ambasandā, it is said that the village was situated not far from a grove of mango trees; therefore, it is called "Ambasandā."

Regarding Vediyaka Mountain, it is said that the mountain was surrounded on all sides by a dark green forest grove, which grew at the foot of the mountain and resembled a polished jeweled pedestal (maṇivedikā); therefore, it came to be known as "Vediyaka Mountain."

Regarding the Indasāla Cave, in the past, that cave was situated between two mountains, and there was an Indasāla tree (nabbai tree) at its entrance; therefore, it came to be known as the "Indasāla Cave." At that time, people enclosed the cave with walls, fitted it with a main door and windows, and having made it a cave-dwelling decorated with well-finished plasterwork, floral designs, and creeper patterns, they offered it to the Blessed One. However, by the power of its former designation, it was still known as the "Indasāla Cave." It is in reference to that cave, which was thus exquisitely prepared and offered, that it is said "Indasālaguhāyaṃ."

"Ussukkaṃ udapādi" means that a righteous zeal (effort) arose. Does not this Sakka frequently visit the Blessed One? There is no assembly of deities where he has not previously come; there is no young deity who dwells in diligence (appamāda) like Sakka. If so, why did zeal arise in him as if he were one who had never visited the Buddha before? It is because he was terrified by the fear of death. At that time, his life-span was exhausted. Having seen the five preliminary signs (pubbanimitta), he knew, "Now my life is exhausted." Among the young deities in whom the signs of death appear, those who were reborn in the celestial realm through small meritorious deeds fall into fear and trembling, thinking, "Where shall we be reborn now?" However, those who were reborn after performing much merit and providing themselves with protection against the fear of death do not fear, reflecting on the gifts they have given, the virtue they have guarded, and the meditation they have practiced, thinking, "We shall enjoy prosperity in the higher celestial realms."

Sakka, the king of devas, having seen the preliminary signs, looked upon all this prosperity—the celestial city of ten thousand leagues, the Vejayanta Palace one thousand leagues high, the Sudhammā celestial assembly hall of three hundred leagues, the Pāricchattaka tree one hundred leagues high, the Paṇḍukambala stone seat of sixty leagues, the celestial retinue of thirty-five million dancers in the two celestial realms, the Nandana Grove, the Cittalatā Grove, the Missaka Grove, and the Phārusaka Grove—and was overcome by fear, thinking, "Alas, this prosperity of mine is about to perish!" Then, searching for someone among recluses, brahmins, or the Great Brahmā, the grandfather of the world, who could pull out the arrow of sorrow (sokasalla) rooted in his heart and make this prosperity permanent, he saw no one. Then he saw again, "The Fully Enlightened Buddha alone is capable of pulling out the arrow of sorrow that has arisen even for a hundred thousand such as I." While he was thus reflecting, at that time, zeal arose in Sakka, the lord of devas, to see the Blessed One.

"Where is the Blessed One dwelling now? In which country, depending on which city, using whose requisites, and to whom is he dwelling while preaching the Dhamma that gives the Deathless Nibbāna?" he pondered. "Addasā kho" means he saw, he realized through penetration. The word "Mārisa" is a term of endearment and is a specific form of address among deities. It also means "one free from suffering."

Why did this Sakka call the deities? He called them for the sake of companionship. It is said that previously, when the Blessed One was dwelling in the Salala hut, Sakka went alone to see him. The Teacher, thinking, "His knowledge is not yet mature; after a few days have passed, while I am dwelling in the Indasāla Cave, he will see the five preliminary signs and, being terrified by the fear of death, will approach me together with the deities from the two celestial realms and ask fourteen questions; at the end of the explanation of the questions on equanimity, he will be established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) along with eighty thousand deities," did not grant him the opportunity. Sakka also thought, "Because I went alone before, the Teacher did not grant me the opportunity; it is certain that I do not have the strong support (upanissaya) for the Path and Fruit. However, if there is a strong support for even one person, the Blessed One will surely preach the Dhamma to the assembly as far as the limits of the universe. There will surely be some deity in the two celestial realms who has the strong support; the Teacher will preach the Dhamma in reference to that deity. By hearing that Dhamma, I too shall appease my own distress." Thinking thus, he called the deities for the sake of companionship.

"Evaṃ bhaddaṃ tavāti kho devā tāvatiṃsā" means the Tāvatiṃsa deities said, "Great King, let it be so. Let us go to see the Blessed One. The arising of a Buddha is rare. May it be a blessing to you, who did not say 'Let us go to play on the mountain peaks or in the rivers,' but instead urged us toward such meritorious matters." "Passassosuṃ" means they respectfully accepted his words and gave their assent.
291:
Sakka, the king of devas, looked upon all this prosperity—the celestial city of ten thousand leagues, the Vejayanta Palace one thousand leagues high, the Sudhammā celestial assembly hall of three hundred leagues, the Pāricchattaka tree one hundred leagues high, the Paṇḍukambala stone seat of sixty leagues, the thirty million dancers (including the fraction), the celestial retinue in the two celestial realms, and the Nandana Grove, Cittalatā Grove, Missaka Grove, and Phārusaka Grove—and was overcome by fear, thinking, "O friends, this prosperity of mine is about to perish!"

Then, searching for someone—a recluse, a brahmin, or a Great Brahmā who is the grandfather of humans—who could well extract the arrow of sorrow rooted in his heart and make this prosperity permanent, he saw no one. But then he saw again, "The Fully Enlightened Buddha alone is capable of extracting the arrow of sorrow that has arisen for a hundred thousand such as I." While he was thus reflecting, at that time, zeal arose in Sakka, the lord of devas, to see the Blessed One.

"Where is the Blessed One dwelling now? In which country, depending on which city, using whose requisites, and to whom is he dwelling while preaching the Dhamma that gives the Deathless Nibbāna?" he pondered. "Addasā kho" means he saw, he realized through penetration. The word "Mārisa" is a term of endearment and is a specific form of address among deities. It also means "dear deity free from suffering."

Why did this Sakka call the deities? He called them for the sake of companionship. It is said that previously, when the Blessed One was dwelling in the Salala hut, Sakka went alone to see him. The Teacher, thinking, "His knowledge is not yet mature; after a few days have passed, while I am dwelling in the Indasāla Cave, he will see the five preliminary signs and, being terrified by the fear of death, will approach me together with the deities from the two celestial realms and ask fourteen questions; at the end of the explanation of the questions on equanimity, he will be established in the Fruit of Stream-entry along with eighty thousand deities," did not grant him the opportunity. Sakka also thought, "Because I went alone before, the Teacher did not grant me the opportunity; it is certain that I do not have the strong support (upanissaya) for the Path and Fruit. However, if there is a strong support for even one person, the Blessed One will surely preach the Dhamma to the assembly as far as the limits of the universe. There will surely be some deity in the two celestial realms who has the strong support; the Teacher will preach the Dhamma in reference to that deity. By hearing that Dhamma, I too shall appease my own distress." Thinking thus, he called the deities for the sake of companionship.

"Evaṃ bhaddaṃ tavāti kho devā tāvatiṃsā" means the Tāvatiṃsa deities said, "Great King, let it be so. Let us go to see the Blessed One. The arising of a Buddha is rare. May it be a blessing to you, Great King, who did not say 'Let us go to play on the mountain peaks or in the rivers,' but instead urged us toward such meritorious matters." "Passassosuṃ" means they respectfully accepted his words and gave their assent.
292:
After calling the devas, why did Sakka, King of Devas, call the Gandhabba celestial youth Pañcasikha separately? It was to make an opening (to request permission). This thought occurred to Sakka: "It is not appropriate to approach the Teacher by bringing all the devas from the two deva worlds as if going to a festival or a dance performance. This celestial youth Pañcasikha is an attendant and a favorite of the Ten-Powered One; he goes at any desired moment to ask questions and listen to the Dhamma. I will send this celestial youth ahead to request permission, and only when permission is granted by him will I approach and ask my questions." Thus, he called him to make an opening.

"O Lord of Devas, let it be so. May it be a blessing to you. You did not say to me, 'Come, dear friend, let us go to see the pleasure gardens or dance festivals,' but instead you say, 'Let us go to see the Buddha and listen to the Dhamma,'" said Pañcasikha, supporting and confirming the words of Sakka, King of Devas, and then he accompanied him.

In that context, 'Beluvapaṇḍu' refers to a lute that has a pale yellow color like a ripe wood-apple. It is said that its bowl was made of gold, its neck of lapis lazuli, its strings of silver, and its tuning pegs of coral. The lute bowl was one gāvuta, the string-fastening area was one gāvuta, and the upper neck was one gāvuta; thus, the lute was three gāvutas in length. Taking that lute, Pañcasikha tuned it to the fifty musical scales, struck it with his fingernails, and produced a sweet melodic sound. Standing to one side, he let the other devas know it was time for Sakka's departure. When the host of devas assembled at the signal of his singing and playing, Sakka, King of Devas... appeared clearly on Mount Vediyaka.

'Atiriiva obhāsajāto' means that while on other days the mountain would be illuminated by the radiance of a single deva, or Māra, or a Brahmā, on that day it was exceedingly radiant due to the light of the devas from the two deva worlds, appearing like a single mass of light similar to the time when a thousand suns and moons have risen. 'Parito gāmesu manussā' refers to the people in the surrounding villages.
