It is said that Sakka went to that mountain at the usual time after the evening meal while children were still playing in the middle of the village; therefore, the people saw it and said: "Indeed, devas usually approach the Blessed One during the middle watch of the night. Why has this one come even in the first watch?" This was asked as a question. The answer given is that he came because he was threatened by the fear of death. "Friends, what is the name of this radiance? Who is this powerful deva or Brahmā approaching the Blessed One today to ask questions and listen to the Dhamma? How will the Blessed One answer the questions and preach the Dhamma? It is a gain for us that the Teacher, who can dispel the doubts of devas like us, dwells in a monastery not far away, where we have the opportunity to offer even a bowl of almsfood or a spoonful of almsfood." Thus, the Blessed One, who is able to dispel the doubts of the devas...
293:
Why did he come during the earlier part of the first watch? Because he was threatened by the fear of death. "Friends, what is the name of this radiance? Who indeed is this powerful deva or Brahmā approaching the Blessed One today to ask questions and listen to the Dhamma? How indeed will the Blessed One answer the questions and preach the Dhamma? It is a gain for us that the Teacher, who dispels the doubts of devas like us, dwells in a monastery nearby, where we get the chance to give even a bowl of almsfood or a spoonful of almsfood." Thus, being moved and with hair standing on end, they stood paying homage with their hands joined in a lotus bud, shining with the light of their ten fingernails, placed upon their heads.

"Durupasaṅkamā" means they are difficult to approach. It means, "I am possessed of greed, hatred, and delusion, while the Teacher is free from greed, hatred, and delusion; therefore, Tathāgatas are difficult to approach by someone like me." "Jhāyī" means one who meditates through both lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna (meditation on characteristics) and ārammaṇūpanijjhāna (meditation on objects). Because he delights only in that jhāna, he is called "Jhānaratā." "Tadantaraṃ paṭisallīnā" means withdrawn in the interval of that approach, or currently secluded. Therefore, he is difficult to approach not only because he is a meditator delighting in jhāna, but also because he is currently in seclusion. "Pasādeyyāsī" means "please propitiate him" or "make an opening for me."

Regarding "Beluvapaṇḍuvīṇaṃ ādāya" (taking the Beluvapaṇḍu lute), if one asks, "Had he not already taken it?" Yes, he had. However, while traveling, it was slung over his shoulder; now, he placed it in his left hand and prepared it for playing, which is why it is said "taking it."

## Explanation of the Verses of Pañcasikha's Song
"Assāvesī" means he made him hear. "Buddhūpasañhitā" means a song that arose concerning the Buddha and based on the Buddha. The same method applies to the remaining terms.

In the verse "Vande te pitaraṃ bhadde, timbaruṃ suriyavacchase," "Suriyavacchasā" refers to one whose body is like the radiance of the sun. It is said that radiance arises from that goddess's feet and ascends to the tips of her hair; thus, she appears like the orb of the rising sun, and so they know her as "Suriyavacchasā." Referring to that goddess Suriyavacchasā, it means: "Dear Suriyavacchasā, I pay homage to your father, the Gandhabba King named Timbaru." "Yena jātāsi kalyāṇီ" means because of that King Timbaru, or depending on that king, you were born endowed with all beautiful major and minor limbs. "Ānandajananī me" means one who increases joy and delight for me. "Vāto va sedattaṃ kanto" means just as a breeze is pleasant and heart-warming to those who are sweating to remove their sweat, so you are beloved to me. "Pānīyaṃ va pipāsato" means like water to one who desires to drink and is oppressed by thirst. "Aṅgīrasī" is so called because there are radiances in the major and minor limbs of that goddess. This is said with the intention of addressing that goddess Suriyavacchasā. "Dhammo arahatā miva" means just as the ninefold supramundane Dhamma is desired and liked by the Arahants. "Bhojanaṃ va jighacchato" means like food to one who desires to eat and is oppressed by hunger.
294:
Depending on that cause, the Gandhabba King Timbaru, you were born, O beautiful one, lovely in every limb. You are the one who increases my joy and delight.

It means: "Just as the wind is desired, loved, and pleasing to those who are sweaty to remove their sweat." It means: "Like drinking water to one who is thirsty and oppressed by thirst." She is called "Angīrasī" because she has radiance in her limbs. It is a form of address referring to that goddess. It means: "Like the ninefold supramundane Dhamma to the Arahants."

It means: "To one who is hungry and oppressed by the desire to eat." It means: "Just as someone might extinguish a blazing fire with a water pot, even so, please extinguish the fever of sensual lust that has arisen in me because of you."

It means: "Mixed with the pollen of lotus filaments." It means: "Like an elephant oppressed by the heat of the sun." It means: "Just as that elephant, having entered a lotus pond and drunk water, remains submerged with only the tip of its trunk visible and finds happiness and pleasure, even so, when shall I descend to your bosom and belly and find happiness and pleasure?"

Like an elephant beyond the hook,
I have conquered the tutta and tomara weapons,
Because I am intoxicated with passion for you who have beautiful thighs,
I no longer know any reason whatsoever.

Here, "tutta" refers to the iron rod used to pierce the base of the ear. "Tomara" refers to the spiked staff used to pierce the feet, etc. "Ankusa" refers to the curved hook used to pierce the head. Just as an elephant in rut, being beyond the hook, does not submit even when pierced and, intoxicated with pride, thinks "I have conquered the tutta and tomara, I do not even submit to the hook" and knows no reason; even so, I, intoxicated with passion for you who have well-proportioned thighs, like a madman, know no reason. Alternatively, like an elephant beyond the hook, I too, intoxicated by your well-proportioned thighs, [know] nothing...
295: From that time on, I no longer know the cause of dispassion. Why? Because, like that elephant who thinks "I have conquered the tutta and tomara" and does not heed anyone's words of advice, I too no longer heed anyone's advice. O lady of well-proportioned thighs, I have a mind bound to you. "Tayī gedhitacittosmi" means having a mind bound by passion for you. Or "gedhitacitto" means having a mind that has reached and stuck to greed. "Cittaṃ vipariṇāmitaṃ" means the mind has abandoned its natural pure state and remains transformed. "Paṭigantuṃ na sakkomi" means being unable to withdraw from that passion. It is like a fish that has swallowed a hook. There is also a reading "ghaso", and the meaning is the same. "Vāmūrū" means a goddess with thighs shaped beautifully, or it means thighs like the trunk of a banana tree. Embrace me! O lady with gentle eyes, women are called "mandalocanā" because they do not look sharply but look gently and softly. "Palissajā" means embrace me from all sides. I have constantly yearned for this embrace. My merit is naturally small. Because of that goddess with hair that curls and waves like a snake, many kinds of defilements have arisen in me. There is also a reading "anekabhāgo". Just as a gift given to Arahants has extraordinary results, my passion is diverse in various ways. May all the collections of merit I have performed, those merits performed towards Arahants endowed with qualities such as patience, ripen together with you only. "Ekodī" means reaching a state of oneness. Wisdom is called "nepakka"; being endowed with that wisdom, one is called "nipaka". Being endowed with mindfulness, one is called "sato". Just as that Sage, the Buddha, seeks the deathless Nibbāna, even so, O Sūriyavaccasā, I seek you. Or it means, just as that Lord wanders seeking Nibbāna, even so I wander seeking you. Just as the Sage, the Buddha, sitting on the Bodhi-throne, having attained omniscience, would rejoice and be glad; even so...
296:
"Nandeyyaṃ" means: "In this way, if I too were to attain union with you and be delighted, if I were to be filled with joy and happiness." 

In the phrase "Tāhaṃ bhadde vareyyāhe," "ahe" is a form of address. The meaning is: "O auspicious Suriyavacchasā, even if Sakka, the king of gods, were to grant a boon saying, 'Suriyavacchasā, will you take the kingship of the two deva worlds?', I would renounce that kingship and say, 'I will take only Suriyavacchasā.' In this way, I would desire, long for, and take you."

"Sālaṃva na ciraṃ phullaṃ" means: At your father's city gate, there is a sal tree that blooms constantly. That sal tree is extremely delightful. It is just like that constantly blooming sal tree. "Pitaraṃ te sumedhase" means: I pay homage and worship while praising your father, who is endowed with great beauty. I pay homage to that father who has such an excellent daughter.

Regarding the word "Saṃsandati": Why did the Blessed One speak in praise of the quality of the song and the sound of the lute? Is there any lustful attachment in the Blessed One towards that sound? No. In such matters, the Blessed One is one who remains indifferent with six-factored equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā). He merely knows the pleasant and the unpleasant, but has no attachment to those objects. It was also said: "Friend, the Blessed One has the eye-sensitivity; the Blessed One sees forms with the eye, but the Blessed One has no desire or lust; the Blessed One has a well-liberated mind. Friend, the Blessed One has the ear-sensitivity..." and so on (SN 4.232). However, if the Blessed One had not spoken in praise, the deva Pañcasikha would not have known, "The Blessed One has given me the opportunity." Then Sakka, thinking "The Blessed One has not given Pañcasikha the opportunity," would have taken the assembly of devas and returned from there. If that happened, it would have been a great loss. Knowing that only when praise was spoken would Sakka know "The Blessed One has given Pañcasikha the opportunity," and then approach with the devas, ask questions, and at the end of the explanation, 80,000 devas would be established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala)—knowing this, He spoke in praise.

In that Pali, "Kadā saṃyūḷhā" means "When did you meet/unite?" "Tena kho panāhaṃ, bhante, samayenāti" means "Venerable Sir, at that time refers to the eighth week after Your attainment of Enlightenment." "Bhaddā nāma Suriyavacchasāti" means she is named Bhaddā by name, and called Suriyavacchasā because of the perfection of her physical beauty. "Bhaginīti" is merely a term of address, meaning "goddess." "Parakāminīti" means desiring or longing for another.
297:
"Upanaccantiyā" means "while dancing." It is said that at one time, she went with the Four Great Kings to perform a dance for Sakka, the king of gods. At that moment, Sakka proclaimed the eight true qualities of the Tathāgata. Thus, going on that day and dancing, she heard (those qualities).

## Commentary on Sakka's Approach

"Paṭisammodati" means that the Blessed One, saying "Friend Pañcasikha, your music accords with my mind," etc., rejoices (approves), and the deva Pañcasikha rejoices in return. When reciting the verses, Pañcasikha speaks joyfully, and the Blessed One rejoices in return. "Āmantesi" means he made it known. It is said that Sakka had this thought: "This Pañcasikha, whom I sent for my own business, is doing his own business. Standing in the presence of such a Teacher, he speaks inappropriate words connected with sensual pleasures. Dancers are indeed shameless; while speaking, he might even show improper behavior. Let me now make my business known to this Pañcasikha." Thinking thus, he called and spoke to him.

"Evaဉ္ca pana tathāgatā" and so on are the words placed by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma (Saṅgāyaka Theras). "Abhivadanti" means they speak with words of praise as a way of accepting the salutation. "Abhivadito" means spoken to with words of praise.

"Urundā samapādī" means (the cave) became wide and open; the darkness within the cave vanished. "Āloko udapādi" means the darkness that was naturally in the cave disappeared, and light arose. All these are the words of the Elders who compiled the Dhamma.

"Cirapaṭikāhaṃ bhante" means "Venerable Sir, I have desired to see You for a long time." "Kehici kehici kiccakaraṇīyehi" means: For the devas, sons and daughters are born on their laps; the goddesses who serve at their feet are born on their beds; the devas who perform the task of decorating and adorning them are born surrounding the bed; those who perform various duties are born within the mansion. For such devas, there is no such thing as a legal dispute. However, regarding those who are born on the boundary between two mansions, being unable to decide "Is it yours or mine?", they have a dispute and ask Sakka, the king of gods. Then Sakka decides, "To whichever mansion it is closer, let it belong to that person."
298:
If both are standing in the same place, it is said, "To whomsoever she stands looking at her mansion, to him she belongs." If she looks at neither, he [the judge/Sakka] makes her his own to settle the dispute between the two. Activities such as playing are also to be performed. Referring to such activities to be performed, it was said, "with certain activities to be performed."

"Salalāgārakē" refers to being in the scented hut (gandhakuṭi) made of pine wood. "Aññatarena samādhinā" means that at that time, the Blessed One, knowing that Sakka's knowledge was not yet mature and not wishing to grant an audience yet, sat in the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). Sakka, not knowing this, said "by a certain concentration." "Bhūjati ca nāma"—Bhūjati is the name of that goddess. "Paricārikā" refers to an attendant goddess who serves at the feet. That goddess had attained two fruits [of the path]; therefore, she had no delight in the deva world. She always came to attend the Blessed One, standing with hands joined in reverence on her head, paying homage to the Blessed One. Regarding the statement "He arose from that concentration due to the sound of the chariot wheels," it should not be said, "Does one in meditative attainment hear sound?" Did the Blessed One not say to Sakka, the lord of the devas, "I arose from that concentration due to the sound of the venerable one's chariot wheels"? Let alone the sound of chariot wheels, one in meditative attainment does not hear the sound of a pair of conchs blown near the ear, nor even a thunderbolt, while within the attainment. However, the Blessed One, having determined, "I will not grant Sakka an audience for this much time," entered the attainment of fruition for that duration. Sakka, thinking, "The Teacher does not grant me an audience now," circumambulated the scented hut, turned the chariot back, and headed toward the deva world. The precinct of the scented hut became filled with the sound of the chariot, like a five-piece orchestra. As the Blessed One emerged from the attainment according to the predetermined time, the first reflection (āvajjanā) arose precisely due to the sound of the chariot; therefore, he spoke thus.

## Gopakavatthuvaṇṇanā

"Sīlesu paripūrakārinī" means one who practices the five precepts to fulfillment. "Itthittaṃ virājetvā" means discarding womanhood. Womanhood is disadvantageous; one cannot enjoy the glory of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), Sakka, Māra, or Brahma, nor reach Paccekabodhi or Sammāsambodhi while remaining in womanhood. Thus, one discards womanhood. This manhood is great, noble, and supreme; only by remaining in manhood can one attain these successes...
299:
In this manner, one develops manhood. That Sākyan princess named Gopikā also did the same. Therefore, it was said, "Having discarded womanhood and developed manhood."

"Hīnaṃ gandhabbakāyaṃ" refers to the lowly assembly of Gandhabbas. Why were those of pure virtue born there? Due to past attachment (nikanti). Even in the past, that was their dwelling place; thus, they were born there through the power of attachment. "Upaṭṭhānaṃ" refers to the Sudhammā assembly hall. "Pāricariyaṃ" refers to the state of service. They came saying, "We will serve you with song and music."

"Paṭicodesi" means he reminded them. Seeing them, that deva Gopaka reflected, "These devas are exceedingly radiant and beautiful; what karma did they perform to come here?" and saw they had been monks. Then, investigating, "Were they monks who fulfilled the precepts?" he saw they were. "Are there other virtues?" he saw they were gainers of jhāna. "Where did they live?" he saw they were his own regular recipients of alms. Those of pure virtue can be reborn in any of the six deva worlds they wish. But these were not born in the higher deva worlds. Those who gain jhāna are born in the Brahma world, but these were not born there. "I, however, established in their advice, was born as the son on the throne of Sakka, the lord of the devas, while they were born in the lowly Gandhabba assembly." Thinking, "These persons are like those who must be pierced deeply by turning an arrow that can pierce bone," he admonished them with words such as "Kutomukhā."

In that context, "Kutomukhā" means: while the Blessed One is teaching the Dhamma directly in front of you, where are your faces turned? Are you occupied with other things, looking here and there, or nodding off? "Duddiṭṭharūpaṃ" refers to an ill-seen nature, an appearance unfit to be seen. "Sahadhammike" refers to fellow practitioners of the Dhamma in the teaching of the same Teacher, fellow performers of merit. "Tesaṃ bhante" means: after the deva Gopaka spoke thus and admonished them further with words like "Oh, you are shameless and fearless," two of the three devas regained mindfulness in that very life.

"Kāyaṃ brahmapurohitaṃ"—those two devas thought: "Dancers, singers, and musicians who come should receive a reward, but this..."
300: However, those devas reflected: "Since this Gopaka devaputta saw us, he has been crackling like a tripod with salt thrown into it; why is this?" Reflecting on their status as monks, their pure virtue, their attainment of jhāna, and their previous visits to Gopaka's house, they realized: "Those with pure virtue are reborn in whatever place they desire in the six deva worlds; those who attain jhāna are reborn in the Brahma world. We were unable to be reborn in the higher deva worlds or the Brahma world. This woman, who stood in our instruction, has been reborn in a higher deva world. Although we were monks and practiced the holy life under the Blessed One, we have been reborn in the inferior Gandhabba realm. That is why this Gopaka devaputta rebukes us so." While listening to the words of Gopaka devaputta, two of those three devas regained mindfulness of the first jhāna. Using that jhāna as a basis, they contemplated conditioned phenomena and established themselves in the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala). At that moment, their meager sense-sphere existence could no longer sustain them, so they passed away immediately and were reborn in the Brahma-purohita realm. That Brahma-purohita body arose while they were still in that Gandhabba deva world. Therefore, it is said: "Venerable Sir, of those three devas rebuked by Gopaka devaputta, two regained mindfulness in this very life and reached the Brahma-purohita realm." In that passage, "diṭṭheve dhamme" means regaining jhāna-mindfulness in that very existence. "kāyaṃ brahmapurohitaṃ" means obtaining the body of a Brahma-purohita Brahma after passing away while staying in that deva world. One deva, however, unable to cut off attachment to the Gandhabba state, delighted in sense pleasures and remained a permanent resident of that Gandhabba realm. "saṅghañcupaṭṭhāsiṃ" means "I served the Saṅgha." "sudhammatāya" means "due to the goodness of the Dhamma." "tidivūpapanno" means "reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa deva world." "gandhabbakāyūpagate vasīne" means "those who have arrived as permanent residents in the Gandhabba realm." The phrase "ye ca mayaṃ pubbe manussabhūtā" should be understood in connection with "we who were formerly human served with food and drink." "pādūpasaṅgayha" means "holding the feet, performing foot-washing and anointing, and worshipping." "sake nivesane" means "in one's own house." This term should also be connected with "served." "paccattaṃ veditabbo" means "to be known and experienced by oneself." "ariyāna subhāsitāni" refers to the well-spoken words of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, taught by you.
301: "While you were attending upon the Excellent One or the unsurpassed Dispensation of the Buddha" means attending upon the Exalted Buddha or the unsurpassed Sāsana. "Brahmacariya" means the excellent practice. "Bhavatūpapatti" means the rebirth of your honors. "agāre vasato mayhaṃ" means "of me living in the midst of the house." "svajja" means "that I today." In the term "gotamasāvākena", this Gopaka deva is called a disciple of Gotama. "samecca" means "having come well." "handa viyāyāma byāyāma" means "come, let us strive, let us especially strive." In the sentence "mā no mayaṃ parapessā ahumhā", "no" is just a particle; it means "let us not be merely the servants (pesanakāraka) of others." "gotamasāsanāni" here refers to the first jhāna which was penetrated naturally; "anussaraṃ" means "remembering" that first jhāna. "cittāni virājayitvā" means "having detached the minds that have the five cords of sensual pleasure as their object." "kāmesu ādīnavaṃ" means they saw the danger in sensual pleasures through the first jhāna by way of suppression, and through the third path (Anāgāmi-magga) by way of eradication. "kāmasamyojanabandhanāni" refers to the fetters of sense-desire and the bonds of sense-desire. "pāpimayogāni" means the bonds of the Evil One (Māra), being those that bind. "duraccayāni" means difficult to overcome. "saindā devā sapajāpatikā" means the devas with Indra as their chief are called "Sainda", and those with Pajāpati the deva-king as their chief are called "Sapajāpatika". "sabhāyupaviṭṭhā" means "seated in the assembly." "vīrā" means brave heroes. "virāgā" means those free from passion. "virajaṃ karontā" means "producing the stainless Path of Non-returning." "nāgovo sannāni guṇāni" means "having cut the bonds of sense-desire like an elephant, they surpassed the Tāvatiṃsa devas." "saṃvegajātassa" refers to Sakka who has been struck with urgency. "kāmābhibhū" means "one who overcomes the two kinds of sense-desires." "satiyā vihīnā" means "devoid of jhāna-mindfulness." "tiṇṇam tesaṃ" means "among those three persons." "āvasinettha eko" means "one alone became a permanent resident in that inferior Gandhabba realm." "sambodhipathānusārino" means "those who follow the Path of Non-returning." "devepi hīḷentī" means "even rebuking the devas..."
302:
Disparaging the two deva worlds and looking downwards, with minds well-concentrated through attainment concentration (appanā-samādhi), they scattered the dust from their feet onto the heads of the devas and ascended into the sky.

In this Dispensation (Sāsana), there is such a proclamation of the Dhamma, through which disciples become endowed with these qualities. Among those disciples, not even a single one has doubt regarding the Buddha and so forth, nor regarding the state of being unattached and unseized in the four directions. Now, wishing to praise the virtues of the Blessed One, he said: "We pay homage to the Buddha, the Conqueror, the Lord of Beings (Janinda), who has crossed the fourfold flood and cut off all doubt." In that verse, 'vicikicchā-chinna' means one who has severed all doubt. 'Janinda' means the one who is supreme in all the worlds.

"The Dhamma which those devas attained" means your Dhamma. "Kāyaṃ brahmā-purohitanti" means attaining the body of a Brahma’s Minister even while we were watching. The meaning is: having understood your Dhamma, two among those three persons attained the stage of the Path and Fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi) and reached the celestial mansion of the Brahma’s Ministers even while we were watching, thus achieving the distinction of the Path and Fruit. We too, dear sirs, have come to attain that Dhamma. "Āgatamhase" means we have arrived. If the Blessed One grants us the opportunity, being those who have been given leave by the Blessed One, we wish to ask a question, dear sir—this is the meaning.

## The Story of Magha the Youth (Maghamāṇavavatthu)

"This yakkha has been pure for a long time" means he has been pure since a long time ago. How long? Since the time of Magha the youth in the village of Macala in the kingdom of Magadha, before the Buddha had appeared. At that time, it is said that one day, having risen early, he went to the place where the people of the village worked in the center of the village. He cleared the dust and rubbish from the spot where he was to stand with his feet and made it pleasant. Another person came and stood there. He, through that much effort, regained mindfulness, cleared a space about the size of a threshing floor in the middle of the village, scattered sand, brought wood, and made a fire during the cold season. Young and old alike came and sat there.
303:
One day, this thought occurred to Magha the youth: "We go to the city and see the King, the King’s great ministers, and so forth. In these mansions of the Moon and Sun, they also say 'the young deva named Canda, the young deva named Suriya.' By performing what deed did they attain such prosperity?" Then, thinking, "It is not by any other means, but only by performing meritorious deeds," he thought, "I too should perform only meritorious deeds that grant such prosperity."

Magha the youth rose early and, having drunk rice gruel, took a billhook, an axe, a hoe, and a pestle in his hand and went to the four-way junction. He lifted the stones in the middle of the road with the pestle and rolled them away. He removed the trees that struck the axles of vehicles. He made the uneven places even. He built a rest house at the four-way junction. He dug a pond. He built a bridge. Having worked all day in this manner, he returned home when the sun set.

Another person asked him, "Friend Magha, you go out early in the morning and return from the forest only in the evening. What work do you do?" "I perform meritorious deeds; I clear the path leading to the deva world," he replied. "Friend, what is this called merit?" he asked. "Do you not know?" he asked in return. "Yes, I do not know," he said. "When you went to the city, have you seen the King, the King’s great ministers, and so forth before?" "Yes, I have seen them before." "They attained that position by performing meritorious deeds. I too perform the work that grants such prosperity. Have you heard before of 'the young deva named Canda, the young deva named Suriya'?" "Yes, I have heard of them before." "I am clearing the path to that heaven," he said. "Is this merit suitable only for you, or is it suitable for others as well?" he asked. "This merit is not forbidden to anyone," he replied. "If so, when you go to the forest tomorrow, give me a call as well."

The next day, he took that man with him. In this way, thirty-three young men in that village became followers of Magha the youth. Being of one mind, they went about performing meritorious deeds. To whatever direction they went, they made the road even, completing it in a single day. Digging ponds, building rest houses, and building bridges—they completed these also in a single day.

Then the village headman (gāmabhojaka) thought: "Formerly, when these men drank liquor and committed acts such as killing living beings, I obtained wealth through coins (kāhāpaṇa) and through fines. Now, since the time they began performing merit, there is no such income. I shall now destroy them in the presence of the royal family." He approached the King and said, "Great King, I see thieves." "Dear man, where do you see them?" the King asked. "I see them in my village," he replied. "Dear man, what kind of thieves are they?" "Deva, they are rebels against the King." "Of what class are they?" "Deva, they are of the householder class." "What can householders do?"
304: When asked, "Why did you not tell me, knowing this?" he replied, "Great King, I did not speak out of fear. Now, please do not find fault with me." Then the King, believing that "This man is making a great outcry to me," said, "In that case, go; you yourself arrest them," and sent him off with a force of soldiers. The village headman went and worked in the forest all day, ate his evening meal, and while sitting in the middle of the village, they were consulting, "What work shall we do tomorrow? Which road shall we make level? Shall we dig a pond? Shall we build a bridge?" Just then, they surrounded the thirty-three men, including the young man Magha, and arrested them, saying, "Do not move; it is the King's command," and led them away. Then their wives, hearing that "Your husbands have been arrested and taken away as 'thieves guilty of crimes against the King,'" said, "For a long time these deceitful men have been spending every day in the forest saying, 'We are doing meritorious deeds.' All work has been ruined, and there is no progress at home. It is very good that they are caught; it is very fitting that they are captured." The village headman also took them and presented them to the King. The King, without investigating or reflecting, commanded, "Have them trampled by an elephant." While they were being led away to be trampled, Magha said to the others, "Friends, will you be able to follow my word?" They replied, "It is only because we followed your word that we have reached this danger; even so, we will continue to follow your word. Friend, tell us, what shall we do?" "Friends, for those wandering in this round of rebirth (saṃsāra), such danger is constant. Are you thieves?" he asked. "We are not," they replied. "In this world, the Act of Truth (saccakiriya) is indeed a refuge. Therefore, all of you make an Act of Truth: 'If we are thieves, let the elephant trample us; but if we are not thieves, let it not trample us.'" They did so. The elephant could not even approach them and fled, trumpeting. Even when they struck the elephant with sticks, spears, and goads, they could not bring it near. They reported to the King, "We cannot bring the elephant near." "In that case, cover them with mats and have them trampled," he commanded. When they were covered with mats, the elephant trumpeted twice as loud and fled again. When the King heard this, he summoned the slanderer and asked, "My man, why does the elephant not wish to trample them?" "Great King, I do not know, but the leader of the youths knows a mantra; this power is only the power of the mantra," he replied. The King summoned the young man Magha and asked, "Is it true that you have a mantra?" "Great King, I have no mantra. However, we performed an Act of Truth: 'If we are thieves of the King, let the elephant trample us; but if we are not thieves, let it not trample us.' This is only the power of our Act of Truth," he replied. "My dear sons, what work do you do?" he asked. "Great King, we make the roads level, and at the crossroads, a rest house..."
305: "...we dig ponds, we build bridges; we have been wandering about performing such meritorious deeds," they replied. The King asked, "For what purpose did this man slander you?" They replied, "When we were negligent, he used to get such and such goods; when we are not negligent, he does not get them. For that reason, he slandered us." The King said, "My dear men, this elephant, though an animal, knows your virtues. I, though a human, did not know your virtues. I give you back your residential village to be your own property. Let this elephant also be yours. Let the slanderer also be your slave. From this day forward, perform meritorious deeds for me as well," and he released them, giving them wealth. Taking the wealth and traveling by turns on the elephant, they consulted, "Friends, although meritorious deeds are said to be done for the sake of future lives, our merit has given fruit in this very life, like a blue lotus blooming in the water. Now, let us perform even more meritorious deeds." When asked, "What merit shall we perform?" they said, "Let us build a strong rest house (sālā) at the crossroads for the multitude to rest. However, let us do it without sharing the portion of merit with women." The reason was that when they were being led away as thieves, not even one of the women felt any anxiety, but instead got up saying, "They are well-caught, they are well-bound." "Therefore, let us not give the portion of merit to those women," they consulted. They returned to their homes and gave the elephant thirty-three balls of rice and thirty-three handfuls of grass. All that food filled the elephant's belly. They entered the forest and cut down trees, and the elephant dragged all the cut timber to the cart-track. They planed the timber and began the work of building the rest house. In the house of the young man Magha, there were four wives: Sujātā, Sudhammā, Cittā, and Nandā. Sudhammā asked the carpenter, "My man, these friends go early and return in the evening; what work are they doing?" The carpenter replied, "Lady, they are building a rest house." "My man, make it so that I also get a share of merit in building the rest house," she said. The carpenter said, "They are saying they will do it without sharing the merit with women." That Sudhammā gave eight kahāpaṇas to the carpenter and said, "My man, by some means or another, make it so that I get a share of the merit." The carpenter agreed, saying, "Very well, lady." First, he took a cross-axe and, standing in the middle of the village, shouted loudly, "Friends, why have you not come out even at this time today?" Knowing that everyone had come out onto the road, he said, "You go on ahead; I have some business that will delay me." He let those thirty-three men go on ahead, then went by another road, felled a tree suitable for making the pinnacle, planed it, made it smooth, brought it, and kept it in Sudhammā's house.
306:
The carpenter sent those men ahead, took another path, cut down a tree suitable for a pinnacle, hewed it, smoothed it, and brought it to Sudhammā's house, instructing her, "On the day I ask for it, please bring it out and give it to me."

Later, when the building work was nearing completion—starting from clearing the ground to laying the foundation, erecting the pillars, joining the beams, and setting up the scaffolding for the pinnacle—the carpenter, sitting on the scaffolding, raised the rafters from the four directions and said, "Friends, there is one part of the building that I forgot to prepare." When they asked, "Friend, what did you forget? Did you forget everything?" he replied, "Friends, where will these rafters rest? It would be proper if we could get a pinnacle." When they asked, "Friend, where can we get one now?" he said, "It might be found in a household; go around and ask."

They entered the village and inquired, and at the door of Sudhammā's house, they asked, "Is there a pinnacle in this house?" She said, "There is." When they said, "Come, take the price for it," she replied, "I do not want the price; if you give me a share of the merit, I will give it." They said, "Friends, come, let us not give a share of the merit to a woman; let us go to the forest and cut a tree," and they departed.

Then the carpenter asked, "Dear friends, did you not get the pinnacle?" They told him the matter. The carpenter, still sitting on the scaffolding, looked up at the sky and said, "Friends, the constellation is favorable today; such a constellation can only be found after another year has passed. The building materials you have brought with great difficulty will rot right here within a year. When we are reborn in the deva world, let there be a rest-house for her in one corner as well; go and bring that pinnacle."

Sudhammā, before they returned, had the words 'This hall is named Sudhammā' carved on the lower surface of the pinnacle, wrapped it in a new cloth, and kept it. The workers came and said, 'Hey, bring the pinnacle, let happen what may; we will give you a share of the merit.' She brought it out and instructed, 'Dear friends, as long as the eight or sixteen rafters are not yet mounted, do not unwrap this cloth.' They agreed, took it, and only after mounting the rafters did they unwrap the cloth.

A man who was the village headman, looking up, saw the letters and, saying, 'Friends, what is this?' called for someone who could read and showed it to him. He...
307:
...said, "This hall is named Sudhammā." They lamented, "Friends, take it away! Although we have built this hall from the beginning, we do not even get the name; this woman, with just a pinnacle-tree worth a gem, makes the hall known by her own name." While they were lamenting, the carpenter inserted the rafters, drove in the pegs, and completed the work on the hall.

They divided the hall into three parts: one part was made as a residence for the powerful, one for the poor, and one for the sick. The thirty-three men arranged thirty-three planks and gave a signal to an elephant: "When a guest comes and sits on a plank spread by someone, take him and establish him in the house of that plank's owner. The responsibility for massaging his feet and back, providing food, drink, and a bed shall belong solely to the owner of that plank." The elephant would take every guest who arrived to the house of the plank's owner, and that owner would perform the necessary duties for the guest on that day.

The young man Magha had a Kovilāra tree planted in a place not far from the hall, and at its base, he had a stone slab spread. His wife named Nandā had a pond dug nearby. Cittā had small flowering plants cultivated. However, the eldest of all the wives, Sujātā, went about merely adorning herself while holding a mirror. Magha said to her, "Lady, Sudhammā has become a sharer in the hall, Nandā has had a pond dug, and Cittā has planted flowers. But you have no meritorious deed; lady, perform some merit." She replied, "For whose sake do you perform it? Is not the merit performed by you mine as well?" and continued to devote herself only to adorning her person.

Magha lived out his lifespan, passed away from there, and was reborn as Sakka in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Those thirty-three villagers also passed away and were reborn as thirty-three devaputtas in the presence of that same Sakka. Sakka's palace, named Vejayanta, rose seven hundred leagues high, and its banner rose three hundred leagues. As a result of planting the Kovilāra tree, the Pāricchattaka Kovilāra tree appeared, with a circumference of three hundred leagues and a trunk fifteen leagues in girth.
308:
As a result of offering a stone slab, the Paṇḍukambala stone throne, sixty leagues in size, appeared at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree. As a result of Sudhammā offering the timber for the pinnacle of the hall, the celestial assembly hall named Sudhammā, three hundred leagues in size, appeared. As a result of Nandā offering a pond, the pond named Nandā, fifty leagues in size, appeared. As a result of Cittā offering a flower garden, the garden named Cittalatā, sixty leagues in size, appeared.

Sakka, the king of the devas, was seated on a golden throne one league in size in the Sudhammā celestial hall, with a white parasol three leagues in size held over him. While surrounded by those young devas, celestial maidens, thirty-five million dancers, and the deities of the two deva realms, he looked upon his great prosperity and saw those three women. "These are clearly visible; but where is Sujātā?" he wondered. Searching, he saw, "This one, by not following my words and only adorning her own body, has been reborn as a female crane in a mountain cleft." He descended from the deva realm and went to that crane. Upon seeing him, the crane recognized him and lowered her head. "You foolish crane, why do you not lift your head now? By not following my words and spending your time only beautifying yourself, you have come to this. Sudhammā, Nandā, and Cittā have attained great prosperity. Come, look at our prosperity!" Saying this, he took her to the deva realm, placed her by the Nandā pond, and sat on his throne.

The celestial dancing women asked, "Great King, where did you go?" Although the king did not wish to tell them, he was pressed by the goddesses and said, "I went to Sujātā." "Great King, where was she reborn?" they asked. "In a mountain cleft," he replied. "Where is she now?" they asked. "I have left her at the Nandā pond," he said. "Friends, come, let us go and see our lady!" they said, and all the goddesses went there. In the past, that crane had been the eldest of all the wives and had looked down upon those younger women. Now, when those goddesses saw the crane, they mocked her, saying, "Friends, look! Our lady's face is just like a spike for piercing crabs!" and so on.

The crane, being greatly distressed and ashamed, said to Sakka, "Great King, what use are these celestial mansions of gold, silver, and jewels, or the Nandā pond to me? Great King, for beings, only their place of birth brings comfort. Please send me back to that mountain cleft." Sakka sent her back to that place and asked, "Will you follow my words?" "I will follow them, Great King," she replied. "Take the Five Precepts and keep them unbroken. In a few days, I will make you the chief of these goddesses," he instructed. The crane followed Sakka's instructions accordingly.
309:
After two or three days had passed, Sakka thought, "I wonder if she can keep her virtue?" He went and, taking the form of a fish, floated on his back on the water in front of the crane. The crane, thinking "It must be a dead fish," went and caught it by the head. The fish moved its tail. The crane thought, "I think it is still alive," and released it into the water. Sakka, standing in the air, said, "Excellent, excellent! You are guarding the precepts. To you who guards them thus, I will make you the chief of the dancers within a few days." That crane lived for five hundred years. Not even for a single day did she get a full stomach; though she became dry, withered, and emaciated, she did not break her virtue. Upon her death, she was conceived in the house of a potter in the city of Vārāṇasī.

Sakka looked to see where she had been reborn and, seeing her, thought, "It is not yet possible to bring her from that house to this deva realm. I will provide her with a means of livelihood." He filled a small cart with golden cucumbers and, taking the form of an old man, sat in the middle of the village and cried out, "Take these cucumbers!" The villagers from all around came and said, "Grandfather, give us some." He asked, "I give them only to those who keep virtue. Do you keep virtue?" They replied, "Grandfather, we do not even know what virtue is. Just give them to us for a price." He said, "I give them only to those who keep virtue." "Hey, who is this old man selling cucumbers?" they said and all went away.

The potter's young daughter asked, "Mothers, you went for cucumbers but have come back empty-handed?" They replied, "Little girl, the old man selling cucumbers says, 'I give only to those who keep virtue.' We do not know if this man's daughters live by eating virtue, but we do not even know what virtue is." The young girl thought, "He must have brought them for me," and went to him, saying, "Grandfather, please give me some cucumbers." He asked, "Little girl, do you keep the precepts?" "Yes, grandfather, I keep them," she replied. "I have brought these golden cucumbers only for you," he said. He left the cart and the cucumbers at the door of her house and departed. The potter's daughter kept her virtue for the rest of her life and, upon her death, was reborn as the daughter of Vepacitti, the Asura king. Due to the result of her virtue, she was possessed of a beautiful and inspiring appearance. The Asura king said, "I will hold a marriage ceremony for my daughter," and gathered the Asuras together.

Sakka looked to see where she had been reborn and, seeing that she was in the Asura realm and that they were going to hold a marriage ceremony that day, thought, "Now I must take her by creating some pretext." He disguised himself as an Asura and went to stand among the Asuras.
310:
"Choose your husband," said the father, placing a garland in his daughter's hand. "Throw it upon the one you desire," he said as he gave it. Looking around, the Asura maiden saw Sakka. Due to the affection arising from having lived together in a past life, she thought, "This is my husband," and threw the garland over Sakka. Sakka took the Asura maiden by the arm and flew up into the sky. At that moment, the Asuras realized what had happened. They pursued them, shouting, "Seize him! Seize the old Sakka, our enemy! We will not give our young daughter to this old Sakka!" Vepacitti, the Asura King, asked, "Who took her away?" "Great King, the old Sakka took her," they replied. He said, "Among all the other gods, this Sakka alone is noble. Let them go." Sakka took the Asura maiden and appointed her as the chief of his three crores of celestial dancers. She asked for a boon from Sakka: "Great King, I have no mother, father, brother, or sister in this celestial realm. Wherever you go, Great King, please take me with you." Sakka gave his word, saying, "Very well."

Thus, seeing the purity of Sakka since his time as the youth Magha in Macala village, the Blessed One said, "For a long time, this Yakkha (Sakka) has been pure." "Atthasaṃhitaṃ" means based on one's own benefit and the benefit of others, or based on the cause of welfare and happiness.

## Pañhaveyyākaraṇavaṇṇanā
"Kiṃsaṃyojanā" means having what kind of fetters, or being bound by what bond? "Puthukāyā" means many people. "Averā" means being without enmity. "Adaṇḍā" means being free from the punishment of weapons or the punishment of wealth (fines). "Asapattā" means being without enemies or rivals. "Avyāpajjhā" means being free from sorrow and distress. "Viharemu averino" means "Oh, how good it would be if we could live without enmity toward anyone! If we could enjoy the wealth obtained by a mere snap of the fingers with a thousand attendants, without giving rise to anger anywhere!" Thus, they make offerings, perform worship, and make such aspirations. "Iti ca nesaṃ hoti" means "Thus is their aspiration." "Atha ca pana" means "Even though there is such an aspiration (they still have enmity)."

"Issāmacchariya-saṃyojanā": Issā (envy) has the characteristic of begrudging the prosperity of others. Macchariya (stinginess) has the characteristic of not being able to share one's own prosperity with others. The fetter of this envy and stinginess exists in those beings. This is the summary here. In detail, envy and stinginess are explained in the Abhidhamma.
311:
Due to stinginess regarding dwellings (āvāsamacchariya), one may become a yakkha or a peta in this life, wandering around carrying the refuse of that dwelling on one's head. Due to stinginess regarding families (kulamacchariya), when seeing others giving alms to that family, one thinks, "Alas, my family is ruined!" Such a person may suffer from bleeding from the mouth, diarrhea, and the intestines coming out in pieces. Due to stinginess regarding gains (lābhamacchariya), if one is stingy with gains belonging to the Saṅgha or a group and uses them as personal property, one may be reborn as a yakkha, a peta, or a great python. Due to stinginess regarding one's physical appearance and virtues, and stinginess regarding the scriptures (pariyatti), if one praises only one's own virtues and disparages others' by saying, "What kind of appearance does he have?" and does not give even a little of the scriptural knowledge to anyone, one may become ugly, mute, or stammering. 

Furthermore, due to āvāsamacchariya, one is cooked in the Iron House Hell. Due to kulamacchariya, one has few gains. Due to lābhamacchariya, one is reborn in the Excrement Hell (Gūthaniraya). Due to vaṇṇamacchariya, one will not have a beautiful appearance in a new life. Due to dhammamacchariya, one is reborn in the Hot Ashes Hell (Kukkuḷaniraya). These fetters of envy and stinginess are abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga). As long as these fetters are not abandoned, even though devas and humans aspire to be free from enmity, they are not liberated from it. "My doubt in this matter is crossed over" means that upon hearing the Blessed One's answer, the doubt is cleared; it does not mean the doubt is cleared by the power of the Path. "Uncertainty is gone" means the thoughts of "How is this? How is that?" have been removed. 

The meanings of terms like "Nidāna" (source/origin) are as previously stated. "Sourced from the beloved and unbeloved" (piyāppiyanidāna) means that stinginess is sourced from beloved beings, and envy is sourced from unbeloved beings. Or both are sourced from both. For a monk, his co-residents and pupils, and for a layperson, children, elephants, horses, etc., are beloved beings. They cannot bear not seeing them even for a moment. When such a person sees another obtaining such a beloved being, he becomes envious. When others request, "We have some business with this person; please give him to us for a moment," he becomes stingy, saying, "I cannot give him; he will be tired or distressed," and so on. In this way, both are sourced from beloved beings. For a monk, requisites like the bowl and robes, and for a layperson, ornaments and utensils are beloved and pleasant. That person...
312:
Seeing such a thing (a beloved structure) arise for another, one feels envy, thinking, "Oh, would that such a thing did not happen to him!" Or, even when asked, one feels stinginess, thinking, "We too cherish this so much that we have not yet used it; we cannot give it." Thus, both envy and stinginess have loved formations as their cause. Even when obtaining unloved beings and formations that are disagreeable to oneself, due to the perverted nature of the defilements, one feels envy, thinking, "Who else but me should obtain such a thing?" Or, even when asked for a temporary loan, one feels stinginess, being unwilling to give. Thus, both have unloved beings and formations as their cause.

In this phrase "chanda-nidāna" (rooted in desire), there are five types of desire: the desire for seeking (pariyesanachanda), the desire for obtaining (paṭilābhachanda), the desire for consumption (paribhogachanda), the desire for hoarding (sannidhichanda), and the desire for spending (vissajjanachanda).

What is the desire for seeking? Here, someone, being insatiable and filled with desire, seeks visible forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangible objects; he seeks wealth. This is called the desire for seeking.

What is the desire for obtaining? Here, someone, being insatiable and filled with desire, obtains visible forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangible objects; he obtains wealth. This is called the desire for obtaining.

What is the desire for consumption? Here, someone, being insatiable and filled with desire, consumes visible forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangible objects; he consumes wealth. This is called the desire for consumption.

What is the desire for hoarding? Here, someone, being insatiable and filled with desire, hoards wealth, thinking, "It will be useful when dangers arise." This is called the desire for hoarding.

What is the desire for spending? Here, someone, being insatiable and filled with desire, spends and gives wealth to elephant-riders, horse-riders, charioteers, and archers, thinking, "These people will protect me, keep me safe, cherish me, and surround me." This is called the desire for spending. These are the five types of desire. In this sutta, only craving (taṇhā) is intended; therefore, this is said with reference to that craving.

In this phrase "vitakka-nidāna" (rooted in thought), the thought of decision (vinicchaya-vitakka), which is spoken of as "decision based on gain," is called thought (vitakka). Regarding "decision" (vinicchaya), there are two types of decision.
313:
There are the decision of craving (taṇhā-vinicchaya) and the decision of views (diṭṭhi-vinicchaya). The one hundred and eight modes of craving are called the decision of craving, and the sixty-two types of wrong views are called the decision of views. Through the power of the aforementioned decision of craving, the differentiation of desirable and undesirable objects, or loved and unloved objects, is not possible. This is because the very same object may be desirable to one person but undesirable to another. This is like the difference in desire for earthworms and venison between the kings of the border regions and the kings of the Middle Country. However, regarding the object obtained through the decision of craving, the differentiation—"This much will be for visible forms, this much for sounds, this much for smells, this much for tastes, this much for tangible objects; this much will be for me, this much for others; this much I will bury, this much I will give to others"—occurs through the decision of thought (vitakka-vinicchaya). Therefore, the Blessed One said, "O Sakka, Lord of Devas, desire is rooted in thought."

"Papañca-saññā-saṅkhā-nidāna" refers to the three types of proliferation (papañca): the proliferation of craving, the proliferation of conceit, and the proliferation of views. Among these, the one hundred and eight modes of craving are called the proliferation of craving. The nine types of conceit are called the proliferation of conceit. The sixty-two types of wrong views are called the proliferation of views. In this sutta, the proliferation of craving is intended. In what sense is it called "papañca"? It is called "papañca" in the sense of leading to a state of heedlessness and intoxication. Perception associated with that craving is called "papañca-saññā." As in the Pali passages such as "saññā-nidānā hi papañca-saṅkhā," the word "saṅkhā" means a portion or a group. Therefore, "papañca-saññā-saṅkhā-nidāna" means thought rooted in the group of perceptions of conceptual proliferation.

"Papañca-saññā-saṅkhā-nirodha-sāruppa-gāminī" refers to the questioning about the Path (magga) along with insight (vipassanā), which is suitable for the cessation (Nibbāna) resulting from the exhaustion of that group of conceptual proliferations, and which leads to that cessation.

## Explanation of the Meditation Subject of Feeling (Vedanākammaṭṭhāna-vaṇṇanā)

Then, the Blessed One taught the three types of feeling to Sakka, starting with "Somanassaṃpāhaṃ" (I say joy...). Did the Blessed One explain what was asked, or what was not asked? Did He explain with a connection (anusandhi), or without a connection? He explained only what was asked, not what was not asked. He explained only with a connection, not without a connection. For to the devas, the mental (arūpa) is more evident than the physical (rūpa), and among mental phenomena, feeling (vedanā) is more evident. Why is that? Because the physical bodies (karajakāya) of the devas are subtle, and their kamma-born matter (kammajarūpa) is powerful. Due to the subtlety of the physical body and the power of the kamma-born matter, the devas cannot survive even if they miss a single meal.
314:
Everything should be understood according to the method stated in the Brahmajāla Sutta, just as a lump of butter placed on a hot stone melts away (so do material phenomena perish). Therefore, the Blessed One began teaching the meditation subject to Sakka based on the three types of feeling. Indeed, there are two kinds of meditation subjects: the meditation subject of materiality (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) and the meditation subject of mentality (arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna). These two are also called the discernment of materiality (rūpa-pariggaha) and the discernment of mentality (arūpa-pariggaha).

Among those two, for a person to whom materiality is apparent, the Blessed One teaches the meditation subject of materiality by expanding on the definition of the four elements (catudhātu-vavatthāna), either in brief or in detail. For a person to whom mentality is apparent, He teaches the meditation subject of mentality. Even when teaching that, He does so only after showing the meditation subject of materiality which is the basis for that mentality. However, for the devas, the meditation subject of mentality is more apparent; therefore, He began the teaching based on feelings by way of the meditation subject of mentality.

Indeed, there are three ways of entering into the meditation subject of mentality: by way of contact (phassa), by way of feeling (vedanā), and by way of consciousness (citta). How? For some individuals, after discerning the meditation subject of materiality either in brief or in detail, contact (phassa) becomes apparent—arising as the first impact of the mind and mental factors on that object, touching that object. For some, feeling (vedanā) becomes apparent, arising as the experience of that object. For some, consciousness (viññāṇa) becomes apparent, arising as the cognition of that object after discerning it.

Among those three types of individuals, for the one to whom contact is apparent, it is not that contact alone arises; along with that contact, feeling that experiences the same object also arises, perception (saññā) that recognizes it arises, volition (cetanā) that coordinates it arises, and consciousness (viññāṇa) that cognizes it also arises. Thus, he discerns only the group of five starting with contact (phassa-pañcamaka). For the one to whom feeling is apparent, it is not that feeling alone arises; along with that feeling, contact that touches the same object also arises, perception that recognizes it arises, volition that coordinates it arises, and consciousness that cognizes it also arises. Thus, he discerns only the group of five starting with contact. For the one to whom consciousness is apparent, it is not that consciousness alone arises; along with that consciousness, contact that touches the same object also arises, feeling that experiences it arises, perception that recognizes it arises, and volition that coordinates it also arises. Thus, he discerns only the group of five starting with contact.

As that person investigates, "On what do these five states starting with contact depend?", he understands, "They depend on a physical basis (vatthu)." The physical body (karajakāya) is called the basis, referring to which...
315:
It is also said: "And this consciousness of mine is supported here, bound here." In terms of meaning, that [body] consists of both the primary elements (bhūta-rūpa) and derived materiality (upādā-rūpa). Thus, in this context, he sees only mentality and materiality, [understanding] that the physical basis is materiality and the five states starting with contact are mentality. Materiality here is the aggregate of materiality (rūpakkhandha), and mentality is the four immaterial aggregates; thus there are only the five aggregates. Indeed, there are no five aggregates apart from mentality and materiality, nor is there mentality and materiality apart from the five aggregates.

As that person investigates, "What is the cause of these five aggregates?", he sees, "They have ignorance and so forth as their cause." Thereafter, [he realizes], "This is both the cause and the result; there is no other being or person; it is merely a heap of pure formations (saṅkhāra-puñja)." Thus, by way of mentality and materiality with their causes, he applies the three characteristics and wanders contemplating "impermanence, suffering, and non-self" through the sequence of insight (vipassanā). Aspiring for penetration this very day, and having obtained suitable weather, person, food, or hearing of the Dhamma on such a day, he brings insight to its peak while sitting in a single cross-legged posture and is established in the fruit of Arahantship. In this way, the meditation subject was taught to these three types of people up to the stage of Arahantship.

In this sutta, however, the Blessed One, when teaching the meditation subject of mentality, taught it by making feeling the head (the starting point). The reason is that if it were taught by way of contact or consciousness, it would not be apparent to that assembly of devas; it would seem like a mass of darkness. But it becomes apparent when taught by way of feeling. Why? Because of the distinctness of the arising of feelings. Indeed, the arising of pleasant and painful feelings is distinct.

When pleasant feeling arises, it arises while moving, massaging, pervading, and drenching the whole body, as if one were eating butter washed a hundred times, or being anointed with oil cooked a hundred times, or as if one were quenching a fever with a thousand jars [of water], causing one to utter, "Oh, what bliss! Oh, what bliss!" When painful feeling arises, it arises while moving, massaging, pervading, and drenching the whole body, as if a hot iron plate were being inserted, or as if one were being poured with molten copper, or as if a bundle of torches were being thrown into a forest of dry grass and trees, causing one to lament, "Oh, what pain! Oh, what pain!" Thus, the arising of pleasant and painful feelings is distinct.

Neutral feeling (neither-painful-nor-pleasant), however, is difficult to point out; it is as if overwhelmed by darkness. It becomes apparent to one who grasps it by way of the method: "Neutral feeling is that which exists in the middle state by way of rejecting both the pleasant and the unpleasant when pleasure and pain have disappeared." How? Just as [the tracks of] a deer that has fled by climbing onto a flat rock...
316:
Just as a hunter, seeing footprints on both the near and far sides of a flat rock but not in the middle, knows by inference, "He ascended from here, he descended from there, and he must have traveled across this part of the middle of the flat rock"; so too, the arising of pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) is evident like the footprint at the place of ascent, and the arising of painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā) is evident like the footprint at the place of descent. To one who takes it by way of inference, "Having ascended from here and descended from there, he went thus in the middle," the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkhamasukha-vedanā)—which is a neutral state characterized by the rejection of both the agreeable and the disagreeable in the absence of pleasure and pain—becomes evident. In this way, the Blessed One first taught the meditation on form (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) and later showed the meditation on the formless (arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) by directing it through the power of feeling (vedanā).

Not only in this Sakkapañha Sutta did He show it thus, but also in many discourses such as the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta, the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya, the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta, the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta, the Cūḷavedalla Sutta, the Mahāvedalla Sutta, the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta, the Māgaṇဍiya Sutta, the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta, the Āneñjasappāya Sutta, and the entire Vedanā Saṃyutta; He first taught the meditation on form and later showed the meditation on the formless by directing it through the power of feeling. Just as He showed in those various discourses, so too in this Sakkapañha Sutta, He first taught the meditation on form and later showed the meditation on the formless by directing it through the power of feeling. In this sutta, however, the meditation on form is merely the object of feeling and is summarized; therefore, it might not appear directly in the Pali text.

To show the path of attention (manasikāra) through the power of feeling that was evident to Sakka, the Lord of Devas, in the meditation on the formless, He said: "Lord of Devas, I say that joy (somanassa) is also of two kinds," and so forth. In that Pali, "duvidhena" means in two ways, or by two portions. "Such joy should not be pursued" means that such household-based joy (gehasita-somanassa) should not be pursued. What is called household-based joy is this: "Therein, what are the six household-based joys? Joy arises in one who obtains, or regards as obtained, forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasant, charming, and connected with worldly baits; or in one who recollects such forms that were previously obtained, which are now past, ceased, and changed. Such joy as this is called household-based joy." Thus, it is the joy based on the cords of sensual pleasure taught in relation to the six sense doors.
317:
"Such joy should be pursued" means that such renunciation-based joy (nekkhammasita-somanassa) should be pursued. What is called renunciation-based joy is this: "Therein, what are the six renunciation-based joys? Having known the impermanence, change, fading away, and cessation of forms, joy arises in one who sees with right wisdom as it really is: 'Formerly as well as now, all these forms are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.' Such joy as this is called renunciation-based joy" (as stated in the Majjhima Nikāya). Thus, it refers to the joy that arises from the delight of one who is able to exert effort by initiating insight (vipassanā) into desirable objects that have come into range at the six sense doors, by way of impermanence and so forth, thinking, "My insight has been well-exerted." Joy that arises through the power of renunciation, insight, recollection (anussati), the first jhāna, and so forth, is called joy that should be pursued.

Among those joys, "that joy which is with thought (savitakka) and examination (savicāra)" should be understood as the joy accompanied by vitakka and vicāra arising through the power of renunciation, insight, recollection, and the first jhāna. "That joy which is without thought (avitakka) and without examination (avicāra)" should be understood as the joy without vitakka and vicāra arising through the power of the second and third jhānas. "Those joys which are without thought and without examination are more sublime" means that between those two types, the joy without thought and without examination is more sublime.

What is meant by this statement? It refers to the attainment of Arahantship by two types of persons. How? It is said that one monk initiates insight into joy that is with thought and examination, and while investigating, "On what does this joy depend?" he realizes, "It depends on the physical base (vatthu)." Then, following the method mentioned in the "group of five starting with contact" (phassapañcamaka), he gradually establishes himself in Arahantship. Another monk initiates insight into joy that is without thought and without examination and, following the same mentioned method, establishes himself in Arahantship. Among those joys thus attended to, the one without thought and examination is more sublime than the one with thought and examination. Insight based on joy without thought and examination is also more sublime than insight based on joy with thought and examination. The attainment of the fruition (phalasamāpatti) of joy without thought and examination is also more sublime than the attainment of the fruition of joy with thought and examination. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Those which are without thought and without examination are more sublime."
318:
“Such displeasure should not be cultivated” means that one should not cultivate the displeasure (domanassa) based on the household life, which is of a nature to cause the increase of unwholesome states and the decrease of wholesome states. What is household-based displeasure (gehasita-domanassa)? It is said: ‘Therein, what are the six kinds of household-based displeasure? When one does not obtain, or sees as not obtaining, forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, charming, and connected with worldly gain; or when one remembers a past form that was not obtained before, or has ceased and changed—displeasure arises. Such displeasure as this is called household-based displeasure.’ This refers to the displeasure rooted in the cords of sensual pleasure that arises in one who reflects, ‘I did not experience, I will not experience, or I do not experience’ a desirable object at the six sense doors.

“Such displeasure should be cultivated” means that one should cultivate the displeasure based on renunciation (nekkhamma-sita-domanassa), which is based on the state of a monk who has gone forth from the bond of the household life. What is renunciation-based displeasure? It is said: ‘Therein, what are the six kinds of renunciation-based displeasure? Having known the impermanence of forms, their change, fading away, and cessation through old age and death, and seeing with right wisdom as it really is: “Formerly and now, all these forms are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change,” one awakens a longing for the supreme liberations (vimokkha) known as the Noble Fruit (ariya-phala), thinking: “When shall I enter and abide in that base which the Noble Ones (Ariyas) now enter and abide in?” For one who awakens such longing for the supreme liberations, displeasure arises due to that longing. Such displeasure as this is called renunciation-based displeasure.’ This refers to the displeasure that arises in one who, when a desirable object appears at the six sense doors, awakens a longing for the Noble Fruit called supreme liberation, and being unable to exert effort in insight (vipassanā) based on impermanence etc. to attain that Noble Fruit, grieves: ‘I have not been able to reach the Noble stage even in this fortnight, this month, or this year.’ Displeasure that arises through renunciation, insight, recollection (anussati), or the first jhāna, etc., is called displeasure that should be cultivated.

Regarding that displeasure, ‘that which is with initial and sustained thought (savitakka-savicāra)’ means that among the two types of displeasure, only household-based displeasure is called displeasure with initial and sustained thought. Displeasure arising through renunciation, insight, recollection, or the first and second jhānas should be understood as displeasure without initial and sustained thought (avitakka-avicāra). However, in the strict sense (nippariyāyena), there is no such thing as displeasure without initial and sustained thought. For the faculty of displeasure (domanassindriya) is invariably unwholesome and accompanied by initial and sustained thought. Nevertheless, it is described as ‘with initial and sustained thought’ or ‘without initial and sustained thought’ according to the monk’s reflection. The meaning of this reflection is: in this Dispensation, a monk takes up the states with initial and sustained thought and the states without initial and sustained thought which are the causes of displeasure, and the path and fruit states that arise solely because of the cause of that displeasure. By observing the practice of others, he reflects: ‘When shall I develop insight based on displeasure caused by jhāna with initial and sustained thought? When shall I develop insight based on displeasure without initial and sustained thought? When shall I produce the fruit caused by displeasure based on jhāna with initial and sustained thought?’ Thus, he takes up a practice to be fulfilled in three, six, or nine months. Taking up the practice to be fulfilled in three months, in the first month, he purifies his mind for one watch and allows himself to sleep for two watches. In the middle month, he purifies his mind for two watches and allows himself to sleep for one watch. In the final watch...
319:
In this regard, this is the method—here, in this Dispensation, a monk takes the states accompanied by initial and sustained application of mind (savitakka-savicāra) and those without initial and sustained application of mind (avitakka-avicāra), which are the causes of distress (domanassa), as well as the states of the Path and Fruit which arise solely due to the cause of distress based on those states. By observing the practice of others, he considers it as 'distress' and reflects: 'When will I be able to establish insight (vipassanā) into the distress that has its cause in jhāna with initial and sustained application? When will I be able to establish insight into the distress without initial and sustained application?' and 'When will I be able to produce the fruition attainment (phala-samāpatti) of distress caused by initial and sustained application? When will I be able to produce the fruition attainment of distress caused by the absence of initial and sustained application?' Thinking thus, he undertakes a three-month, six-month, or nine-month course of practice.

Having undertaken the three-month practice, in the first month, he remains awake and purifies his mind for one watch and allows himself to sleep for two watches. In the middle month, he remains awake for two watches and allows himself to sleep for one watch. In the final month, he spends his time only in walking and sitting. Practicing in this way, if he attains the fruit of Arahatship, it is well. If he does not attain it, he specifically undertakes the six-month practice. In that six-month practice, he practices each two-month period according to the method mentioned above. If he still cannot attain Arahatship, he specifically undertakes the nine-month practice. In that nine-month practice, he practices each three-month period in the same manner. For the person who still cannot attain Arahatship, distress arises as he reflects, 'Alas, I have not gained the opportunity to perform the pure Pavāraṇā ceremony together with my fellow monks,' and a stream of tears flows, just as it happened to the Elder Mahāsīva, a resident of Gāmantapabbhāra.

## The Story of Elder Mahāsīva

It is said that the Elder taught eighteen great groups of students. Established in his instruction, thirty thousand monks attained the fruit of Arahatship. Then, a certain monk reflected, 'As for me, the internal virtues are immeasurable; I wonder what the virtues of my teacher are like.' Seeing that his teacher was still a worldling (puthujjana), he thought, 'Our teacher is a refuge for others, but he cannot yet be a refuge for himself. I will give him an admonition.' He traveled through the air, descended near the monastery, approached the teacher who was sitting in his daytime resting place, performed his duties, and sat in a suitable place.

The Elder asked, 'Friend, monk who observes the dhutaṅga of alms-round, for what reason have you come?' He replied, 'Venerable sir, I have come to learn a single verse of appreciation (anumodanā).' The Elder said, 'Friend, there will be no opportunity.' The monk said, 'Venerable sir, I will ask when you are at the meditation platform.' The Elder replied, 'Others ask me there.' The monk said, 'Venerable sir, I will ask on the road for alms.' The Elder replied, 'Others ask me there too.' The monk said, 'Venerable sir, at the place where you change your inner robe, where you robe yourself in the upper robe, or where you take out your bowl...'
320:
'Venerable sir, I will ask when you have wandered through the village and are drinking gruel in the refectory.' The Elder said, 'Friend, at that time, the Elders who teach the Commentaries clear their own doubts.' The monk said, 'Venerable sir, I will ask when you leave the village.' The Elder said, 'Friend, others ask me then as well.' The monk said, 'Venerable sir, I will ask on the road, or at the end of the meal in the refectory, or at your daytime resting place, or when you wash your feet, or when you wash your face.' The Elder said, 'At those times too, others ask me.' The Elder continued, 'Friend, from the time of washing the face until dawn, others ask me.' The monk said, 'Venerable sir, I will ask when you take the tooth-wood and go to wash your face.' The Elder said, 'Others ask then too.' The monk said, 'Venerable sir, I will ask when you return after washing your face.' The Elder said, 'Others ask then too.' The monk said, 'Venerable sir, I will ask when you have entered your dwelling and are sitting down.' The Elder said, 'Others ask then too.' The monk then said, 'Venerable sir, after washing your face and entering your dwelling, should there not be a time of leisure for you who sit cross-legged three or four times to let the heat subside and perform the work of wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra)? Venerable sir, you will not even get the opportunity for the moment of death. Venerable sir, you are like a wooden plank. You are only a refuge for others; you are not able to be one for yourself. I have no need for your appreciation.' Saying this, he rose into the air and departed.

Elder Mahāsīva realized, 'This monk has no need for study; he came to be like a goad to admonish me.' Thinking, 'Now there is no opportunity; I will go at dawn,' he placed his bowl and robes nearby. After teaching the Dhamma throughout the day and during the first and middle watches, he took his bowl and robes and departed at dawn along with another monk who had just finished his lesson. The resident disciples thought, 'The teacher has gone out for some business.' The monk who left with him also thought, 'He is just a fellow monk traveling together.'

The Elder thought, 'How can attaining Arahatship be difficult for someone like me? I will return after reaching it within two or three days.' Without informing his disciples, he departed on the thirteenth day of the waxing moon of Āsāḷha, went to a mountain cave near a village, and ascended the walking path. Although he reflected on the meditation subject, he was unable to attain Arahatship on that day. When the Uposatha day arrived, he thought, 'I came thinking I would attain Arahatship in two or three days, but I could not. I will consider these three months as three days and strive until the Great Pavāraṇā.' Even after entering the Rains Retreat (Vassa) and striving, he could not attain it. On the Pavāraṇā day, he reflected, 'I came thinking I would take Arahatship in two or three days. I have striven for three months but could not. My fellow monks are performing the pure Pavāraṇā.' As he thought this, tears flowed from the Elder.
321:
“I came [thinking I would attain the fruit of Arahantship in two or three days], but though I have striven for three months, I have not been able to succeed. My fellow practitioners have performed the pure Pavāraṇā,” he thought. As he thought thus, streams of tears flowed from the Elder. Then he thought, “The Path and Fruit will not arise for me in the four postures while on the couch. Without reaching the fruit of Arahantship, I shall neither stretch my back on the couch nor wash my feet.” Having thought so, he set the couch aside. Again, when the rainy season arrived, he was still unable to attain the fruit of Arahantship. Streams of tears flowed until the twenty-ninth Pavāraṇā. Village children used thorns to sew up the cracked areas on the Elder's feet. Even while doing so, they mocked him, saying, “May [our feet] be like the feet of the Great Elder Mahāsīva.”

On the day of the Great Pavāraṇā in the thirtieth year, the Elder stood leaning against a support plank and thought, “It has now been thirty years since I began practicing the recluse's Dhamma. I have not been able to reach the fruit of Arahantship. Surely, there is no Path or Fruit for me in this existence.
