I have not had the opportunity to perform the pure Pavāraṇā together with my fellow practitioners.” Even as he was thinking this, displeasure (domanassa) arose in him, and streams of tears flowed. Then, a goddess stood crying not far away. When asked, “Who is crying here?” she replied, “Venerable sir, I am a goddess.” When asked, “Why are you crying?” she replied, “Venerable sir, assuming that the Path and Fruit can be produced by crying, I am crying with the intention that I too might produce one or two fruits of the Path.”

Then the Elder admonished himself, “O Great Elder Mahāsīva, even the deities are mocking you. This mockery by the deities is indeed unbecoming of you.” He then developed insight (vipassanā) and attained the fruit of Arahantship together with the Analytical Knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Thinking, “Now I shall lie down,” he tidied the sleeping quarters, prepared the couch, placed water ready at the washing place, and sat on the plank at the head of the stairs, thinking, “I shall wash my feet.” His disciples also reflected, “It has been thirty years since our teacher went to practice the recluse's Dhamma. Has he been able to produce the special attainment or not?” Seeing him sitting to wash his feet after reaching Arahantship, they thought, “While disciples like us are present, it is improper for our teacher to wash his own feet. I shall wash them! I shall wash them!” Saying so, thirty thousand monks came through the air, paid homage, and requested, “Venerable sir, let us wash your feet.”
322:
“Venerable sir,” they said. “Friends, it has now been thirty years since my feet were last washed. You all stay back; I shall wash them myself,” he said. Sakka, the King of Devas, also reflected, “My lord, the Great Elder Mahāsīva, has reached the fruit of Arahantship. He did not allow the thirty thousand disciples who came to wash his feet to do so. While an attendant like me is present, it is improper for my lord to wash his own feet. I shall wash them myself.” Having made this resolution, he appeared in the presence of the Saṅgha of monks together with Queen Sujātā. Sakka, placing the Asura maiden Sujātā in front, made way by saying, “Step aside, venerable sirs, a woman is coming.” He approached the Elder, paid homage, sat in a crouching position in front of him, and said, “Venerable sir, I shall wash your feet.”

“Kosiya, it has now been thirty years since my feet were last washed. To deities, the odor of the human body is naturally loathsome. Even when standing a hundred yojanas away, it is like a rotting carcass tied to the neck. Therefore, I shall wash them myself,” he said. “Venerable sir, this body odor is not apparent to me. Only the scent of your virtue (sīlagandha) pervades, transcending the six deva worlds and reaching up to the highest point of existence (bhavagga). There is no scent more excellent or superior than the scent of virtue. Venerable sir, I have come because of the scent of your virtue,” he replied. He then held the ankle joint with his left hand and massaged the sole of the foot with his right hand. The feet became like those of a young boy. After washing the feet and paying homage, Sakka returned to the deva world.

Thus, it should be understood that based on the displeasure (domanassa) that arose in the monk who reflected, “I no longer have the opportunity to perform the pure Pavāraṇā with my fellow practitioners,” through the power of mindfulness, the access concentration (upacāra-jhāna) which is the object of insight, insight itself, the Path, and the Fruit are described in the Pali as “domanassa with initial and sustained application” (savitakka-savicāra-domanassa) and “domanassa without initial and sustained application” (avitakka-avicāra-domanassa).

In this regard, one monk begins insight on domanassa with initial and sustained application and, investigating “What does this displeasure depend on?”, realizes it depends on the physical base (vatthu). In this manner, following the method described in the five factors starting with contact (phassapañcamaka), he gradually established himself in the fruit of Arahantship. Another monk begins insight on domanassa without initial and sustained application and, in the same manner described, established himself in the fruit of Arahantship. Among those types of displeasure thus contemplated, that which is without initial and sustained application is more sublime than that with initial and sustained application. Insight on domanassa without initial and sustained application is also more sublime than insight on domanassa with initial and sustained application. Likewise, the fruition attainment (phalasamāpatti) of domanassa without initial and sustained application is indeed more sublime than the fruition attainment of domanassa with initial and sustained application.
323:
(Those states) are exceedingly noble. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "There are states that are without initial thought and without sustained thought; those states are exceedingly noble."

"Such a kind of equanimity should not be cultivated" means that this kind of household-based equanimity (gehasita-upekkhā), which is based on the home life of sensual pleasures, should not be cultivated. What is household-based equanimity? "Among them, what are the six household-based equanimities? When an unlearned, foolish worldling, who has not seen the danger, who has not overcome the results [of kamma], who has not overcome the defilements, and who is ignorant, sees a form with the eye, equanimity arises. Such a kind of equanimity that exists cannot transcend the form; therefore, that equanimity is called household-based." (Thus it is taught). In this way, when a pleasant object appears at the six doors, like a fly landing on a lump of molasses, the equanimity based on sensual pleasures arises, being stuck and attached to that very object without being able to transcend forms and so on; such equanimity should not be cultivated.

"Such a kind of equanimity should be cultivated" means that this kind of renunciation-based equanimity (nekkhamma-sita-upekkhā) should be cultivated. What is renunciation-based equanimity? "Among them, what are the six renunciation-based equanimities? Having known the impermanence of forms, their change, fading away, and cessation, and seeing with right wisdom as it really is that 'formerly as well as now, all these forms are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change,' equanimity arises. Such a kind of equanimity that exists transcends the form; therefore, that equanimity is called renunciation-based." (Thus it is taught). In this way, when pleasant or unpleasant objects appear at the six doors, it is the equanimity associated with insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) that arises by observing with even-mindedness without being deluded, not being attached to the pleasant and not being irritated by the unpleasant. Furthermore, the equanimity of specific neutrality (tatra-majjhattūpekkhā), which is of the same nature as the feeling, is also taken as equanimity here. Therefore, it means that the equanimity arising by power of renunciation, insight, the stations of recollection (anussatiṭṭhāna), and the first, second, third, and fourth jhanas should be cultivated.

Here, "the state that is with initial thought and with sustained thought" should be understood as the equanimity with initial and sustained thought (savitakka-savicāra) arising by power of renunciation, insight, the stations of recollection, and the first jhana among those renunciation-based equanimities. "The state that is without initial thought and without sustained thought" should be understood as the equanimity without initial and sustained thought (avitakka-avicāra) arising by power of the second jhana and so on. "Those states that are without initial thought and without sustained thought are exceedingly noble" means that between these two, the equanimity without initial and sustained thought is more noble. What is meant by this statement?
324:
Is it so? It is the teaching of the Fruit of Arahantship for two types of persons. Indeed, one monk, having established insight (vipassanā) in the equanimity with initial and sustained thought, and reflecting, 'On what does this equanimity depend?', understands that it depends on the physical basis (vatthu). In this way, following the sequence mentioned in the method of 'contact as the fifth,' he becomes established in the Fruit of Arahantship. Another monk, having established insight in the equanimity without initial and sustained thought, becomes established in the Fruit of Arahantship by the same mentioned method. Among those equanimities thus applied, the one without initial and sustained thought is more noble than the one with initial and sustained thought. Even compared to insight based on equanimity with initial and sustained thought, insight based on equanimity without initial and sustained thought is more noble. Even compared to the attainment of the fruit (phala-samāpatti) of equanimity with initial and sustained thought, the attainment of the fruit of equanimity without initial and sustained thought is indeed more noble. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Those that are without initial thought and without sustained thought are exceedingly noble."

"O Sakka, Lord of Devas, a monk who has practiced in this way is one who has practiced the path suitable for reaching the cessation of the perceptions and categories of mental proliferation (papañca-saññā-saṅkhā-nirodha)." Thus the Blessed One concluded the teaching by setting the Fruit of Arahantship as the summit. Sakka, however, attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). For the intention of the Buddhas is never low; it is only exalted. Whether teaching the Dhamma to one or to many, they take the Fruit of Arahantship as the summit. Beings, however, remaining in their own suitable supporting conditions (upanissaya), some become Stream-enterers, some Once-returners, some Non-returners, and some Arahants. Indeed, the Blessed One is like a King, and those to be guided (veneyya) are like young princes. Just as a King, when taking a meal, takes a morsel of food according to his own capacity and gives it to the young princes, and those young princes make a mouthful from that food only according to the size of their own mouths; in the same way, the Blessed One, with a teaching suitable to his own intention, takes the Fruit of Arahantship as the summit. Those to be guided, according to the capacity of their own supporting conditions, take from that teaching only the Fruit of Stream-entry, or the Fruit of Once-returning, Non-returning, or Arahantship. Sakka, however, became a Stream-enterer. Having become a Stream-enterer, he passed away right in front of the Blessed One and was instantly reborn as a young Sakka. For the departure and arrival of the bodies of devas who are passing away is not perceived; it is like the movement of a lamp's flame. Therefore, the other devas did not know. Only two persons knew: Sakka himself, because of his passing away, and the Blessed One, because of his unimpeded knowledge. Then Sakka thought: "The Blessed One has taught me only the result (Path and Fruit) produced in three places. But this Path or Fruit cannot be seized instantly like a bird leaping and catching [prey]; there must be a preliminary practice (pubbabhāga-paṭipadā) that leads to it. Now, I shall ask about the preliminary practice for the higher state of one who has destroyed the taints (an Arahant)."
325:
## Explanation of the Restraint of the Pātimokkha

At that time, Sakka, the king of devas, wishing to ask about the prior practice of that Arahant, spoke these words: "Venerable sir, how do you practice?" and so forth. In that context, the phrase "for the sake of the restraint of the Pātimokkha" (pātimokkhasaṃvarāya) refers to the virtue of the Pātimokkha restraint, which is superior to and greater than all other mundane virtues. The words beginning with "bodily conduct also" (kāyasamācārampi) were spoken for the purpose of showing the restraint of the Pātimokkha by way of bodily conduct that should be cultivated, and so on. This discourse on virtue (sīlakathā) should be explained either by way of the courses of action (kammapatha) or by way of prescriptions (paṇṇatti).

Among these two, if explained by way of the courses of action, bodily conduct that should not be cultivated is first explained through killing living beings, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct. If explained by way of prescriptions, it is explained through the transgression of the training rules prescribed for the body-door. Bodily conduct that should be cultivated is explained through abstinence from killing living beings and so forth, as well as through the non-transgression of the training rules prescribed for the body-door. Verbal conduct that should not be cultivated is explained through verbal misconduct such as false speech and so forth, as well as through the transgression of the training rules prescribed for the speech-door. Verbal conduct that should be cultivated is explained through abstinence from false speech and so forth, as well as through the non-transgression of the training rules prescribed for the speech-door.

Seeking (pariyesanā), however, is only seeking through body and speech. Although such seeking is included within the categories of bodily and verbal conduct, because the virtue with livelihood as the eighth (ājīvaṭṭhamakasīla) arises only at these two doors—the body-door and the speech-door—and not in the air, it is mentioned separately for the purpose of showing the virtue with livelihood as the eighth. Among those types of seeking, seeking that should not be cultivated is explained as ignoble search (anariyapariyesanā). Seeking that should be cultivated is explained as noble search (ariyapariyesanā). Thus it was also said:

"Monks, there are these two types of search: the ignoble search and the noble search. And what, monks, is the ignoble search? Here, monks, someone being himself subject to birth seeks only what is subject to birth. Being himself subject to aging, subject to sickness, subject to death, subject to sorrow, and subject to defilement, he seeks only what is subject to defilement.

And what, monks, would you say is subject to birth? Wife and children, monks, are subject to birth. Female and male slaves are subject to birth. Goats and sheep are subject to birth. Poultry and pigs are subject to birth. Elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to birth. Gold and silver are subject to birth."
326:
Monks, these acquisitions (upadhi) such as wife and children are subject to birth. This being, who is attached to, infatuated with, and indulged in these sensual pleasures, being himself subject to birth, seeks only what is subject to birth.

Monks, and what would you say is subject to aging? Monks, wife and children are said to be subject to aging... he seeks only what is subject to aging.

Monks, and what would you say is subject to sickness? Monks, wife and children are said to be subject to sickness. Female and male slaves are said to be subject to sickness. Goats and sheep are said to be subject to sickness. Poultry and pigs are said to be subject to sickness. Elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are said to be subject to sickness. Monks, these acquisitions such as wife and children are subject to sickness. This being, who is attached to, infatuated with, and indulged in these acquisitions, being himself subject to sickness, seeks only what is subject to sickness.

Monks, and what would you say is subject to death? Monks, wife and children are said to be subject to death... he seeks only what is subject to death.

Monks, and what would you say is subject to sorrow? Wife and children... he seeks only what is subject to sorrow.

Monks, and what would you say is subject to defilement? ... Gold and silver are said to be subject to defilement. Monks, these acquisitions of sensual pleasure such as wife and children are subject to defilement. He who is attached to, infatuated with, and indulged in these acquisitions of sensual pleasure, being himself subject to defilement, seeks only what is subject to defilement. Monks, this search is called the ignoble search (anariyapariyesanā).

Furthermore, all unfitting searches (anesanā) occurring in these ways—the fivefold search by way of scheming (kuhanā) and so forth, the sixfold search by way of wrong resorts (agocara), and the twenty-one-fold search by way of medical practice (vejjakamma) and so forth—should be understood as only the ignoble search.

"And what, monks, is the noble search (ariya pariyesanā)? Here, monks, someone being himself subject to birth, having understood the danger in what is subject to birth, seeks the unborn, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna. Being himself subject to aging, sickness, death, sorrow, and defilement, having understood the danger in what is subject to defilement, he seeks the undefiled, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna. Monks, this search is called the noble search."

In another way, seeking righteously and in accordance with the Dhamma through alms-gathering, while avoiding the five kinds of scheming and so forth, the six kinds of wrong resorts, and the twenty-one kinds of unfitting searches, should also be understood as only the noble search. To continue, among those bodily and verbal conducts, whichever bodily and verbal conduct is said to be not to be cultivated, that bodily and verbal conduct is indeed not to be cultivated from the moment one seeks tools such as poisoned weapons for the sake of killing living beings and so forth, or when one makes an appropriate effort for killing and so forth, or when one sets out for the purpose of killing and so forth. Bodily and verbal conduct other than this is indeed to be cultivated from the beginning. A monk who is unable [to act] should at least arouse the mind. In another way, for the sake of causing a schism in the Saṅgha and so forth...
327:
One seeks Nibbāna, which is unsurpassed and the security from the four bondages (yogakkhema). Such seeking is called the Noble Quest (ariya-pariyesanā). (M. Ni. 1.275).

Furthermore, it should be understood that seeking alms righteously and fairly, while avoiding the five types of scheming (kuhanā) and so forth, the six improper resorts (agocara), and the twenty-one types of improper seeking (anesana), is also indeed the Noble Quest.

In this context, whatever bodily and verbal conduct is said to be "not to be associated with" should not be associated with from the very beginning—starting from the time of seeking the materials, making the effort, and going for the purpose of killing living beings and so forth. Other bodily and verbal conduct should be associated with from the start; if one is unable to do so, one should at least arouse the intention. Furthermore, bodily conduct like that of Devadatta and others who strive for the purpose of causing a schism in the Saṅgha and so forth should not be associated with. Bodily conduct like that of the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, and the Great Elder Mahāmoggallāna, which proceeds by way of going to attend upon the Triple Gem two or three times a day, should be associated with. Verbal conduct (vacī-samācāra) like that of Devadatta and others who break their word by sending archers and so forth should not be associated with. Verbal conduct like that of the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, and the Great Elder Mahāmoggallāna, which proceeds by way of praising the virtues of the Triple Gem and so forth, should be associated with. Seeking like that of Devadatta and others who pursue an ignoble quest should not be associated with. Seeking like that of the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, and the Great Elder Mahāmoggallāna, who pursue only the Noble Quest, should be associated with.

"A person who practices in this way" means: O Lord of Devas, a monk who practices for the fulfillment of those things to be associated with, having abandoned the bodily conduct, verbal conduct, and seeking that are not to be associated with, is said to be practicing for the sake of the restraint of the Pātimokkha and for the sake of the supreme and foremost restraint of virtue. Thus, the Blessed One taught the practice that is the preliminary part of the path leading to Arahantship.

## Description of the Restraint of the Faculties

In the second question, "for the restraint of the faculties" (indriya-saṃvarāya) means for the purpose of closing the faculties, because of having guarded doors and having restrained doors. In that answer, "forms cognizable by the eye" and so forth are spoken of for the purpose of showing the restraint of the faculties by way of forms and so forth that should be associated with. In that answer, "when this was spoken" means that because he had heard the answers to the questions on joy (somanassa) and so forth below, Sakka had a well-formed intuition that "these forms and so forth must also be of such a nature." Thus, when the Blessed One spoke in this way, the Lord of Devas...
328:
The Lord of Devas, Sakka, addressed the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I understand (the meaning) of this statement," and so forth. The Blessed One also gave the Lord of Devas the opportunity and remained silent. Indeed, even if one wishes to speak but is unable to complete the meaning, or if one is able to complete the meaning but does not wish to speak, the Blessed One does not grant him the opportunity. However, because this Lord of Devas both wished to speak and was able to complete the meaning, the Blessed One granted him the opportunity.

In that (explanation by Sakka), regarding "such a form should not be associated with" and so forth, this is the summary: the form which, when seen, causes lust and so forth to arise, should not be associated with, should not be looked at, and should not be gazed upon. However, the form which, when seen, causes the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā) to be established, or causes faith (pasāda) to arise, or leads to the acquisition of the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā), should be associated with.

The sound which, even if it has ornate letters and ornate syllables, causes lust and so forth to arise when heard, such a sound should not be associated with. However, the sound which is based on the goal and based on the Dhamma—even the song of a potter's maid—which, when heard, causes faith to arise or causes revulsion (nibbidā) to be established, such a sound should be associated with.

The odor which, when smelled, causes lust and so forth to arise, such an odor should not be associated with. However, the odor which, when smelled, leads to the acquisition of the perception of foulness and so forth, such an odor should be associated with.

The taste which, when tasted, causes lust and so forth to arise, such a taste should not be associated with. However, the taste which, when tasted, causes the perception of repulsiveness in food (āhāre paṭikūlasaññā) to arise, and by which one is able to enter the Noble stage by relying on bodily strength resulting from that taste, or by which the destruction of defilements occurs even while consuming it, like the novice Sīva, the nephew of the Great Elder Mahāsīva, such a taste should be associated with.

The tangible object which, when touched, causes lust and so forth to arise, such a tangible object should not be associated with. However, the tangible object which, when touched, leads to the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya) like in the case of the Elder Sāriputta and others, and by which energy is well-exerted, and by which future generations are supported by providing an example to follow, such a tangible object should be associated with.

It is said that the Elder Sāriputta did not stretch his back on a couch (did not sleep lying down) for thirty years. Likewise, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna. The Elder Mahākassapa did not stretch his back on a couch for one hundred and twenty years. The Elder Anuruddha for fifty years. The Elder Bhaddiya for thirty years. The Elder Soṇa...
329:
For eighteen years (he did not stretch his back on a couch). The Elder Raṭṭhapāla for twelve years; the Elder Ānanda for fifteen years; the Elder Rāhula for twelve years; the Elder Bākula for eighty years; and the Elder Nāḷaka, until his parinibbāna, did not stretch his back on a couch (did not lie down).

When one reflects on mental objects (dhammā) cognizable by the mind-consciousness, lust and so forth arise. Covetousness (abhijjhā) and so forth come into focus in such a way as: "Oh, would that what belongs to others, their wealth and equipment, were mine!" Such states should not be cultivated. States such as loving-kindness, in the manner of "May all beings be free from enmity," or the practices of the three elders, such states should be cultivated.

It is heard that: On the day of entering the Rains (Vassa), three elders made a pact: "Unwholesome thoughts such as sensual thoughts should not be entertained." Then, on the day of Pavāraṇā, the senior elder asked the junior monk: "Friend, during these three months of the Rains, how far did you allow your mind to wander?" He replied: "Venerable sir, I did not allow it to wander outside the boundary of the monastery (pariveṇa)." He asked the second: "And you, friend?" He replied: "Venerable sir, I did not allow it to wander outside the room where I reside." Then both asked the senior elder: "And you, venerable sir?" He said: "Friends, I did not allow the mind to wander outside my own internal five aggregates." They remarked: "Venerable sir, you have performed a difficult task." Such mental objects cognizable by mind-consciousness should be cultivated.

"Ekantavādā" means having only one side to their doctrine; because there are no divergent doctrines, they are called "ekantavādā". It asks, "Do they speak only of a single view?" "Ekantasīlā" means having uniform conduct. "Ekantachandā" means having uniform belief. "Ekanta-ajjhosānā" means having a uniform final goal (Nibbāna).

"Lord of the Devas, Sakka, this world has many elements (dhātu), diverse elements" means: Sakka, this multitude of beings has many dispositions, diverse dispositions. When one wishes to go, another wishes to stay. When one wishes to stay, another wishes to sleep. It is rare to find even two beings with the same disposition. In this world of many and diverse elements, whatever disposition or element beings tenaciously cling to and take up, that alone they firmly grasp through the power of views or through wrong misapprehension, and they speak of it, describe it, and praise it, saying: "This alone is the truth, any other view is empty." This means: "Only this word of ours is true; the words of others are empty, hollow, and useless."
330:
In the term "accantaniṭṭhā", "anta" refers to destruction. Because they have a final goal (Nibbāna) that transcends destruction, it is called "accantaniṭṭhā". Their final goal, the supreme solace which is Nibbāna, is called "nicca" (permanent) because it transcends all destruction. "Yogakkhema" is simply a name for Nibbāna. Because they have Nibbāna, which is safety from the four yokes and transcends destruction, they are called "accantayogakkhemī". Because they practice the Noble Path called "brahma" in the sense of being excellent, they are called "brahmacārī". Because they practice for the sake of the benefit that transcends destruction, they are called "accantabrahmacārī". "Pariyosāna" is also a name for Nibbāna. Because they have an end (Nibbāna) that transcends destruction, they are called "accantapariyosānā".

In the term "taṇhāsaṅkhayavimuttā", "taṇhāsaṅkhaya" (destruction of craving) refers to both the Path and Nibbāna. The Path is called "taṇhāsaṅkhaya" because it exhausts (destroys) craving. Nibbāna is called "taṇhāsaṅkhaya" because craving is exhausted (destroyed) depending on it. Those who are liberated by the Path that destroys craving, or those who are liberated (inclined) towards Nibbāna where craving is exhausted, are called "taṇhāsaṅkhayavimuttā".

By this much, the Blessed One has answered the fourteen great questions. The fourteen great questions are: envy and stinginess (issā-macchariya) is one question; the dear and the undear (piyāppiya) is one; desire (chanda) is one; thought (vitakka) is one; proliferation (papañca) is one; joy (somanassa) is one; grief (domanassa) is one; equanimity (upekkhā) is one; bodily conduct (kāyasamācāra) is one; verbal conduct (vacīsamācāra) is one; pursuit (pariyesanā) is one; restraint of the faculties (indriyasaṃvara) is one; many elements (anekadhātu) is one; and the ultimate goal (accantaniṭṭhā) is one.

"Ejā" refers to craving (taṇhā) in the sense of trembling. That craving is called "disease" (roga) in the sense of oppressing; it is called "boil" (gaṇḍa) in the sense of destroying from within; it is called "dart" (salla) in the sense of piercing. Therefore, when it is said "this man," it is because craving pulls a man to be reborn here and there according to the kamma he has performed; thus, that man reaches high or low states by the power of those various existences. He is high in the Brahma world, low in the deva world. High in the deva world, low in the human world. High in the human world, low in the states of deprivation (apāya).

"Yesāhaṃ bhante" means "Venerable sir, those among whom I..." Here, "yesāhaṃ" is formed by the power of euphonic combination (sandhi). "I shall preach the Dhamma" as I have heard and learned it refers to preaching the Dhamma of the seven vows (sattavatapada) for being Sakka. "I am not their (disciple)" means I am not their disciple...
331:
I am not confused. By the words "Venerable Sir, I am indeed..." and so forth, he makes known his state of being a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna).

## Explanation of the Acquisition of Joy

"Acquisition of knowledge" (vedapaṭilābha) means the acquisition of satisfaction. "War between Devas and Asuras" (devāsura-saṅgāma) is the battle between the devas and the asuras. "Drawn up" (samupabyūḷho) means well-arrived, as if reaching a state of striking forehead against forehead. It is said that these devas and asuras sometimes have battles on the surface of the great ocean. In those battles, there is no such thing as killing or harming one another by cutting or piercing; it is merely a matter of victory or defeat, like the fighting of wooden rams. Sometimes the devas win, and sometimes the asuras win. Among those battles, referring to the battle in which the devas defeated the asuras so that they could not return, he said, "Venerable Sir, in that battle..." and so forth.

"Both of these" (ubhayam-etaṃ) refers to these two. "In this deva realm, only the devas will enjoy both kinds of essence"—reflecting thus, powerful rapture and joy (pīti-somanassa) arose in that Sakka. "Accompanied by punishment" (sadaṇḍāvacaro) means being with the taking up of weapons; it shows that he was with the taking up of sticks and swords, and had not laid down his weapons. "For absolute disenchantment" (ekantanibbidāya) means for the purpose of being weary of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa). All the remaining words are just as stated in the Mahāgovinda Sutta.

"Proclaimed" (pavedesi) means he preached or showed. "Right here" (idheva) means in this very place. "While I was a deva" (devabhūtassa me sato) means while I was a deity. "I have gained life again" (punarāyu ca me laddho) means "I have obtained life again due to the result of another kamma." By this, he makes clear his passing away (cuti) and his rebirth (upapatti).

"From divine bodies" (diviyā kāyā) means from divine forms of existence. "Leaving behind non-human life" (āyuṃ hitvā amānusaṃ) means having abandoned the divine lifespan. "I will enter the womb unconfused" (amūḷho gabbhamessāmi) means being one of certain destiny, he will enter the mother's womb without confusion. "Wherever my mind delights" (yattha me ramatī mano) means "Wherever my mind shall delight, there in the Khattiya families and so forth, I will enter the womb." By this, he shows the meaning that he will be reborn seven times among devas and seven times among humans.

"I will live by the right method" (ñāyena viharissāmi) means that even when born among humans, because he is incapable of things such as taking his mother's life, he will live according to reason and fairness.

The words "And there will be enlightenment" (sambodhi ca bhavissati) are said with reference to the Path of Once-returning (sakadāgāmi-magga). By this, he shows the meaning that he will become a Once-returner. "I will live as one who knows" (aññāto viharissāmi) means he will live desiring to know the extraordinary Dhamma which is the Fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala). "That will be the end" (sveva anto bhavissati) means that state of being a Non-returner will be the end in the human world. "Again I will be a deva, supreme in the deva world" (puna devo bhavissāmi devalokasmim uttamo) means he will again be Sakka, the lord of devas, the supreme one in the deva world. "When existing in the final [birth]" (antime vattamānamhi) means when being in the last existence. "That will be the dwelling" (senaivāso bhavissati) means the dwelling of the Akaniṭṭha devas—who are not inferior in terms of lifespan or wisdom, but are superior and more excellent than all other devas and Brahmas—will be his final dwelling. This Sakka, having attained the Path of Non-returning in that very existence, becomes a "Non-returner who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm" (uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī); having been reborn in the Aviha realm and so forth, he will finally be reborn in the Akaniṭṭha realm. It is with reference to this that he spoke thus.
332:
The words "There will be enlightenment" refer to the Path of Once-returning, showing "I will become a Once-returner." "I will live as one who knows" (aññātā viharissāmi) means I will live desiring to know the extraordinary Dhamma of the Fruit of Non-returning. "That will be the end" (sveva anto bhavissati) means that state of being a Non-returner will be my end in the human world.

"Again I will be a deva, supreme in the deva world" means he says he will again be Sakka, the lord of devas, supreme in the deva world.

"When existing in the final [birth]" (antime vattamānamhi) means when being in the last existence. "That will be the dwelling" (so nivāso bhavissati) means the dwelling of the Akaniṭṭha Brahmas—who are great in terms of lifespan and wisdom, and are more excellent and superior to all devas and Brahmas—will be my home in the final existence. This Sakka, after passing away from that state of being Sakka, because of having attained the Path of Non-returning in that existence, becomes a "Non-returner who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm" (uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī); being reborn in realms such as Aviha, he will finally be reborn in the Akaniṭṭha realm. It is with reference to that fact that he spoke thus. He will live for one thousand kappas in the Aviha realm, two thousand kappas in the Atappa realm, four thousand kappas in the Sudassa realm, eight thousand kappas in the Sudassī realm, and sixteen thousand kappas in the Akaniṭṭha realm, enjoying the lifespan of Brahmas for a total of thirty-one thousand kappas. Sakka the king of devas, Anāthapiṇḍika the householder, and Visākhā the great female lay follower—these three have equal lifespans in terms of kappas. Among beings who delight in the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa), there are none who have a share of happiness equal to these.

"One whose wishes are not yet fulfilled" (apariyosita-saṅkappo) means one whose heart's desire is not yet completed. "I recognize the recluses" (yassu maññāmi samaṇe) means "I recognize those recluses who dwell in seclusion."

"Accomplishment" (ārādhanā) means the fulfillment of the Noble Path. "Failure" (virādhanā) means non-fulfillment. "They are not able" (na sampāyanti) means they are not able to speak so as to fulfill [the meaning].

"Kinsman of the Sun" (ādiccabandhunaṃ) is said because the Sun is of the Gotama lineage and the Blessed One is also of the Gotama lineage. "That which we do" (yaṃ karomase) refers to the homage previously paid to Brahmā. "Together with the devas" (samaṃ devehi) shows that from this day forward, there is no longer a need for us to pay homage to Brahmā. "We pay homage" (sāmaṃ karoma) means we shall perform the act of paying homage.
333:
"Having touched" (parāmasitvā) means having a delighted mind, as if striking a friend's hand with one's own hand, he struck the earth; or he struck it for the sake of witnessing, meaning: "Just as you (the earth) are unshakable, so am I unshakable in my devotion to the Blessed One." "Requested questions" (ajjhiṭṭhapañhā) are the problems that were requested and longed for. The remaining meanings are clear in all places.

## The Commentary on the Sakkapañha Sutta is finished.
334:
## 9. Commentary on the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta
## Commentary on the Section of the Summary (Uddesavāra)

The discourse beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta. In this discourse, the following is the commentary on the meanings of the words (not previously explained): Why did the Blessed One teach this discourse, saying, "Bhikkhus, this path is the sole way"? It was because the inhabitants of the Kuru country were capable of receiving deep teachings. The monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen living in the Kuru country, being endowed with favorable conditions such as climate and so forth, and by constantly enjoying the suitable climate of that country, always possessed healthy bodies and healthy minds. Because of their health of both mind and body, they possessed the power of wisdom that had been nurtured, and thus were capable of receiving deep Dhamma teachings. Therefore, the Blessed One, seeing their capability to receive such deep teachings, taught this Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta of profound meaning, incorporating meditation subjects into twenty-one sections leading up to Arahantship. Just as a man, having obtained a golden flower-basket, might place various flowers in it, or having obtained a golden casket, might place the seven gems in it, even so, the Blessed One, having found the audience of the Kuru country, taught this deep discourse. For this very reason, other discourses of profound meaning were also taught in this Kuru country: the Mahānidāna Sutta in the Dīgha Nikāya; and in the Majjhima Nikāya, the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta, the Sāropama Sutta, the Rukkhopeama Sutta, the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta, the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta, and the Āneñjasappāya Sutta.

Furthermore, in that district, the fourfold assembly naturally lived devoted to the practice of the development of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna-bhāvanā). Even the lowest servants, laborers, and attendants spoke only words connected with mindfulness. Even at places such as the water-landing or the spinning-place, there was no such thing as useless or idle talk. If a woman were asked, "Mother, which development of mindfulness are you reflecting upon?" and she replied, "None at all," they would rebuke her, saying, "Your life is blameworthy; though living, you are like one who is dead." Then, after admonishing her, "From now on, do not do this again," they would teach her one of the subjects of mindfulness. But if she said, "I am reflecting upon such-and-such a mindfulness," they would applaud her, saying, "Sadhu! Sadhu!" and praise her, saying, "Your life is a life well-lived; you have truly attained human status; it is for your sake that the Fully Enlightened One has appeared." Not only were the human beings here devoted to the reflection on mindfulness, but even the animals living in dependence on them were also so devoted.
335:
Regarding the reflection on meditation by these animals, there is this story: It is said that a certain dancer wandered about with a young parrot he had caught and trained. Having stayed near a nunnery, he forgot the young parrot and left it behind when he departed. The novice nuns took it and cared for it, naming it "Buddharakkhita." One day, seeing the parrot sitting in front of her, the Great Elder Nun called out, "Buddharakkhita!" When it replied, "What is it, Venerable Lady?" she asked, "Do you have any reflection on meditation?" It replied, "No, Venerable Lady." She said, "Dear parrot, one who lives in the presence of monastics should not live with a neglected self; some form of reflection is desirable. If you are unable to reflect on other meditation subjects, then practice the recitation: 'Bones, bones.'" Following the instruction of the Elder Nun, that parrot wandered about reciting, "Bones, bones."

One day, early in the morning, while the parrot was sitting on top of an archway basking in the morning sun, a hawk snatched it with its talons as if in a cage. The parrot cried out, "Kiri! Kiri!" The novice nuns heard it and said, "Venerable ladies, Buddharakkhita has been snatched by a bird; let us rescue him!" They took stones and other things, pursued the bird, and caused it to release him. When the parrot was brought back and placed before her, the Elder Nun asked, "Buddharakkhita, what were you thinking when the bird snatched you away?" It replied, "Venerable Lady, I did not think of anything else; I thought only that a heap of bones is carrying away a heap of bones, and in which place will it be scattered? Thus, Venerable Lady, I thought only of a heap of bones." The nun said, "Sadhu! Sadhu! Buddharakkhita, in the future, this will be a condition for you for the destruction of existence (Nibbāna)." In this way, even the animals in that Kuru country were devoted to the reflection on mindfulness. Therefore, the Blessed One taught this discourse to generate the wisdom of mindfulness in them.

In that discourse, "Ekāyano" means a single path. Indeed, there are many names for the word "magga" (path):
"Maggo, pantho, patho, pajjo, añjasaṃ, vaṭumaṃ, ayanaṃ,
nāvā, uttarasetu ca, kullo ca, bhisi, saṅkamo."
Here, that path is taught by the name "ayana." Therefore, in the Pāḷi "Bhikkhus, this path is ekāyano," the meaning should be understood as: "Bhikkhus, this path is a single path, not a path that is divided into two." Alternatively, it is called "ekāyana" because it is to be traveled by one alone. "By one alone" means by one who has abandoned the company of the crowd and possesses a secluded and detached mind. It is to be traveled, to be practiced. Or else, it is called "ayana" because they go by means of this path.
336:
It is called *ekāyana* because it goes from *saṃsāra* to *nibbāna*. It is called *ekāyana* (*eka* + *ayana*) because it is the path of a single person. 'Single' refers to the most excellent person. Since the Blessed One is more excellent than all beings, in this context, it means 'the path of the Blessed One.' Although others (Paccekabuddhas and noble disciples) also travel by this path, it is called only the path of the Blessed One because the Blessed One Himself brought it into existence. As it is said in the Majjhima Nikāya: 'Brahmin, that Blessed One is the arouser of the path that had not yet arisen,' and so on. Alternatively, it is called *ayana* because it occurs; it means it goes or proceeds. It is called *ekāyana* because it occurs in only one dispensation; it means it occurs only in this Dhamma-Vinaya and not in the dispensations of other sectarians (*titthiya*). As it is said in the Dīgha Nikāya: 'Subhadda, only in this Dhamma-Vinaya is the Noble Eightfold Path found.' This is merely a difference in the method of teaching, but in meaning, it is only one. Furthermore, it is called *ekāyana* because it goes to a single [goal], *nibbāna*. This means that although in the preliminary stage it proceeds by various methods of meditation, in the later stage it goes only to the single *nibbāna*. Brahma Sahampati also addressed this:

'The One who sees the end of the destruction of birth,
Compassionate and concerned for welfare, knows the sole way.
By this path, they crossed the flood in the past,
They will cross in the future, and they are crossing now.'

Some teachers, however, say it is *ekāyana* because one goes to *nibbāna* only once, according to the method of the verse 'They do not go to the further shore twice' (*na pāraṃ diguṇaṃ yanti*). But that is not appropriate. If that were the meaning, the expression should be *sakiṃ ayana* (going once). If one were to explain the meaning as 'occurring only once,' the expression might be grammatically possible, but the meaning is inappropriate in both ways. Why? Because here, the preliminary path (*pubbabhāga-magga*) is intended. For here, the preliminary path of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna-magga*) occurring in the four objects such as the body is intended, not the supramundane path (*lokuttara-magga*). That mundane path occurs many times, and its occurrence is frequent.

In the past, there was a discussion among the Great Elders regarding this term. The Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga said it is the 'preliminary path of mindfulness.' However, his teacher, the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷasuma, said it is the 'mixed path' (*missaka-magga*). When [Cūḷanāga] asked, 'Venerable Sir, is it the preliminary path?', [the teacher] replied, 'It is the mixed path, friend.' As the teacher repeatedly stated this...
337:
(The Elder Cūḷanāga) remained silent without contradicting his teacher's words. They rose from their seats without resolving the question. Then, the teacher Elder, while going to the bathhouse, thought: 'I said it is the mixed path (the path mixing mundane and supramundane), but Cūḷanāga holds it to be the preliminary path (the path prior to the supramundane). What is the conclusion here?' While reviewing the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta from the beginning, he noticed this point: 'Bhikkhus, should any person develop these four foundations of mindfulness in this way for seven years...' There is no such thing as the supramundane path arising and lasting for seven years. The mixed path I mentioned is not possible. Realizing that only the preliminary path seen by Cūḷanāga is possible, he went when the announcement for the Dhamma preaching was made on the eighth day.

It is said that the Elders of old were lovers of hearing the Dhamma; upon hearing the announcement, they would gather all at once, saying, 'I first! I first!' On that day, it was the Elder Cūḷanāga's turn to preach. Therefore, while the Elder Cūḷanāga was sitting on the Dhamma-seat, holding the fan and reciting the introductory verses, the teacher Elder, standing at the back of the seating area, thought: 'I will not speak while sitting in private.' This is because the Elders of old were not envious. They did not go about exalting their own views like carrying a bundle of sugar cane; they accepted only what was reasonable and rejected what was unreasonable. Therefore, the Elder called out, 'Friend Cūḷanāga!' Recognizing it as his teacher's voice, Cūḷanāga paused the preaching and said, 'What is it, Venerable Sir?' 'Friend Cūḷanāga, the mixed path I spoke of is not possible. Only the preliminary path of mindfulness you spoke of is possible.'

The Elder (Nāga) thought: 'Our teacher is proficient in all the scriptures, a bearer of the Tipiṭaka, and a Buddha of great learning (*sutabuddha*). If even such a person can be confused by this question, in the future, my younger brothers (fellow monks) will also be confused by it.' Thinking, 'I will make this question firm by citing the Pāli Canon,' he brought forth and presented the text from the Paṭisambhidāmagga: 'The preliminary path of mindfulness is called the *ekāyana* path,' and the Sutta verses:

'Of paths, the eightfold is the best; of truths, the four parts (Four Noble Truths) are the best.
Detachment is the best of states; and of two-legged beings, the Seeing One (the Buddha) is the best.
This is the only path; there is no other for the purification of vision.
Enter upon this path, for it is the discomfiter of Māra's host.
Having entered upon this path, you will make an end of suffering.'
338:
"Maggo": In what sense is it called the Path (Magga)? It is called the Path because it is the means for going to Nibbāna, and because it is that which is to be sought by those who desire Nibbāna.

"Sattānaṃ visuddhiyā" means for the purification of beings whose minds are defiled by impurities such as lust (rāga), and by corruptions (upakkilesa) such as covetousness (abhijjhā) and deviant greed. This statement is true. Only by this journey of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), starting from the Buddhas named Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, Saraṇaṅkara, and Dīpaṅkara—who appeared in a single aeon (kappa) more than four incalculables (asaṅkheyya) and a hundred thousand aeons ago—down to the Sakyamuni (Gotama) Buddha, as well as many hundreds of Paccekabuddhas and countless Noble Disciples (ariyasāvaka), all these beings have washed away the impurities of the mind and reached supreme purification. There is no designation of defilement or purification by way of the impurity of the physical body (rūpa). This statement is true—

'The Great Sage (Mahesi) did not declare: "Beings are defiled by a defiled body, and they are purified when the body is pure."
The Great Sage declared: "Beings are defiled by a defiled mind, and they are purified when the mind is pure."

As the Blessed One said: "Monks, through the defilement of the mind, beings are defiled; through the purification of the mind, they are purified." And that purification of the mind occurs only through this path of the foundations of mindfulness. Therefore, he said, "sattānaṃ visuddhiyā."

"Sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāya" means for the surmounting and abandoning of sorrow (soka) and lamentation (parideva). For the cultivation of this path leads to the surmounting of sorrow, as in the case of the minister Santati and others, and to the surmounting of lamentation, as in the case of Paṭācārā and others. Therefore, he said, "sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāya." Indeed, the minister Santati, upon hearing this verse:

"Cleanse what is past; let there be nothing for you in the future.
If you do not grasp what is in the middle, you will wander at peace."

attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Paṭācārā, upon hearing this verse:

"Sons are no refuge, nor father, nor kinsmen;
for one seized by the Ender (Death), there is no refuge among kin."

(established herself in the fruit of Stream-entry).
339:
Upon hearing this verse, she was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). However, since there is no such thing as meditation (bhāvanā) without contemplating one of the phenomena among body, feeling, mind, or mental objects (dhamma), it should be understood that they too overcame sorrow and lamentation by this very path of the foundations of mindfulness. 'Dukkha-domanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāya' means for the disappearance and cessation of these two: physical pain (dukkha) and mental grief (domanassa). Indeed, when this path is developed, it leads to the disappearance of pain, as in the case of Elder Tissa and others, and to the disappearance of grief, as in the case of Sakka and others. 

To clarify this meaning: In Sāvatthī, a son of a householder named Tissa, having renounced forty crores of wealth and ordained, lived in a forest far from any village. His younger brother's wife sent five hundred thieves, saying, "Go and deprive that monk of his life." They went, surrounded the Elder, and sat down. The Elder asked, "Lay followers, why have you come?" "We have come to deprive you of your life." The Elder pleaded, "Lay followers, take a guarantee from me and give me my life for just this one night." "O monk, who will be a guarantee for you in this place?" The Elder took a large stone, broke both his thigh bones, and said, "Lay followers, the guarantee is sufficient." They moved away, made a fire at the head of the walkway (caṅkama), and lay down. The Elder, having suppressed the pain and reflecting on his virtue (sīla), felt joy and gladness (pīti-pāmojja) based on his pure virtue. Then, gradually increasing insight (vipassanā) and practicing the monk's duty (samaṇa-dhamma) throughout the three watches of the night, he attained Arahantship at dawn and uttered this inspired utterance (udāna):
'Having broken both my legs,
I shall give you a guarantee;
I am weary of and ashamed of
Dying with lust (sarāga).
Having thought thus,
I contemplated things as they really are;
When dawn arrived,
I attained Arahantship.'

Another thirty monks, having taken a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) from the Blessed One, entered the rains-retreat in a forest monastery and lived there, saying, "Friends, we must practice the monk's duty throughout the three watches of the night; let us not come to one another." While they were practicing the monk's duty and nodding off at the time of dawn, a tiger came and took the monks one by one. No one even uttered the words, "A tiger is seizing me." When five or ten monks had been eaten in this way, on the Uposatha day, they asked, "Friends, where are the rest of the monks?" and thus they came to know. They lived saying, "Now, the monk who is seized by the tiger is no longer like the others." Then, a certain young monk was seized by the tiger in the same manner as before. That young monk cried out, "Venerable sirs, a tiger is taking me!" The monks, carrying walking sticks and torches, followed, saying, "Let us rescue him." The tiger climbed onto a broken cliff where the monks could not reach and began to eat that monk starting from his toes. The other monks...
340:
"Friends, where is he?" they asked, and upon learning, they lived saying, "Now the monk taken by the tiger has become [one who attained distinction]." Then, a tiger seized another young monk in the same manner as before. He said, "Venerable sirs, a tiger has seized me." The monks, taking walking sticks and torches, followed, saying, "We will rescue him." The tiger climbed a broken cliff where the monks could not follow and began to eat that monk starting from his big toe. The remaining monks said, "Good man, there is nothing more we can do now; the distinction of monks must be made manifest in such a place as this."

While lying in the tiger's mouth, that young monk dispelled the pain and developed insight (Vipassanā). By the time he was eaten up to his ankles, he became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna); by the time he was eaten up to his knees, a Once-returner (Sakadāgāmī); by the time he was eaten up to his navel, a Non-returner (Anāgāmī). Before his heart-base was eaten, he reached Arahatship along with the analytical knowledges (Paṭisambhidā) and uttered this inspired utterance:

"Possessed of virtue and fulfilled in vows, wise and well-concentrated, due to a moment of negligence, I have been oppressed by a tiger. Seized in this cage [of a body] and placed upon a rock, let the tiger eat me as it wishes, desiring bone and sinew; I shall exhaust the defilements and touch liberation."

Another person named Pītamalla Thera had been a standard-bearer in three kingdoms during his lay life. Having come to the island of Tambapaṇṇi and seen the King, he received royal patronage. One day, while passing by the door of a mat-seller's shop, he heard the words: "Monks, form is not yours; abandon it. Your abandoning of it will be for your long-term welfare and happiness." He thought, "Indeed, form is not self, nor is feeling." Using that very meaning as a goad to control the wild elephant of his mind, he left the lay life, went to the Mahāvihāra, and requested ordination. After ordaining and receiving full admission (Upasampadā), he mastered the two Mātikās. Taking thirty monks with him, he went to the Gabalavāliya area and practiced the recluse's Dhamma. When his feet could no longer carry him, he practiced walking meditation on his knees. One night, a hunter, mistaking him for a deer, stabbed him with a spear. The spear pierced through his body. The Elder had the spear removed, filled the wound with a grass-plug, sat upon a stone slab, and having made the opportunity, developed insight...
341:
...filling the spear wound with a grass-plug and seating himself on a stone slab, he developed insight and reached Arahatship along with the analytical knowledges. He briefly declared his attainment of Arahatship to the monks who arrived at the sound of his coughing and uttered this inspired utterance:

"The word spoken by the Excellent Buddha, the speaker of the supreme in all the world: 'Monks, this form is not yours; you should abandon it.'
Impermanent indeed are formations! They are of the nature to arise and pass away. Having arisen, they cease; their subsiding is bliss."

In this way, first of all, this path leads to the cessation of suffering, as it did for Tissa Thera and others.

Sakka, the Lord of Devas, having seen his own five premonitory signs and being terrified by the fear of death and overcome with distress, approached the Blessed One and asked a question. At the conclusion of the explanation of the question on equanimity, he was established in the fruit of Stream-entry along with eighty thousand deities. His rebirth as a deva occurred just as before.

The young deva Subrahma was also enjoying celestial splendor, surrounded by a thousand nymphs. Among those thousand nymphs, five hundred passed away while picking flowers from trees and were reborn in hell. Subrahma, wondering, "Why are these nymphs taking so long?" looked and saw their rebirth in hell. Then, examining "How long is my own life span?" he realized his life was exhausted and saw that after passing away, he too would be reborn in that very hell. Terrified and deeply distressed, he thought, "Only the Teacher can dispel this distress of mine, no one else." Taking the remaining five hundred nymphs, he approached the Blessed One and asked this question:

"Venerable Sir, this heart is always terrified; this mind is always agitated, both by troubles that have not yet arisen and by those that have already occurred. If there is a cause for fearlessness, please tell it to me who asks."

Then the Blessed One said to him:
"Other than through the knowledge of the path of Arahatship, other than through noble practice (tapa), other than through the restraint of the sense faculties, and other than through the relinquishment of all defilements, I see no safety for living beings."

At the end of the teaching, that young deva, along with the five hundred nymphs, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. Having made that celestial splendor stable, he returned to the deva realm.

"For the attainment of the Way (Ñāyassa adhigamāya)": The Noble Eightfold Path is called "Ñāya." It means for the sake of obtaining or reaching that path. Indeed, it should be understood that when this mundane path of mindfulness is developed in the preliminary stage, it leads to the attainment of the supramundane path. Therefore, He said, "For the attainment of the Way." "For the realization of Nibbāna (Nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya)" means...
342:
At the conclusion of the discourse, that deity, together with five hundred celestial nymphs, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Having made that celestial attainment permanent, he returned to the celestial realm. Thus, it should be understood that when this path is developed, it leads to the cessation of grief, just as it did for Sakka and others.

"Ñāyassa adhigamāya" means: the Noble Eightfold Path is called "Ñāya"; it means for the sake of attaining or reaching that path. In fact, when this mundane (lokiya) path of Satipaṭṭhāna is developed in the preliminary stage, it leads to the attainment of the supramundane (lokuttara) path. Therefore, He said, "Ñāyassa adhigamāya." "Nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya" means: for the realization, for the personal witnessing, of the Deathless Nibbāna, which is so named because it is free from the "vāna" (binding) of craving (taṇhā). When this path is developed, it gradually accomplishes the realization of Nibbāna. Therefore, He said, "Nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya."

Among those [five phrases starting with 'for the purification of beings'], when "for the purification of beings" (sattānaṃ visuddhiyā) is preached, the overcoming of sorrow and so forth are already established by meaning. However, except for those skilled in the logic of the Teaching (Sāsana), such as in the Truths and Dependent Origination, it is not clear to others. The Blessed One does not first make people skilled in the Teaching and then preach the Dhamma. Rather, He makes the respective meanings known through that very Sutta. Therefore, in this Sutta, wishing to make clear whichever meanings this One-way Path accomplishes, He preached "for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation" (sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāya), and so forth. Alternatively, because the purification of beings occurs through the One-way Path, that purification happens through the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation. The overcoming of sorrow and lamentation happens through the disappearance of pain and grief. The disappearance of pain and grief happens through the attainment of the Path (Ñāya). The attainment of the Path happens for the realization of Nibbāna. Therefore, wishing to show this sequence as well, He said "for the purification of beings" and then "for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation," and so forth.

Furthermore, this is the praising of the One-way Path. Indeed, just as the Blessed One spoke praise with eight phrases in the Chachakka Sutta, saying: "Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; I will proclaim the holy life (brahmacariya) that is perfectly complete and pure, with its meaning and spirit, namely, the six sets of six"; and just as in the Ariyavaṃsa Sutta: "Monks, these four noble lineages (ariyavaṃsa) are foremost, long-standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated, never before adulterated..."
343:
"...not criticized, and will not be criticized in the future, not loathed by wise recluses and brahmins" (in Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.28), He spoke praise [of the Ariyavaṃsa] with nine phrases. Similarly, He spoke praise of this Satipaṭṭhāna, which is the One-way Path, with seven phrases such as "for the purification of beings." Why did He speak this praise? It was to inspire effort (ussāha) in those monks. Indeed, when those monks hear the words of praise, they will think: "This path surely destroys the four afflictions: sorrow (soka) which is the burning of the heart, lamentation (parideva) which is verbal wailing, pain (dukkha) which is bodily unpleasantness, and grief (domanassa) which is mental unpleasantness. It brings about the three distinctions: purification (visuddhi), the Noble Path (ñāya), and Nibbāna." Thus inspired, they will learn, study, memorize, and recite this Dhamma teaching, and they will consider this path as something to be developed. Thus, He spoke the praise to inspire effort in those monks, just as blanket merchants speak of the qualities of their blankets.

For example, even if a merchant selling a pale red blanket (paṇḍukambala) worth a hundred thousand cries out, "Buy the blanket!", people do not yet know what kind of blanket it is. This is because blankets woven from human hair or animal fur, which have a foul smell and a rough touch, are also called "blankets." But when that merchant cries out, "This is a red blanket from Gandhara, fine, bright, and pleasant to the touch," then those who can afford it buy it, and even those who cannot afford it desire to see it. In the same way, even when it is said, "Monks, this is a one-way path," it is not yet clear what kind of path it is. This is because various wrong paths that do not lead out of suffering are also called "paths." However, when "for the purification of beings" and so forth are spoken, they will think: "This path surely destroys the four afflictions and brings about the three distinctions," and thus inspired, they will learn, study, memorize, and recite this Dhamma teaching, and they will consider this path as something to be developed. Wishing to speak praise with this intention, He said "for the purification of beings," and so forth. Just as with the analogy of the merchant of the pale red blanket worth a hundred thousand, analogies of merchants selling Jambunada gold, rubies, pearls, coral, and so forth should also be brought in here.

"Yadidaṃ" is an indeclinable (nipāta), meaning "which are these [Satipaṭṭhānas]." The word "cattāro" (four) is a numerical limitation. By that, He shows the limitation of Satipaṭṭhāna, that they are neither less than four nor more than four. In the word "satipaṭṭhānā," there are three types of Satipaṭṭhāna: the object of mindfulness, the Teacher's state of being beyond resentment and attraction when disciples practice in three ways, and mindfulness itself.
344:
“Monks, I will teach the origin and the disappearance of the four foundations of mindfulness. Listen to that... Monks, what is the origin of the body (kāya)? The body originates from the origin of nutriment (āhāra).” In such passages from the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the object of mindfulness is called 'satipaṭṭhāna'. Similarly, in passages from the Paṭisambhidāmagga such as, “The body is the foundation (upaṭṭhāna), not mindfulness; but mindfulness is both the foundation and mindfulness,” the object of mindfulness is also called 'satipaṭṭhāna'. The meaning of this 'satipaṭṭhāna' is: it is called 'paṭṭhāna' because mindfulness stands (patiṭṭhāti) in this object. What stands? Mindfulness stands. Because it is the standing place of mindfulness, it is called 'satipaṭṭhāna'. Alternatively, 'paṭṭhāna' means a principal place (ṭhāna). Just like an elephant stable or a horse stable, the principal place of mindfulness is called 'satipaṭṭhāna'.

“The Blessed One resorts to the three foundations of mindfulness; the Teacher who resorts to those foundations of mindfulness is worthy of instructing the group of disciples.” In this sutta from the Majjhima Nikāya, the Teacher's state of being free from aversion (paṭigha) and attraction (anunaya) towards disciples who practice in three ways is called 'satipaṭṭhāna'. Its meaning is: it is called 'paṭṭhāna' because it should be established (paṭṭhapetabba) or set in motion (pavattayitabba). By what is it established? It is established by mindfulness. Because it is established by mindfulness through effort, it is called 'satipaṭṭhāna'.

“The four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment.” In such passages, mindfulness itself is called 'satipaṭṭhāna'. Its meaning is: it is called 'paṭṭhāna' because it stands firmly. It means 'paṭṭhāna' because it occurs by entering into, rushing into, and spreading out over the object. Mindfulness itself is the foundation of mindfulness. Alternatively, it is 'sati' in the sense of recollecting (saraṇa), and 'paṭṭhāna' in the sense of establishing (upaṭṭhāna). Thus, because it is both mindfulness and the foundation, it is 'satipaṭṭhāna'. This is the meaning intended here in this Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta.

If mindfulness itself is called 'satipaṭṭhāna', why is the plural form 'satipaṭṭhānā' used? It is because of the plurality of mindfulness. These mindfulnesses are many due to the diversity of objects. If they are so many, why is the singular form 'maggo' (path) used? It is because they are one in the sense of being a path. These four mindfulnesses reach oneness in the sense of being a path.

“In what sense is the path called 'magga'? It is called 'magga' because it goes to Nibbāna and because it is sought (magganiya) by those desiring Nibbāna,” so the Blessed One has said. These four mindfulnesses also go to Nibbāna while fulfilling their functions regarding objects such as the body in the subsequent stage, and they are sought by those desiring Nibbāna from the very beginning; therefore, all four are called 'the one path'. In this way, according to the connection of words, this teaching is a connected discourse. It is like in the suttas such as: “Monks, I will teach you the path that crushes the army of Māra. Listen to that... Monks, what is the path that crushes the army of Māra? It is these seven factors of enlightenment.” Just as in that sutta, the term 'crusher of Māra's army' and the term 'seven factors of enlightenment' are one in meaning, and only the phrasing (byañjana) here...
345:
(In meaning) it is distinct. Similarly, the term "Ekāyanamaggo" and the term "Cattāro Satipaṭṭhānā" are identical in meaning; here, only the phrasing is different. Therefore, the singular is used because of the oneness in the sense of the path (magga) as the way out of suffering. It should be understood that the plural is used because of the multiplicity of mindfulness in terms of the variety of objects.

Why did the Blessed One teach exactly four foundations of mindfulness, neither more nor less? It is for the benefit of those to be guided (veneyya). Among those of craving temperament, view temperament, those who take tranquility as their vehicle (samathayānika), and those who take insight as their vehicle (vipassanāyānika), there are two types each: those of dull faculties and those of sharp faculties. For the one of craving temperament with dull faculties, the gross contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā) is the path to purification. For the one of craving temperament with sharp faculties, the subtle contemplation of feeling (vedanānupassanā) is the path to purification. For the one of view temperament with dull faculties, the contemplation of the mind (cittānupassanā), which does not have many divisions, is the path to purification. For the one of view temperament with sharp faculties, the contemplation of phenomena (dhammānupassanā), which has very many divisions, is the path to purification. For the one of tranquility vehicle with dull faculties, the first foundation of mindfulness, which has a sign to be attained without difficulty, is the path to purification. For the one of tranquility vehicle with sharp faculties, the second foundation of mindfulness is the path, because they do not settle on a gross object. For the one of insight vehicle with dull faculties, the third foundation of mindfulness, which has an object without many divisions, is the path to purification. For the one of insight vehicle with sharp faculties, the fourth foundation of mindfulness, which has an object with very many divisions, is the path to purification. Thus, exactly four foundations of mindfulness are taught, neither more nor less.

Alternatively, they are taught for the purpose of abandoning the perversions (vipallāsa) of beauty, happiness, permanence, and self. Although the body (kāya) is foul, beings have the perversion of perceiving it as beautiful. To abandon that perversion by showing the foul nature therein, the first foundation of mindfulness is taught. Although feelings and so on are grasped as happy, permanent, and self, feelings are suffering, the mind is impermanent, and phenomena are non-self. To abandon those perversions by showing the nature of suffering and so on to beings who have the perversions of happiness, permanence, and self in those [feelings, etc.], the remaining three foundations of mindfulness are taught. Thus, it should be understood that exactly four foundations of mindfulness are taught, neither more nor less, for the purpose of abandoning the four perversions. It should be understood that four are taught not only for abandoning the perversions, but also for abandoning the four floods (ogha), the four yokes (yoga), the four taints (āsava), the four ties (gantha), the four clingings (upādāna), the four wrong courses (agati), and for the full understanding of the four nutriments (āhāra). This is the method according to the Netti Pakaraṇa.

In the Commentary, however, it is said that the foundation of mindfulness is only one by way of refuge and by way of convergence into oneness, but four by way of objects. For example, in a city with four gates, those coming from the East take the goods produced in the East and enter the city through the East gate. Those coming from the South, West, and North take the goods produced in the North and enter the city through the North gate; this should be understood accordingly. Like the city...
346:
The great city of Nibbāna is like a city; the Noble Eightfold Path is like the gate; the body and so on are like the East and other directions.

Just as those coming from the East take the goods produced in the East and enter the city through the East gate, so too, those who come by way of contemplation of the body, having developed the fourteenfold contemplation of the body, enter the single Nibbāna by the Noble Path produced by the power of the development of contemplation of the body. Just as those coming from the South take the goods produced in the South and enter the city through the South gate, so too, those who come by way of contemplation of feeling, having developed the ninefold contemplation of feeling, enter the single Nibbāna by the Noble Path produced by the power of the development of contemplation of feeling. Just as those coming from the West take the goods produced in the West and enter the city through the West gate, so too, those who come by way of contemplation of the mind, having developed the sixteenfold contemplation of the mind, enter the single Nibbāna by the Noble Path produced by the power of the development of contemplation of the mind. Just as those coming from the North take the goods produced in the North and enter the city through the North gate, so too, those who come by way of contemplation of phenomena, having developed the fivefold contemplation of phenomena, enter the single Nibbāna by the Noble Path produced by the power of the development of contemplation of phenomena. Thus, it should be understood that the foundation of mindfulness, which is only one by way of refuge and by way of convergence into oneness, is taught as four by way of objects.

"Which four?" (Katamē cattāro): This question is asked out of a desire to explain. "Here" (Idha) means in this Dispensation (Sāsana). "O Monks" (Bhikkhave) is an address to the persons receiving the Dhamma. "Monk" (Bhikkhu) is a designation for the person who fulfills the practice. Although others, such as devas and humans, also fulfill the practice, the term "Monks" is used because of the excellence of the practice and because the state of a monk is shown through the practice. Indeed, among those who receive the Blessed One's instruction, the monk is the best because he is the vessel for all types of instruction. Therefore, because of excellence, He said "Monks". When the monk is taken, the rest are also taken, just as when the king's going is mentioned, the rest of the retinue is included. Also, whoever follows this practice is called a monk; thus, He said "Monks" to show the state of a monk through the practice. Whether it be a deva or a human, one who practices is certainly reckoned as a "monk". How is it taught? —
347:
## 
“Even if one is adorned, if one should lead a balanced life, is peaceful, tamed, established in the path, a celibate, and has laid down the rod towards all beings, he is a Brahmin, he is a Samana, he is a Bhikkhu.” (Dhammapada, 142).

‘Kāye’ refers to the physical body (rūpakāya). In this context, the physical body is intended as ‘kāya’ in the sense of a collection (samūha) of major and minor limbs and things such as hair, etc., similar to an elephant corps or a chariot corps. Just as it is intended as ‘kāya’ in the sense of a collection, it is likewise intended as ‘kāya’ in the sense of being the place of origin (āya) of loathsome things such as hair, etc. Because it is the place of origin of extremely loathsome things like hair, it is called the physical body. ‘Āya’ means the place of origin. The definition of the word ‘āya’ is: they arise from it, therefore it is ‘āya’. What things arise? Loathsome things such as hair, etc., arise. Thus, because it is the place of origin of loathsome things, it is called ‘kāya’.

‘Kāyānupassī’ means one who has the habit of repeatedly contemplating the body, or one who is repeatedly contemplating the body. It should be understood that although ‘kāye’ is said, the use of the word ‘kāya’ for a second time in ‘kāyānupassī’ is to show the determination of the object without mixing with others, and the breaking down of the perception of compactness (ghana-vinibbhoga), etc. By saying so, it means that one is not a contemplator of feelings (vedanānupassī) or a contemplator of mind or mental objects (cittadhammānupassī) in the body, but only a contemplator of the body (kāyānupassī). Thus, by showing only the mode of body-contemplation on the object called the body, the unmixed determination is shown.

Likewise, one does not contemplate a single phenomenon separate from the major and minor limbs in the body, nor does one contemplate a woman or a man separate from the hair, body hair, etc. In this body, there is that which is called the body, which is a collection of primary elements (bhūta) and derived matter (upādā) such as hair, body hair, etc. Even in that physical body, one does not contemplate a single phenomenon separate from the primary elements and derived matter. Rather, like one who contemplates the parts of a cart, one contemplates the collection of major and minor limbs; like one who contemplates the components of a city, one contemplates the collection of hair, body hair, etc.; and like one who peels the layers of a banana trunk or one who opens an empty fist, one repeatedly contemplates only the collection of primary elements and derived matter. Thus, by showing the object called the body only by way of various collections, the breaking down of the perception of compactness is shown.

In this physical body, there is no body, woman, man, or any other phenomenon separate from the aforementioned collection. However, beings wrongly cling to only that aforementioned collection of phenomena in such and such ways. Therefore, the ancient teachers said: ‘What one sees (with wrong view), that is not the seen (the sense-object). What is seen (the sense-object), that one does not see (with wisdom). The fool, not seeing, is bound; being bound, he is not released.’
348:
In the phrase “for the sake of seeing the breaking down of compactness, etc.,” the following meaning should also be understood by the word ‘ādi’ (etc.). In detail, it means that this person dwells repeatedly contemplating only the body in this physical body, and does not dwell repeatedly contemplating phenomena other than the foul (asubha). Just as people repeatedly contemplate water in a mirage although it is not water, one should not dwell repeatedly contemplating permanence, happiness, self, and beauty in this physical body which is only impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul. Instead, it means that one dwells repeatedly contemplating only the collection of modes of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness in the physical body.
