Alternatively, the meaning should also be understood as “contemplating the body in the body” because of contemplating all that is called the body in this very body—starting from the breath and ending with the bones scattered in pieces as described later in the passage: “Here, monks, a monk having gone to the forest... he, mindful, breathes out,” etc., and as described in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: “Here, someone contemplates the collection of earth, the collection of water, the collection of fire, the collection of air, the collection of hair, the collection of body hair, the collection of outer skin, the collection of inner skin, the collection of flesh, the collection of blood, the collection of tendons, the collection of bones, and the collection of bone marrow as impermanent.”

Alternatively, the meaning should be seen as “contemplating the body as a collection of phenomena such as hair, etc.” because of not contemplating any object that could be grasped as “I” or “mine” in the sense of self (atta) or what belongs to self (attaniya) in the physical body, but instead contemplating only that collection of various phenomena such as hair, body hair, etc., which is the body produced by four causes (catusamuṭṭhānika kāya).

Furthermore, the meaning should also be seen as “contemplating the body in the body” because of contemplating the body, which is called a collection of modes such as the characteristic of impermanence, etc., in its entirety according to the method found in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: “In this body, one contemplates as impermanent, not as permanent,” etc. Indeed, this monk who has entered upon the practice of contemplation of the body in the body contemplates this physical body as impermanent, not as permanent, by way of the seven contemplations such as the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā). He contemplates it as suffering, not as happiness. He contemplates it as non-self (beyond control), not as self (under control). He becomes weary (nibbindati), not delighted. He becomes dispassionate (virajjati), not lustful. He causes [defilements] to cease (nirodheti), not to arise. He relinquishes (paṭinissajjati), not grasps. He, contemplating that physical body as impermanent, abandons the perception of permanence (nicca-saññā). Contemplating it as suffering, he abandons the perception of happiness (sukha-saññā). Contemplating it as non-self, he abandons the perception of self (atta-saññā). Becoming weary, he abandons delight (nandī).
349:
It should be understood that one abandons lust (rāga) by becoming dispassionate; one abandons the origin (samudaya) by causing it to cease; one abandons grasping (ādāna) by relinquishing it.

'Viharati' (dwells) means maintaining the four postures. 'Ātāpī' (ardent): it is called 'ātāpa' because it burns away the defilements (kilesas) in the three realms of existence; this 'ātāpa' is a name for energy (vīriya). Because that monk possesses that energy which intensely burns away the defilements, he is called 'ātāpī'. 'Sampajāno' (clearly comprehending) means being endowed with the knowledge known as clear comprehension (sampajañña), which understands without distortion. 'Satimā' (mindful) means being endowed with mindfulness (sati) that grasps and delimits the physical body (rūpakāya). Furthermore, this person, having grasped the object with mindfulness, contemplates it repeatedly with wisdom. Indeed, for one devoid of mindfulness, there is no such thing as contemplation (anupassanā). Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, I declare that mindfulness is necessary in all circumstances (in both the shrinking mind and the scattered mind)." Therefore, by this phrase alone, "kāye kāyānupassī viharati" (contemplating the body in the body, he dwells), the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā satipaṭṭhāna) is already stated. Alternatively, for a person without effort, the shrinking of the mind causes danger to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). A person without wisdom becomes confused regarding the grasping of what is the cause and the avoiding of what is not the cause. A person who has lost mindfulness is unable to relinquish what is not the cause and to grasp what is the cause. Because of such inability, the meditation subject does not reach fulfillment for that yogi. Therefore, it should be understood that this phrase "ātāpī sampajāno satimā" was spoken to show those qualities—namely energy, wisdom, and mindfulness—by whose power that meditation subject reaches fulfillment.

Having thus shown the contemplation of the body in the body and its associated factors, He now spoke the words "vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ" (having removed covetousness and grief in the world) to show the factors to be abandoned. In that text, "vineyya" means having removed [them] either by the removal of substitution (tadaṅga-vinaya) or by the removal by suppression (vikkhambhana-vinaya). "Loke" (in the world) refers to that very physical body (rūpakāya). Indeed, in this context, the physical body is intended as "the world" (loka) because of its nature of breaking up and disintegrating. However, for that yogi, covetousness and grief are not abandoned only in the physical body; they are also abandoned in feelings and so forth. Therefore, in the Vibhaṅga, it was said: "The five aggregates of clinging are called the world." Alternatively, because it is called "the world," this was spoken by way of extracting the meaning of those states such as feeling, etc. In the statement, "Therein, what is the world? That very body is the world," only the aforementioned meaning should be noted. The connection of the words should be noted as: "having removed covetousness and grief in that world." Furthermore, in this text, by the inclusion of "covetousness" (abhijjhā), sensual desire (kāmacchanda) is included; by the inclusion of "grief" (domanassa), ill-will (byāpāda) is included. Therefore, it should be understood that by showing these two powerful states included among the hindrances (nīvaraṇas), the abandoning of all hindrances is stated.
350:
In this context, specifically, by the removal of covetousness (abhijjhā), the abandoning of compliance (anurodha) rooted in bodily success is mentioned; by the removal of grief (domanassa), the abandoning of opposition (virodha) rooted in bodily failure is mentioned. By the removal of covetousness, the abandoning of delight in the physical body is mentioned; by the removal of grief, the abandoning of lack of delight in the cultivation of the body is mentioned. By the removal of covetousness, the abandoning of the superimposition of non-existent beauty and happiness upon the body is mentioned; by the removal of grief, the abandoning of the removal of the existing foulness and suffering of the body is mentioned. By stating such abandonment, the power of the practitioner's (yogāvacara) meditation and their capability for meditation are illustrated. For this is the power of meditation: that one becomes free from compliance and opposition, endures both delight and non-delight, and is free from superimposing the non-existent and removing the existent. One who is free from compliance and opposition, endures delight and non-delight, does not superimpose the non-existent, and does not remove the existent, is capable of meditation.

In another way, in the phrase "kāye kāyānupassī" (contemplating the body in the body), the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is stated by 'contemplation' (anupassanā). In the word "viharati" (dwells), the maintenance of the physical body by the practitioner through the stated dwelling is mentioned. In terms such as "ātāpī" (ardent), Right Effort (sammappadhāna) is stated by 'ardor' (ātāpa). By 'mindfulness and clear comprehension' (sati-sampajañña), the universal meditation subject (sabbattha-kammaṭṭhāna) or the means of maintaining the meditation subject is stated. Alternatively, it should be understood that tranquility (samatha) obtained through the power of contemplation of the body is stated by 'mindfulness' (sati), insight (vipassanā) by 'clear comprehension' (sampajañña), and the power of cultivation (bhāvanā) by the removal of covetousness and grief.

In the Vibhaṅga, however, regarding "anupassī": In that term, what is contemplation (anupassanā)? It is the wisdom (paññā), knowing, investigation, scrutiny, investigation of phenomena (dhammavicaya), marking, close marking, repeated marking, sagacity, proficiency, examination, discrimination, reflection, analysis, breadth of wisdom, guiding wisdom, insight (vipassanā), clear comprehension (sampajañña), the goad, wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the sword of wisdom, the palace of wisdom, the light of wisdom, the radiance of wisdom, the splendor of wisdom, the jewel of wisdom, non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view. This wisdom is called 'contemplation'. One who is endowed with, fully endowed with, possessed of, fully possessed of, gifted with, and provided with this contemplation is called "anupassī". "Viharati" means one moves, proceeds, guards, sustains, keeps going, carries on, and dwells; therefore, it is called "viharati". Regarding "ātāpī": In that term, what is ardor (ātāpa)? It is the mental inception of energy, exertion, endeavor, effort, striving, zeal, vigor, strength, fortitude, state of unflinching endeavor, state of not abandoning the desire, state of not abandoning the task, the firm grasping of the task, energy, the faculty of energy, the power of energy, right effort. This is called 'ardor'. One who is endowed with... possessed of this ardor is called "ātāpī". Regarding "sampajāno": In that term, what is clear comprehension (sampajañña)? It is the wisdom, knowing, investigation, scrutiny, investigation of phenomena, marking, close marking, repeated marking, sagacity, proficiency, examination, discrimination, reflection, analysis, breadth of wisdom, guiding wisdom, insight, clear comprehension, the goad, wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the sword of wisdom, the palace of wisdom, the light of wisdom, the radiance of wisdom, the splendor of wisdom, the jewel of wisdom, non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view. This is called 'clear comprehension'. One who is endowed with... possessed of this clear comprehension is called "sampajāno". Regarding "satimā": In that term, what is mindfulness (sati)? It is the mindfulness, recollection, recall, mindfulness, the state of remembering, the state of bearing in mind, the state of non-drifting, the state of non-forgetfulness, mindfulness, the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness...
351:
Right mindfulness (sammāsati) is the quality of remembering deeds done long ago, words spoken long ago, and so forth; it is the quality of repeatedly remembering, and remembering well. This quality is called mindfulness (sati). One is endowed with this mindfulness... and thus is called mindful (satimā).

In the phrase 'having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world,' what is the world? The physical body (rūpakāya) beginning with hair, which is the object of that mindfulness, is itself called the world. The five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā) are also called the world. These things are called the world. Among that world, covetousness, and displeasure, what is covetousness (abhijjhā)? It is the lust, intense lust, fawning, compliance, delight, intense delight, and the intense lust of the mind towards an object. This is called covetousness. Among those, what is displeasure (domanassa)? It is mental unpleasantness, mental suffering, and the unpleasant and painful feeling born of mental contact. This is called displeasure. Thus, both this covetousness and this displeasure are removed in this world, abandoned, calmed, stilled, subsided, gone to destruction, gone to complete destruction, perished, utterly perished, dried up, completely dried up, and made to vanish. Therefore, it is said, 'having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world.'

Thus, the meaning of these words has been stated. This method of the Commentary should be understood as it harmonizes with that Vibhaṅga Pali. This is the explanation of the meaning of the summary (uddesa) of the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā).

Now, in this passage: 'In feelings... in the mind... in dhammas, he dwells contemplating dhammas... having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world,' the purpose of repeating the words 'feelings' and so on in 'contemplating feelings in feelings' should be understood in the same way as stated in the contemplation of the body.

In the passage 'contemplating feelings in feelings, contemplating the mind in the mind, contemplating dhammas in dhammas,' feelings refer to the three kinds of feelings, and they are only mundane (lokiya). The mind is also mundane, and likewise, the dhammas such as the hindrances are also mundane. The classification of those feelings, mind, and dhammas will become clear in the exposition section (niddesavāra). However, here, in whatever way feelings should be contemplated, one who contemplates those feelings in that way should be understood as 'one who contemplates feelings in feelings.' This same method applies to the mind and dhammas.

How should feelings be contemplated? First, pleasant feeling should be seen as suffering. Painful feeling should be seen as a dart. Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling should be seen as impermanent. As the Blessed One said: 'One who sees pleasant feeling as suffering, painful feeling as a dart, and peaceful neutral feeling as impermanent, when seeing rightly...'
352:
“He who saw the pleasant as suffering,
And saw the painful as a dart;
And saw the peaceful neutral [feeling]
As something impermanent;
That monk, seeing rightly,
Will indeed wander at peace.” (SN 4.253)

All these feelings should also be contemplated as 'suffering.' For it was said: “Whatever is felt, I say that is included in suffering.” (SN 4.259). Furthermore, they should be contemplated in terms of being pleasant or painful. As it was said: “Pleasant feeling is pleasant when it persists, and painful when it changes.” (MN 1.465). All this should be understood in detail. Moreover, they should be contemplated by way of the seven contemplations, such as impermanence. The remaining distinctions will become clear in the exposition section (niddesavāra) itself.

Regarding the mind and dhammas: first, the mind should be contemplated by way of distinctions such as object (ārammaṇa), predominance (adhipati), conascence (sahajāta), plane (bhūmi), kamma, result (vipāka), and functional (kiriya), and by way of the seven contemplations such as impermanence, and by way of the distinctions such as 'with lust' (sarāga) that appear in the exposition section. Dhammas should be contemplated by way of individual characteristics (paccatta-lakkhaṇa) and general characteristics (sāmañña-lakkhaṇa), by way of the nature of emptiness (suññata) which is void of self, by way of the seven contemplations such as impermanence, and by way of the distinctions such as 'peaceful' (santa) that appear in the exposition section. The rest is just as previously stated. Although in this context, if covetousness and displeasure have been abandoned in the world called the body for a person, they are certainly abandoned for that person in feelings and so on as well. However, it is taught in all the foundations of mindfulness by way of different individuals and by way of the development of the foundations of mindfulness occurring in different thought-moments. Or, it should be understood that this is said to show the abandonment in one of those—feelings and so on—because when it is abandoned in one place, it is abandoned in the rest as well.

## The Commentary on the Summary Section is Finished.
## Contemplation of the Body: The Section on Mindfulness of Breathing

Now, just as a skilled bamboo worker, wishing to make utensils such as coarse mats, fine mats, baskets, boxes, and cases, might obtain a large bamboo, split it into four, and then take each piece of bamboo, split it further, and make those various utensils; in the same way, the Blessed One, wishing to enable beings to attain various kinds of distinctions through the teaching of the foundations of mindfulness, divided the single Right Mindfulness into four parts based on the objects to be contemplated, such as the body, in the manner beginning: “There are four foundations of mindfulness.”
353:
What are the four? "Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body"—having divided the objects into four in this manner, and taking each foundation of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) individually, desiring to analyze the body, he begins the exposition (niddesavāra) with the words "And how, monks?"

In that exposition, the question beginning with "And how?" is an inquiry made with the desire to explain in detail. The summary of the meaning here is: Monks, in what way does a monk dwell contemplating the body in the body? This method should be understood in all sections of inquiry. "A monk in this Dispensation" means a monk who exists in this Dispensation of the Buddha. In this context, the word "here" (idha) indicates the Dispensation which is the support for the person who brings about the contemplation of the body in all its aspects, and it serves to exclude the possibility of such a thing in other dispensations. Thus it has been said: "Monks, only here is there a first recluse... other doctrines are void of recluses" (M. Ni. 1.139). Therefore, it is said, "a monk in this Dispensation."

"Whether gone to the forest, or gone to the root of a tree, or gone to an empty hut"—this indicates his acquisition of a lodging (senāsana) suitable for the development of the foundations of mindfulness. For the mind of this monk, which has long been distracted by objects such as visible forms, does not wish to enter the path of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna); it runs only onto the wrong path, like a chariot yoked to a wild ox. Therefore, just as a cowherd, wishing to tame a wild calf that has grown up drinking all the milk from a wild cow, would take it away from the cow and, having driven a large post into the ground in a suitable place, would tie it there with a rope. Then that calf, though struggling this way and that, being unable to run away, would only sit or lie down near that very post. In the same way, this monk, wishing to tame the corrupt mind that has grown up drinking the flavors of objects such as visible forms for a long time, should take it away from objects such as visible forms and, having entered the forest, the root of a tree, or an empty hut, should tie it with the rope of mindfulness to the post of the foundation of mindfulness object. Thus, even if that mind wanders here and there, not finding the objects it was previously accustomed to, and being unable to break the rope of mindfulness and run away, it sits and lies down close to that very meditation object by the power of access concentration (upacāra) and absorption concentration (appanā). Therefore, the ancients said:

"Just as a man here would tie a calf to a post to tame it,
So should one firmly tie one's own mind to the object with mindfulness."
354:
In this way, this lodging is suitable for meditation for that monk. Therefore, it is said, "This indicates his acquisition of a lodging suitable for the development of the foundations of mindfulness."

Furthermore, because this Ānāpānassati meditation—which is the pinnacle of mindfulness of the body and the basis for the attainment of distinction and for dwelling in happiness in the present life for all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples—is not easy to accomplish without abandoning a village-adjacent monastery crowded with the sounds of women, men, elephants, horses, and so on, because sound is a thorn to jhāna. However, in a forest far from a village, it is easy for a practitioner (yogāvacara) to grasp this meditation subject, produce the fourth jhāna of Ānāpāna, and then, using that very jhāna as a basis, to comprehend the formations (saṅkhāra) and reach the supreme fruit, Arahatship. Therefore, the Blessed One, showing him the suitable lodging, said "Whether gone to the forest," and so on.

The Blessed One is like a master of site-planning (vatthuvijjācariya). Just as a master of site-planning, having looked at the site for a city and examined it well, instructs, "Build a city here," and when the city is completed safely, he receives great honor from the royal family; in the same way, the Blessed One, having examined the suitable lodging for the practitioner, instructs, "The meditation subject should be practiced here." Then, when the meditating monk practicing the meditation subject in that lodging reaches Arahatship in due course, the Blessed One receives great honor, with the monk thinking, "The Blessed One is indeed the Fully Enlightened One."

This monk is said to be like a leopard (dīpi). Just as a great king of leopards, depending on a thicket of grass, a thicket of trees, or a mountain thicket in the forest, hides and catches animals such as wild buffaloes, elk, and boars; in the same way, this monk practicing the meditation subject in the forest and other such places, in due course catches (attains) the four paths and the four noble fruits. Therefore, the ancients said:

"Just as a leopard catches prey by lying in wait,
So this son of the Buddha, diligent in yoga and a practitioner of insight,
Having entered the forest, catches the supreme fruit."

Therefore, the Blessed One, showing the forest lodging as the suitable ground for the speed of his exertion, said "Whether gone to the forest," and so on. From this point forward, whatever should be said in this section on Ānāpāna has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga. Indeed, this simile of the skilled turner (bhamakāro) and the mention of absorption (appanā) in the phrase "thus internally in the body" are the only parts not found there; the rest is already included.
355:
Among the words not yet mentioned, in the term 'dakkha', the meaning of 'skilled' should be understood. 'Whether pulling long' refers to the act of stretching the hands and feet to pull a long stroke when turning large drum-heads and the like. 'Whether pulling short' refers to the act of pulling a short stroke slowly when turning small ivory pins, needle cases, and the like. In the same way, this monk, by means of the out-breaths and in-breaths occurring through a long duration or a short period, clearly knows, 'I breathe out long' when breathing out long... and trains himself, 'I shall breathe in.' For that monk who trains in this way, the four jhānas arise based on the sign (nimitta) of the out-breaths and in-breaths. Emerging from the jhāna, he grasps either the out-breaths and in-breaths or the jhāna factors.

Among those two, the monk who takes the out-breaths and in-breaths as his basis grasps materiality (rūpa) thus: 'On what do these out-breaths and in-breaths depend? They depend on the physical base (vatthu). The physical base is the physical body (karajakāya); the physical body consists of the four great elements and derived materiality (upādārūpa).' Thereafter, he grasps the mental states (nāma) beginning with contact (phassa) as the fifth, which have that materiality as their object. Having thus grasped mind and matter (nāmarūpa), while searching for their cause, he sees dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) beginning with ignorance (avijjā) and, having crossed over doubt by realizing, 'This is merely a phenomenon of cause and effect; there is no other being or person,' he applies the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa) to mind and matter along with their causes. As he develops insight (vipassanā), he gradually reaches the fruition of Arahatship (arahattaphala). This is the path of exit from the round of suffering up to Arahatship for one monk.

The monk who takes the jhāna as his basis also defines mind and matter by grasping: 'On what do these jhāna factors depend? They depend on the physical base. The physical base is the physical body; the jhāna factors are mind (nāma), and the physical body is matter (rūpa).' While searching for the cause of that mind and matter, he sees the mode of causes beginning with ignorance and, having crossed over doubt by realizing, 'This is merely a phenomenon of cause and effect; there is no other being or person,' he applies the three characteristics to mind and matter along with their causes. As he develops insight, he gradually reaches the fruition of Arahatship. This too is the path of exit from the round of suffering up to Arahatship for another monk.

'Thus internally' means he dwells repeatedly contemplating the body in his own collection of out-breaths and in-breaths. 'Or externally' means contemplating in the collection of out-breaths and in-breaths of another. 'Or internally and externally' means contemplating at times in his own out-breaths and in-breaths, and at times in those of another. By this phrase, the time of moving back and forth between them without setting aside the familiar meditation subject is stated. However, both cannot be attained at the same time.
356:
One who repeatedly contemplates the nature of arising means—just as the wind moves back and forth depending on the blacksmith's bellows, the nozzle, and the appropriate effort for that wind, in the same way, the collection of out-breaths and in-breaths moves back and forth depending on the monk's physical body, the nostrils, and the mind. The phenomena such as the physical body are 'phenomena of arising'; one who sees these is said to 'dwell repeatedly contemplating the nature of arising in the body.'

One who repeatedly contemplates the nature of vanishing means—just as when the bellows are removed, the nozzle is broken, and the appropriate effort is absent, that wind does not occur; in the same way, when the physical body is broken, the nostrils are destroyed, and the mind has ceased, the collection of out-breaths and in-breaths does not occur. Thus, seeing that the cessation of out-breaths and in-breaths is due to the cessation of the physical body and so forth, he is said to 'dwell repeatedly contemplating the nature of vanishing in the body.'

One who repeatedly contemplates the nature of both arising and vanishing is one who contemplates arising at one time and vanishing at another. Alternatively, the mindfulness is established for that monk that 'there is only a collection of matter.' He reflects: 'It is not a being, not a person, not a woman, not a man, not a self, not something belonging to a self, not I, not mine, not anyone, and not belonging to anyone.'

The word 'yāvad-eva' (only to the extent) defines the limit of the purpose. This is what is meant: the mindfulness that is established is not for any other purpose, but only to the extent of the measure of knowledge and the measure of mindfulness for the sake of further and higher stages, meaning for the sake of the growth of mindfulness and clear comprehension.

He dwells independent, not depending on the supports of craving and views. He does not cling to anything in the world, such as materiality... or consciousness, thinking, 'This is my self' or 'This belongs to my self.' In the term 'evampi', the syllable 'pi' has the sense of connecting with the meaning to be stated above. With this phrase, the Blessed One shows the conclusion of the Section on Mindfulness of Breathing.

In that teaching, the mindfulness that grasps the out-breaths and in-breaths is the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). The prior craving that originates that mindfulness is the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca). The non-occurrence of both is the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca). The Noble Path that fully understands the Truth of Suffering, abandons the Truth of the Origin, and has the Truth of Cessation as its object is the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca). Having thus made an effort by way of the Four Noble Truths, he reaches Nibbāna. This is the path of exit from the round of suffering up to Arahatship for a monk who applies his mind by way of out-breaths and in-breaths.

## The Section on Mindfulness of Breathing is finished.
357:
## Commentary on the Section on Postures (Iriyapathapabbavaṇṇanā)

Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of in-breaths and out-breaths, he now says "And again..." etc., to analyze it by way of postures. In that teaching, even animals like dogs and jackals know "we are going" when they go; however, it is not with reference to such knowing that this was said. For such knowing does not abandon the perception of a being (sattūpaladdhi), does not uproot the notion of a self (attasaññā), and is neither a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) nor the development of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā). But the knowing of this monk abandons the perception of a being, uproots the notion of a self, and is both a meditation subject and the development of the foundations of mindfulness. This was said with reference to clear comprehension (sampajānana) such as: "Who goes? Whose going is it? For what reason does one go?" The same method applies to standing and so forth.

Among those questions, "Who goes?" means: No being or person whatsoever goes. "Whose going is it?" means: It is not the going of any being or person. "For what reason does one go?" means: One goes because of the diffusion of the air element (vāyodhātu) born of mental activity. Therefore, this practitioner knows thus: The thought "I will go" arises; that thought produces the air element; the air element produces bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti); the movement of the whole body forward through the diffusion of the air element born of mental activity is called "going". The same method applies to standing and so forth.

In standing and so forth: The thought "I will stand" arises; that thought produces the air element; the air element produces bodily intimation; the upright state of the whole body from the feet upwards through the diffusion of the air element born of mental activity is called "standing". The thought "I will sit" arises; that thought produces the air element; the air element produces bodily intimation; the contraction of the lower body and the upright state of the upper body through the diffusion of the air element born of mental activity is called "sitting". The thought "I will lie down" arises; that thought produces the air element; the air element produces bodily intimation; the horizontal extension of the whole body through the diffusion of the air element born of mental activity is called "lying down".

To that practitioner who knows thus, it occurs: "A being goes, a being stands" is said in the world, but in the ultimate sense (atthato), there is no being at all who goes or stands. For example, "A cart goes, a cart stands" is said, but there is no such thing as a cart that goes or stands by itself; only when four oxen are yoked and a skilled driver drives it, is it said "A cart goes, a cart stands"...
358:
...it is merely a conventional expression (vohāramatta). In the same way, the body is like the cart because it lacks volition (ajānanatṭhena), the air elements born of mind are like the oxen, and the mind is like the driver. When the thought "I will go, I will stand" arises, the air element arises producing bodily intimation. Through the diffusion of the air element born of mental activity, going and so forth proceed. Therefore, it is merely a conventional expression: "A being goes, a being stands, I go, I stand". Hence it was said —

"As a boat goes by the force of the wind,
As an arrow goes by the force of the bowstring,
So this physical body goes,
Driven by the wind [of the mind].
As a machine moves by the power of a string,
So this body-machine moves, stands, or sits
By the power of the mind-string.
What being is there here who, without causes and conditions,
Could stand or go by its own power?"

Therefore, this meditating monk who clearly discerns going and so forth as proceeding only by the power of causes and conditions should be understood as: "When going, he knows 'I am going'; when standing, sitting, or lying down, he knows 'I am lying down'." Furthermore, the statement "In whatever way his body is disposed, he knows it accordingly" is an all-inclusive statement. This means: in whatever posture his body is placed, he knows it in that way. When it is in the posture of going, he knows "he goes". When it is in the posture of standing, sitting, or lying down, he knows "he lies down".

"Thus internally" means he dwells contemplating the body in the body by grasping his own four postures. "Or externally" means by grasping the four postures of another. "Or internally and externally" means he dwells contemplating the body in the body by grasping the four postures sometimes of himself and sometimes of another. In the passages such as "contemplating the nature of arising", the arising and passing away of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) should be extracted by way of the five modes, such as "with the arising of ignorance, form arises". With reference to those five modes, it was said here "contemplating the nature of arising" and so forth. The statement "Or else, mindfulness that 'there is a body'" and so forth is just the same as what has been said before.
359:
In this Section on Postures, the mindfulness that grasps the four postures is the Truth of Suffering. The preceding craving that causes that mindfulness is the Truth of the Origin. The non-occurrence of both is the Truth of Cessation. The Noble Path, which fully understands the Truth of Suffering, abandons the Truth of the Origin, and takes the Truth of Cessation as its object, is the Truth of the Path. Thus, by striving through the power of the Four Truths, one reaches Nibbāna, the state of peace. This should be understood as the way of deliverance from the round of rebirths unto the Fruit of Arahantship for a monk who grasps the four postures.

## The Section on Postures is finished.

## Commentary on the Section on the Fourfold Clear Comprehension
Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of postures, he now says "Again, monks..." and so forth, to analyze it by way of the fourfold clear comprehension. In that text, the words beginning with "Abhikkante" have already been explained in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta. "Thus, internally..." means that by grasping the fourfold clear comprehension in this way, one dwells contemplating the body either in one's own body, or in another's body, or at times in one's own and at times in another's body. Here too, in the passage beginning with "contemplating the nature of arising and vanishing," only the arising and vanishing of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) should be extracted. The remaining text is just as previously stated.

In this Section on Clear Comprehension, the mindfulness that grasps the fourfold clear comprehension is the Truth of Suffering. The preceding craving that causes that mindfulness is the Truth of the Origin. The non-occurrence of both is the Truth of Cessation. The Noble Path of the aforementioned kind is the Truth of the Path. Thus, by striving through the power of the Four Truths, one reaches the state of peace. This is the way of deliverance from the round of rebirths unto the Fruit of Arahantship by power of a monk who grasps the fourfold clear comprehension.

## The Section on the Fourfold Clear Comprehension is finished.

## Commentary on the Section on Attention to Repulsiveness
Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of the fourfold clear comprehension, he now says "Again, monks..." and so forth, to analyze it by way of attention to repulsiveness (paṭikūlamanasikāra). In that text, whatever needs to be said regarding "this very body" and so forth, has all been stated in full detail in every aspect in the Visuddhimagga, in the section on the meditation subject of mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati). "Open at both ends" (ubhatomukhā) means provided with two openings, at the bottom and at the top. "Of various sorts" (nānāvihitassa) means of various kinds.
360:
The comparison of the simile here is as follows: This physical body composed of the four great elements is like a bag with openings at both ends. The various types of grain mixed and put into that bag are like the thirty-two parts, such as hair of the head and so forth. The man with good sight is like the meditator (yogāvacara). Just as the time when the various grains become clear to the man when he unties the bag and examines it, so should the time when the thirty-two parts become clear to the meditating monk be understood. "Thus, internally..." means that by grasping hair of the head and so forth in this way, one dwells contemplating the body either in one's own body, or in another's body, or at times in one's own and at times in another's body. From here on, it is exactly as previously described. Specifically, in this Section on Attention to Repulsiveness, the mindfulness that grasps the thirty-two parts is the Truth of Suffering; thus, by applying this method, the way of deliverance should be understood. The rest is just as previously stated.

## The Section on Attention to Repulsiveness is finished.

## Commentary on the Section on Attention to Elements

Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of attention to repulsiveness, he now says "Again, in another way" and so forth, to analyze it by way of attention to elements (dhātumanasikāra). In that Section on Attention to Elements, the explanation of the meaning along with the simile is as follows: Just as a certain butcher or a butcher's apprentice who is supported by his wages, having slaughtered a cow and dissected it, might sit at a crossroads, which is the central point of the main roads going in the four directions, having divided it into portions; even so, a monk reflects on this very body, however it is placed and however it is disposed, as it stands in any of the four postures, thus: "There are in this body the earth element... the air element."

What is meant is this: To the butcher, while he is rearing the cow, while he is bringing it to the slaughterhouse, while he is tying it up there, while he is slaughtering it, and while he is looking at the slaughtered dead cow, the perception "cow" does not disappear as long as he has not yet dissected it and divided it into parts. But to the butcher who has divided it and is sitting there, the perception "cow" disappears and the perception "meat" arises. To him...
361:
While a butcher is raising a cow, leading it to the slaughterhouse, binding it there, killing it, or looking at the dead cow, for as long as he has not yet butchered it into pieces, the perception of 'cow' does not disappear. However, for the butcher who has butchered the cow and is sitting there, the perception of 'cow' disappears and only the perception of 'meat' arises. It does not occur to that butcher, 'I am selling a cow; these people are taking away a cow.' Rather, it only occurs to him, 'I am selling meat; these people are taking away meat.' In the same way, for this monk, whether as a foolish worldling in the past while a layman or after ordaining, as long as he does not dissect this very body, just as it stands and is positioned, into its elements and contemplate them, the perception of 'being' or 'person' does not disappear. But for the yogi who contemplates by way of the elements, the perception of 'being' disappears and the mind becomes established through the power of the elements alone. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'He contemplates this very body, just as it stands and is positioned, by way of the elements: "In this body there are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element."' In the Pali passage 'Just as a butcher... (etc.)... air element,' the yogi should be understood as the butcher; the perception of 'being' as the perception of 'cow'; the four postures as the four-way crossroads; and the contemplation by way of elements as the sitting after butchering into pieces. This is the explanation of the Pali text here. The detailed discussion regarding the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga. 'Thus, internally...' means that by grasping the four elements in this way, one dwells contemplating the body in one's own body, or in another's body, or at times in one's own and at times in another's body. What follows is according to the method already mentioned. Specifically, here, the mindfulness that grasps the four elements is the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca); thus, by connecting it, the way of exit from the round of rebirth should be understood. The rest is the same as what was said before.

## The Section on Attention to Elements is finished.

## Explanation of the Nine Cemetery Contemplations

Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of attention to the elements, the Blessed One now spoke the words beginning with 'Again, further,' to analyze it by way of the nine cemetery contemplations. In that Pali, 'seyyathāpi passeyya' means 'as if one were to see.' 'Sarīraṃ' refers to a dead corpse. 'Sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ' means a corpse discarded in a cemetery. A corpse that has been dead for one day is called 'ekāhamata.' A corpse that has been dead for two days is called 'dvīhamata.' A corpse that has been dead for three days is called 'tīhamata.' It is called 'uddhumāta' (bloated) because it is swollen upward with air like a blacksmith's bellows due to the exhaustion of life. 'Uddhumāta' is the same as 'uddhumātaka.' Alternatively, it is called 'uddhumātaka' because it is a loathsome bloated corpse. A corpse with a blue-black color is called 'vinīla.' 'Vinīla' is the same as 'vinīlaka.' Alternatively, it is called 'vinīlaka' because it is a loathsome blue-black corpse. This name applies to a corpse that has a red color in fleshy parts, white in pus-filled parts, and mostly a blue-black color. Or it is the name of a corpse that appears as if covered with a blue-black cloth. A corpse with pus oozing from burst places and from the nine orifices is called 'vipubba.' 'Vipubba' is the same as 'vipubbaka.' Alternatively, it is called 'vipubbaka' because it is a loathsome festering corpse. It is called 'vipubbakajāta' because it has reached the state of oozing pus. 'This very body' means that the monk compares this body of his own with that dead corpse through wisdom. How does he compare it?
362:
A corpse with a distorted color is called 'vinīla'; 'vinīla' is the same as 'vinīlaka.' Or it is called 'vinīlaka' because it is loathsome. It refers to the appearance of a corpse that is red in fleshy parts, white in parts where pus collects, and generally blue-black, as if wrapped in a blue cloth. A corpse with pus trickling from broken places or from the nine orifices is called 'vipubba'; 'vipubba' is the same as 'vipubbaka.' Or it is called 'vipubbaka' because it is loathsome. Having reached the state of being festering, it is called 'vipubbakajāta.'

'He [compares] this very body' means that the monk compares and contemplates his own physical body with that dead corpse through wisdom. How does he contemplate? He contemplates: 'This body too is of such a nature, will become such, and cannot escape this.' The meaning is: as long as these three things—life (life faculty), heat (kamma-born heat), and consciousness—exist, this body can perform actions such as standing and walking. But when these things depart, this body too is of such a putrid nature; it will reach such various states as being bloated (uddhumāta), and it cannot escape the state of being bloated. Thus, by grasping the bloated state and so on, he dwells contemplating the body in his own body, or in another's body, or at times in his own and at times in another's body.

'Being devoured' (khajjamāna) refers to a corpse being eaten by animals that perch on the belly and so on, and pluck out the flesh of the belly, the lips, the eye-sockets, and so forth. 'With flesh and blood' refers to a corpse possessing remaining flesh and blood. 'Fleshless but smeared with blood' refers to a corpse where the flesh is gone but the blood has not yet dried. 'In another direction' means in a different spatial direction. 'Hand-bones' refers to the sixty-four types of hand-bones scattered individually. The same method applies to foot-bones and so on.

'More than a year old' refers to bones that have passed one year. 'Rotted' refers to bones that, when left in the open, rot over a long time due to contact with wind, sun, and rain; bones inside the earth, however, last much longer. 'Reduced to powder' refers to bones that have become fine powder and are scattered. In all the charnel ground sections, the phrase 'he [compares] this very body' should be applied by way of the states such as 'being devoured,' according to the method already stated. Thus, by grasping from the state of being devoured up to the state of being reduced to powder, he dwells contemplating the body in his own body, or in another's body, or at times in his own and at times in another's body.
363:
At this point, the nine cemetery contemplations (nava-sivathika) should be understood collectively. One is the corpse that is "one day dead" and so forth; one is the corpse "being devoured by crows" and so forth; one is "a skeleton with flesh, blood, and sinews"; one is "a skeleton without flesh but smeared with blood and held together by sinews"; one is "a skeleton without flesh and blood but held together by sinews"; one is "bones disconnected from sinews" and so forth; one is "bones white like the color of a conch shell"; one is "bones heaped up for more than a year"; and one is "bones rotted and crumbled into powder"—thus there are nine.

The Buddha spoke the words "Thus, monks" after showing these nine cemetery contemplations, intending to conclude the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā). Therein, the mindfulness that grasps these nine cemetery contemplations is the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). The prior craving that causes that mindfulness to arise is the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca). The non-occurrence of both is the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca). The Noble Path that fully understands suffering, abandons the origin, and has cessation as its object is the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca). Thus, by making an effort through the power of the Four Noble Truths, one reaches Nibbāna, the state of peace. This is the gateway to liberation from the round of rebirths, up to the fruit of Arahantship, for monks who grasp the nine cemetery contemplations.

## The Section on the Nine Cemetery Contemplations is Finished.

With this sequence of words, the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā) consisting of fourteen sections—namely, the section on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna-pabba), the section on postures (iriyāpatha-pabba), the section on fourfold clear comprehension (catusampajañña-pabba), the section on reflection on repulsiveness (paṭikūlamanasikāra-pabba), the section on reflection on the elements (dhātumanasikāra-pabba), and the nine cemetery contemplations (nava-sivathika-pabba)—is completed. Among these fourteen, only these two—the section on mindfulness of breathing and the section on reflection on repulsiveness—are attainment meditation subjects (appanā-kammaṭṭhāna). Because the cemetery contemplations are taught by way of contemplating danger (ādīnavānupassanā), the remaining twelve sections are only access meditation subjects (upacāra-kammaṭṭhāna).

## The Contemplation of the Body is Finished.

## Commentary on the Contemplation of Feelings

Having thus taught the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna) in fourteen ways, the Blessed One now says "And how, monks," etc., to teach the contemplation of feelings (vedanānupassanā) in nine ways. In that text, "a pleasant feeling" means that when experiencing a pleasant feeling, whether bodily or mental, one understands, "I experience a pleasant feeling." In this regard, even infants lying on their backs understand when they experience pleasure while drinking milk, "We experience pleasure." However, it is not with reference to such understanding that it is said "one understands." This is because such understanding does not abandon the perception of a being, does not remove the perception of a self, and is neither a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) nor the development of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna-bhāvanā). Indeed, the understanding of this monk abandons the perception of a being, removes the perception of a self, and is both a meditation subject and the development of mindfulness. It is spoken with reference to the experiencing of one who understands clearly in this way: "Who feels? To whom does the feeling belong? For what reason does the feeling arise?"
364:
Indeed, even infants lying on their backs understand when they experience pleasure at times such as nursing, "We experience a pleasant feeling." However, it is not with reference to such understanding that this is said. For such understanding does not abandon the grasp of a being, does not remove the perception of a self, and cannot be a meditation subject or the development of mindfulness. But the understanding of this monk abandons the grasp of a being, removes the perception of a self, and is both a meditation subject and the development of mindfulness. This is spoken with reference to experiencing with clear comprehension, thus: "Who feels? To whom does the feeling belong? For what reason does the feeling arise?"

Among those questions, "Who feels?" means that no being or person feels. "To whom does the feeling belong?" means that the feeling does not belong to any being or person. "For what reason does the feeling arise?" means that the feeling arises only because of the physical base (vatthu) and the object (ārammaṇa). Therefore, that monk understands: "Depending on various bases and objects such as pleasure, it is only the feeling that feels. Based on the occurrence of that feeling, it is merely a conventional expression to say 'I feel.'" Thus, the monk who notes that only the feeling feels, depending on the base and the object, should be understood as "understanding that he experiences a pleasant feeling." He is like a certain Elder on Cittalapabbata.

It is said that when that Elder was unwell, he was rolling back and forth, groaning due to intense pain. Then a young monk asked, "Venerable sir, which part of you is hurting?" The Elder replied, "Friend, there is no such thing as a specific place that hurts. Depending on the base and the object, it is only the feeling that feels." The young monk asked, "Venerable sir, from the time of knowing this, is it not proper to endure?" The Elder said, "Friend, I shall endure." The young monk said, "Venerable sir, endurance is noble." So the Elder endured. The wind (ailment) pierced up to his heart, and his intestines lay in a heap on the couch. The Elder showed the young monk, "Friend, is this much endurance sufficient?" The young monk remained silent. The Elder, balancing his energy, attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) and passed away as a samasīsī (one who simultaneously attains the end of defilements and the end of life).

Just as with pleasure, so with pain... (and so forth) ... when experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling free from worldly attachments (nirāmisa), one understands, "I experience a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling free from worldly attachments." Thus, having taught the meditation on materiality (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna), the Blessed One, wishing to teach the meditation on immateriality (arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna), found that if it were taught by way of contact (phassa) or by way of consciousness (citta), it would not be clear and would appear like a mass of darkness. However, because the arising of feelings is clear, the meditation subject becomes clear when taught by way of feelings. Therefore, just as in the Sakkapañha Sutta, in this sutta as well, He taught the meditation on immateriality by way of feelings. In that teaching:
365:
"There are two kinds of meditation subjects: meditation on materiality and meditation on immateriality," and so on—this sequence of words should be understood in the same way as taught in the Sakkapañha Sutta.

In those words beginning with "pleasant feeling" (sukhaṃ vedanaṃ), this is another method of understanding. In saying "he understands that he feels a pleasant feeling," because there is no painful feeling at the moment a pleasant feeling arises, the person feeling a pleasant feeling understands specifically, "I feel only a pleasant feeling." By understanding in this way, that painful feeling which existed previously no longer exists now, and this pleasant feeling did not exist before this moment; thus, he clearly understands regarding those feelings that "feeling is impermanent, unstable, and subject to change." This has also been taught by the Blessed One:

"Aggivessana, at the time when one feels a pleasant feeling, at that time one does not feel a painful feeling, nor does one feel a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; at that time one feels only a pleasant feeling. Aggivessana, at the time when one feels a painful feeling... (pe) ... a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, at that time one does not feel a pleasant feeling, nor does one feel a painful feeling; at that time one feels only a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Aggivessana, a pleasant feeling is also impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to passing away, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation. A painful feeling is also... (pe)... Aggivessana, a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is also impermanent... (pe)... subject to cessation. Seeing thus, Aggivessana, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with pleasant feeling, becomes disenchanted with painful feeling, and becomes disenchanted with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, the knowledge arises: 'It is liberated.' He understands: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state to come,'" (M. Ni. 2.205).

In the words beginning with "or a worldly pleasant feeling" (sāmisaṃ vā sukhaṃ), what is called worldly pleasant feeling (sāmisa-sukha) refers to the six types of joy based on the household life (gehasita-somanassa) which are dependent on the worldly bait of the five cords of sensual pleasure. What is called unworldly pleasant feeling (nirāmisa-sukha) refers to the six types of joy based on renunciation (nekkhamma-sita-somanassa). What is called worldly painful feeling (sāmisa-dukkha) refers to the six types of grief based on the household life (gehasita-domanassa). What is called unworldly painful feeling (nirāmisa-dukkha) refers to the six types of grief based on renunciation (nekkhamma-sita-domanassa). What is called worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (sāmisa-adukkhamasukha) refers to the six types of equanimity based on the household life (gehasita-upekkhā). Unworldly...
366:
...neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (nirāmisa-adukkhamasukha) refers to the six types of equanimity based on renunciation (nekkhamma-sita-upekkhā). The classification of these feelings has already been taught in the Sakkapañha Sutta.

Thus, by defining and grasping pleasant feelings and so on, he dwells contemplating feelings in his own feelings, or in the feelings of others, or at times in his own and at times in the feelings of others. In the phrase "or contemplating the nature of arising and passing away" (samudayawayadhammānupassī vā), it should be understood that he dwells contemplating the arising and passing away of feelings through the five modes each, such as "with the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of feeling," and so on. He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in feelings, or he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in feelings, or at times he dwells contemplating the nature of arising and at times the nature of passing away in feelings. What follows this is the same as the method stated in the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā). However, in this contemplation of feelings, it should be understood that the mindfulness that defines and grasps feeling is the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca); thus, the way of exit from the round of existence for the monk who defines feeling should be understood. The rest of the explanation is the same.

## The Contemplation of Feeling is Finished.

## Explanation of the Contemplation of the Mind

Having thus taught the foundation of mindfulness of the contemplation of feeling in nine ways, he now speaks the words beginning with "And how, bhikkhus" (kathañca bhikkhave) to teach the contemplation of the mind in sixteen ways. In that passage, "with lust" (sarāgaṃ) refers to the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed. "Without lust" (vītarāgaṃ) refers to mundane wholesome and indeterminate (avyākata) consciousness. Since this term is only for investigation (sammasana) and not for the combination of states (dhamma-samodhāna), supramundane consciousness is not obtained in any single term here. The remaining four unwholesome types of consciousness are included neither in the former term nor in the latter term. "With hate" (sadosaṃ) refers to the two types of consciousness accompanied by aversion (domanassa). "Without hate" (vītadosaṃ) refers to mundane wholesome and indeterminate consciousness. The remaining ten unwholesome types of consciousness are included neither in the former term nor in the latter term. "With delusion" (samohaṃ) refers to the two types of consciousness: that accompanied by doubt (vicikicchā) and that accompanied by restlessness (uddhacca). However, since delusion arises in all unwholesome consciousness, the remaining unwholesome types of consciousness are also appropriate in this term "with delusion." In this dyad of delusion alone, all twelve unwholesome types of consciousness are completely encompassed. "Without delusion" (vītamohaṃ) refers to mundane wholesome and indeterminate consciousness. "Shrunken" (saṅkhittaṃ) refers to the mind overcome by sloth and torpor (thina-middha). This is called a shrunken mind (saṅkuṭita-citta). "Scattered" (vikkhittaṃ) refers to the mind accompanied by restlessness (uddhacca). This is called a distracted mind (pasaṭa-citta).

"Great" (mahaggataṃ) refers to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara) consciousness. "Not great" (amahaggataṃ) refers to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) consciousness. "Surpassable" (sauttaraṃ) refers to the sense-sphere consciousness. "Unsurpassable" (anuttaraṃ) refers to the fine-material sphere and immaterial sphere consciousness. Among those (great) types of consciousness, the fine-material sphere consciousness is "surpassable" (when compared to the immaterial sphere).
367:
The 'unexcelled' (anuttara) mind refers only to the formless-sphere (arūpāvacara) mind. The 'concentrated' (samāhita) mind is a mind that possesses either absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) or access concentration (upacāra-samādhi). The 'unconcentrated' (asamāhita) mind is a mind devoid of both types of concentration. The 'liberated' (vimutta) mind is a mind freed from defilements through 'liberation by substitution of opposites' (tadaṅga-vimutti) and 'liberation by suppression' (vikkhambhana-vimutti). The 'unliberated' (avimutta) mind is a mind devoid of both types of liberation. As for 'liberation by eradication' (samuccheda-vimutti), 'liberation by tranquillization' (paṭippassaddhi-vimutti), and 'liberation by escape' (nissaraṇa-vimutti), there is no occasion for them here.

Regarding the phrase "Thus, in his own mind..." and so forth, by distinguishing through the presence of lust and so on, one dwells observing the mind repeatedly—either in one's own mind, in another's mind, or at times in one's own and at times in another's mind—noting whatever mind arises at whatever moment. In the phrase "observing the nature of arising and passing away," the arising and passing away of consciousness should be brought out through five aspects each, such as "with the arising of ignorance, consciousness arises." From this point onward, the method is the same as previously stated. However, it should be understood that in this contemplation of the mind, the mindfulness that grasps the mind is the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). Thus, by connecting the terms, the way of exit from the round of rebirth for the monk who grasps the mind should be known. The remaining passages are just as described before.

## The Contemplation of the Mind is finished.

## Contemplation of Phenomena: Explanation of the Section on Hindrances

Having thus taught the Contemplation of the Mind (cittānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna) in sixteen ways, the Buddha now says "And how, bhikkhus..." and so forth to teach the Contemplation of Phenomena (dhammānupassanā) in five ways. Alternatively, the Blessed One taught the grasping of pure matter (rūpa) through the Contemplation of the Body, and the grasping of pure mentality (nāma) through the Contemplation of Feeling and the Contemplation of the Mind. Now, to teach the grasping of mixed matter and mentality, he says "And how, bhikkhus..." and so forth. Or, only the grasping of the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha) was taught by the Contemplation of the Body, only the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) by the Contemplation of Feeling, and only the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha) by the Contemplation of the Mind. Now, to also teach the grasping of the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha) and the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), he says "And how, bhikkhus..." and so forth.

In that text, "present" (santam) means existing clearly within one's own continuity by way of frequent occurrence. "Absent" (asantam) means not existing, either due to non-occurrence or because it has been abandoned. "And how" (yathā ca) refers to the cause by which sensual desire arises. "And he knows that" (tañca pajānāti) means he knows that cause of the arising of sensual desire. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all terms.

In this context, sensual desire (kāmacchanda) arises due to unwise attention (ayonisomanasikāra) to a beautiful object (subhanimitta). A beautiful object (subhanimitta) refers to both a beautiful thing itself and the sign of beauty.
368:
Unwise attention (ayonisomanasikāra) means attention that is not a means to reach desired welfare, attention on a wrong path, or attention to the impermanent as permanent, the painful as pleasant, the non-self as self, or the foul as beautiful. For a person who frequently applies such unwise attention to a beautiful object, sensual desire arises. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, there is the sign of beauty; frequently applying unwise attention to it is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sensual desire or for the growth and increase of arisen sensual desire."

However, the abandoning of that sensual desire occurs through wise attention (yonisomanasikāra) to the sign of foulness (asubhanimitta). The sign of foulness (asubhanimitta) refers to both foulness (the absorption of foulness) and the object of foulness. Wise attention (yonisomanasikāra) means attention that is a means to reach desired welfare, attention on the right path, or attention to the impermanent as impermanent, the painful as painful, the non-self as non-self, or the foul as foul. For a person who frequently applies such wise attention to the sign of foulness, sensual desire is abandoned. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, there is the sign of foulness; frequently applying wise attention to it is the nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen sensual desire or for the abandoning of arisen sensual desire."

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of sensual desire: learning the sign of foulness, devotion to the meditation on foulness, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, noble friendship, and suitable talk. In detail, sensual desire is abandoned for one who learns the ten kinds of foulness signs, for one who develops them, for one who has the doors of the sense faculties closed, and for one who knows moderation in eating by having the habit of drinking water to sustain oneself while there is still space for four or five mouthfuls of food. Thus it was said:

"Without eating four or five mouthfuls, one should drink water;
This is sufficient for the comfortable dwelling of a monk with resolute intent."

Sensual desire is also abandoned for one who associates with noble friends who delight in the meditation on foulness, such as the Elder Tissa who practiced the meditation on foulness, and by engaging in suitable talk related to the ten kinds of foulness while standing, sitting, and so forth. Therefore, I have said, "Six things lead to the abandoning of sensual desire." One knows distinctly that for a person who has abandoned sensual desire through these six things, there is no future arising of it by the Path of Arahatship.
369:
Ill-will (byāpāda) arises due to unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) to the sign of repulsion (paṭigha-nimitta). In this context, both anger itself is called the sign of repulsion, and the object of anger is also called the sign of repulsion. Unwise attention has the same characteristic across all signs of repulsion. For one who frequently applies unwise attention to that sign, ill-will arises. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Bhikkhus, there is the sign of repulsion; frequently applying unwise attention to it is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen ill-will, or for the growth and abundance of arisen ill-will.'

Ill-will is abandoned through wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) to the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (mettā-cetovimutti). In this context, when 'loving-kindness' (mettā) is mentioned, it refers to both access concentration (upacāra) and absorption (appanā); however, when 'liberation of mind' (cetovimutti) is mentioned, it refers only to absorption. Wise attention has the characteristic already described. For one who frequently applies wise attention to that liberation of mind through loving-kindness, ill-will is abandoned. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Bhikkhus, there is the liberation of mind through loving-kindness; frequently applying wise attention to it is the nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen ill-will, or for the abandoning of arisen ill-will.'

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of ill-will: learning the sign of loving-kindness, devotion to the meditation on loving-kindness, reflection on the ownership of one's kamma (kammassakatā), frequent reflection, good friendship (kalyāṇamittatā), and suitable talk (sappāyakathā). Ill-will is abandoned for one who learns loving-kindness by way of pervading the directions, whether specifically or non-specifically. It is also abandoned for one who develops loving-kindness by way of pervading, whether with limits or without limits.

'What can you do to this person by being angry? Can you destroy his virtue and so forth? Have you not come by your own kamma and will you not go by your own kamma? Being angry at another is like wanting to strike another after picking up glowing coals, a red-hot iron rod, or excrement. What can he do to you by being angry? Can he destroy your virtue and so forth? He has come by his own kamma and will go by his own kamma. Like a gift not accepted, or like a handful of dust thrown against the wind, his anger will fall back upon his own head.' Thus, ill-will is abandoned for one who reflects on the ownership of kamma of oneself and others, for one who stands in reflection having considered the ownership of kamma of both, for one who associates with good friends who delight in the meditation on loving-kindness like the Elder Assagutta, and for one who engages in suitable talk related to loving-kindness while standing, sitting, etc. Therefore, I said: 'Six things lead to the abandoning of ill-will.' Ill-will abandoned by these six things never arises again through the path of non-returning (anāgāmi-magga).

Sloth and torpor (thina-middha) arise through unwise attention to discontent (arati) and so forth. Discontent (arati) means boredom. Laziness (tandī) means physical lethargy. Stretching (vijambhitā) means bending the body in various ways. Food-drowsiness (bhattasammada) means the mental discomfort (confusion) caused by food. Sluggishness of mind (cetaso līnattatta) is the state of a shrinking mind. For one who frequently applies unwise attention to these things such as discontent, sloth and torpor arise. Thus the Blessed One said: 'Bhikkhus, there is discontent, laziness, stretching, food-drowsiness, sluggishness of mind...'
370:
"Six things lead to the abandonment of ill-will" (as has been said). One understands that ill-will abandoned by these six things does not arise again in the future through the Path of Non-Returning (anāgāmi-magga).

Sloth and torpor (thīna-middha) arise due to unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) to discontent (arati) and so forth. Discontent (arati) means boredom. Laziness (tandī) means physical sluggishness. Stretching (vijambhitā) means stretching the body or bending it in various ways. Food-drowsiness (bhattasammada) means the mental malaise (confusion) that occurs after eating. Sluggishness of mind (cetaso līnattam) means the state of the mind shrinking back. For one who frequently applies unwise attention to these things like discontent, sloth and torpor arise. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there are discontent, laziness, stretching, food-drowsiness, and sluggishness of mind. Frequently applying unwise attention to them is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sloth and torpor, or for the growth and increase of arisen sloth and torpor."

Sloth and torpor can be abandoned through wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) to the element of initial effort (ārambha-dhātu) and so forth. The element of initial effort is the first exertion of energy. The element of exertion (nikkama-dhātu) is stronger than the initial effort because it emerges from laziness. The element of progressive endeavor (parakkama-dhātu) is even stronger than the element of exertion because it overcomes successive stages. For one who frequently applies wise attention to these three types of energy, sloth and torpor are abandoned. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there are the element of initial effort, the element of exertion, and the element of progressive endeavor. Frequently applying wise attention to them is the nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen sloth and torpor, or for the abandonment of arisen sloth and torpor."

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandonment of sloth and torpor: reflecting on the cause (of sloth and torpor) in overeating, changing postures, attending to the perception of light (āloka-saññā), living in the open air, having good friends, and suitable talk. For one who eats excessively—like the eating styles of Brahmins known as āharahatthaka, tatravaṭṭaka, alaṃsāṭaka, kākamāsaka, and bhuttavamitaka—and then sits in a place for the night or day to practice the Dhamma of a recluse, sloth and torpor come upon him like a great elephant. However, for a monk who leaves space for four or five mouthfuls, drinks water, and eats only enough to sustain himself, that sloth and torpor do not occur. Thus, for one who reflects on the cause in overeating, sloth and torpor are abandoned. For one who changes to another posture when sloth and torpor descend in a particular posture, or for one who attends to the light of the moon, a lamp, or a torch at night, or the light of the sun during the day...
371:
...for one who lives in the open air, or for one who associates with good friends who have abandoned sloth and torpor, such as the Venerable Mahākassapa Thera, sloth and torpor are abandoned. It is also abandoned through suitable talk related to the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) while standing, sitting, and so forth. Therefore, it is said: "Six things lead to the abandonment of sloth and torpor." One understands that sloth and torpor abandoned by these six things do not arise again in the future through the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga).

Restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca) arise due to unwise attention to the unpeacefulness of mind. Unpeacefulness means the state of being unpeaceful, which in essence is restlessness and remorse itself. For one who frequently applies unwise attention to that unpeacefulness, restlessness and remorse arise. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there is unpeacefulness of mind. Frequently applying unwise attention to it is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen restlessness and remorse, or for the growth and increase of arisen restlessness and remorse."

Restlessness and remorse can be abandoned through wise attention to the peace of mind known as concentration (samādhi). Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there is peace of mind. Frequently applying wise attention to it is the nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen restlessness and remorse, or for the abandonment of arisen restlessness and remorse."

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandonment of restlessness and remorse: great learning (bāhussacca), inquiry, understanding the nature of Vinaya, associating with elders, having good friends, and suitable talk. Through great learning, for one who learns one, two, three, four, or all five Nikāyas in terms of both the text (Pāli) and the meaning, restlessness and remorse are abandoned. Also for one who frequently inquires about what is allowable and what is not (kappiya-akappiya), for one who understands the nature of Vinaya through mastery of the Vinaya rules, for one who approaches senior elder monks, and for one who associates with good friends who are experts in Vinaya like the Venerable Upāli Thera, restlessness and remorse are abandoned. It is also abandoned through suitable talk related to what is allowable and what is not while standing, sitting, and so forth. Therefore, it is said: "Six things lead to the abandonment of restlessness and remorse." One understands that among the restlessness and remorse abandoned by these six things, restlessness (uddhacca) does not arise again in the future through the Path of Arahantship, and remorse (kukkucca) does not arise again through the Path of Non-Returning.

Doubt (vicikicchā) arises due to unwise attention to things that are grounds for doubt. Things that are grounds for doubt are previous instances of doubt, as they are the cause for doubt to arise again and again. For one who frequently applies unwise attention to that doubt, doubt arises. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there are things that are grounds for doubt. Frequently applying unwise attention to them is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen doubt, or for the growth and increase of arisen doubt." Doubt can be abandoned through wise attention to states such as wholesome states. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there are wholesome and unwholesome states; there are blameworthy and blameless states; there are states to be cultivated and states not to be cultivated; there are low and exalted states; there are states with dark and bright sides. In those states..."
372: Because it is the cause of doubt, it is doubt itself. Doubt arises in one who frequently applies unwise attention to those things that are the basis for doubt. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there are things that are the basis for doubt; frequently applying unwise attention to them is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen doubt, and for the growth and expansion of arisen doubt." By wise attention to wholesome and other states, the abandonment of that doubt occurs. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there are wholesome and unwholesome states, blameworthy and blameless states, states to be cultivated and not to be cultivated, low and exalted states, dark and bright states. Frequently applying wise attention to them is the nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen doubt, and for the abandonment of arisen doubt." Furthermore, six things lead to the abandonment of doubt: great learning, inquiry, skill in the Vinaya, abundance of resolution (faith), good friendship, and suitable talk. For through great learning, doubt is abandoned in one who learns even one... or all five Nikāyas, both in text and in meaning. It is also abandoned in one who is frequent in inquiry concerning the Three Jewels, in one who has achieved mastery in the Vinaya, in one who has an abundance of resolution consisting of faith that descends into the Three Jewels, and in one who associates with good friends like the Elder Vakkali, who was foremost in faith. Doubt is also abandoned by suitable talk concerning the virtues of the Three Jewels while standing, sitting, etc. Therefore, it is said: "Six things lead to the abandonment of doubt." One understands that for doubt abandoned by these six things, there is no future arising by means of the Path of Stream-entry. "Thus, internally..." as stated, by thus discerning the five hindrances, one dwells contemplating the Dhamma in one's own dhammas, or in the dhammas of another, or at times in one's own and at times in another's dhammas. Here, the rise and fall should be extracted according to the method already stated for the five hindrances by way of unwise attention and wise attention regarding the sign of the beautiful, the sign of the foul, and so on. From here on, the method is just as stated. Indeed, in this Section on Hindrances...
373:
Mindfulness that discerns the hindrances is called the Truth of Suffering. Having made such a connection, the way of exit for the bhikkhu who discerns the hindrances should be understood. The rest is just as described.

## The Section on Hindrances is finished.

## Explanation of the Section on Aggregates

Having thus analyzed the contemplation of Dhamma by way of the five hindrances, he now says "Again, monks..." and so on, to analyze it by way of the five aggregates. In that passage, "in the five aggregates of clinging" (pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu) means the aggregates of clinging, which are the groups of states or masses of states that serve as the basis for clinging. This is the summary here. For a detailed account, the "Discussion on the Aggregates" (Khandhakathā) has been stated in the Visuddhimagga.

"Thus is form" means one understands form according to its nature, thinking: "This is form, this much is form, there is no form beyond this (primary and derived matter)." The same method applies to feeling and the others. This is the summary here; in detail, however, form and the others have been stated in the "Discussion on the Aggregates" of the Visuddhimagga itself. "Thus is the origin of form" means one understands the origin of form in five ways by way of the origin of ignorance and so on. "Thus is the passing away of form" means one understands the passing away of form in five ways by way of the cessation of ignorance and so on. The same method applies to feeling and the others. This is the summary here; the detail has been stated in the "Discussion on the Knowledge of Rise and Fall" (Udayabbayañāṇakathā) of the Visuddhimagga.
