"Thus, internally..." means by thus discerning the five aggregates, one dwells contemplating the Dhamma in one's own dhammas, or in the dhammas of another, or at times in one's own and at times in another's dhammas. In this Section on Aggregates, the rise and fall should be extracted by way of the fifty characteristics stated for the five aggregates, such as "With the origin of ignorance, there is the origin of form." From this point on, the method is just as stated. Indeed, in this Section on Aggregates, mindfulness that discerns the aggregates is called the Truth of Suffering. Having made such a connection, the way of exit for the bhikkhu who discerns the aggregates should be understood. The rest is just as described.

## The Section on Aggregates is finished.
374:
## Commentary on the Section on Sense Bases

Having thus analyzed the contemplation of phenomena (dhammānupassanā) by way of the five aggregates, [the Teacher] now says "And again, monks..." etc., to analyze it by way of the sense bases (āyatana). In that passage, "in the six internal and external sense bases" means in these six internal sense bases: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; and in these six external sense bases: forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects. "He knows the eye" means he knows the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) analytically by way of its characteristic and function as they really are. "He knows forms" means he knows the external matter produced by the four causes analytically by way of its characteristic and function as they really are. "And he knows the fetter that arises dependent on both" means he knows how the ten types of fetters—namely, the fetter of sensual desire (kāmarāga-saṃyojana), the fetter of aversion (paṭigha-saṃyojana), the fetter of conceit (māna-saṃyojana), the fetter of wrong view (diṭṭhi-saṃyojana), the fetter of doubt (vicikicchā-saṃyojana), the fetter of adherence to rites and rituals (sīlabbata-parāmāsa-saṃyojana), the fetter of desire for existence (bhavarāga-saṃyojana), the fetter of envy (issā-saṃyojana), the fetter of stinginess (macchariya-saṃyojana), and the fetter of ignorance (avijjā-saṃyojana)—arise dependent on both the eye-sensitivity and forms; and he knows those fetters analytically by way of their characteristics and functions as they really are.

How does that fetter arise? Firstly, for one who enjoys and delights in an agreeable object (iṭṭhārammaṇa) that has come into range at the eye-door by way of sensual gratification, the fetter of sensual desire arises. For one who is angry at a disagreeable object (aniṭṭhārammaṇa), the fetter of aversion arises. For one who thinks, "Who else but me is able to make this object clear?", the fetter of conceit arises. For one who takes it as, "This form-object is permanent and stable," the fetter of wrong view arises. For one who doubts, "Is this form-object a being, or does it belong to a being?", the fetter of doubt arises. For one who longs for existence, thinking, "May we easily obtain this form-object in a happy state of existence!", the fetter of desire for existence arises. For one who undertakes [a practice] thinking, "In the future too, such a form-object can be obtained by undertaking the bovine practice (sīlabbata)," the fetter of adherence to rites and rituals arises. For one who is envious, thinking, "Oh, may others not obtain that form-object!", the fetter of envy arises. For one who is stingy regarding the form-object obtained by oneself, the fetter of stinginess arises. By way of the unknowing (moha) that is co-nascent with all fetters, the fetter of ignorance arises.

"[He knows] how the unarisen [fetter arises]" means he knows analytically the cause for the arising of those ten types of fetters which have not yet arisen due to lack of habitual recurrence. "[He knows] how the arisen [fetter is abandoned]" means he knows analytically the cause for the abandonment of those ten types of fetters which have arisen either because they have not yet been abandoned or due to habitual recurrence. "[He knows] how the abandoned [fetter does not arise again]" means he knows analytically the cause—namely, the Path of Stream-entry—by which those ten types of fetters, though already abandoned by way of abandonment of factors (tadaṅga-pahāna) or abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna), will not arise again in the future.
375:
...he knows the cause by which the non-arising in the future of the fetter occurs. By what cause does the non-arising in the future of that fetter occur? Firstly, the non-arising in the future of the fivefold fetters consisting of wrong view, doubt, adherence to rites and rituals, envy, and stinginess occurs through the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). The non-arising of the coarse pair of the fetter of sensual desire and the fetter of aversion occurs through the Path of Once-returning (sakadāgāmi-magga); the subtle pair through the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmi-magga). The non-arising in the future of the triad of fetters—conceit, desire for existence, and ignorance—occurs through the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga). In the passages "He knows the ear and he knows sounds," etc., the method is the same. Furthermore, the discussion on the sense bases here should be understood in detail according to the method stated in the "Description of the Sense Bases" (Āyatana-niddesa) of the Visuddhimagga.

"Thus internally..." means that by grasping the internal sense bases, he dwells contemplating phenomena in his own phenomena; or by grasping the external sense bases, in the phenomena of others; or at one time in his own and at another time in the phenomena of others. Regarding the origin and passing away (samudaya-vaya) here, they should be extracted according to the method stated: for the sense base of forms (rūpāyatana) in the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) as "with the arising of ignorance, the eye arises"; for the sense base of mind (manāyatana) among the immaterial sense bases in the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha); and for the sense base of mental objects (dhammāyatana) in the remaining aggregates. Supramundane phenomena (lokuttara-dhamma) should not be taken. From this point onwards, the method is as already stated. In fact, in this section on sense bases, it should be understood that the mindfulness that grasps the sense bases is the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca); thus, by making this connection, the gateway to liberation for the monk who grasps the sense bases should be known. The rest is just as previously described.

## The Section on Sense Bases is Finished.

## Commentary on the Section on the Factors of Enlightenment

Having thus analyzed the contemplation of phenomena by way of the six internal and external sense bases, [the Teacher] now says "And again, monks..." etc., to analyze it by way of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). In that section, "in the factors of enlightenment" (bojjhaṅgesu) means in the factors of a being who is awakening [to the Four Noble Truths]. "Existing" (santaṃ) means clearly present in one's own continuity by way of attainment. "The enlightenment factor of mindfulness" (sati-sambojjhaṅga) means the enlightenment factor known as mindfulness. Here, the meditator (yogāvacara) is called "enlightenment" (sambodhi) because he understands well from the time he begins insight (vipassanā). Alternatively, the harmony of the seven factors beginning with mindfulness, by which he awakens from the sleep of defilements or penetrates the Truths, is called "enlightenment" (sambodhi). Because it is a factor of that well-understanding meditator, or a factor of that harmony of factors, it is called an "enlightenment factor" (bojjhaṅga). Therefore, it is said: "the enlightenment factor known as mindfulness." In the case of the remaining enlightenment factors, the meaning of the terms should be understood in this same way.
376:
"Asanti" means non-existence due to non-attainment. In the passages beginning with "Yathā ca anuppannassa," first regarding the enlightenment factor of mindfulness: "Bhikkhus, there are states that are the basis for the enlightenment factor of mindfulness; frequently applying wise attention to them is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of mindfulness, or for the growth, expansion, and fulfillment by development of the arisen enlightenment factor of mindfulness." In that passage, mindfulness itself is the basis for the enlightenment factor of mindfulness. Wise attention has the characteristics already mentioned. For one who frequently applies wise attention to those bases, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness arises.

Furthermore, four things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness: mindfulness and clear comprehension, avoiding persons of muddled mindfulness, associating with persons of established mindfulness, and inclination towards that enlightenment factor of mindfulness. Indeed, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness arises through mindfulness and clear comprehension in the seven instances such as moving forward; by avoiding persons of muddled mindfulness who are like crows dropping rice; by associating with persons of established mindfulness like the Elder Tissadatta and the Elder Abhaya; and by having a mind inclined towards establishing mindfulness in postures such as standing and sitting. It should be understood that this enlightenment factor of mindfulness, arisen through these four causes, reaches fulfillment of development through the Path of Arahantship.

Regarding the enlightenment factor of investigation of states: "Bhikkhus, there are wholesome and unwholesome states... states that have a dark side and a bright side; frequently applying wise attention to them is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of investigation of states, or for the growth, expansion, and fulfillment by development of the arisen enlightenment factor of investigation of states."

Furthermore, seven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of investigation of states: being inquisitive, cleansing the basis, balancing the faculties, avoiding unwise persons, associating with wise persons, reviewing the conduct of deep knowledge, and inclination towards that enlightenment factor of investigation of states. Among these, "being inquisitive" means frequent discussion and inquiry based on the meaning of the aggregates, elements, bases, faculties, powers, enlightenment factors, path factors, jhāna factors, serenity, and insight. "Cleansing the basis" means making the internal and external bases clean. Indeed, when the hair, nails, and body hair of that practitioner are long, or when the body is full of defects such as phlegm and smeared with sweat and dirt, then the internal basis is unclean and impure. When the robe is worn out...
377:
...soiled and foul-smelling, or the dwelling is messy, then the external basis is unclean and impure. Therefore, the internal basis should be made clean by having the hair etc. cut, by making the body light through emetics and purgatives etc., and by anointing and bathing. The external basis should be made clean by sewing, washing, dyeing, and bordering [the robes] etc.

Truly, when these internal and external bases are unclean, the knowledge in the arising consciousness and mental factors is also unclean and impure, like the light of a lamp flame depending on an impure lamp-bowl, wick, and oil. But when the internal and external bases are clean, the knowledge in the arising consciousness and mental factors is also clean and pure, like the light of a lamp flame depending on a pure lamp-bowl, wick, and oil. Therefore, it is said: "Cleansing the basis leads to the arising of the enlightenment factor of investigation of states."

"Balancing the faculties" means making the faculties such as faith etc. equal to one another. For if one's faculty of faith is strong and the other faculties are weak, then the faculty of energy cannot perform the function of exertion, the faculty of mindfulness cannot perform the function of establishing, the faculty of concentration cannot perform the function of non-distraction, and the faculty of wisdom cannot perform the function of seeing. Therefore, that faculty of faith should be diminished either by reflecting on the nature of things or by not attending to it in the way that made it strong. The story of the Elder Vakkali is an illustration here. If the faculty of energy is strong, then the faculty of faith cannot perform the function of decision-making, and the other faculties cannot perform their respective functions. Therefore, that energy should be diminished by developing tranquility etc. There, the story of the Elder Soṇa should be shown. Thus, it should be understood that in the case of the other faculties as well, when one is excessively strong, the others are incapable of their functions.

In particular, among these faculties, the equality of faith and wisdom, and of concentration and energy, is praised. For one with strong faith but weak wisdom is blindly devoted and gains confidence in what is not a proper basis. One with strong wisdom but weak faith falls into the side of cunning; like a disease caused by medicine, he is difficult to cure. Thinking excessively that "merit occurs merely by the arising of a thought," he does not perform acts of giving etc. and is liable to be reborn in hell. Only through the equality of both does one have confidence in the Triple Gem, which is the proper basis. One with strong concentration but weak energy is overcome by sloth because concentration belongs to the side of sloth. One with strong energy but weak concentration is overcome by agitation because energy belongs to the side of agitation. But when concentration is joined with energy, it cannot fall into sloth; when energy is joined with concentration, it cannot fall into agitation...
378:
(It is) not possible to fall (into sloth or restlessness). Therefore, those two (concentration and energy) should be balanced. For it is only through the balance of both that absorption (appanā) occurs.

Furthermore, for one practicing tranquillity (samatha) meditation, strong faith (saddhā) is appropriate. Only with such faith and conviction will one reach absorption. Between concentration and wisdom, however, for one practicing samatha meditation, strong one-pointedness (ekaggatā) is appropriate. Only when one-pointedness is strong can that person reach absorption. For one practicing insight (vipassanā), strong wisdom (paññā) is appropriate. Only when wisdom is strong can that person reach the penetration of the three characteristics. Nevertheless, absorption also occurs through the balance of those two (concentration and wisdom). Mindfulness (sati), however, is required to be strong in all circumstances. For mindfulness protects the mind from falling into restlessness through the power of faith, energy, and wisdom, which belong to the side of restlessness; and from falling into sloth through the power of concentration, which belongs to the side of sloth. Therefore, that mindfulness is desired in all matters, just as salt is desired in all dishes, and just as a chief minister is desired in all royal affairs. Hence, the Blessed One said: “Mindfulness, I declare, is useful in all things. For what reason? The mind has mindfulness as its refuge, and mindfulness is manifested as protection; without mindfulness, there can be no uplifting or restraining (governing) of the mind.”

Avoiding unwise persons means keeping far away from foolish people who lack deep insight into the categories such as the aggregates (khandha). Associating with wise persons means associating with those endowed with the knowledge of arising and passing away (udayabbaya-ñāṇa), which grasps the fifty characteristics of balanced wisdom. Reflecting on the conduct of profound knowledge means reflecting on the distinctions of profound wisdom occurring in profound subjects such as the aggregates. Inclination towards that state means having a mind that is bent, sloped, and inclined towards the arising of the Enlightenment Factor of Investigation of States (dhamma-vicaya-sambojjhaṅga) while standing, sitting, etc. One understands that the dhamma-vicaya-sambojjhaṅga thus arisen reaches the fulfillment of development through the Path of Arahantship.

Regarding the Enlightenment Factor of Energy (vīriya-sambojjhaṅga): “Monks, there is the element of inception (ārambha-dhātu), the element of exertion (nikkama-dhātu), and the element of progressive endeavor (parakkama-dhātu). Frequent wise attention to these elements of energy leads to the arising of the unarisen vīriya-sambojjhaṅga, or to the further growth, expansion, and fulfillment of the development of the arisen vīriya-sambojjhaṅga.” Thus, its arising is known.

Furthermore, eleven things lead to the arising of the vīriya-sambojjhaṅga: reflecting on the fear of woeful states, seeing the benefits of energy, reflecting on the path to be traveled (to Nibbāna), honoring the alms food, reflecting on the greatness of the inheritance, reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher (the Buddha), reflecting on the greatness of one's birth, reflecting on the greatness of fellow practitioners, avoiding lazy persons, associating with energetic persons, and having a mind inclined towards that energy.
379:
Among those (eleven factors), in the hells, from the time of being tortured by the fivefold binding onwards while experiencing great suffering; in the animal realm, when being caught by nets, traps, etc.; when being driven and pierced by goads and thorns while pulling a cart; in the realm of hungry ghosts (peta), when being oppressed by hunger and thirst for many thousands of years or even for the interval between two Buddhas; among the Kālakañjika Asuras, when experiencing suffering due to wind and heat with a body sixty or eighty cubits in height consisting only of skin and bones—at such times, it is not possible to arouse the Enlightenment Factor of Energy (vīriya-sambojjhaṅga). “Monk... this present time alone is the time for you to make an effort.” Thus, for one who reflects on the fear of woeful states, the vīriya-sambojjhaṅga arises.

A lazy person cannot attain the nine supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma); only one with aroused energy can attain them. “This is the benefit of energy.” Thus, for one who sees the benefit, the vīriya-sambojjhaṅga arises. The path traveled by all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Great Disciples must be traveled; that path cannot be traveled by a lazy person. Thus, for one who reflects on the path to be traveled, the vīriya-sambojjhaṅga arises. These people who support you with alms food and so on are not your relatives, nor your slaves or servants; nor do they give these excellent robes and so on intending to live depending on you. Rather, they give expecting great fruit from their own meritorious deeds. Even the Teacher (the Buddha) did not allow these requisites for you with the intention: “Let this monk live happily, becoming stout in body by using these four requisites.” On the contrary, he allowed them with the intention: “Let this monk, using these requisites, perform the recluse’s duties and be liberated from the suffering of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa-dukkha).” This being so, if you now live lazily, you do not honor that alms food. Only a monk with aroused energy is said to honor the alms food. Thus, for one who reflects on honoring the alms food, like Elder Ayya-Mitta, the vīriya-sambojjhaṅga arises.

To elaborate, the Elder lived in a cave named Kassaka. In his alms-resort village, a great laywoman (upāsikā) looked after the Elder, treating him like a son. One day, as she was about to go to the forest, she said to her daughter: “Dear daughter... in this place is old rice, here is ghee, here is milk, and here is molasses. When your brother, Elder Ayya-Mitta, arrives, cook the meal and offer it to him along with the milk, ghee, and molasses; you should eat too. As for me, I ate yesterday’s stale rice with sour gruel.” When the daughter asked, “Mother, what will you eat for lunch?” she replied, “Daughter, just throw in some leaves and cook a sour rice-gruel with broken rice grains.”
380:
The Elder, while putting on his robe and taking out his alms-bowl (from its bag), heard that (great laywoman's) voice and admonished himself thus: "The great laywoman eats stale rice with sour gruel; in the day, she will eat sour congee with leaves. For your sake, however, she gives instructions (to cook) old rice and so on. Depending on you, this great laywoman does not long for fields, houses, food, or clothing; rather, she gives while aspiring for the three types of prosperity. Will you be able to give those prosperities to this great laywoman, or will you not?" (Thus he questioned and admonished himself). "You, who are possessed of lust, hatred, and delusion, are not worthy of receiving this alms-food," he reflected. He put the bowl back into the bag, unfastened the button, and turning back, he went only to the Kassaka Cave. Placing the bowl under the couch and the robe on the robe-rack, he sat down, having resolved his energy: "I shall not go out without attaining Arahantship."

That monk, who had lived heedfully for a long time, developed insight and attained Arahantship even before the mealtime in the morning. Becoming a great Arahant whose taints were exhausted, like a blooming lotus, he sat smiling. The deity dwelling in the tree at the cave entrance uttered this inspired exclamation:

"Homage to you, O noble man! Homage to you, O supreme man!
To you whose taints are exhausted, you are worthy of offerings, dear sir."

After uttering this exclamation, the deity said, "Venerable sir, by offering alms to Arahants like you who enter for alms, these elderly women will be released from suffering." The Elder rose, opened the door, and looking at the time, realized, "It is still early." Taking his bowl and robes, he entered the village.

The young girl, having prepared the meal, sat looking at the door, thinking, "Now my brother will come, now he will come." When the Elder reached the door of the house, she took the bowl, filled it with milk-rice mixed with ghee and molasses, and offered it into his hands. The Elder said, "May you be happy," and after performing the appreciation (anumodanā), he departed. The girl also stood watching the Elder. Indeed, at that time, the Elder's complexion was exceedingly pure, his faculties were especially clear, and his face was exceedingly radiant, like a ripe palm fruit fallen from its stalk.

The great laywoman returned from the forest and asked, "Dear daughter, did your brother come?" The girl told her everything that had happened. The laywoman (thought, "Today my son will become a monk / has become a true monk")...
381:
Knowing, "Today my son's task of monkhood has reached its pinnacle," she said, "Dear daughter, your brother delights greatly in the Buddha's Dispensation; he is not dissatisfied."

The inheritance of the Teacher, called the seven types of Noble Wealth, is indeed very great. A lazy person cannot receive that inheritance. Truly, just as parents cast out a son who behaves wrongly, saying "This is not our son," and he does not receive the inheritance when they pass away, so too a lazy person cannot receive this inheritance of Noble Wealth; only one with aroused energy can receive it. Thus, the Enlightenment Factor of Energy (viriya-sambojjhaṅga) also arises through reflecting on the greatness of the inheritance.

Your Teacher, the Buddha, is truly great. At the time of your Teacher's conception in his mother's womb, his renunciation, his enlightenment upon realizing the Four Noble Truths, his preaching of the Dhammacakka, his performance of the Twin Miracle, his descent from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, his relinquishing of the life-force, and his Parinibbāna, the ten-thousandfold world system shook. Is it proper for you to be lazy while having ordained in the Dispensation of such a Teacher? Thus, the Enlightenment Factor of Energy also arises through reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher.

By birth also, you are not of low birth now. You are born in the Okkāka royal lineage, descended from the unbroken line of King Mahāsammata. You are the grandson of King Suddhodana and Queen Mahāmāyā, and the younger brother of Rāhula. It is not proper for a son of the Conqueror (Jinaputta) like you to live lazily. Thus, the Enlightenment Factor of Energy also arises through reflecting on the greatness of birth.

Venerable Sāriputta, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, and the eighty Great Disciples realized the supramundane Dhamma only through energy and effort. Will you follow the path of these fellow practitioners, or will you not? Thus, the Enlightenment Factor of Energy also arises through reflecting on the greatness of fellow practitioners.

The Enlightenment Factor of Energy also arises by avoiding lazy persons who have abandoned physical and mental effort and are like pythons lying with full bellies; by associating with persons of aroused energy whose minds are directed towards Nibbāna; and by having a mind that is inclined, leaned, and sloped towards arousing energy in postures such as standing and sitting. It is known that this arisen Enlightenment Factor of Energy reaches the fulfillment of development through the Path of Arahantship.

Regarding the Enlightenment Factor of Joy (pīti-sambojjhaṅga): "Bhikkhus, there are things that are the basis for the Enlightenment Factor of Joy. Frequently applying wise attention to them is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen Enlightenment Factor of Joy, and for the growth, increase, and fulfillment by development of the arisen Enlightenment Factor of Joy." Thus (one knows) the arising of the Enlightenment Factor of Joy.
382: It is so. Among those states, joy (pīti) itself is the state that is the basis for the enlightenment factor of joy. Wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) directed towards it is the attention that produces it. Furthermore, eleven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of joy: recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati), recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, recollection of deities, recollection of peace, avoiding coarse persons, associating with refined persons, reflecting on inspiring discourses, and inclination towards that enlightenment factor of joy. Indeed, for one who repeatedly recollects the qualities of the Buddha, the enlightenment factor of joy arises, pervading the entire body with sublime mind-produced matter caused by joy, reaching as far as access concentration (upacāra). It also arises for one who repeatedly recollects the qualities of the Dhamma and the Saṅgha; for one who reflects on the fourfold purification of virtue (catu-pārisuddhi-sīla) kept unbroken for a long time; for laypeople who reflect on the ten precepts or the five precepts; for one who, having given fine food to fellow practitioners (sabrahmacārīs) during times of fear such as famine, reflects on their own generosity, thinking, 'We have given such a gift'; for laypeople who reflect on gifts given to the virtuous at such times; for one who reflects on the existence within themselves of qualities such as faith through which deities attained their divine state; for one who reflects on the non-arising of defilements, thinking, 'The defilements suppressed by attainment (samāpatti) have not occurred for sixty or seventy years'; for one who avoids coarse persons who show a lack of reverence when visiting shrines, Bodhi trees, or elders—persons who are coarse like dust on a donkey's back because they lack the 'sap' of devotion toward the Buddha and others; for one who associates with refined persons who have much devotion toward the Buddha and others and who possess a gentle mind; for one who reflects on inspiring discourses that illustrate the qualities of the Triple Gem; and for one who has a mind inclined, leaning, and slanting toward producing joy while standing, sitting, and so forth. He understands that this enlightenment factor of joy, having thus arisen, reaches fulfillment through development by the Path of Arahantship. Regarding the enlightenment factor of tranquility: 'Monks, there is tranquility of the body (kāya-passaddhi) and tranquility of the mind (citta-passaddhi). Frequently applying wise attention to them is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of tranquility, or for the increase, expansion, and fulfillment through development of the arisen enlightenment factor of tranquility.' Thus is its arising. Furthermore, seven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of tranquility: using fine food, using a comfortable climate, using a comfortable posture, balanced application (majjhatta-payogatā), avoiding restless persons, associating with tranquil persons, and inclination towards that enlightenment factor of tranquility. Indeed, for one who eats fine, smooth, and suitable food; for one who, among cold and hot climates and postures such as standing, uses a suitable climate and posture...
383: ...for one who uses a suitable climate and posture, the enlightenment factor of tranquility arises. However, this is not said with reference to a person of the nature of a Great Being (mahāpurisajātika) who is able to endure all climates and postures. It refers only to a person who distinguishes between suitable and unsuitable climates and postures. For such a person, the enlightenment factor of tranquility arises when they avoid unsuitable climates and postures and use suitable ones. Balanced application (majjhatta-payogatā) is said to be the reflection on the ownership of one's own and others' kamma (kammassakatā). Through this balanced application, the enlightenment factor of tranquility arises. It also arises by avoiding restless persons who wander about harassing others with clods of earth, sticks, and so forth; by associating with tranquil persons who have restrained feet and hands; and by having a mind inclined, leaning, and slanting toward producing tranquility while standing, sitting, and so forth. He understands that this enlightenment factor of tranquility, having thus arisen, reaches fulfillment through development by the Path of Arahantship. Regarding the enlightenment factor of concentration: 'Monks, there is the sign of serenity (samatha-nimitta) and the sign of non-distraction (abyagga-nimitta). Frequently applying wise attention to them is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of concentration, or for the increase, expansion, and fulfillment through development of the arisen enlightenment factor of concentration.' Thus is its arising described. In that statement, serenity itself is the sign of serenity. It is also called the sign of non-distraction in the sense of non-wavering. Furthermore, eleven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of concentration: making the physical basis clean, balancing the faculties, skill in the sign, uplifting the mind at the proper time, restraining the mind at the proper time, gladdening the mind at the proper time, looking on with equanimity at the proper time, avoiding unconcentrated persons, associating with concentrated persons, reflecting on the jhanas and liberations (vimokkha), and inclination towards that concentration. Among these, making the physical basis clean and balancing the faculties should be understood in the manner already stated. Skill in the sign means skill in grasping the kasina sign (kasiṇa-nimitta). Uplifting the mind at the proper time means uplifting the mind by giving rise to the enlightenment factors of investigation of states (dhammavicaya), energy (viriya), and joy (pīti) at a time when the mind is slack due to overly lax energy and so forth. Restraining the mind at the proper time means restraining the mind by giving rise to the enlightenment factors of tranquility (passaddhi), concentration (samādhi), and equanimity (upekkhā) at a time when the mind is restless due to overly exerted energy and so forth. Gladdening the mind at the proper time means gladdening the mind by reflecting on the eight grounds for urgency (saṃvega-vatthu) at a time when the mind is listless due to weak application of wisdom or due to not attaining the bliss of peace...
384:
He causes [the mind] to be stirred. The eight grounds for urgency (saṃvega-vatthu) are: birth (jāti), aging (jarā), sickness (vyādhi), and death (maraṇa)—these four; the suffering of the lower realms (apāya-dukkha) as the fifth; the suffering rooted in the round of rebirths in the past; the suffering rooted in the round of rebirths in the future; and the suffering rooted in the search for nutriment in the present. He also inspires confidence by recollecting the virtues of the Triple Gem. This is called "gladdening at the proper time" (samaye sampahamsanatā).

Equanimity at the proper time (samaye ajjhupekkhanatā) means the occasion when, by means of right practice, the mind is not sluggish, not restless, and not infatuated, but proceeds evenly on the object, having entered the path of serenity (samatha). At that time, he does not concern himself with encouraging, restraining, or gladdening that mind, just as a charioteer does not concern himself with horses that are running evenly. This is called "samaye ajjhupekkhanatā." Avoiding persons who are not concentrated means keeping far away from persons who have not attained access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) or absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) and whose minds are distracted. Cultivating concentrated persons means associating with, frequenting, and attending to persons whose minds are concentrated through access or absorption concentration. Inclining towards that concentration means having a mind that is bent, sloped, and inclined towards the production of concentration while standing, sitting, etc. For one practicing in this way, this enlightenment factor of concentration (samādhi-sambojjhaṅga) arises. He understands that this arisen enlightenment factor of concentration reaches fulfillment in development through the path of Arahatship (arahattamagga).

Regarding the enlightenment factor of equanimity (upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga): "Bhikkhus, there are things that are the basis for the enlightenment factor of equanimity; frequently applying wise attention to them is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of equanimity, or for the growth, increase, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of equanimity." Thus is the manner of its arising stated. Therein, equanimity itself is called the things that are the basis for the enlightenment factor of equanimity.

Furthermore, five things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of equanimity: equanimity towards beings (satta-majjhattatā), equanimity towards formations (saṅkhāra-majjhattatā), avoiding persons who cherish beings and formations, cultivating persons who are equanimous towards beings and formations, and inclining towards that equanimity. Among these five, one arouses equanimity towards beings in two ways: by reflecting on ownership of kamma (kammasakatā), "You have come by your own kamma and will depart by your own kamma; this person too has come by his own kamma and will depart by his own kamma; whom are you cherishing?"; and by reflecting on the absence of a being (nissatta), "In the ultimate sense, there is no being; whom then are you cherishing?" One arouses equanimity towards formations in two ways: by reflecting on masterlessness (assāmika-bhāva), "This robe will gradually reach a state of discolouration and wear, becoming a foot-wiping rag, and will eventually be fit to be discarded with the tip of a stick; if this robe...
385:
...had a master who owned it, he would not allow it to perish in this way"; and by reflecting on its temporary nature (tāvakālika-bhāva), "This robe does not last long; it is only temporary." (Thus he arouses equanimity towards formations). As with the robe, so should it be applied to the bowl and so forth.

In the phrase "avoiding persons who cherish beings and formations" (satta-saṅkhāra-kelāyana-puggala-parivajjanatā), the decision is as follows: A person, whether a layperson or a monk, who cherishes his own sons and daughters, or his own pupils, fellow-preceptors, etc. He himself performs for them such tasks as shaving their hair, sewing, washing and dyeing their robes, and baking their bowls. If he does not see them even for a moment, he looks here and there like a frightened deer, asking, "Where is such-and-such a novice? Where is such-and-such a young monk?" Even when asked by another to "send such-and-such a novice for a moment" for the purpose of shaving hair, etc., he does not give him, saying, "We ourselves do not make him work; if you take him, you will tire him out." This person is called one who cherishes beings (satta-kelāyana).

One who cherishes robes, bowls, cups, walking sticks, etc., and does not allow even another's hand to touch them, and when asked for temporary use, says, "We ourselves cherish this so much that we do not use it; how can we give it to you?"—this person is called one who cherishes formations (saṅkhāra-kelāyana). One who is neutral and indifferent towards both these kinds of objects is called one who is equanimous towards beings and formations (satta-saṅkhāra-majjhatta). Thus, this enlightenment factor of equanimity (upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga) arises for one who avoids from afar such persons who cherish beings and formations, for one who associates with persons who are equanimous towards beings and formations, and for one who has a mind bent, sloped, and inclined towards the production of that enlightenment factor of equanimity while standing, sitting, etc. He understands that this arisen enlightenment factor of equanimity reaches fulfillment in development through the path of Arahatship (arahattamagga).

"Thus, internally..." means that he dwells contemplating dhammas in dhammas, having grasped either his own seven enlightenment factors, or those of another, or at times his own and at times another's. In this section on the enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga-pabba), arising and vanishing should be understood by way of occurrence and cessation. From here on, the method is exactly as previously stated. Specifically, in this section on the enlightenment factors, the mindfulness that grasps the enlightenment factors is the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca); thus, having made the connection, the way of exit [from the round] for the monk who grasps the enlightenment factors should be understood. The rest is the same as what was said before.

## The Section on the Factors of Enlightenment is Finished.
386:
## Commentary on the Section on the Four Noble Truths

Having thus analyzed the Satipaṭṭhāna of the Contemplation of Phenomena by way of the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), the Buddha now speaks the words beginning with "Puna caparaṃ" (And again) in order to analyze it by way of the Four Noble Truths. In that passage, "He understands as it really is: 'This is suffering'" means that, excluding craving (taṇhā), he understands the collection of phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence as "This is suffering" according to their nature of oppression, without distortion and in various ways. He understands the preceding craving, which is the producer and the root cause of that very suffering, as "This is the origin of suffering" according to its true nature. He understands Nibbāna, which is the non-occurrence of both the truth of suffering and the truth of the origin, as "This is the cessation of suffering" according to its nature of peace, without distortion. He understands the Noble Path (ariya magga), which fully knows the truth of suffering, abandons the truth of the origin, and realizes the truth of cessation, as "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering" according to its nature of escape, without distortion. The remaining discourse on the Noble Truths, excluding the word-by-word analysis (padabhājana) of birth (jāti) and so forth, has already been detailed in the Visuddhimagga.

## Commentary on the Exposition of the Truth of Suffering

In the word-by-word analysis, regarding the phrase "Monks, what is birth?", the meaning should be understood in all questions as: "Monks, there is that birth which is said to be 'Birth is also suffering'; what is that birth?" The phrase "of those various beings" is a comprehensive term for all beings because there is no specific designation such as "of beings with such and such a name." The phrase "in those various orders of beings" is also a comprehensive term for all groups of beings. The names "janana" and "jāti" are designations for the first arising of the aggregates (khandhas) together with the transformation known as arising (uppāda). The word "sañjāti" is a synonym for that same birth, adorned with a prefix. That same birth is called "okkanti" (descent) because of its nature of entering into the womb. It is called "abhinibbatti" (production) because of its nature of being produced, which is known as arising. Thus, these four are conventional descriptions (sammuti-kathā). However, the phrase "the manifestation of the aggregates" is an ultimate description (paramattha-kathā). In realms of one-constituent existence (ekavokāra-bhava) and so forth, there is only the manifestation of the aggregates, which are divided into one, four, or five; there is no manifestation of a "person." When those aggregates exist, it is merely a conventional expression to say "a person is manifest." "The acquisition of the sense bases" means that when the sense bases manifest, they are said to be acquired; it refers to the acquisition known as the manifestation of those sense bases.

"Jarā" (aging) is a description of the nature. "Jīraṇatā" (decay) is a description of the state or mode. The words beginning with "khaṇḍicca" (brokenness) are descriptions of the transformation. Indeed, in youth, the teeth are even and white. As those teeth age, they gradually undergo transformation in color and fall out here and there. Then, based on the fallen teeth and the remaining teeth, one is called "broken-toothed" (khaṇḍita). The state of being broken-toothed is called "khaṇḍicca." Hair and body hair that gradually become white are called "palita" (gray). Because that person has white hair, he is called "palita" (a gray-haired person). The state of being a gray-haired person is called "pālicca." Struck by the wind of aging...
387:
One who is broken-toothed is called "khaṇḍita." The state of those who are broken-toothed is called "khaṇḍicca." Hair and body hair that have gradually become white are called "palita." Because of the state of having white hair, one is called "palita" (a gray-haired person); the state of being a gray-haired person is called "pālicca." One who has wrinkles in the skin because of the state of having dried-up flesh and blood due to being struck by the wind of aging is called "valittaca" (wrinkled-skinned); the state of such a person is called "valittacatā." By this much, evident aging (pākaṭa-jarā), which becomes manifest through the demonstration of transformation in the teeth, hair, body hair, and skin, has been shown.

Indeed, just as the path taken by water, wind, or fire becomes evident through the destruction, total ruin, or burning of grass, trees, and so forth, yet that path is not the water and so forth itself; in the same way, the path taken by aging is evident through the brokenness of teeth and so forth, and can be perceived even by opening the eyes, yet the brokenness of teeth and so forth is not aging itself. For aging is not cognizable by eye-consciousness. However, because life (āyu) wanes for one who has reached aging, aging is called "the waning of life" (āyuno saṃhāni) by way of metonymy (phalūpacāra), attributing the effect to the cause. Because the faculties (indriya) such as the eye, which in youth were very clear and capable of easily grasping even subtle objects, become mature, disturbed, and unclear for one who has reached aging, being unable to grasp even gross objects, aging is also called "the maturation of the faculties" (indriyānaṃ paripāka) by way of metonymy.

In the exposition of death (maraṇaniddesa), "yaṃ" (which) is a neuter designation referring to death (maraṇa). The construction here is: "That death which is called 'cuti' (passing away) and is called 'cavanatā' (the state of passing away)." Among those, "cuti" is a description of the nature (sabhāva-niddesa). "Cavanatā" is a description of the state of the mode (ākāra-bhāva-niddesa). For one who has reached death, the aggregates break up, disappear, and go to invisibility; therefore, that death is called "breaking up" (bheda) and "disappearance" (antaradhāna). "Maccu-maraṇa" refers only to death as the end of life (maccu-maraṇa), not to momentary death (khaṇika-maraṇa). "Kālakiriyā" (making an end of time) means the act of dying. All these are merely conventional descriptions (sammuti-kathā). However, "the breaking up of the aggregates" (khandhānaṃ bhedo) is an ultimate description (paramattha-kathā). In realms of one-constituent existence and so forth, there is only the breaking up of the aggregates, which are divided into one, four, or five; there is no breaking up of a "person." When those aggregates break up, it is merely a conventional expression to say "the person has died."

"The laying down of the carcass" (kaḷevarassa nikkhepo) means the laying down of the physical body (attabhāva). For the physical body of one who has reached death falls like a useless log; therefore, that death is called the laying down of the carcass. The cutting off of the life-faculty (jīvitindriyassa upaccheda), however, is death in the ultimate sense in every aspect.
388:
This cessation of the life-faculty is also called conventional death (sammuti-maraṇa). This is because worldly people, based on the cessation of the life-faculty, say, "Tissa is dead, Phussa is dead."

"Byasanena" means by any kind of loss among the loss of relatives and so on. "Dukkhadhammena" means by causes of suffering such as killing, binding, and so on. "Phuṭṭhassa" means of one who is overwhelmed or oppressed. "Soka" is the sorrow characterized by grieving that arises in one who is oppressed by any of the losses of relatives or by killing, binding, and so on. "Socitattaṃ" is the state of sorrowing itself. Because this sorrow arises drying up [the person] within and drying up [the person] all around, it is called "inner sorrow" (antosoka) and "inner consuming sorrow" (antoparisoka).

Because one wails referring to "my daughter, my son," and so on, that sound of wailing is called "ādeva." Because one wails proclaiming various virtues and qualities, it is called "parideva." The next two terms are expressions that merely indicate the state of that lamentation.

"Kāyikaṃ" refers to what is based on the physical sensitivity of the body (kāyaprasāda). It is called "dukkha" because of the sense of being hard to bear. "Asātaṃ" means what is unpleasant. "Kāyasamphassajaṃ dukkhaṃ" is the suffering born of body-contact. "Asātaṃ vedayitaṃ" is an unpleasant feeling.

"Cetasikaṃ" refers to what is associated with the mind. The remaining terms are to be understood in the same way as explained for bodily pain.

"Āyāsa" is mental exhaustion reaching the state of sinking and despondency. Intense "āyāsa" is called "upāyāsa." The next two terms are descriptions showing the state of not being one's own or one's possession.

"Jātidhammānaṃ" refers to those whose nature is to undergo rebirth. "Icchā uppajjati" means craving (taṇhā) arises. "Aho vata" is a longing. "Na kho panetaṃ icchāya" means that this non-coming of birth cannot be attained by mere wish without the development of the Path (magga-bhāvanā). In the term "idampi," the word "pi" is spoken in consideration of not obtaining the non-coming of aging and so on, which will be mentioned later, even if one longs for it. "Yampicchaṃ" means not obtaining what one desires when wishing for something unobtainable; that wishing for an unobtainable object is suffering. This method should be understood everywhere.
389:
In the description of the aggregates (khandha-niddesa), the decision should be understood by the method already mentioned. Form is both form and an aggregate that is an object of clinging; therefore, it is called the form-clinging-aggregate (rūpupādānakkhandha). In all terms, the analysis (vigraha) should be made in this same way.

## Explanation of the Description of the Truth of the Origin

"Yāyaṃ taṇhā" refers to that craving. "Ponobbhavikā" means it has the nature of producing a new existence again. "Nandīရာဂသဟဂတာ" means it arises together with lust that delights. In terms of meaning, it means it has reached a state of oneness with delighting lust. "Tatratatrābhinandinī" means wherever an individual existence (attabhāva) arises, it delights in that very place. Or, among objects such as visible forms, it delights in those various forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects. "Seyyathidaṃ" is an indeclinable. It should be understood as "What is that craving?" "Kāma-taṇhā" is the craving for the five objects of sensual pleasure (vatthu-kāma). This is the name for lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Bhava-taṇhā" is craving for existence. This is a designation for the lust for fine-material and immaterial existence accompanied by the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi) arising through the power of longing for existence, and for the attachment to meditative absorption (jhāna). "Vibhava-taṇhā" is craving for the cessation of existence. This is a designation for lust accompanied by the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi).

Now, to show the basis of that craving in detail, he said "That [craving] indeed..." and so on. Among those words, "uppajjati" means it is born. "Nivisati" means it becomes established through repeated occurrence. "Yaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ" means whatever in the world is of a lovable nature and an agreeable nature.

In the passages starting with "The eye in the world," the decision should be understood thus: Beings in the world who are obsessed with the eye, etc., as "mine," being established in prosperity, following the taking of signs in mirrors, etc., regard their own eye—the fivefold clear sensitivity which is especially clear—as like a jeweled lion-window opened in a golden mansion. They regard the ear as like a silver tube or a symmetrical string. They regard the nose, which is called "high-nosed," as like a prepared ball of yellow orpiment. They regard the tongue as like a red woolen sheet, soft, smooth, and delighting in good tastes. They regard the body as like a sal-column or a golden archway. They regard the mind as noble and unlike the minds of others. They regard visible forms as like the color of golden kaṇikāra flowers, etc. They regard sounds as like the song of the intoxicated karavīka bird or the Indian cuckoo, or the sound of a jeweled flute softly blown. They regard the objects of smell, etc., born of the four causes which they have obtained, thinking, "Who else has such smells, etc., as these?" To those who regard them thus, those eyes, etc., become endearing and agreeable. Then, craving that has not yet arisen for those endearing and agreeable things like the eye, etc., arises.
390:
Craving that has not yet arisen arises, and craving that has already arisen remains by way of repeated occurrence. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "In the world, the eye is of a lovable nature, of an agreeable nature; here this craving, when arising, arises," and so forth. In that passage, "arising" (uppajjamānā) means: whenever it arises, it arises here in these lovable and agreeable objects. This method should be understood in all instances.

## Exposition of the Description of the Truth of Cessation

All the terms beginning with "the fading away and cessation without remainder" (asesavirāganirodho) are synonyms for Nibbāna. Indeed, depending on Nibbāna, craving fades away and ceases without remainder; therefore, Nibbāna is called "the fading away and cessation without remainder of that very craving." And depending on Nibbāna, craving is given up, relinquished, released, and not clung to; therefore, Nibbāna is called "giving up, relinquishment, freedom, and non-attachment."

Although Nibbāna is only one, its names are many by way of being the opposite of the names of all conditioned things (saṅkhata). They are as follows: fading away without remainder, cessation without remainder, giving up, relinquishment, freedom, non-attachment, the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion, the destruction of craving, non-arising, non-occurrence, the signless, the desireless, non-exertion, non-rebirth, non-reappearance, non-destination, the unborn, the unaging, the unailing, the deathless, the sorrowless, the lamentation-less, the despair-less, and the undefiled.

Now, in order to show the non-existence of craving in those very objects where its arising was previously shown—both for craving that has been cut off by the Path and for craving that has reached non-occurrence depending on Nibbāna—the Blessed One said: "That very [craving]..." and so forth. In this regard, there is a simile: just as a man, seeing a bitter gourd vine growing in a field, might search for the root starting from the tip and cut it; that bitter gourd vine would gradually wither and reach a state of disappearance. Then it would be said that the bitter gourd vine in that field has ceased and vanished. In the same way, craving in the eye and so forth should be understood like the bitter gourd vine in the field. That craving, having its root cut by the Noble Path, reaches non-occurrence depending on Nibbāna. Craving that has reached this state is no longer perceived in those objects, just like the bitter gourd vine in the field.

Furthermore, to use another simile: just as if thieves were taken from a forest and executed at the south gate of the city; from then on, it would be said that the thieves in the forest are dead or have been killed. In the same way, craving in the eye and so forth should be understood like the thieves in the forest. Because that craving has ceased depending on Nibbāna, like the thieves at the south gate, it is said to have ceased in Nibbāna. Craving that has ceased in this way is no longer perceived in those objects, just like the thieves in the forest. Therefore, showing the cessation of that craving in those very objects...
391:
Desiring to show the cessation of craving in things of a lovable and pleasant nature, the Buddha spoke the words: "In the world, the eye is of a lovable nature and a pleasant nature; here this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; here, when ceasing, it ceases," and so forth.

## Commentary on the Exposition of the Truth of the Path (Magga-sacca-niddesa-vaṇṇanā)

"Ayam eva" (This alone) is a restriction for the purpose of excluding any other path imagined by others. "Ariyo" (Noble) is so called because it is far from the defilements that are to be killed by each respective path, and because it makes one a Noble One.

By the words "Knowledge of suffering" (dukkhe ñāṇaṃ) and so forth, the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) of the Four Truths is shown. Among those Four Truths, the first two truths are called the Round (vaṭṭa), and the last two truths are called the Ending of the Round (vivaṭṭa). Among those truths, a monk has the application of the meditation subject in the Round, but there is no application [of the preliminary meditation] in the Ending of the Round. This is because the practitioner (yogāvacara) performs the work [of meditation] by learning the first two truths from a teacher—both in brief as "The five aggregates are suffering, craving is the origin," and in detail by the method of "What are the five aggregates? They are the aggregate of form," and so forth—and by reciting them repeatedly with the voice.

Regarding the other two truths, however, he performs the work [of meditation] merely by hearing that "The truth of cessation is desirable, lovely, and pleasing; the truth of the path is desirable, lovely, and pleasing." A yogi who practices in this way penetrates the Four Truths with a single penetration and realizes them with a single realization. He penetrates suffering by the penetration of full understanding (pariññā-paṭivedha), the origin by the penetration of abandoning (pahāna-paṭivedha), cessation by the penetration of realization (sacchikiriyā-paṭivedha), and the path by the penetration of development (bhāvanā-paṭivedha). He realizes suffering through the realization of full understanding... and the path through the realization of development.

Thus, for that yogi, in the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga), there is penetration through learning, questioning, hearing, retaining, and examining regarding the first two truths; but regarding the other two truths, there is penetration only through hearing. In the later stage (aparabhāga), there is penetration by way of function (kicca) regarding three truths, and penetration by way of object (ārammaṇa) regarding the truth of cessation. Reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā), however, occurs only for the person who has reached the truths. Since this yogi is a beginner (ādikammika), that reviewing is not mentioned here.

For this monk, prior to the grasping of the meditation subject, there is no reflection, attention, or reviewing such as "I shall fully understand suffering, I shall abandon the origin, I shall realize cessation, I shall develop the path"; it exists only from the time of grasping onwards. In the later stage, suffering is indeed fully understood... and the path is indeed developed. Among those truths, two truths are deep because they are difficult to see, and two are difficult to see because they are deep. The truth of suffering is evident through its occurrence; it even reaches the point where one must say "Oh, what suffering!" when struck by a stump or a thorn. The origin is also evident through its occurrence by way of the desire to eat, the desire to enjoy, and so forth. However, in terms of the penetration of their characteristics, both are deep. Thus, they are deep because they are difficult to see. The effort to see the other two truths is like stretching out the hand to grasp the peak of existence (bhavagga), or stretching out the foot to touch the edge, or trying to touch one end with the end of a seven-jointed bamboo. Therefore, they are difficult to see because they are deep. Regarding these Four Truths which are difficult to see and deep, and deep and difficult to see, the arising of knowledge in the preliminary stage by the power of learning and so forth is described as "This is the knowledge of suffering," and so forth.
392:
It is like stretching out the hand, or like stretching out the foot to touch the Avīci hell, or like touching the tip of a hair with the tip of a hair that has been split into a hundred parts. Thus, because they are profound, these Truths are difficult to see. Because of this difficulty in seeing them, and because of their profundity among profound things, the Buddha taught, "This is the knowledge of suffering," and so forth, referring to the arising of preliminary knowledge (pubbabhāga-ñāṇa) through the power of learning and so on regarding the four Truths which are difficult to see. However, at the moment of penetration (paṭivedha-kkhaṇa), that path-knowledge is only one.

Right Intention (nekkhamma-saṅkappa) and the others are diverse in the preliminary stage because of the diversity of perceptions (saññā) involved in abstaining from sensual desire, ill will, and cruelty. However, at the path-moment (magga-kkhaṇa), a single wholesome intention arises, fulfilling the path-factor by way of achieving the non-recurrence of unwholesome intentions by cutting off their path in these three instances (sensual desire, ill will, and cruelty). This is called Right Intention (Sammā-saṅkappa).

Abstinence from false speech and so forth are also diverse in the preliminary stage because of the diversity of perceptions involved in abstaining from false speech and so forth. However, at the path-moment, a single wholesome abstinence arises, fulfilling the path-factor by way of achieving the non-recurrence of the unwholesome volition of immorality (dussīlya-cetanā) that arises in these four instances (false speech, etc.) by cutting off its path. This wholesome abstinence is called Right Speech (Sammā-vācā).

Abstinence from taking life and so forth are also diverse in the preliminary stage because of the diversity of perceptions involved in abstaining from taking life and so forth. However, at the path-moment, a single wholesome abstinence arises, fulfilling the path-factor by way of achieving the non-recurrence of the unwholesome volition of immorality that arises in these three instances (taking life, etc.) through non-action and by cutting off its path. This wholesome abstinence is called Right Action (Sammā-kammanta).

Wrong Livelihood (micchā-ājīva) refers to bodily and verbal misconduct performed for the sake of food, edibles, and so forth. "Having abandoned" (pahāya) means having avoided. "By Right Livelihood" (sammā-ājīvena) means by a livelihood praised by the Buddha. "Leads his life" (jīvitaṃ kappeti) means he carries out the process of living. Right Livelihood is also diverse in the preliminary stage because of the diversity of perceptions involved in abstaining from scheming and so forth. However, at the path-moment, a single wholesome abstinence arises, fulfilling the path-factor by way of achieving the non-recurrence of the volition of immorality of wrong livelihood that arises in these seven instances by cutting off its path. This wholesome abstinence is called Right Livelihood (Sammā-ājīva).

"Of unarisen" (anuppannānaṃ) refers to states that have not arisen for oneself in a particular life or in such an object. Seeing them arising in others, one thinks, "Oh, may such evil unwholesome states not arise in me!" Thus, for the unarisen evil...
393:
...for the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states. "He arouses desire" (chandaṃ janeti) means he arouses the desire of energy (vīriya-chanda) that accomplishes the practice of non-arising of those states. "He strives" (vāyamati) means he makes an effort. "He exerts energy" (vīriyaṃ ārabhati) means he initiates energy. "He upholds the mind" (cittaṃ paggaṇhāti) means he makes the mind upheld by energy. "He exerts" (padahati) means he initiates exertion, thinking, "Let only skin, sinews, and bones remain."

"Of arisen" (uppannānaṃ) refers to states that have previously arisen for oneself through habitual practice. He arouses desire to abandon those states, thinking, "Now I will not let such states arise." "Of unarisen wholesome states" (anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ) refers to the first jhana and so forth which have not yet been attained. "Of arisen" (uppannānaṃ) refers to those same states, such as the first jhana, which have been attained. "For the maintenance" (ṭhitiyā) means for the sake of remaining by way of the continuity of repeated arising. "For non-disappearance" (asammosāya) means for the sake of non-destruction. "For increase" (bhiyyobhāvāya) means for the sake of arising in higher stages. "For abundance" (vepullāya) means to reach the state of abundance. "For the fulfillment of development" (bhāvanāya pāripūriyā) means for the sake of fulfilling the development (bhāvanā). This Right Effort is also diverse in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of thoughts such as the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states. However, at the path-moment, a single wholesome energy arises, fulfilling the path-factor by way of accomplishing the task in these four instances. This is called Right Effort (Sammā-vāyāma).

Right Mindfulness (Sammā-sati) is also diverse in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of minds that grasp the body and so forth. However, at the path-moment, a single mindfulness arises, fulfilling the path-factor by way of accomplishing the task in the four instances. This is called Right Mindfulness (Sammā-sati).

Jhanas are diverse both in the preliminary stage and at the path-moment. In the preliminary stage, they are diverse by way of attainments (samāpatti). At the path-moment, they are diverse by way of the various paths. Indeed, for one person, the first path is associated with the first jhana; the second path and others may also be associated with the first jhana or with any other jhana among the second jhana and so forth. For another person, the first path may be associated with any other jhana among the second and so forth, and the second path and others may also be associated with any other jhana among the second and so forth, or with the first jhana. Thus, the four paths may be similar, dissimilar, or partially similar by way of jhana. This distinction occurs according to the determination of the basis jhana (pādaka-jhāna).

According to the determination of the basis jhana, first, for a person who has attained the first jhana and practices insight (vipassanā) after emerging from the first jhana, the path that arises is associated with the first jhana. In this path based on the first jhana, the path-factors and enlightenment-factors (bojjhaṅga) are indeed complete. For one who practices insight after emerging from the second jhana, the path that arises is associated with the second jhana. In this path based on the second jhana, there are seven path-factors. For one who practices insight after emerging from the third jhana, the path that arises is associated with the third jhana. In this path based on the third jhana, the path-factors...
394:
There are six factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). This same method applies to the path (magga) that arises for a person who, having emerged from the fourth jhāna, contemplates with insight up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana).

In the formless realm (arūpa-bhūmi), the fourth and fifth jhānas occur; it is said that these are only supramundane (lokuttara) and not mundane (lokiya). How does this occur in the formless realm (without a basic jhāna)? In this formless realm, for a person who has emerged from any one of the jhānas such as the first jhāna, attained the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), and then developed the formless attainments and is reborn in the formless realm, the three higher paths arise in that realm based on those jhānas. Thus, it is only the basic jhāna (pādaka-jhāna) that determines (the jhāna of the path).

Some elders say, "The aggregates (khandha) which are the objects of insight determine it." Some say, "The person's inclination determines it." Some say, "Emerging insight (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā) determines it." The decision regarding these elders' views should be understood according to the method stated in the section on emerging insight in the Visuddhimagga.

"Monks, this is called Right Concentration (sammā-samādhi)" means this Right Concentration which is mundane in the preceding stage and supramundane in the subsequent stage.

"Thus, either in himself" means either by grasping one's own four noble truths, or by grasping another's four noble truths, or at times one's own and at times another's four noble truths, he dwells frequently contemplating the truths within the truths. In this section on the four truths (catu-sacca-pabba), the arising and passing away of the four noble truths should be understood as far as possible by way of their occurrence and cessation. The words stated hereafter follow the same method already mentioned. In fact, in this section on the four truths, the mindfulness that discerns the four noble truths is called the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca); thus, by connecting it in this way, the way of exit (from the round of suffering) for the monk who grasps the truths should be understood. The remaining words are just the same.

## The Section on the Four Noble Truths is Finished.

By this much, there are twenty-one meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna): the section on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna-pabba), the section on the four postures (iriyāpatha-pabba), the section on the four kinds of clear comprehension (sampajañña-pabba), the section on the thirty-two parts of the body (dvattiṃsākāra-pabba), the section on the analysis of the four elements (dhātuvavatthāna-pabba), the section on the nine cemetery contemplations (navasivathika-pabba), the contemplation of feelings (vedanānupassanā), the contemplation of consciousness (cittānupassanā), the grasping of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa-pariggaha), the grasping of the aggregates (khandha-pariggaha), the grasping of the sense bases (āyatana-pariggaha), the grasping of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga-pariggaha), and the grasping of the truths (sacca-pariggaha). Among those twenty-one meditation subjects, eleven subjects—namely mindfulness of breathing, the thirty-two parts of the body, and the nine cemetery contemplations—are absorption meditation subjects (appanā-kammaṭṭhāna). However, the Elder Mahāsīva, a reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya, said, "The nine cemetery contemplations are taught by way of the contemplation of danger (ādīnavānupassanā)." Therefore, according to that elder's view, only two (mindfulness of breathing and the thirty-two parts) are absorption meditation subjects, while the remaining are access meditation subjects (upacāra-kammaṭṭhāna). How is it then, in all these meditation subjects...
395:
...does the application of insight (abhinivesa) occur in all these twenty-one meditation subjects? It does not. In fact, it should be understood that the application of insight does not occur in the postures (iriyāpatha), clear comprehension (sampajañña), hindrances (nīvaraṇa), and factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), but it occurs only in the remaining meditation subjects. However, the Elder Mahāsīva said, "The application of insight occurs in these subjects as well. This is because this meditating monk discerns thus: 'Do I have the four postures or not? Do I have the four kinds of clear comprehension or not? Do I have the five hindrances or not? Do I have the seven factors of enlightenment or not?' Therefore, the application of insight occurs in all meditation subjects."

"Whoever, O monks" (yo hi koci, bhikkhave) refers to anyone, whether a monk, a nun, a layman, or a laywoman. "Should thus develop" (evaṃ bhāveyya) means to develop according to the sequence of meditation taught from the beginning. "May be expected" (pāṭikaṅkha) means it should be expected, it is desired, it is inevitable. "Gnosis" (aññā) is the fruit of Arhatship (arahatta-phala). "If there is a residue of clinging" (sati vā upādisese) means if the residue of clinging has not yet been exhausted. "The state of a non-returner" (anāgāmitā) means the state of an Anāgāmī.

Thus, having shown the nature of the Dispensation as a way of exit from the round of suffering by way of a seven-year period, and wishing to show it again in periods shorter than those seven years, he said the words beginning with "Let alone, monks" (tiṭṭhantu bhikkhave). All this is taught by way of a person of medium temperament who is to be led (veneyya). However, with reference to a person of sharp wisdom, it is said, "If instructed in the morning, he will attain distinction in the evening; if instructed in the evening, he will attain distinction in the morning." Thus, the Blessed One, having shown, "Monks, my Dispensation is thus a way of exit," and wishing to conclude the teaching which was taught with Arhatship as the summit in all twenty-one places, said, "Monks, this path is a one-way path... etc. That which was said, was said in reference to this." The remaining words are clear in meaning. At the conclusion of the teaching, thirty thousand monks were established in Arhatship.

## The Commentary on the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta is Finished.
396:
## 10. Commentary on the Pāyāsi Sutta

The words beginning with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' constitute the Pāyāsi Sutta. In this sutta, the following is the explanation of terms not previously explained. The word 'Āyasmā' (Venerable) is a term of endearment. 'Kumārakassapa' is the name of that Elder. Because he ordained while still a youth (kumāra), when the Blessed One said, "Call Kassapa; give this fruit or this food to Kassapa," and was asked, "To which Kassapa should it be given?", He replied, "Give it to Kumārakassapa." Having received the name in this way, he continued to be called "Kumārakassapa" even when he was grown. Alternatively, he was known as Kumārakassapa because he was the foster son of King Pasenadi of Kosala.

This is the account of the Elder's past efforts. It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, the Elder was the son of a wealthy merchant. One day, seeing the Blessed One appoint a disciple who was an eloquent speaker (citrakathī) to the foremost position (etadagga), he gave alms to the Blessed One for seven days and made a wish: "Venerable Sir, may I also become a disciple who is an eloquent speaker under a future Buddha, just like this Elder." Having performed such meritorious deeds, he later ordained during the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, but was unable to attain any special realization. At that time, as the dispensation was declining after the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One Kassapa, five monks built a ladder, climbed a mountain, and practiced the Dhamma. The senior monk (Saṅghathera) attained Arahantship on the third day, and the next senior monk (Anuthera) became a Non-returner (Anāgāmī) on the fourth day. The remaining three monks, unable to attain special realization, were reborn in the celestial realm.

While those three enjoyed prosperity in the celestial and human realms throughout the interval between two Buddhas, one was reborn into the royal family in the city of Takkasilā and became a king named Pukkusāti. Having ordained out of devotion to the Blessed One and traveling toward Rājagaha, he heard the Blessed One's Dhamma teaching in a potter's shed and attained the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala). Another was reborn in a family at a seaport. While traveling by boat, the boat was wrecked; he then wore robes made of bark (dārucīra) and received much gain and honor. When the thought arose in him, "I am an Arahant," a Suddhāvāsa Brahma, who was his former companion in Dhamma, urged him out of compassion, saying, "You are not an Arahant; go, approach the Teacher and ask him questions." Following that advice, he attained the fruit of Arahantship (Arahattaphala).

The remaining one was conceived in the womb of a woman from a certain family in Rājagaha. That woman had first pleaded with her parents to ordain but did not receive permission. She then went to her husband's house and became pregnant...
397:
...she became pregnant. Without even knowing she was pregnant, she pleased her husband and, with his permission, ordained among the bhikkhunīs. Seeing the signs of her pregnancy, the bhikkhunīs questioned Devadatta. He declared, "She is not a true recluse." They then questioned the Ten-Powered One (the Buddha). The Teacher assigned the task of settlement to the Venerable Upāli. The Elder summoned the families living in Sāvatthī and the laywoman Visākhā to investigate. He then declared, "The pregnancy occurred before she became a nun; her status as a nun is blameless (pure)." The Teacher gave his approval to the Elder, saying, "The case has been well-decided." That bhikkhunī gave birth to a son who resembled a golden statue. King Pasenadi of Kosala took the boy and had him raised. He named the boy "Kassapa" and later, having adorned him, brought him to the Teacher and had him ordained as a novice. Thus, he was also known as "Kumārakassapa" because he was the foster son of the King. One day, while he was practicing the Dhamma in the Andhavana forest, a deity (Brahma) who desired his welfare taught him certain questions and said, "Ask these questions to the Blessed One." The Elder asked the questions, and at the conclusion of the answers, he attained Arahantship. The Blessed One also appointed him to the foremost position among the monks who are eloquent speakers (citrakathī).

'Setabyā' is the name of that city. 'Uttarena Setabyaṃ' means to the north of Setabyā. 'Rājanyo' refers to a king who has not yet been consecrated. 'Diṭṭhigataṃ' means simply a (wrong) view. Just as when one says 'gone to dung' or 'gone to urine,' there is nothing other than dung etc., so too 'diṭṭhigata' is just a view. 'Itipi natthi' means he speaks thus, citing various reasons, saying "For such a reason, it does not exist." 'Purā...pe... saññāpeti' means as long as he has not yet been fully convinced.

## Commentary on the Simile of the Moon and Sun

Regarding the words, "Venerable Kassapa, these moons and suns," it is said that when questioned by the Elder, King Pāyāsi thought: "This recluse first brought up the simile of the moon and sun; he must be like the moon and sun in wisdom, and cannot be overcome by another. If I say, 'The moon and sun are in this world,' he will entangle me with questions such as 'What do they depend on? What is their size? How high are they?' and so on. I will not be able to untangle that. I will tell him instead that 'The moon and sun are in the other world'." Therefore, he spoke in that way.
398:
The Blessed One had preached the Sudhābhojanīya Jātaka not long before that [the conversation between Venerable Kumāra Kassapa and King Pāyāsi]. In that Jātaka, it is mentioned: "In the moon is the deity Canda, in the sun is the deity Suriya." The Jātaka or Sutta preached by the Blessed One becomes famous throughout the entire Jambudīpa. Therefore, King Pāyāsi, thinking that he could no longer say "There are no deities living in this moon and sun," said, "Those are gods, they are not humans."

"Rājañña, is there a reason (pariyāya) for this view?" he asks. "Ābādhikā" means being possessed of an affliction (ābādha) known as disharmonious feeling. "Dukkhitā" means having reached suffering. "Bāḷhagilānā" means being extremely ill. "Saddhāyikā" means "I believe you; may you be those whose words are to be believed by me." "Paccayikā" means "I trust you; may you be those who are to be trusted by me."

## Commentary on the Simile of the Thief and Others (Corādi-upamā-vaṇṇanā)

"Uddisitvā" means having shown oneself and the stored goods to those friends and relatives and having entrusted them. "Vippalapantassa" means wailing in various ways such as "My son, my daughter, my wealth." "Nirayapālesu" refers to the beings who perform the punishment in hell. Those who say, "Kamma alone performs the punishment, there are no hell-wardens," contradict the Devadūta Sutta which states, "Monks, the hell-wardens [take] him..." Just as there are people who perform punishments in the royal families in the human world, so there are hell-wardens in hell.

"Veḷupesikāhi" means with bamboo splints. "Sunimmajjathā" means to wipe away or cleanse thoroughly so that it is well-cleaned.

"Asuci" means being unpleasant. "Asucisaṅkhāto" means being a heap of impurity or being known as impure. "Duggandho" means having the smell of a corpse. "Jeguccho" means being associated with what is loathsome. "Paṭikūlo" means bringing about repulsion (aversion) merely by being seen.
