"Ubbādhatī" means that even the scent of humans such as Universal Monarchs (Cakkavatti), who bathe twice a day, change clothes three times, and are adorned with noble ornaments, oppresses (stinks to) the deities who are a hundred yojanas away, like a rotting corpse hanging from their necks.
399:
Furthermore, he speaks by virtue of those who undertake and practice the five precepts, such as abstaining from taking life. Regarding the word "Tāvatiṃsānaṃ," he means: "Let those deities born in that distant realm not come yet; why do these [others] not come?"

"Jaccandhūpamo maññe patibhāsī" means appearing like a person blind from birth. In "araññavanapatthāni," they are called "araññāni" (forests) because they possess the factors of a forest-dwelling, and "vanapatthāni" (forest thickets) because they are large jungle groves. "Pantāni" means remote places.

"Kalyāṇadhamme" refers to those who have a good nature by that very virtue. "Dukkhapaṭikūle" refers to those who do not desire suffering. "Seyyo bhavissati" means that there will be the happiness of a happy destination (sugati) in the next world.

"Upavijaññā" means one whose time of giving birth is near, who is heavily pregnant, and will give birth before long. "Opabhoggā bhavissati" means she will be an attendant (wife) at his feet. "Anayavyasanaṃ" means great suffering and ruin. "Aya" means happiness, and "anaya" means non-happiness, which is suffering. That suffering is called "vyasana" because it destroys and scatters happiness in every way. Thus, suffering itself is "anayavyasana" (great ruin/suffering) because it destroys prosperity and happiness. "Ayoniso" means without a proper cause (improperly). "Apakkaṃ na paripācenti" means they do not prematurely cut off a life that is not yet ripe or exhausted. "Paripākaṃ āgamenti" means they wait for the time of the ripening of life (the time of death). This point was also stated by the General of the Dhamma (Venerable Sāriputta):

"I do not delight in death, I do not delight in life;
I await the time, as a hireling waits for his wages."

"Ubbindhitvā" means having destroyed the coating of fine clay. "Rāmaṇeyyakaṃ" means a delightful state. "Velāsikā" refers to women who are playful and frolicsome. "Komārikā" refers to young girls. "Tuyhaṃ jီvaṃ" means asking, "Do you see the life-principle (soul) that goes out or enters at the time of dreaming?" Here, the movement of the mind (cittācāra) is taken as "life" (jīva). This is because that person has the perception of a "soul" (jīvasaññī) in that mental occurrence.

"Jiyāya" means having encircled the neck with a bowstring. "Patthinnataro" means being more rigid and stiff. What is shown by this? When you [observe] a being at the time it has life...
400:
It is said that while a being is alive, there are five aggregates (khandhas). However, at the time of death, only the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) remains; the three mental aggregates do not occur, and the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha) departs. Although the remaining aggregate of form should be lighter, it actually becomes heavier. Therefore, this shows the meaning that there is no one who goes anywhere.

Nibbuta means having the heat (tejo) extinguished.

Anupahacca means without destroying. Āmato hoti means being half-dead and in the process of dying. Odhunātha means "turn it this way." Sandhunātha means "turn it that way." Niddhunātha means "turn it back and forth." 'Tañcāyatanaṃ na paṭisaṃvedeti' means not clearly perceiving (seeing) that base of form with that eye. This method is the same in all cases.

Saṅkhadhama means a conch-blower. Upalāpetvā means by blowing.

Aggika means a fire-worshipper. Āpādeyyaṃ means if I were to accomplish it, or if I were to bring life to an end. Poseyyaṃ means if I were to nourish with food and so forth. Vaḍḍheyyaṃ means if I were to make it grow. Araṇīsahita refers to the pair of fire-sticks (the rubbing board and the drill).

Tirorājāno pi means kings in other foreign regions also know. Abyatta means one who is unclear (obscure) or unskilled. Kopena pi means "I will wander holding onto this wrong view even out of anger that arises toward those who speak to me in this way." Makkhena means with contempt (makkha), which has the characteristic of disparaging the proper reasons you have stated. Palāsena means with rivalry (palāsa), which has the characteristic of competing for dominance with you.

Haritakapaṇṇa means any green leaf; it means that there is not even a green blade of grass left. Sannaddhakalāpa means having a bound quiver of arrows. Āsittodakāni vaṭumāni means there are paths and ravines filled with water. Yoggāni refers to oxen.

Bahunikkhantara means having gone out in great numbers, or having gone out for a long time. Yathābatena bhaṇḍena means with the goods—such as grass, wood, and water—just as you have carried them, just as they were loaded, just as they were taken.

Appasārāni means things of little value. Paṇiyāni refers to trade goods or merchandise.
401:
## Explanation of the Simile of the Dung-Carrier and Others

"Mama ca sūkarabhattaṃ" means "And this is food for my pigs." Uggharantam means overflowing upwards. Paggharantam means trickling downwards. In the phrase "Tumhe khvettha bhaṇe," it should be parsed as "Tumhe kho ettha bhaṇe." Or this is simply the reading. "Tathā hi pana me sūkarabhattaṃ" means "For that very reason, this dung is food for my pigs."

"Swallows the losing die that comes again and again" (āgataāgataṃ kaliṃ gilati) means swallowing the die that causes defeat whenever it comes. Pajjohissāmi means I will perform an offering in various ways, or I will make a sacrificial offering (bali). Akkhehi dibbissāma means we will play with dice. Littaṃ paramena tejasā means smeared with a poison of supreme potency.

Gāmapaṭṭa refers to an old village site that people have abandoned and fled from. There is also a reading Gāmapada; the meaning is the same. Sāṇabhāra means a load of hemp. Susannaddho means well-bound. Tvaṃ pajānāhi means "You should know." It means "If you wish to take it, take it."

Khoma refers to cloth made in the Khoma region (linen). Aya means black iron. Loha means copper. Sajjha means silver. Suvaṇṇa means a gold coin (māsaka). Abhinandinsu means they were delighted and rejoiced.

Attamano means having a mind that is delighted within oneself. Abhiraddho means being very confident (devoted). Pañhāpaṭibhānāni means the flashes of insight (ready wit) that appear in the intellect to answer questions. Paccanīkaṃ kattabbaṃ means "I will consider it as something to be done in opposition," meaning one stands holding a contrary view.

"Fall into destruction" (saṅghātaṃ āpajjanti) means they reach ruin and death. Na mahapphalo means not of great fruit in terms of the result (vipāka). Na mahānisaṃso means not of great benefit in terms of spiritual advantage. Na mahājutiko means not of great splendor in terms of power and radiance. Na mahāvipphāro means not of great pervasiveness in terms of the spread of the result. Bījanaṅgala means seed and plough. Dukkhette means in a bad field, a field without essence. Dubbhūme means in an uneven piece of ground. Patiṭṭhāpeyya means if one were to place or plant. Khaṇḍāni means those that are broken or fragmented. Pūtīni means things that are rotten or without essence.
402: Seeds that are damaged by wind and sun, whose vitality and power to germinate are exhausted, are called 'vātātapahata'. Seeds that are mere chaff, devoid of the essence of the rice grain, are called 'asārādāna'. Those seeds that have been dried and stored by being poured into a granary are called 'sukhasayita' (well-stored seeds). These seeds, however, are not of that kind. 'Anuppaveccheyya' means that the rain does not fall properly—it does not rain every fortnight, every ten days, or every five days. 'Api nu tāni' is a question: if there are such defects in the field, the seeds, and the rain, would those seeds reach growth upwards through sprouts, roots, and leaves, flourish downwards, and attain abundance all around? Rājañña, such a sacrifice [gift] does not yield great fruit because it is impure—due to the offerings being obtained by oppressing others, and because of the donor and the recipient. Rājañña, such a sacrifice yields great fruit because of the offerings obtained without oppressing others, because of the virtuous donor who does not harm others, and because of the recipient endowed with qualities such as right view. If one finds a recipient who has just emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), which is a superior quality, and if the intention is abundant, it yields results even in the present life. After hearing this Dhamma discourse from the Elder Kumāra Kassapa, Pāyāsi Rājañña invited the Elder, gave a great gift for seven days, and from then on, established a gift for the multitude. Referring to that gift, it is said, 'Then Pāyāsi Rājañña...' and so on. In that passage, 'kaṇājaka' means coarse rice meal along with bran. 'Bilaṅgadutiya' means food where sour gruel is the second [the accompaniment]. 'Dhorakāni vatthāni' means coarse clothes. 'Guḷavālakāni' means clothes with large tassels or fringes that hang in clusters. 'Evaṃ anuddisati' means thus he directs or points out. 'Pādāpi' means even with the foot (kicking). 'Asakkaccaṃ' means a gift without faith, lacking respect. 'Asahatthā' means not with one's own hand. 'Acittīkataṃ' means lacking care; giving without establishing a respectful manner and without a noble mind. 'Apaviddhaṃ' means giving carelessly, as if discarding it. 'Suññaṃ Serīsakaṃ' means reaching an empty silver mansion named Serīsaka. It is said that there was a large Serīsa tree at its gate, which is why it is called 'Serīsaka'. In a past life as a human, Venerable Gavampati had been the leader of cowherd boys. At that time, he cleaned the area at the foot of a large Serīsa tree, spread sand, and invited a monk who was a piṇḍapātika (alms-food eater) to sit at the foot of the tree, and offered him the food he had obtained. Due to that meritorious deed, when he passed away, he was reborn in that silver mansion. At the gate of that mansion, the Serīsa tree...
403:
The Elder Gavampati, in a previous life as a human, was the leader of cowherd boys. Having cleared the ground at the foot of a large Sirīsa tree and spread sand, he invited an elder who was an alms-food gatherer to sit at the foot of that tree and offered him the food he had obtained. When he passed away, by the power of that merit, he was reborn in that silver mansion (vimāna). A Sirīsa tree stood at the door of the mansion. That tree fruits once every fifty years. When fifty years had passed, the deva was struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Later, in the time of our Blessed One, he was reborn among humans, and after hearing the Buddha's teaching, he attained Arahatship. Due to his past habit, he frequently went to that very mansion for his day-rest (divāvihāra), as the climate there was pleasant for him. It was with reference to this that it was said, "At that time, the Venerable Gavampati..." and so on.

That youth Uttara respectfully gave the gift, even though it belonged to another. He also announced, "Give gifts respectfully," and so forth. Hearing the elder's announcement, many people gave gifts respectfully and were reborn in the deva world. Although the attendants of King Pāyāsi also gave gifts respectfully, they were reborn in the presence of King Pāyāsi himself due to their attachment (nikanti) to him. That mansion was a "wandering mansion" (disācārika-vimāna) located in the Vaṭṭani forest. One day, the deva Pāyāsi showed himself to some merchants and told them of the deeds he had done in the past.
